PREFACE 
a: 
The World Tax Series consists of reports on national tax systems of 
countries throughout the world. 
There is generally one country report 
in each volume. 
Each report contains a description of the tax system as a 
whole and a detailed analysis of the most important taxes, especially the 
income tax. 
As far as possible, the contents of the reports are arranged 
according to a uniform pattern which is explained in the Introduction. 
The United Nations, and the League of Nations before it, had long 
recognized the need for providing systematic information on national 
tax systems and had initiated a series of publications, dealing especially 
with the taxation of foreign income and foreign taxpayers. 
In August, 
1951, the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations passed the 
following resolution, which was recommended to it by the Fiscal Com- 
mission, where the United States Delegate had originally proposed it: 
The Economic and Social Council 
Having in mind that the promotion of trade and investment between 
countries is of great importance in the economic development of Member 
countries; 
Having in mind that the establishment of a modern tax structure con- 
stitutes an important factor in attracting foreign trade and investment and 
in promoting national development; 
Having in mind that the availability of comprehensive and authentic 
information on the tax systems of Member countries serves these aims; and 
Having in mind that the United Nations is best suited to obtain the basic 
information on national tax systems from Member governments; 
Requests the Secretary-General to consider: 
(a) The publication of a world tax service, providing a continuous service 
of information on national tax laws and administration; 
(b) Keeping this service on a current basis by the publication of loose- 
leaf or booklet supplements; 
(c) Inviting governments in each of the countries to be covered by the 
world tax service to cooperate in supplying the legislative documentation 
and other materials; 
(d) The possible cooperation of universities in this undertaking. 
The Harvard Law School offered to cooperate in response to this 
resolution. 
Officials of the United Nations Secretariat, working in close 
collaboration with members of the Law School faculty, prepared an 
outline and plan of organization for the contemplated series of reports 
on national tax systems. 
Further discussions led, in 1952, to the estab- 
lishment at the Law School of an International Program in Taxation, 
which has been carried forward as part of the Harvard Law School 
program in International Legal Studies. 
Training and research activities 
xv

PREFACE 
xvi 
were started with the aid of a grant from the Ford Foundation. 
The 
World Tax Series project was undertaken as a part of the Program in 
1954, when the minimum financial support necessary to commence this 
work was obtained from the contributions of corporations. 
A uniform method of preparation is generally followed for all of the 
reports of the World Tax Series. 
Preliminary drafts are prepared by the 
staff with the assistance of correspondents abroad and consultants both 
here and abroad. 
In some cases, the correspondent has provided basic 
information for use by the staff, and a number of correspondents have 
come to Cambridge to assist in completing the drafts for their respective 
countries. 
The final draft of a report is reviewed before publication both 
by members of the staff and by correspondents, with the advice of officials 
of the United Nations. 
The collection of laws, regulations, and basic 
texts in the Harvard Law Library which has formed the foundation for 
each report is available to all interested persons. 
An advisory board, composed of persons familiar with international tax 
problems, has assisted the staff by making recommendations on the scope 
and arrangement of the Series. 
Particular reports have been checked by 
members of the Advisory Board and other tax experts here and abroad. 
The final arrangement of the material has been worked out with the 
advice of consultants from the United Nations Secretariat and from tax 
publishing houses. 
The World Tax Series is designed to present a comprehensive perspec- 
tive of the various tax systems. 
It is not expected that reports will furnish 
final answers to all the questions that can arise under a particular tax 
system. 
The over-all description of the tax structure and the detailed 
analysis of the principal taxes in each report of the World Tax Series 
provide basic tools for comparative tax research. 
This research has 
hitherto been difficult because of the lack of any convenient source 
where information could be obtained on a comparative basis. 
The Series 
also provides tax practitioners in the United States and elsewhere with 
technical information which will enable them to discuss tax questions 
with their advisers abroad. 
It may be useful to governments engaged in 
tax reforms or in international tax negotiations. 
The information on the 
techniques used in other countries may be helpful to teachers of taxation 
as well as to those carrying on technical assistance in the fiscal field. 
Only through the use of the reports will their shortcomings become 
evident. 
Readers are urged to suggest specific improvements for consid- 
eration in the preparation of future reports and the periodic supplements 
by means of which it is planned to keep the information in the basic™ 
volumes up-to-date. 
The ultimate purpose is to achieve a design for a 
truly comparative approach which may be useful not only in the field of 
taxation but in other fields of law as well.

INTRODUCTION 
The Arrangement of the Reports 
The World Tax Series seeks to achieve two basic goals: (1) to describe 
each tax system in its own legal and administrative terms, and (2) to 
present each system so it can be compared, point by point, with others. 
Therefore, each report in the Series presents in Part I a description of the 
tax system of a country and in Part II a detailed analysis, under uniform 
topic headings, of its income tax. 
If, in any country, taxes other than 
the income tax require detailed treatment, they are covered in Part III. 
Part | 
The four chapters of Part I describe the background and the entire tax 
structure in its own setting. 
Chapter 1 gives the background information needed for an under- 
standing of the tax structure as a whole. 
Chapter 2 summarizes taxes on 
net income. 
It serves as more than an introduction to their detailed 
analysis in Part II in that it presents an over-all perspective of them in 
terms of their own legislative and administrative design. 
Chapter 3 
describes the various taxes on capital, and Chapter 4 describes taxes on 
transactions. 
Those taxes which are analyzed in detail in Part III are 
merely summarized here. 
Readers should examine Part I to understand the framework of the 
~whole tax system before they look up any specific point of law in Part 
II or Il, 
Part Il 
In Part II of each report, Chapters 5 through 13 contain a detailed 
analysis of the income tax and these chapters all have the same titles 
and the same major subdivisions in each report. 
As the Table of Contents 
shows, the analysis follows the over-all sequence of answering these 
questions: Who pays the income tax? What is the tax imposed on? How 
is the tax computed? How is the tax administered? 
While this sequence is broad enough to embrace all the problems 
presented by any income tax, it is designed primarily for analysis of 
detailed provisions and does not follow the legislative and administrative

INTRODUCTION 
xviii 
pattern of the particular country’s income tax, which is described in 
Chapter 2. 
Part Ill 
In Part III the taxes other than the income tax which deserve detailed 
treatment are analyzed. 
These taxes differ in each report, but they 
usually include those which are summarized in Chapters 3 and 4. Where 
a particular tax is an integral part of the income tax structure, it may 
be included in Part II. 
Location of Certain Material 
Individuals, corporations, and other taxpayers. 
In describing who pays 
the income tax, each report makes the basic distinction between individ- 
uals and corporations. Where the distinction is between physical persons 
and juridical persons, the latter are referred to as “entities” in the Series. 
The first section of Chapter 5 of each report describes the status of indi- 
viduals as taxpayers, and the second describes the status of corporations. 
The various types of organization and association, some of which are 
taxpayers and some of which are not, are described separately and, as 
far as possible, in terms of comparison and contrast with the tax status 
of individuals and of corporations. 
The international aspects of income taxation. 
In order to emphasize 
international problems related to income taxation, the technical definitions 
of resident and nonresident are included among the criteria identifying 
the various classes of taxpayers described in Chapter 5, at the beginning 
of the analysis of the income tax. 
There are references throughout the 
income tax chapters to the sections of Chapter 11 (International Aspects 
of Income Taxation) where equivalent problems are discussed in relation 
to nonresidents or to foreign income. 
The last section of Chapter 11, 
relating to tax treaties, covers only the major effects of those treaties on 
the basic internal law. 
The United Nations series on International Tax 
Agreements, of which seven volumes have been published so far (in 
English, French, and Spanish editions), provides full texts of the agree- 
ments and comprehensive data on their current legal status. 
Schedular and global income tax systems. 
The characterization of a 
system as “schedular” or “global” is retained in the descriptive material 
on income taxes in Part I, but it does not affect the arrangement of Part II. 
Income tax return forms. 
An important part of each report in the 
Series is the reproduction in Chapter 12 of the country’s most recent 
available individual and corporate income tax return forms, with transla- 
tions where necessary. 
The forms are not always facsimiles, but they 
show each item in the position corresponding to its place on the page 
of the original return.

INTRODUCTION 
The Numbering System 
Each topic in this, and in other, books in the Series is numbered. 
These numbers furnish a complete system of cross reference. 
By giving 
the same numbers to the same topics in each book, considerable uni- 
formity has been provided throughout the Series. 
In Part I, only the 
chapters are identical, but in Part II both the chapters and the major 
headings are virtually the same in every report. 
In Part III, a separate 
chapter covers each of the principal taxes requiring analysis. 
Each chapter is indicated by its number followed by a diagonal stroke. 
Thus, 5/ always refers to Chapter 5. The major headings within each 
chapter are numbered consecutively following the stroke. 
For example, 
in every report Chapter 7 is “Business Income” and the second major 
heading is “Deductions.” 
Thus, its number is 7/2. 
Subheadings are 
numbered consecutively following the period (e.g., “Compensation for 
Services” under “Deductions” is usually 7/2.3), but rules of taxation vary 
so widely from country to country that these subheadings cannot be 
uniform. 
In general, where the same subject matter appears in different 
countries, the titles and numbers of the subheadings are the same in each 
report, but the editorial staff of the Series considered it unwise to impose 
a perhaps artificial and misleading uniformity merely for its own sake. 
Cross references and references in the Index are made to heading 
numbers rather than pages. 
Thus, 9/10.5 is a reference to Chapter 9, 
tenth major heading, fifth subheading. 
The Table of Contents in the 
front of the book lists each major heading, its title, and the number of 
the page on which it begins. 
An examination of a detailed Table of 
Contents at the beginning of a chapter will familiarize the reader with 
the workings of the system. 
Bibliography and Sources 
In each report of the Series, the Bibliography includes a narrative 
description of the sources of tax law in the country, an explanation of 
how they are reported, and a list of abbreviations. 
It also lists books, 
articles, and other works either used as source material for the text or 
recommended for further reference. 
Citations 
The method of citing any volume of the World Tax Series is as follows: 
WTS: India, 1/5.6. 
In the report there are many citations to relevant sections of laws and 
regulations, but few direct quotations or translations. 
The substance and 
effects of tax provisions are explained instead of merely paraphrased. 
Wherever possible, examples further clarify the explanations, but there

INTRODUCTION 
XX 
are no explicit comparisons with laws of the United States or of any 
other country. 
References 
At the end of the text, the section of the book called References gives a 
Table of Statutes and Regulations mentioned in the report and the 
numbers of the sections in which they appear. 
In common law countries, 
a Table of Cases is also provided. 
This section is designed to help 
readers find the application or interpretation of any particular section 
of a statute or judicial decision. 
The Index 
All subjects and terms in the Index, both in English and in the language 
of the taxing country, are in one alphabetical list. Each foreign word or 
term in the list is cross-referenced to its English equivalent. 
In addition 
to consulting the Index, readers are advised to use the detailed Tables of 
Contents at the beginning of each chapter. 
The Terminology of the Reports 
A difficulty in preparing the World Tax Series has been the variety of 
words used, both from country to country and within particular countries, 
to describe concepts which are functionally identical. 
Wherever such 
variety exists, one word that best describes the function has been applied 
consistently throughout the Series. 
One of the best examples of the verbal confusion in this field is the 
variety of words used to describe the way total amounts received and 
accrued during a taxable period are reduced to establish taxable income. 
Some of them are abatements, allowances, credits, deductions, exclusions, 
and exemptions. 
Within every system different items are covered by each 
of these terms with little consistency. 
In the preparation of these reports a standardized vocabulary is being 
developed. 
It is by no means complete yet, but the following income tax 
terms and definitions represent a beginning. 
Gross receipts. 
“Gross receipts” is the total amount, both in cash and 
accruals and in goods, services, or other benefits, received by a taxpayer 
during the taxable period. 
In addition to items that are within the 
definition of income, “gross receipts” is used to include any items received 
which are not so considered. 
' 
Exclusion. 
“Exclusion” is that amount received by a taxpayer which is 
not considered within the concept of income for tax purposes. 
Examples 
of “exclusions” might be gifts, life insurance proceeds, or capital receipts. 
Gross income. 
“Gross income” is the total of all the items included in 
the concept of income that a taxpayer receives during a taxable period.


<!-- page 25 of 600 -->

India 
xxi 
INTRODUCTION 
The term “gross profits” is equivalent to gross income less cost of goods 
sold. 
“Gross taxable income” is gross income as reduced by those items 
which, while included in the concept of income, are eliminated from the 
scope of the tax. 
Exemption. 
“Exemption” as used in the analysis of the income tax 
has two applications: (1) to classes of taxpayers, and (2) to items of 
income. 
1. An “exemption” granted to a taxpayer is the elimination, by law, of that 
individual or entity from the operation of the tax. 
Foreign diplomatic 
personnel and charitable institutions are frequent examples of persons 
exempt from tax. 
2. The word “exemption” applied to income means the elimination of a 
certain item from the scope of tax, even though that item is recognized 
as income. 
An example of an exemption from income might be interest 
from certain government securities. 
As applied to taxes on capital or transactions, the term “exemption” has 
a similar dual application. 
It may refer to a person or to a type of capital 
or transaction declared by law to be beyond the scope of the tax. 
Deduction. 
A “deduction” is an amount that the law declares a tax- 
payer may subtract from his gross taxable income in arriving at net tax- 
able income. 
“Deductions” may include both expenses incurred by the 
taxpayer in acquiring his gross income, and other disbursements not 
directly related to the income-earning activity. 
Examples of the former 
may be wages, rent, and advertising expenses, and of the latter, medical 
expenses, charitable contributions, and interest due on the taxpayer's 
personal debts. 
Net income. 
“Net income” is the amount remaining after subtracting 
exemptions and deductions from gross income. 
This term means income 
before the subtraction of taxes on income. 
The term for income as 
reduced by taxes thereon is “net income after tax.” 
Allowance. 
“Allowance” is any part of net income on which the tax 
rate is zero. 
As opposed to deductions, “allowances” do not correspond 
to actual expenses but are concrete amounts or percentages established 
by the tax law. The most common “allowances” are those granted to the 
_ taxpayer for himself and for his dependents (often called personal exemp- 
tions), and the minimum amounts which entities must earn before they 
become subject to tax. 
Thus “allowances” may enter into the tax calculations of both indi- 
viduals and entities. 
They differ from exemptions in that they apply to 
definite amounts or percentages of income, while exemptions apply to 
types of income or classes of taxpayers. 
Taxable income. 
“Taxable income” is the result obtained after sub- 
tracting allowances from net income. 
It is the amount to which the 
_ jncome tax rates are applied in computing the tax liability.


<!-- page 26 of 600 -->

India 
INTRODUCTION 
xxii 
Presumed income. 
“Presumed income” is the amount presumed to 
have been derived from some activity of or property owned by the tax- 
payer, without reference to how much income, if any, he actually received. 
Credit. 
“Credit” is any amount that a taxpayer is permitted to subtract 
from the total tax computed according to the process described above. 
“Credits” are usually granted by a government for taxes already paid. 
Examples of possible credits are those for taxes withheld on wages or 
salaries during the taxable period; or those for tax on income earned 
abroad when the country of origin has taxed that income. 
Another fre- 
quent example of a credit is the fixed amount certain governments allow 
taxpayers to subtract from their total tax liability for dependents. 
A 
“credit” against tax must not be confused with a deduction from income. 
Real property and movables. 
The term “real property” ordinarily 
designates land and interests therein, accretions, buildings, and fixtures. 
Whether or not a particular interest is considered an interest in land 
depends on local law. Where the term “immovables” has a specialized 
meaning different from “real property’ which is relevant to taxation, 
that difference is explained. 
All other kinds of property are “movable.” 
“Personal property” and 
“personalty” seem inadequate because of the confusion that may result 
from speaking of the personal property of an entity. “Movable property” 
includes intangible as well as tangible property, though the distinction 
between the two is made whenever necessary throughout the Series. 
Resident and nonresident. 
Some countries distinguish between tax- 
payers with unlimited tax liability and those with limited tax liability. 
In these reports, the distinction is drawn between a “resident” and a 
“nonresident.” 
In general, an individual with close ties to the taxing 
country is taxed by that country on his income from all sources. 
The tie 
that usually decides the extent of his tax liability is his presence in the 
country for a specified length of time during the tax year, and the word 
usually applied to him is “resident.” 
However, nationality or some other 
criterion may determine the extent of an individual’s tax liability in a 
particular country. 
The individual who does not meet the requirements 
is a “nonresident.” 
The term “resident” is applied to corporations and other entities 
which are subject to unlimited tax liability. 
As in the case of an indi- 
vidual, the extent of the tax liability of a corporation or other entity 
depends upon the ties between it and the taxing country. In some coun- 
tries, mere organization under the laws of the country may be sufficient 
to subject the corporation of other entity to unlimited tax liability. How-* 
ever, the place of organization is often irrelevant and other ties with the 
taxing country may determine the extent of tax liability. 
In each 
report, the criteria which determine who is a “resident” are given in 
Chapter 5, and the legal consequences of that determination are analyzed 
in Chapter 11.

Legislative Materials 
Central and state acts are cited by short title and year; the numbers 
of acts are sometimes given in addition, but are not used in this volume. 
The India Code is the current compilation of the unrepealed central acts. 
Current central acts are published annually in Acts of Parliament and 
monthly in the unofficial All India Reporter; current central acts and 
current acts of some states are published monthly in the unofficial Current 
Indian Statutes. 
Treatises on particular taxes usually contain reprints of 
the pertinent acts, rules, and notifications; see below under Treatises. 
References in this volume to the Income-tax Act of 1922, which is the 
main source of law on the income tax, are designated by a section symbol 
in the following manner: § 7(2). 
References to other central acts are 
designated by an abbreviation of the name of the act, followed by a 
section symbol. 
For example, “WTA § 3” designates a reference to the 
Wealth-tax Act of 1957.

Case Materials 
Any case cited in this volume for which no court designation is given 
is a decision of one or another of the High Courts. 
A citation to a 
decision of any other court is followed by an abbreviation of the name 
of the court; for example, decisions of the Supreme Court are designated 
Cc. 
In this volume reference is made to United Kingdom decisions which 
have been cited with approval by the Indian courts and to United 
Kingdom decisions which in the judgment of the authors may be helpful 
in resolving questions of Indian tax law. 
Although the tax systems of 
__the two countries are different in structure and content, basic concepts 
are the same in many areas, and a number of Indian statutory provisions 
are derived from United Kingdom statutes. 
Consequently, Indian de- 
cisions frequently follow the authority established by United Kingdom 
decisions 
in comparable 
situations. 
Although 
reference 
to United 
- Kingdom authority is helpful where there is no Indian authority, par- 
ticularly when questions of concept or principle are involved, caution 
is always required because a United Kingdom decision which appears 
to be in point may be based on a statutory provision which differs from 
the governing Indian provision. 
All United Kingdom cases cited in this 
volume are designated “U.K.”

Historical and Political Background 
171.1 
Historical Background 
India possesses one of the oldest civilizations in the world. 
The 
early Indus civilization with archeological remains 
at Harappa and 
Mohenjo-Daro 
in the Punjab is believed to date back 5,000 years. 
Indian recorded history begins with the Aryans, who came into India 
about 1500 s.c. 
The Aryans, also known as Indo-Europeans, came 
from the Caucasian area of Eurasia and are from the same stock as the 
peoples who migrated to Persia and Europe during the same period. 
At the time of the Aryan incursion into India the country was populated 
by the Dravidians, a dark-skinned, broad-nosed people of obscure origin 
who already possessed a high degree of civilization. 
The Aryans first 
settled in the Indus Valley, after surging into the country through the 
Khyber Pass, and then pushed on into the Gangetic Plain, driving the 
Dravidians 
south. 
There was, of course, intermingling of the two 
racial groups. 
This historical process still bears its stamp on India in 
both the physical and the cultural characteristics of the Indian people. 
The people of the Punjab are more Aryan whereas the people of Madras 
“are more Dravidian in physical characteristics. 
The north Indian lan- 
guages are based on the Sanskrit of the Aryans, whereas the south 
Indian languages are based on the Tamil of the Dravidians. 
The two 
language 
groups 
are fundamentally 
different 
in sound, 
script, and 
, alphabet. 
There are 14 different languages in India and several hundred 
dialects. 
Hindu religion and philosophy, however, have welded these 
two major groups into a single civilization which largely surmounts this 
basic division of the people of India. 
Thus, India is not unlike multi- 
lingual Europe, which is welded together by Christianity. 
The Vedas, the religious scriptures of the Aryans, are the cultural 
foundation of the Hindu civilization. 
In addition there are two great 
epic poems, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. 
The latter is similar 
to the Iliad of the Greeks, another Aryan people. 
The most notable


<!-- page 42 of 600 -->

1/1.1 
| 
India 
DESCRIPTION 
OF 
TAX 
SYSTEM 
6 
feature of the Hindu civilization is the caste system. 
It has complex 
historical and religious origins. 
The caste system was created by the 
Aryans and formalized in the Institutes of Manu, the early legal code 
of the Hindus. 
Suffice it to say here that there are four basic castes 
with numerous subcastes. 
At the top are the Brahmans, the priestly 
and scholarly class. 
Next are the Kshatriyas, the warrior and ruling 
class, then the Vaisyas or merchant class, and last, the Sudras or farmers. 
In addition, there is a group of outcastes, untouchables, who were not 
taken into any of the four Aryan incastes. 
The Hindus were poor historical chroniclers, and much less is known 
of their history than of their contemporaneous 
sister civilizations in 
western Asia and Egypt. 
In the sixth century B. c. there was a strong 
protestant movement within Hinduism which brought forth two great 
religious 
figures, Gautama Buddha and Mahavira, 
the founders 
of 
Buddhism and Jainism. 
For centuries these two movements competed 
for the minds and hearts of the Indians until Emperor Asoka, one of 
the great kings of Indian history, who reigned from 273 to 232 B.c., 
adopted Buddhism and made it the religion of his Indian empire. 
More- 
over, he sent missionaries abroad to Tibet, China, Ceylon, Burma, and 
Thailand, so that Buddhism became one of the great religions of Asia 
and the world. 
Several centuries later, 
a Brahmanic revival restored 
the Hindu religion in India. 
Jainism, however, continues until today as 
a minor religion. 
The second era of note in Indian history is the period of the Gupta 
Empire from the fourth to the sixth century a. p. 
Indian agriculture, 
industry, commerce and art flourished during this period. 
The Univer- 
sity of Nalanda had over 10,000 students. 
Indian scientists deduced and 
proved that the world was round. 
The mathematical developments of 
this period later formed the basis of Arabian mathematics, which in 
turn was adopted by the Europeans. 
Iron and steel making reached a 
point which was not again achieved anywhere until the latter part of the 
nineteenth century. 
The unrusted wrought iron pillar at Delhi, 24 feet 
in length and weighing 6 tons, dates from this period. 
From the fall of the Gupta Empire to the rise of Muslim power in 
north India, the country was fragmented into numerous small states 
whose history is obscure and poorly recorded. 
The Arab Muslims first 
landed in the Sind during the ninth century a. p. but it was not until the 
Turko-Afghan Muslims established their rule in Delhi during the latter 
part of the twelfth century that India came under Muslim rule. 
In this era, Muslim power over north India was organized around 
the Delhi Sultanate, which lasted until the rise of the Mughal Empire 
during the sixteenth century. 
Although there was considerable integra- 
tion, the Muslim conquerors remained throughout a ruling caste apart 
from the Indian society. 
Such success as the Muslim conquerors were


<!-- page 43 of 600 -->

India 
T/1.1 
7 
BACKGROUND 
able to achieve in converting the Indians from Hinduism to Islam was 
with the outcastes and lower castes of the Indian society 
The Muslims during this period were never able to penetrate to extreme 
south India, where an independent south Indian civilization flourished 
from the ninth to the sixteenth century under the Pallava, Chola, and 
Vijayanagar Empires. 
A distinctive and highly-developed south Indian 
art flourished during this period, particularly in sculpture and _archi- 
tecture. 
The Cholas were great colonizers and mainly responsible for 
transplanting Hindu culture to Indo-China and Indonesia from the 
ninth to the thirteenth century. 
The climax of Muslim power in north India came with the rise of 
the Mughal Empire. 
The Mughals were of Turko-Mongolian origin; 
their ancestry can be traced to the great Kublai-Khan through Timurlane 
and Babur. 
Babur first came to India in 1525, but Mughal power 
was not consolidated in India until the rise of Akbar, another of the great 
kings of India, in 1558. 
The Mughals intermarried with the Rajputs, the 
fierce Hindu warriors of Rajasthan, whom they could not conquer by 
arms; and the Mughal Empire was therefore a true blend of the Muslim 
and Hindu societies, although Islam remained the state religion. 
During the height of the Mughal Empire, India became the most 
prosperous and fabulous country in the world. Indian silks and cottons 
were in great demand in international trade. 
Other exports were spices, 
indigo, opium, and other drugs. The world’s gold and silver flowed into 
India in exchange for these products. 
The Mughals were master 
builders; Shajahan, the grandson of Akbar, built the famous Taj Mahal 
at Agra and other beautiful mosques, monuments, and palaces. 
The 
Mughal Empire, however, was short-lived. 
Because of internal disinte- 
gration and external pressure from the Persians and the Europeans, it 
was in decay by the end of the seventeenth century. 
The European advent into India began with the Portuguese in 1503 
when de Albuquerque landed in south India. 
Unlike previous invaders, 
~who had come by land, the Europeans came by sea. 
The Portuguese 
were followed by the Dutch, by the French, and in 1608 by the English, 
when the East India Company founded its first factory at Surat on the 
western coast of the Indian peninsula above Bombay. 
Factories were 
soon established in Madras, Calcutta, and other parts of India. 
For a 
century and a half the British carried on a brisk trade with the Indians 
without getting involved deeply in the politics of the country. 
But the 
political void left by the disintegrating Mughal Empire gradually brought 
the English and the French into the political arena of the country. 
In 
their competitive trade efforts, the British and French pitted one local 
ruler against another until the Battle of Plassey in 1757, in which a 
prince favored by the British defeated one favored by the French and 
with British support became the ruler of Bengal. 
After this date,

British power rose in India and the East India Company gradually took 
over political control of large parts of the country. 
This control centered 
administratively 
in the three Presidencies 
of Calcutta, Madras, and 
Bombay. 
The city of Calcutta became the capital of British rule in 
India until the government was transferred to Delhi in 1911. 
At the time of its first arrival in India, the East India Company, then 
styled the “Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading 
into the East Indies,” operated purely as a trading company under a 
charter granted by Queen Elizabeth I in 1600.1 
Successive royal charters 
through the seventeenth century continued the company’s monopoly and 
increased its judicial powers over English subjects in the East. 
In 1694, 
the validity of the monopoly granted to the “London Company” by the 
Crown was successfully challenged in Parliament, which in 1698 estab- 
lished a new company, known 
as the “English Company,” with a 
monopoly of trade to the East Indies from 1701. 
In 1708, Parliament 
formed a “United Company” from the London and English companies. 
Although this Company’s monopoly on trade to India continued until 
1813, successive acts of Parliament which extended the territorial juris- 
diction of the Company and increased its legislative and judicial powers 
also subjected the conduct of its affairs to increasing supervision by the 
Crown.? 
Under the Charter Act of 1833 % and the Government of India 
Act of 1853,4 the Company was essentially an agency of government 
rather than a trading company. 
Until 1854, the Company governed only 
the Presidencies of Bombay, Bengal, and Madras, but the Government of 
India Act of 18545 empowered the Governor General in Council to take 
control of other areas in which the Company operated and govern them 
through Chief Commissioners. 
After the Indian Mutiny of 1858, Parliament placed British India, in- 
cluding the provinces administered through Chief Commissioners, under 
the direct political control of the Crown as a branch of the British Em- 
pire. The powers of government were vested in a Secretary of State for 
India, assisted by an advisory Council with special powers over finance, 
who was responsible to Parliament and who governed India through a 
Governor-General (later called Viceroy) and his Council in India. 
The latter part of the nineteenth century witnessed the beginnings of 
the Indian independence movement. 
The Congress Party came into be- 
ing in 1888 and formed the rallying unit for Indian demands for greater 
political autonomy and self-determination. 
In 1906, many Indian Mus-

lims separated from the Congress movement and formed an independence 
movement of their own in the Muslim League. 
These efforts for greater 
self-rule gradually brought about a restoration of political power to the 
Indians. 
The Morley-Minto reforms in 1909 marked an important step 
in the introduction of representative government in British India.?- 
They 
were followed by the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919, which fur- 
thered the movement toward representative government by establishing 
provincial governments with a large measure of political autonomy.® 
This reform established the roots of the present federal system of gov- 
ernment in India. 
The Government of India Act of 1935, which forms 
the basis of the present Indian Constitution, divided legislative and ad- 
ministrative powers between the central government and autonomous 
provincial governments which were responsible to elected legislatures. 
This dual system of government has had, and continues to have, far- 
reaching effect on the fiscal and tax policies of India. 
During the later years of British rule, there were over 500 native Indian 
States which were not subject to the political control of British India. 
Hyderabad and Kashmir were each as large as the United Kingdom, 
while some states contained only a few acres. 
Some of the states pre- 
dated the Muslim invasion; some were ruled by Muslim dynasties; and 
others existed by virtue of recognition by the British during the con- 
solidation of British power. 
Between 1757 and 1857, the East India Com- 
pany had entered into treaties or engagements with the rulers of these 
independent states, guaranteeing the external and internal stability of 
their governments; the Company exacted in return the promise of favor- 
able conditions for its operations, together with grants of varying degrees 
of power, through control over the internal affairs of the states, to en- 
sure that favorable conditions were maintained. 
During the later years 
of East India Company rule, a number of native Indian States were an- 
nexed outright to British India. 
When the Crown took over the control 
_of British India in 1858, it succeeded to the treaties and engagements 
with the remaining states;'° and abandoning the policy of annexation, 
it negotiated new agreements consolidating the system of “paramountcy” 
developed by the East India Company. 
The terms of the agreements 
varied widely; but in general the Crown exercised complete control over 
- 
the external affairs of the states, and the control which the various rulers 
retained over internal affairs was subject to the “paramount power” of 
the Crown. 
The states were politically and fiscally independent of 
British India.

The Congress and Muslim League movements for independence re-

two separate and independent dominions of India and Pakistan. 
Under 
this Act, the suzerainty of the Crown over the native Indian States 
lapsed,!’ and these states have been either merged in or integrated with 
the rest of India. From 1947 to 1950, the Indian government continued 
to operate under the Government of India Act, 1935, subject to the 
authority of a Constituent Assembly established to provide for the consti- 
tution of the dominion.1* 
The Constituent Assembly abolished the 
jurisdiction of the British Privy Council over Indian appeals and petitions 
in 1949.16 
1/1.2. 
The Constitution of India 
The Constitution of India, enacted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 
November 1949 and inaugurated on 26 January 1950, forms the basis of 
the political organization of the country. 
It is a written Constitution 
with 395 articles and 9 schedules. 
The procedure for amendment is 
simple, and amendments have been frequent. 
The Constitution draws 
for precedent on the written constitutions of Ireland, Australia, and the 
United States. 
India is a sovereign democratic republic. 
While it 
chooses to remain a member of the British Commonwealth, this mem- 
bership involves no legal or constitutional surrender of her sovereignty. 
India is a secular state in which every citizen is guaranteed the right 
of religious freedom. 
Every citizen of India who is 21 years of age or 
older is entitled to vote in central and state elections, and 120 million 
people voted in the second national election in 1957. 
The Constitution continues the federal type of government established 
by the Government of India Act of 1935 (1/1.1). 
Originally it provided 
for 28 states.

dent through Chief Commissioners, Lieutenant-Governors, or the gov- 
ernments of neighboring states, with provision for the creation by Parlia- 
ment of legislatures and councils of ministers in such states. 
One “Part 
D” state,” a territory administered by British India, was administered by 
the President independently of the legislative jurisdiction of Parliament. 
The States Reorganization Act of 1956, and the Constitution (Seventh 
Amendment) Act of 1956, abolished the distinction between Part A and 
Part B states, reorganized the states along demographic, ethnic, and 
linguistic lines, and reduced their number to 14 as follows:24 Andhra 
Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Bombay, Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala, Madhya 
Pradesh, Madras, Mysore, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, 
West Bengal.

Union

Andaman 
and Nicobar 
Islands; 
Delhi; Himachal

The Indian Constitution defines in greater detail than most constitutions 
the division of legislative, executive, and administrative powers between 
the central and state governments. 
Unlike the situation in the United 
States, the constitutional powers of the central and state governments are 
contained in a single document. 
Part IV of the Constitution sets forth 16 principles of policy which are 
not enforceable by any court but which the central and state govern- 
ments are enjoined to follow in framing legislation.2? 
Among them are 
the establishment of a social order based on social, economic, and politi- 
cal justice; the organization of village panchayats (1/1.5); assurance of

improvement of wages and working and living conditions; provision of 
free compulsory education for children; elevation of the level of nutrition 
and the standard of living (including prohibition of the consumption of 
alcohol and drugs); and the modernization of agriculture.

The Central Government 
a, THE LEGISLATURE. 
The central legislature 2° is known as the Union 
Parliament. 
It consists of the President and two houses: the Council of 
States or Rajyasabha, and the House of the People or Lok Sabha. 
With 
the exceptions noted at 1/6.2, legislation must be approved by both 
houses. 
The Council of States is a permanent body, elected indirectly. 
Pro- 
vision is made for 250 seats, a third of which become vacant every second 
year. 
Twelve members are nominated by the President from among 
artists, writers, scientists, and social workers. 
The remainder are elected 
by the members of the state legislative assemblies. 
The Council is pre- 
sided over by the Vice-president. 
Only citizens 30 years of age or over 
qualify for membership. 
The House of the People consists of not more than 500 members elected 
by the voters in the states and not more than 20 members representing 
the Union territories. 
Representatives of the states are elected by ter- 
ritorial constituencies established on the basis of population. 
The normal 
life of the House of the People is five years. 
A speaker and a deputy 
speaker of the House are elected by its members. 
Only citizens 25 
years of age or over qualify for membership. 
Parliament is called into session by the President, who is required 
to summon each house within six months of its last sitting in its pre- 
vious session.2° 
Under the rules of Parliament, 
there are two 
ses- 
sions annually: the Budget Session opening in February, at which the 
principal business is the budget, and the Autumn Session, which is 
the principal 
legislative 
session, 
running 
from September 
through 
December. 
The President has the power to legislate by the promulgation of ordi- 
nances when either house of Parliament is not in session; but such ordi- 
nances must be submitted to Parliament, and expire six weeks after the 
reassembly of Parliament if they have not been invalidated by resolu- 
tions of both houses before that time.?*

b. THE EXECUTIVE. 
The Constitution provides for a parliamentary form 
of government, resembling 
that of Great Britain, rather than a presidential 
form, like that of the United States.28 
Although all executive powers are 
exercised in the name of the President, they actually reside in the Council 
of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, who is normally the head 
of the party in power in the Union Parliament. 
The President *° is the head of the Indian Republic. 
He is elected by 
an electoral college consisting of electoral members of both houses of 
Parliament and of the legislative assemblies of the states. 
The election 
is held on the basis of proportional representation by single transferable 
vote. 
The President holds office for five years, is eligible for re-election, 
and can be removed from office only by impeachment. 
Any citizen of 
India over 35 years of age who is eligible for election as a member of 
the House of the People is qualified for the office of President. 
The Vice- 
president *° is ex officio chairman of the Council of States. 
Any citizen 
age 35 years and above and qualified for membership in the Council of 
States can be elected to this office by both the houses of Parliament. 
The real executive of the Indian Republic is the Council of Ministers 
with the Prime Minister as its leader.*! 
It is collectively responsible to 
the House of the People and holds power while it retains the confidence 
of this legislative body. 
The Prime Minister, as head of the Council, 
provides the link between it and the President. 
The Prime Minister is 
appointed by the President, and the other ministers are appointed by the 
President on the advice of the Prime Minister. 
The ministers hold office 
at the pleasure of the President, and must be, or within six months of their 
appointment must become, members of one of the houses of Parliament. 
As presently constituted, the Council of Ministers consists of the Cabinet 
Ministers, each of whom is responsible for one or more departments of 
government, the Ministers of State, who administer the departments of 
government but who are not members of the Cabinet, and the Deputy 
_ Ministers. 
India has a well-developed civil service, administration service, and 
police service. 
¢. THE yupictary. 
The Constitution *” establishes a Supreme Court of 
India, consisting of a Chief Justice of India and 10 other judges. 
Parlia- 
ment has the power to establish additional courts to administer laws on 
matters within its jurisdiction.** 
The judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President and

No person who has held office as a judge of the

The Supreme Court is a court of record with all the powers of such a 
court, including the power to punish for contempt. 
The seat of the court 
is in Delhi. 
The Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction in any 
dispute between states or between a state and the government of India.** 
The appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court extends to appeals from 
any judgment, decree, or final order of a High Court (1/1.4c) in civil, 
criminal, or other proceedings, if the High Court certifies that the case 
involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the 
Constitution. 
If the High Court refuses such a certificate, the Supreme 
Court may grant special leave to appeal.*® 
An appeal also lies to the 
Supreme Court from a High Court in civil matters when the amount or 
value of the subject matter in dispute is not less than Rs 20,000 or when 
the High Court certifies the case to be a fit one for appeal to the Supreme 
Court.?® 
In criminal matters, an appeal lies to the Supreme Court from 
any judgment, final order, or sentence of a High Court if the High Court 
has on appeal reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and 
sentenced him to death, or if the High Court has withdrawn the case 
from a subordinate court and in a trial before itself convicted the accused 
person and sentenced him to death, or if the High Court has certified 
that the case is a fit one for appeal.37_ The Supreme Court also has discre- 
tion to grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, sentence, 
or order in any matter passed by any court or tribunal in India.8 
Article 32 of the Constitution guarantees the right to move the Supreme 
Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of “fundamental 
rights”; and for the enforcement of such rights the Court has the right to 
issue directions, orders, or writs in the nature of habeas corpus, man- 
damus, prohibition, quo warranto, or certiorari, as may be appropriate.

The State Governments 
The territories, organization, and powers of the state governments are 
prescribed by the Constitution of India; unlike the states of Australia or 
the United States, the states have no “residual powers” arising inde- 
pendently of the Constitution. 
a. THE LEGISLATURE. 
The Constitution provides for bicameral legislatures 
in 10 states and for unicameral legislatures in the other states.4° 
The 
bicameral legislatures are modeled after the Union Parliament. 
The 
upper house is the Legislative Council; the lower house, or the single 
house of a unicameral legislature, is the Legislative Assembly. 
The 
Legislative Council is a permanent body with one third of its members 
retiring every second year. 
Half of its members are elected from local 
bodies, from university graduates of three years’ standing, and from 
teachers who have worked at least three years in an educational institu- 
tion not lower than a secondary school; a third of the members are 
elected by the Legislative Assembly from among others than its own 
members; and the rest are nominated by the government from among 
men of eminence in literature, art, science, and social service.*1 
The 
Legislative Assembly is elected on the basis of adult franchise at the 
time of the elections for the Union Parliament unless a special by-election 
_is necessary because of failure of the last elected parliamentary govern- 
ment in the state (1/3.2). 
It has not less than 60 and not more than 
500 members. *” 
b. THE EXECUTIVE. 
The Constitution of India vests the executive power 
of each state in a Governor,** who is appointed by the President of India 
to serve a five year term. 
Only an Indian citizen who has attained the 
age of 35 years and is not a member of Parliament or a state legislature 
is eligible for appointment. 
As in the central government, executive

The Constitution provides for the establishment of a 
High Court in each state,*7 although Parliament may establish a com- 
mon High Court for two or more states.#® 
The judges of a High Court 
are appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice

A judge of a High Court holds office until he attains the 
age of 60 years. 
Only a citizen of India who has either held judicial office 
for 10 years or practiced as an advocate for 10 years is qualified for ap- 
pointment as a judge of a High Court.*® 
A permanent judge of a High 
Court is prohibited from practicing law before that court after leaving the

Courts.®° 
A High Court is a court of record and has all the powers of 
such courts, including the power to punish for contempt.*! A High Court 
exercises control over the administration of all subordinate courts within 
its jurisdiction.®? 
The subordinate courts which were in existence at the time of the 
adoption of the Constitution continued to exercise their functions under 
its provisions.’ 
Under the Constitution, their judges are appointed by 
the Governor of the state.*4 
The membership and jurisdiction of the lower courts vary. 
Generally 
speaking, one district and sessions judge is appointed for each district.

1/1.5 
Local Government 
In those parts of India which were subject to British rule, the system 
of local government established by the British still functions. 
At first 
under Crown charters and later by acts of Parliament, municipal corpora- 
tions were established during the period of the East India Company in 
the Presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras, and other munici- 
palities were later formed in other parts of British India by Indian 
legislation. 
Subject to varying degrees of control by the state govern- 
ment, exercised either directly, through a Director of Local Authorities, 
or through a District Collector, the local governments 
control such 
matters as roads, sanitation, public health, and education within their 
“borders. 
The principal officer of local administration under the British 
was the District Collector, who had broad powers over land revenue, 
police, and the administration of justice. 
When local authorities were 
established, they frequently operated either in association with or under 
the control of the Collector. 
~ 
Historically, the foundation of local self-government in India was the 
panchayat, a council which originally consisted of five persons, but which 
is now usually larger, entrusted with the administrative and judicial 
responsibility of a village or group of villages. During the periods of 
Muslim and European domination, panchayat government was 
sup- 
planted by state or central government control, but its revival has been 
explicitly adopted as a policy by the government of India.®

Regulatory Boards, Statutory Corporations, and 
Public Utilities 
In pursuit of its goal of industrial development through a mixed 
economy (1/2.4), the government has resorted, through various types 
of instrumentalities, to regulation, financial support, and direct partici- 
pation in industry. 
Statutory boards have been given broad powers in 
the implementation of government policies on the regulation of certain 
industries and the control of their development; examples are the boards 
established under the Rubber Act of 1947, the Central Silk Board Act 
of 1948, and the Tea Act of 1953 (formerly governed by the Central Tea 
Board Act of 1949). 
A number of central government corporations 
(1/3.3a) have been established for the purpose of providing long-term 
financing for private agricultural and industrial development (1/2.6). 
In addition, the Reserve Bank of India, the State Bank of India, and the 
Life Insurance Corporation of India are owned and operated by the 
central government. 
Under the Damodar Valley Corporation Act of 
1948, the government has undertaken a program of flood control, irriga- 
tion, generation of electric power, navigation, and development of the 
economic and social welfare of the Damodar River valley. 
Central gov- 
ernment corporations established under the Air Corporations Act of 1953 
handle most of India’s air transportation cf passengers and freight. 
The 
central government has owned and operated practically all of India’s 
railroad system since 1937. 
Under their inherent powers and independ- 
ently of any legislative action, both the central government and state 
governments have established corporations to carry out industrial and 
commercial activities of various kinds. 
Thus, the central government 
now operates three steel mills, two locomotive factories, an airplane 
factory, and a plant for the production of antibiotics. 
Facilities for the road transport of passengers are always entirely owned 
and operated by public bodies established by the states under authority 
of the Road Transport Corporations Act of 1950. 
The generation and 
distribution of electricity is controlled by state electricity boards, under 
the general supervision of a Central Electricity Authority, established 
under the Electricity (Supply) Act of 1948.

Except for 
the island territories, they are under the legislative jurisdiction of Parlia- 
ment’ and are subject to the central tax laws. 
Sales taxes are also in 
force in some of the Union territories. 
Each Union territory is under 
the jurisdiction of the High Court of a neighboring state.

BACKGROUND 
1/2. 
Economic and Fiscal Background 
1/2.1 
Resources 
India is a vast country; its area of some 1,270,000 square miles—almost 
half the size of the United States and more than all of western Europe— 
justifies its classification, with Pakistan, as a subcontinent, separated from 
the rest of Asia by the Himalayas. 
Below the mountains, the Indo- 
Gangetic Plain covers the broad northern part of the continent from 
Karachi to Calcutta. 
Composed of rivers and silt, this plain forms one 
of the most extensive sheets of rich and level cultivable land in the 
world. 
On the south, it is joined by a triangular peninsula of hills and 
plateaus ranging mostly between 1,000 and 3,000 feet above sea level, 
also well adapted to agriculture. 
The southern peninsula is characterized 
by a tropical climate of even temperature, in contrast to the extremes 
in weather variations found in the north. 
In the north, tributaries of the 
two vast river systems, the Indus on the east and the Ganges on the west, 
provide perennial water. 
In contrast, the five southern peninsular river 
systems depend primarily on the rains; they flow in torrents during the 
monsoon season and then shrivel into sand. 
Indeed, the outstanding 
phenomenon of Indian weather is the monsoon, still the decisive factor 
in India’s agriculture and perhaps its entire economy. 
In the four mon- 
soon months, roughly mid-May through mid-September, India receives 
essentially all its internal rainfall. 
It is this concentration which is 
responsible for the fact that in the past India has not been able to use 
more than 7% of its annual rainfall; in considerable part, it explains the 
efforts devoted to the expansion of various kinds of facilities for water 
storage, from vast dams to small tanks, in order to provide more evenly 
distributed means of irrigation. 
Not more than 35% of India’s land area is cultivated on a regular 
basis. 
Optimistic estimates envisage that perhaps as much as 10% to 
“12% more of the land surface might be cultivated, but the investment 
required for clearance and soil improvement probably means that a figure 
half this large represents the actual maximum. 
Irrigation is extended 
less to bring new land into cultivation than to assure the supply of 
.. water on land already being used for crops, and perhaps to provide an 
opportunity for double cropping. 
There is a growing awareness of the 
opportunities 
for expanding agricultural output through intensifying 
production as against its extension over broader areas. 
By raising yields 
per acre to levels prevailing in comparable countries, agricultural pro- 
duction in India might be almost doubled.

figures for averages of selected prewar (1933-1934) and recent (1954-

1/2.2 
Population 
The potential resources of India are better appraised in the light of 
its population. 
Thus, the cultivated area in 1951 was less than one acre 
per person, a very low figure for a large country.®® 
Given India’s rela- 
tively low yields per acre and early stage of industrial development, 
measurements of output per head of population in agriculture, industry, 
and power are all low. 
This is consistent with the fact that India’s 
national income in 1951, at the start of the planned development programs, 
stood at US$51.50 per person. 
The census of 1951 reported a total population of 356.9 million as of 
1 March.®® 
Despite high birth rates, the high death rates tended to 
keep the rate of natural increase very low until 1951; it was especially 
low in the years between 1891 and 1921. 
Even in the 1941-1951 decade,

In 1951, this meant an annual addition

Under the spur 
of recent public health measures, which have had particularly dramatic 
effects upon infant mortality and upon the incidence of such diseases as 
malaria and tuberculosis, the rate of natural increase has been expanding; 
_ the current population is in excess of 400 million. 
There has been an 
average increase of more than 5.5 million persons in each year since 1951; 
and today, there is evidence that the population may be growing by as 
much as 7.5 million persons annually. 
Where the Census Commissioner 
for 1951 projected a total of 520 million persons by 1981,*! recent esti- 
mates place a minimum figure for 1981 at 562 million and a probable 
figure well in excess of 600 million.® 
In general, neither India’s population growth nor economic expansion 
has altered the distribution of population over the subcontinent. Most 
Indians still live in the Gangetic Plain from Amritsar to Calcutta and 
along the coastal areas of Bombay, Madras, and Southwestern India. 
More than 80% of India’s population still lives in rural areas in villages 
with populations averaging less than 600 persons. 
No less than 72.5% 
of all the 143 million members of the labor force in 1950-1951 was 
employed in agriculture and similar activities. 
As can be seen in Table 2, 
the structural pattern of the labor force is essentially that of the classic 
breakdown for a nonindustrial economy. 
The vast bulk of the working 
force is engaged in agriculture, and of the remainder, a large proportion, 
17% of the total work force, are in service activities. 
Thus, commerce 
and transport alone have over 10 million workers, and government and 
professional services together also account for over 10 million. 
Finally, the other productive sector, mining and industry, tends to be 
dominated by forms of economic endeavor in which, as in agriculture, 
output per man is low. 
If small-scale and handicraft activity is consid- 
ered separately, what might be called modern industry in 1951 provided 
employment for less than 3 million people, only 2.1% of the total work 
force. 
It does not appear likely that the percentage of the population working 
in industry has increased, although there has been some shift in favor 
of modern industry within this component. 
Nor has there been any 
_appreciable alteration in proportion of workers who are engaged in 
agriculture and related activities.

proceeded at a somewhat more rapid rate after 1951, urban unemploy-

Despite the emphasis which planning has placed upon growth in the

product is produced by private enterprise. 
Even the expanding role 
which government plays in industrial enterprise will probably not alter 
this ratio significantly over the next decade and perhaps longer. 
Indeed, 
among nations for which national income statistics are available, India 
ranks lowest with respect to the relative importance of governmental 
transactions.®® 
One factor which contributes to the importance of private 
activity is the predominant position of agriculture, which is primarily in 
private hands. 
The fact that in rural enterprise many transactions are 
in goods rather than in money complicates the problems of measuring 
national income, of inducing economic change in rural areas, and of 
increasing the degree of government control over the economy. 
1/2.4 
The Five-year Plans 
From the time of independence, the economic and political scene in 
India has been dominated by organized planning efforts. 
Today, India 
is drawing to the close of its second plan. 
Preparation of the third 
plan is well underway. 
The Planning Commission is responsible for preparing the plans; its 
work constitutes the background blueprint for the central and state 
governments, whose operating ministries and agencies conduct the actual 
development projects. 
The individual plans are specific components of 
a long-range perspective which anticipates that national income will be 
doubled by 1967-1968, that is, in the 17 years following 1950-1951, with 
per capita income doubled about 10 years later.°* 
The five-year plans 
themselves are now viewed as a framework for specific annual programs 
formulated on the basis of actual progress year by year. 
The relationship of private activity to the governmental planning effort 
is based upon India’s fundamental objective of attaining a “socialist pat- 
tern of society,” but this does not imply a doctrinaire approach to broad- 
scale nationalization of the economy. 
Public ownership of enterprises 
is expected to expand, but primarily in fields which the government 
believes might otherwise be neglected. 
In any case, as noted earlier, 
the bulk of the economy is left to private ownership and development.

BACKGROUND 
Two major problem areas arise in such a mixed economy. 
One con- 
cerns the responsibility for industrial development, where the govern- 
ment will be treading new ground. 
The other is the more general 
concern with the pattern of public-private interplay not only in industry, 
but throughout the economy. 
On the first problem, the major policy is presented in the Industrial 
Policy Resolution of 30 April 1956 which revised an earlier resolution 
dated 6 April 1948.8 
The resolution outlined three categories of indus- 
try. 
The first category, in which government has the primary respon- 
sibility, includes arms and ammunition, atomic energy, iron and steel, air- 
craft and air transport, railway transport, ship building, and generation 
and distribution of power, among others. 
The second category includes 
such important modern industrial activities as the manufacture of machine 
tools, fertilizers, chemicals, synthetic rubber and others; here both public 
and private control will operate, with a clear indication that government 
operations will tend to expand relatively. 
The third category, in which 
the private sector is expected to continue to play the dominant if not the 
exclusive role, consists of all remaining industries. 
The government itself 
anticipates that this allocation might double its relative importance in 
industrial production; currently it is responsible for less than 5%. 
It 
should be noted that this policy statement applied to both domestic and 
foreign private investment. 
India does not treat foreign private capital 
differently from domestic private capital. 
The 1956 policy statement makes clear that the categories are not water- 
tight compartments. 
The flexibility in the interpretation of the first cate- 
gory is illustrated by the current expansion of steel production by a con- 
cern in the private sector. 
While the plan establishes objectives and pri- 
orities for economic expansion, the government cannot compel the private 
sector to undertake any specific project. Through the Industries (Devel- 
opment and Regulation) Act of 1951, which provides for the registration 
of existing enterprises and the licensing of future undertakings in some 
“42, categories of industry, the government can exercise various restraints 
on the private entrepreneur desiring to invest. 
To this end, a licensing 
committee was set up under the Act to function as an advisory body to 
the government. 
Development councils for individual industries in the 
_private sector were also established to participate in the formulation of 
programs of industrial development in the plans. 
Moreover, the govern- 
ment has taken steps to facilitate private enterprise through income tax 
concessions for new undertakings, through tariff protection, and through 
the creation of new credit facilities. 
Industrial financing corporations 
have been established by the central government as well as by a number 
of individual state governments.

As can be seen in Table 4, the public emphasis has shifted from

Current expectations are that the

be renewed efforts to expand agricultural output significantly and a 
stepped up program of industrialization will give particular attention to 
the production of heavy machinery. 
Programs for community development and small-scale industry are of 
special importance in these plans. 
These are efforts to accelerate the 
process of change for the bulk of the population engaged in agriculture, 
handicrafts, and other small enterprises. 
They are meant to provide a 
link between the government program and private responsibility and to 
stimulate employment in sectors affected by joblessness and underemploy- 
ment. 
By 1955-1956, national income had increased by 17% or 18% over the

The United States provided about half of this assistance. 
Important 
contributions were made by the International Bank, the International 
Monetary Fund, the United Kingdom, the Federal Republic of Germany, 
Canada, Japan, and other Colombo Plan countries. 
Russia and the com- 
munist bloc also participated in the aid program for the second plan. 
They have provided about 12% of the total to date. 
However, India has

ings as well as in the effectiveness with which new investment has been 
converted into an increased flow of national income. 
Agricultural output in 1955-1956 exceeded the levels planned, partly 
as a result of the unusually favorable weather conditions of 1953-1955. 
Currently, the prospects for achieving the 1960-1961 targets are not fa- 
vorable. 
For 1960-1961 industrial production, the general index will 
probably fall appreciably below the level anticipated. 
Actually, there is 
considerable variation in the relative achievements in individual com- 
modities. 
Industrial output has been lagging in considerable measure 
because the private sector finds limited demand in India’s domestic 
market. 
Since agriculture and rural production play a major role in the 
Indian economy, private industry cannot expand significantly unless there 
is greater progress in agriculture. 
Therefore, governmental emphasis for 
the third plan is again being directed toward a major forward movement 
in this basic sector. 
Agricultural progress at a rate of 5% to 8% per year 
is considered both necessary and possible.

Public Finance 
Fiscal authority resides in the powerful Ministry of Finance, which has 
control over all revenues and expenditures, the budgetary process, and 
all matters of internal and external finance connected with the economic 
affairs of the country. 
It maintains continuous control over the ex- 
penditures of the other ministries and agencies of government by assign: 
ing its own finance officers to serve in them. 
The government of India operates with a general budget and a con- 
solidated fund. A separate railway budget is presented by the Ministry 
of Railways but eventually is consolidated with the general budget. 
All

_ consolidated fund and used-only for budgetary expenditures approved 
by Parliament. 
The budget is separated into revenue and capital accounts. 
The rev- 
enue budget embraces current, recurring governmental receipts and ex- 
penditures. 
The capital budget is for capital expenditures of the govern- 
ment, including those for economic development. 
Revenue surpluses, 
if any, are carried over to the capital budget and an over-all surplus (or

1/2.6 
Banking System 
India has a modern central banking system and a well-developed com- 
mercial banking system which is equipped to provide suitable financing 
arrangements for facilitating the flow of internal trade, especially for 
large enterprises. 
The organized banking system is only beginning to 
meet these needs for the small enterprises which dominate the Indian 
economic scene. 
Indigenous bankers and moneylenders, whose rates are 
usually high, still fill most of this role, particularly in rural areas. 
Commercial bank advances are not available for long enough periods 
to finance development effectively. 
The government is attempting to fill 
these needs in agriculture through the Reserve Bank’s newly established 
National Agricultural Credit Fund, and in industry through such organi- 
zations as the Industrial Finance Corporation, various parallel state or- 
ganizations, the Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation (a private 
financing group to which the government has given a loan), the National 
Industrial Development Corporation, and the National Small Industries 
Corporation. 
These have in common the objective of providing reason- 
ably long-term investment resources to private enterprises—small and 
large—which need capital. 
The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 and was 
nationalized on 1 January 1949. 
Prior to that time, the banking system 
was dominated by the Imperial Bank of India, established in 1921. 
The 
Imperial Bank was nationalized 20 December 1954 and established as 
the State Bank of India for the purpose of improving the remittance sys- 
tem and promoting rural credit supplies to facilitate agricultural devel- 
opment. 
These two banks form the core of the modern banking system 
of the country. 
A 
The substructure of the system consists of Indian joint-stock banks, 
branches of foreign banks, and cooperative banks.

Companies Act of 1949, the Reserve Bank is empowered to license banks

Currency 
The unit of currency in India is the rupee, which as of 1960 is worth 
approximately 21 cents in United States currency or ls. 6d. sterling. 
The 
rupee is one of the currencies of the sterling bloc and therefore tied to 
the pound sterling. 
It is one of the most stable currencies in the world; 
it has maintained its value steadfastly since September 1949 when it was 
reduced from 30 United States cents on the devaluation of the pound 
sterling by the United Kingdom. 
Large amounts of rupees are frequently 
expressed in terms of “lakhs” and “crores”: Rs 1 lakh is Rs 100,000, and

In order to facilitate computa- 
tion with lakhs and crores, high numbers are often punctuated, begin- 
ning to the left of the thousands column, to indicate multiplication by 
100 instead of multiplication by 1,000. 
Thus, Rs 1 lakh is frequently

1/2.8 
Foreign Trade and Investment 
Like the United States and Russia, India is a nation which is relatively 
self-sufficient. 
For example, imports and exports tend to be a low per- 
centage of national income—usually about 7%. 
As in the case of the 
Chinese mainland, however, India’s self-sufficiency is accompanied by 
low levels of living. 
Over the years of major development activity, im- 
ports needed for the expanded investment program must be provided 
by its international transactions. 
Particular attention is therefore being 
given to the expansion of exports, the reduction of imports for which 
demand can be curtailed or domestic substitutes generated, and the in- 
flow of foreign investment, all of which operate in the direction of making 
possible greater imports for development. 
In pursuit of these objectives, India has maintained and expanded its 
system of foreign exchange controls. 
Under the administration of the 
Reserve Bank of India, the program seeks to centralize all receipts of 
foreign currencies and to allocate their use, either by government or by 
the private sector in conformance with a system of priorities. 
Thus, the 
system of licensing in industrial plant expansion and in other capital 
construction is tied in with arrangements for release of any foreign ex- 
change needed for these purposes. 
Similarly, the Indian system of im- 
port and export control, originally instituted as a war-time measure in 
1940, is still maintained and provides basic policy and procedures for 
allocating foreign exchange to importers. 
This requires reasonably flexi- 
ble administration; ordinarily, the specifics of the government's import 
policy are announced twice a year to guide importers seeking licenses. 
In general, capital goods and industrial requirements are given priority, 
while the availability of exchange for imports of consumer goods is varied 
dependent upon the foreign exchange position at the time. 
The govern- 
ment’s system of tariffs and export duties must be considered not only 
as a device to raise revenue but also as a means to further the objectives 
for its international accounts. 
As in the case of other developing coun- 
tries, India’s participation in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 
and in Commonwealth preference schemes, is fitted into the basic pro- 
gram of directing India’s foreign trade pattern so that it contributes to the 
development objectives. 
In preplan years, India tended to run a small deficit in its commodity 
trade, and this was usually more or less balanced by a surplus in the 
current service account due to net earnings on transportation, insurance, 
and private remittances from abroad. 
Tea, jute, and cotton manufactures 
have long been the main export staples, while imports consisted of a wide 
miscellany including grains and raw cotton plus capital goods and indus- 
trial raw materials. 
Over the plan years this picture has been changing. 
Data for 1958, for example, show commodity imports as Rs 1,044.5 crores, 
almost twice the preplan level, while exports are Rs 565.1 crores, not very

The vast bulk of India’s imports comes from western Europe and the

Exports to the dollar area, however,

The foreign market for India’s basic exports is

Insofar as India’s export markets

The foreign assistance mentioned earlier was devoted to financing these

The large reduction in India’s own foreign exchange bal-

Thus, the total figure is unofficially estimated at Rs

Small though the net additions 
may be, the technical skills and processes which they bring, especially 
through joint foreign and Indian industrial ventures, give this private

In General 
The law of business organizations and commercial transactions in 
India is almost entirely based on central or state legislation.

extended throughout the territory of India. 
At that time, the laws of 
the former provinces of British India were also extended to the territories 
of former Indian States which had been merged with them. 
The transfer 
of territories to different states in the reorganization of 1956 (1/1.2) did 
not itself affect the laws in force in the territories transferred, but the 
states are gradually unifying their laws by suitable legislation (1/5.3). 
Legislation now also governs the Hindu law of succession, adoption 
and maintenance, marriage, minority and guardianship, and to some 
extent the law of inheritance, transfers, bequests and partition. 
Formerly 
these matters were governed by the Mitakshara school of Hindu law, 
except in Bengal, where the Dayabhaga school was prominent. 
In gen- 
eral, the effect of the statutory changes is to remove the former disabilities 
of women and restrictions of alienation of property. 
The Hindu law was 
derived in part from custom, in part from the sruti (that which was 
heard—the words of the deities), but principally from smriti (that which 
was remembered—recollections of the words of the deities passed down 
by ancient sages). 
The most important of these latter were the Code of 
Manu, which originated between 200 B.c. and 200 a.p.; the Code of 
Yajnavalkya, 400 a.v.; and the Code of Narada, dating from between 
500 and 600 a.p. 
The most important characteristic of the Hindu society is the joint 
family (Hindu undivided family). 
A joint family consists of all male 
Hindus descended in the male line from a common ancestor, their wives, 
and their unmarried daughters. 
The control of the family vests in the 
Karta, who is usually the eldest male member. 
When a daughter is 
married, she ceases to be a member of her father’s family and becomes 
a member of her husband’s family. 
Female members of the family are 
entitled to maintenance, but a woman can acquire an interest in the 
family property only by inheritance from her husband. 
A member 
of the family who has an interest in the family property is called a 
coparcener. 
Each coparcener is entitled to claim a partition and to 
receive a share of the family property on partition. 
A partition may 
either sever the interest of the coparcener seeking partition, leaving the 
rest of the family property intact, or divide the entire family property 
among all the coparceners. 
When a Hindu inherits property from his 
father, or father’s father, or father’s farther’s father, then it is ancestral 
property. 
But property which he inherits from other relatives or accu- 
mulates on his own 
is separate property. 
Thus, if a man _ inherits 
ancestral property and has a son, grandson, or great grandson, or all of 
them, all acquire a share in the property by reason of and from the 
moment of birth. 
But a man is absolute owner of his separate property 
and can dispose of it according to his will. 
Yet once it passes to his son 
it becomes ancestral property in the hands of the son. 
It is the ancestral 
property which is divided by a partition.
