The High Courts and their predecessors under the East India Company 
had applied general English statutory and common law in litigation 
between Englishmen where there was no applicable Indian legislation 
or applicable British legislation expressly affecting India.73 
In general, 
the courts did not apply English law in litigation involving Indians unless 
there was no applicable indigenous law. 
British statutory and case law 
in effect in India which was not expressly repealed was not necessarily 
abrogated either by the enactment of the Indian Independence Act or 
by the adoption of the Constitution. 
However, Indian legislation has 
now displaced most of the English statutory law which applied to India, 
and torts and conflict of laws are the only fields in which English 
common law is the principal source of Indian authority. 
English and 
other Commonwealth cases may, however, be helpful in interpreting 
Indian legislation.

Central and State Legislative Powers 
The Constitution establishes three categories of legislative subjects: 
the “Union List,” comprising those which are within the exclusive juris- 
diction of Parliament; the “State List,” comprising those which are within 
_the exclusive jurisdiction of the state legislatures; and the “Concurrent 
| List,” composed of those on which Parliament and the state legislatures 
have concurrent jurisdiction, subject to the supremacy of parliamentary 
action.7! 
The power to legislate on any matter not enumerated in the 
State List or the Concurrent List is reserved to Parliament.” 
All matters 
“relating to the Union territories are within the exclusive jurisdiction 
of Parliament.”®

a. CORPORATIONS. 
The formation and operation of business corporations 
(companies ) in India is governed by the Companies Act of 1956, which 
replaced an act of 1913. 
The two types of corporate business organiza- 
tion permitted in India are the private company and the public company. 
A private company is one which, by its articles of incorporation, restricts 
the right to transfer its shares, limits the number of shareholders to 50, 
and prohibits any invitation to the public to subscribe to any of its shares 
or debentures.°? 
A company whose articles of incorporation do not 
contain these restrictions and limitations is a public company. 
The new 
Companies Act contains elaborate and detailed provisions on the manage- 
ment and administration of companies in India.® 
The new law permits only two kinds of share capital, namely, equity 
share capital and preference share capital.°2 
Every holder of equity 
share capital must have the right to vote in proportion to his share of 
the paid-up equity capital in the company.®? 
Preference shares may be 
issued with preferential rights with respect to either dividends 
or 
liquidation.°* 
An Indian company may also issue debentures but cannot 
grant the holders any voting rights.®* 
It may, however, make the de- 
bentures perpetual. 
Convertible debentures are also permitted. 
A foreign company which establishes a place of business in India is 
_required to deliver to the Registrar in the state in which its place of 
business is located a certified copy of its charter, the address of its 
principal office, a list of the directors and secretary of the company, the 
name and address of a person or persons resident in India authorized to 
accept service of process and other notices on behalf of the company, and 
-~ the address of its principal office in India.°*

b. MANAGING AGENCIES. 
A unique and controversial form of business 
organization in India is the managing agency. 
A managing agent is an 
individual, 
a Hindu undivided family, a corporation, or a partnership 
which, under a long-term contract for a fee or percentage of profits, 
manages 
another company’s business and provides 
it with a wide 
range of financial and technical services. 
Some of the large manag- 
ing agents control 50 or more companies. 
The bulk of the engineer- 
ing, coal, jute, tea, paper, flour, and rice industries are managed this 
way. 
The managing agency system served and still serves a useful function 
in the development of industries in India. 
Since there is a shortage of 
capital and managerial and technical skills, the managing agency system 
provides an organizational form which makes these limited factors of 
production available to a greater number of individual enterprises. 
On 
the other hand, the system has lent itself to abuse by creating monopolies 
and permitting unconscionable profit taking.

1/3.5 
Legal Practitioners 
Legal practice in India is governed by the Legal Practitioners Act of 
1879, the Indian Bar Councils Act of 1926, and various state acts. 
The 
bar of each High Court includes advocates, who are entitled to practice 
before the High Court and all courts subordinate to it, and pleaders, 
who are entitled to practice before subordinate courts only. 
In the 
High Courts of Bombay and Calcutta there is a third class of practitioners 
called solicitors, who advise clients and instruct advocates and who may 
appear in subordinate courts. 
Solicitors are required, as in England, 
to pass a rigorous examination after apprenticeship to a firm. 
An advo- 
cate must either hold a law degree from an Indian university and pass 
an examination given by the Bar Council, or be a member of the English 
Bar. 
To be admitted to practice before the Supreme Court, an advocate 
must have been enrolled as an advocate of a High Court for seven years, 
and must either have a law degree from an Indian university or be a 
member of the English Bar. 
The Union Cabinet includes 
a Law Minister. 
Outside the Cabinet, the 
principal law officers of the government of India are the Attormmey 
General and the Solicitor General, both of whom are appointed by the 
President. 
Each of the state governments has its own advocate general. The state 
governments usually have their own legal remembrancers and professional 
lawyers as government advocates and assistant advocates.

priated for the expenses of promoting or maintaining any particular 
religious denomination is invalid.1%

d. Loans. 
Although there is no restriction on public borrowing by the 
states, except that prior approval is required when a state is in debt to 
the central government,!** the states are accustomed to borrow from the 
central government, which thereby acquires considerable control over 
state borrowing and expenditure. The states also deposit with the central 
government certain state and local funds which are in effect loans to the 
central government and available to it for general purposes. 
The total amount of outstanding loans from the central government to 
the states has increased greatly in recent years. 
From Rs 43.97 crores 
on 15 August 1947, the amount grew to Rs 195.41 crores on 31 March 
1951 and to Rs 900 crores on 31 March 1956.1°° 
The rate of annual 
borrowing by the states from the central government has also increased 
sharply until 1958-1959, and the amount budgeted for 1959-1960, as 
shown in Table 10, is considerably higher than the final figure for 1957- 
1958, although lower than that for 1958-1959. 
Irrigation and river 
programs, agricultural development, rehabilitation, community develop- 
ment, and industrial housing are among the purposes for which loans are 
currently being made.

of Tax Law 
1/5.1 
In General 
Each central or state tax is levied by a basic act, identified by title 
and year, and sometimes also by number, which establishes the basis 
of the tax, who is to pay it, when it is to become payable, when and how 
it is to be collected, and other details of the taxing machinery. Most 
acts contain general and special provisions for the making of rules by the

provisions have the force of law. Amendments made from time to time 
become parts of the basic act. 
A major revision may be made by repeal 
of the basic act and substitution of a new one. 
The Indian Independence Act,!“° the Constitution,14! and the States 
Reorganization Act of 1956 1*? each provided for the preservation of the 
law in force at its effective date, subject to such adaptation orders issued 
by the central executive as was necessary to ensure conformity with it. 
Hence, none of these constitutional changes, in the absence of subsequent 
legislation under the new distribution of legislative power, affected the 
application, territorial extent, or administration of existing tax measures. 
1/5.2 
Central Acts and Regulations 
Central legislation in force consists of all unrepealed acts of the 
Indian Parliament (1/6.2) and its predecessors, together with the rules 
and notifications issued under authority of such acts (1/6.3). 
Central 
tax legislation was gradually extended to the former native Indian States 
after their accession to federation with the rest of India (1/1.2).14% 
Circulars issued by the Central Board of Revenue, as distinct from 
statutory notifications, are explanatory only and have no legal effect. 
“Press notes,” which are sometimes issued by the Ministry of Information 
or state government information departments, serve merely to explain 
legislation or administrative procedure to the general public, and are 
also without legal effect. 
However, both circulars and press notes are 
reliable indications of official policy. 
1/5.3 
State Acts and Regulations 
The legislation of a state consists of the unrepealed acts of its legis- 
lature and the predecessors of its legislature, together with rules and 
notifications issued under authority of such acts. 
After the accession and merger of the former Indian States (1/1.1), 
all the states extended their tax laws to territories which were merged 
with them. 
It is expected that ultimately each state as reconstituted in 
1956 will extend its tax laws throughout the territory added to it in the 
reorganization. 
This 
process 
will 
involve 
extensive 
administrative 
changes, however, and in the meantime the revenue system and tax laws 
now in force in a particular place may be those of the state to which it 
belonged before 1956 and not those of the state to which it was trans- 
ferred (2/1.1, 16/1.1).

1/5.4 
Judicial Decisions 
Decisions of the Supreme Court are binding on all other courts in 
India.144 
Decisions of a High Court are binding within the jurisdiction 
of the court; they may be cited by other High Courts but do not bind 
them. 
Under the Government of India Act of 1935, the law declared by the 
Federal Court and the law declared by a judgment of the British Privy 
Council was binding on all courts in British India.1° 
Decisions of these 
courts prior to the effective date of the Constitution are binding on all 
Indian courts except the Supreme Court, and decisions of other Indian 
courts prior to the effective date of the Constitution continue to function 
as precedents, as do decisions of the courts in Burma and Pakistan ren- 
dered when those territories were parts of India. 
In the absence of 
subsequent legislation affecting its subject matter, the territorial effect of 
a decision was not modified by the States Reorganization Act of 1956. 
While law declared by the Privy Council after the commencement of 
the Constitution is not binding in India, British and other Commonwealth 
cases are still regarded as persuasive, and some of them are reprinted in 
supplements to the unofficial collections of income tax and sales tax cases. 
1/5.5 
Administrative Decisions 
The decisions of administrative authorities of the central government, 
including the Central Board of Revenue and the Appellate Tribunal, are 
not published. Whether they would be considered binding on the govern- 
ment, assuming the taxpayer had access to them, is doubtful. 
Decisions 
of some of the sales tax appellate tribunals in the states are published 
officially and are used as authorities. 
There are no provisions for obtain- 
ing advance rulings from tax authorities.

1/6.1

The central government department primarily concerned with finan- 
cial and economic policy is the Ministry of Finance, which is in charge 
of a Cabinet Minister. 
All tax legislation is introduced and explained 
in Parliament by the Finance Minister. 
In 1953 the government appointed a Taxation Enquiry Commission to 
examine the structure and functioning of central, state, and local taxation 
as related to the economic and social objectives of the country, and to 
make recommendations for modification of the existing tax system and 
for the addition of new methods of taxation.

In general, legislation in the Indian Parliament originates with the 
government and may be introduced in either house of Parliament. 
All 
bills are published in the Gazette of India before they are introduced. 
A bill passed by Parliament becomes law on receiving the assent of the 
President, and is again published in the Gazette of India in its final form 
as an act of Parliament. 
The enactment of bills dealing with taxation, borrowing, appropria- 
tions, and other financial matters is subject to a number of restrictions.

financial matters is known as a “money bill”; 1° such a bill cannot be 
introduced in the Council of States and cannot be amended or vetoed 
by the Council of States.!"°

People transmits it to the Council of States, which may return it to the 
House with recommendations; but the House is under no obligation to

This statement is supported by the Finance Minister

The taxing proposals of the budget are embodied in the Finance Bill,

1/7. 
Synopsis of the Tax System 
1/7.1 
In General 
Because of the close integration of central and state finances, some 
important trends in central and state revenues as a whole will be discussed 
briefly in this section. 
The taxes imposed by the central government 
and the taxes imposed by the states, with recent collection figures for 
each, are listed in 1/7.2 and 1/7.3 respectively. 
During the nineteenth century, land revenue, as developed by the 
British from the indigenous systems in each province, was the principal 
source of revenue in British India. When the British first began to make 
use of the land revenue system, it placed a heavy burden on agricultural 
production; but because of the rigidity of the tax, its revenues did not 
increase in proportion to the increases in agricultural production and 
in prices which took place in the latter part of the century.'6' 
The 
government therefore turned to customs duties, excise taxes, and the 
income tax for increased revenue. 
During the first four decades of the 
twentieth century, customs duties were the principal source of the com- 
bined revenues of the central, state, and local governments, accounting 
in 1938-1939 for about 34% of total tax revenue as against 8% for income 
taxes.16? 
Jn 1944-1945, as a result of World War II, the share of income 
taxes in a greatly increased total tax revenue rose to 26%, while that of 
customs fell to 5%.1®° 
Although in 1953-1954 the proceeds of income 
taxes and customs were about equal (19% of combined central, state, 
and local tax revenues), income taxes now account for a somewhat 
higher proportion than customs. 
Revenues from excise duties, however, 
have increased even more rapidly and now account for a higher propor- 
tion of total tax revenues than do income taxes. 
The tax system of India appropriates at present something less than 
10% of national income. 
Part of the explanation for this fact is that a 
very small proportion of the total population of the country, which now

This small tax base is in turn partly the result of the absence

The burden already borne by agriculture under the land

Because of the great

and in the native Indian States, the recent land tenure reforms are only 
the first steps toward effective taxation of agricultural production.1® 
1/7.2 
Central Government Taxes 
a. TAXES IMPOSED. 
The various taxes imposed by the central govern- 
ment are summarized in the paragraphs which follow. 
1. Income tax. 
Persons other than corporations are subject to a graduated 
income tax and a graduated supertax; corporations are subject to a flat 
rate income tax, and also to a flat rate supertax known as the “corpora- 
tion tax.” 
Various special rates of supertax are applied to dividends 
received by a corporation from 
a subsidiary and to all income of 
corporations with income of not more than Rs 25,000; to income of 
foreign corporations which have not made prescribed arrangements for 
the deduction of tax from dividends; to income of the government- 
owned life insurance corporation; and to income of cooperative societies. 
Corporations are subject to an additional supertax on stock dividends 
and capitalization of earnings. 
A closely held corporation which fails 
to distribute a specified percentage of profits is also subject to an 
additional supertax. 
The central government distributes to the states 
60% of the proceeds of the income tax, not including the corporation 
tax. 
The tax is summarized in Chapter 2 and considered in detail in 
Chapters 5 through 13. 
2. Net wealth tax. 
<A tax is levied at graduated rates on the net wealth 
of individuals above Rs 200,000 and of Hindu undivided families above 
Rs 400,000. 
The net wealth of corporations above Rs 500,000 is at 
present taxed at a flat rate. 
Banks, insurance companies, shipping 
corporations, 
certain nonprofit corporations, and certain corporations 
established to finance industrial enterprises in India are exempt. 
New 
corporations organized to carry on industrial undertakings in India are

exempt for the first five years. 
However, it is expected that from 
1 April 1960 corporations will be exempted from the tax entirely. 
The 
tax is described in Chapter 14. 
3. Expenditure tax. 
A steeply graduated tax is levied on the personal 
expenditure, above standard allowances, of individuals and their de- 
pendents, and of Hindu undivided families. 
The maximum 
rate 
is 
100%. The tax is described in Chapter 15. 
4, Estate duty. 
A graduated tax is levied on the principal value, above 
standard allowances, of all property of an individual which passes or is 
deemed to pass at death (3/5). 
The proceeds of the tax are appor- 
- 
tioned among the states (1/4.4a). 
5. Gift tax. 
A tax is levied, at rates which for the most part correspond 
to those of the estate duty, on gifts of real property or movables above 
a standard allowance 
(3/6). 
6. Central sales tax. 
A tax is imposed, at rates determined in accordance 
with a central act, on sales of goods in interstate trade (16/1.3). 
The 
tax is intended to supplement the state sales taxes and at the same 
time to regulate the taxation of interstate sales in order to prevent an 
undue burden on interstate commerce. 
The states retain the proceeds, 
which they collect on behalf of the central government. 
The central 
act determines which dealers are liable to tax, determines what con- 
stitutes a taxable sale, and imposes limits on the rates of tax. 
The sales 
tax law of the state in which the movement in interstate trade com- 
mences determines which goods are taxable, determines the rates of tax, 
within the limits set by the central act, and governs the administration 
of the tax. 
7. Union excise duty. 
A tax is imposed at specific rates on a variety of 
manufactured commodities, on tobacco, and on coffee. 
Tires, woolen 
fabrics, footwear and electric batteries and parts are taxed at ad valorem 
rates. 
Liability for taxes on manufactured goods is incurred when the 
process of manufacture is completed, and the tax becomes payable when 
the goods leave the factory or warehouse. 
Liability to the taxes on 
tobacco and coffee is incurred when the goods have been cured and are 
ready for sale, and the taxes become payable either on the expiration 
of a prescribed period or when the goods are removed from licensed 
warehouses. 
Exported goods 
are 
in general exempt. 
The central 
government distributes 25% of the proceeds of the excise duty among 
the states. 
The tax is described in Chapter 17. 
8. Miscellaneous central excise taxes. 
Taxes are levied on a number of 
designated goods, principally to defray the costs of government activities 
undertaken on behalf of the industries producing them (17/4.4). 
Com- 
modities subject to such taxes include cotton, certain fabrics, vegetable 
oils, salt, coal and coke, coffee, rubber, and copra. A central excise tax 
has been imposed on medicinal and toilet preparations 
containing 
alcohol or narcotics, but the proceeds are collected and retained by 
the states. 
Additional excise duties on certain commodities 
of im- 
portance in interstate trade are collected by the central government but 
distributed among the states. 
9. Stamp duties. 
Stamp duties are levied on financial documents at rates 
prescribed by the central government, and on other documents at rates 
prescribed by the states (4/3). 
The proceeds are collected and retained 
by the states,

1/7.3 
State and Local Taxes 
a. TAXES IMPOSED. 
Of the various taxes which states and local authori- 
ties are empowered to levy, land revenue and sales taxes are the most 
important. 
Revenue systems and their administration differ considerably 
from state to state; and as a result of the reorganization of the states in 
1956, variations within the states themselves may still be found (1/5.3). 
The principal state taxes in force!" are summarized in the succeeding 
paragraphs. 
1. Land revenue. 
In all the states taxes are imposed on the value of land 
(3/2). 
The methods of valuation and the rates vary widely from state 
to state, and sometimes within the states, depending on the system of 
land tenure, the indigenous revenue system, and the modifications made 
by British officers to suit local circumstances. 
In most states special 
provision is made, either by law or by executive order, for the assess- 
ment of nonagricultural land on a different basis from the assessment 
of agricultural land. 
Further distinction is sometimes made between 
rural and urban residential land; and urban residential land may be 
further classified according to the incomes of the occupants. 
Urban 
commercial land may be assessed on still a different basis. 
2. Irrigation and betterment charges. 
In most agricultural areas, charges

are made by the states for irrigation (3/2.1). 
In some states, these 
charges are payable by cultivators in return for the service of irrigation; 
in others, the charges are payable by owners in consideration of the in- 
crease of the value of the land. 
. Sales and purchase taxes. 
Every state except Jammu and Kashmir im- 
poses a tax on sales or purchases of goods which take place within its 
borders. 
The taxes are collected from registered dealers whose annual 
gross receipts exceed prescribed limits, and are based on varying per- 
centages of gross receipts. 
The transactions on which the taxes are im- 
posed, taxable goods, and rates differ widely from state to state. There 
are also special taxes on the sale of gasoline or “motor spirit.” 
These 
taxes are described in Chapter 16. 
. Excise duties. 
Excise taxes on alcoholic beverages and narcotics are 
levied in all the states (17/4.5). 
In some states, the yield from these 
taxes has been reduced in recent years as a result of the implementa- 
tion of the national policy of prohibition. 
. Taxes on motor vehicles. 
Motor vehicles are subject to taxes based on 
loaded weight, unloaded weight, or seating capacity. 
The proceeds of 
these taxes are used for the development and maintenance of state 
roads. 
. Entertainment taxes. 
Taxes are levied on the price of admissions to 
various types of entertainment. 
In some states, the power to levy these 
taxes has been delegated to the local authorities. 
. Electricity duties. 
Several states levy taxes on the consumption of elec- 
tricity, although some restrict the tax to domestic consumption. 
The 
bases and rates of tax differ from state to state. 
. Miscellaneous fees and duties. 
Other taxes levied by the states are 
stamp duties and court fees, fees for registration of documents, and 
taxes on betting. 
Under the Constitution, the internal customs duties 
levied by some of the former native Indian States were permitted to re- 
main in effect for a limited time, but these taxes were abolished in 
1955.168 
The taxes listed below are now levied exclusively by local authorities 
(1/1.5) in most of the states in which they are used.1°°

An analysis of the importance of state tax revenues, including 
the states’ share of taxes collected by the central government, and in- 
cluding taxes which are levied by the central government but collected

In 1951-1952, the total ordinary revenue of local bodies other than 
panchayats was Rs 86.78 crores, of which total tax revenue accounted for 
Rs 48.73 crores, or 56.1%. 
The balance of total ordinary revenue con- 
sisted of government grants (20.5%), receipts from local enterprises 
(1.7% ), and miscellaneous receipts (21.7% ). The most important source 
of tax revenue in the municipalities was the property tax (3/3), which

accounting for 9.3% of total local tax and nontax revenues. 
Octroi and 
terminal taxes accounted for 10.1% of total local tax and nontax revenue, 
and profession taxes for less than 1%.17° 
1/8. 
Tax Administration 
1/8.1 
In General 
The agency primarily responsible for the development of central tax 
policy and for the administration of the central taxes is the Department 
of Revenue in the Ministry of Finance. 
The Department consists of a 
Secretary, four Joint Secretaries, and a number of Deputy Secretaries and 
Under Secretaries, and exercises the functions assigned to the Central 
Government under the various tax acts. 
For example, it makes all ap- 
pointments of income tax authorities except in the lower ranks (1/8.3- 
1/8.6), makes the rules for the central excise tax (17/7.1) and the central 
sales tax (16/7.1), and approves the rules made by the Central Board of 
Revenue for the income tax (1/8.2). 
However, most of the functions of 
supervising the administration of the central taxes and of making execu- 
tive decisions relating to those taxes have been assigned under the 
various tax acts to the Central Board of Revenue (1/8.2). 
Although the 
Board is a separate statutory body, its Chairman and members are 
the Secretary and Joint Secretaries of the Department of Revenue, and the 
Deputy Secretaries and Under Secretaries of the Department serve as 
Secretaries and Under Secretaries of the Board. 
Under the direction and control of the Board are Commissioners of 
Income-tax and other administrative officers responsible for the adminis- 
tration of the income tax in various parts of India. 
Each of these officers 
also performs the functions in the administration of the wealth, expendi- 
ture, and gift taxes corresponding to those he performs in the administra- 
tion of the income tax (1/8.3-1/8.6). 
The Central Board of Revenue

administers the central excise tax through Collectors of Central Excise

and the customs duties through Collectors: of Customs (4/5.4). 
The 
central sales tax (16/7.1), the central stamp duty (4/3.1), and the 
central excise tax on medicinal alcohol and narcotics (17/4.4) are ad- 
ministered by the states. 
Although the taxes on income, net wealth, expenditure, and gifts are 
administered by the same officers and, together with the estate duty, are 
regarded as forming a unitary system, they are reported and assessed 
by means of separate returns. 
When Nicholas Kaldor of Cambridge 
University proposed the taxation of net wealth, expenditure, gifts, and 
capital gains, he also recommended that the information pertinent to 
determining a taxpayer's liability under each of these taxes be reported 
and reconciled in a single comprehensive return.!7* 
The form of return 
proposed by Kaldor would reconcile opening and closing net wealth 
without reference to income or expenditure, balance accruals and dis- 
posals, and derive expenditure by adjustments to taxable income.!72_ 
The 
separate returns now employed could be used to reconcile a taxpayer’s 
accounts for purposes of the various taxes, provided certain adjustments 
were made in the method proposed by Kaldor.‘ 
For checking in- 
formation reported by different taxpayers, Kaldor also proposed the 
adoption in India of a comprehensive automatic system, similar to that 
used in Sweden, for reporting property transactions and cash pay- 
ments.1“# 
Administrative problems of the income tax, the wealth tax, and other 
direct taxes have recently been the subject of a study by a Direct Taxes 
Enquiry Committee, which made a report to the government in Novem- 
ber 1959.15

under the Central Board of Revenue Act of 1924 to perform functions 
assigned to it by the Central Government or by other laws. 
Its Chairman 
and four members are appointed by the President and serve also as 
_ Secretary and Joint Secretaries in the Department of Revenue (1/8.1).

The 
Directors of Inspection (1/8.4) are attached to the Board. 
Under section 5 of the Income-tax Act, the rules, orders, instructions, 
and directions of the Board are binding on all officers employed in the 
administration of the tax, but the Board cannot interfere with the dis- 
cretion of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner in the exercise of his 
appellate functions. 
The Board’s powers in the administration of the 
wealth, gift, estate, and expenditure taxes are similar. 
Decisions on 
certain subjects under the Income-tax Act, such as whether an asso- 
ciation is to be taxed as a corporation (5/2.2), the prescription of a 
particular base year for a taxpayer or class of taxpayers (6/3.2), and in 
some cases, approval of the issuance of notice to file a return for an 
additional assessment (13/5.1), are reserved to the Board. 
Subject to 
the control of the Central Government (1/8.1), the Board also exercises 
the power to make rules 
(1/5.2, 1/6.3) under the Income-tax Act 
(§ 59(1) ); it also has the basic rule-making powers for the wealth, expen- 
diture, gift, and estate taxes, and the customs duties. 
Apart from its broad powers to direct the assessment of all the central 
taxes, the Board does not serve as a formal appellate authority except for 
the customs duties (4/5.4) and the central excise tax (17/7.6). 
1/8.3 
Commissioners of Income-tax 
The Commissioners of Income-tax, who are appointed by the Central 
Government (1/8.1), are in charge of income tax administration either 
for particular areas 
or for certain classes of taxpayers, categories of 
income, or types of cases ($5(2)). 
The jurisdiction of each Commis- 
sioner is determined by the Central Board of Revenue; at present, there 
are 16 Commissioners responsible for specified territories and 2 respon- 
sible for cases specially assigned. 
The Commissioners direct the work 
of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioners and the Income-tax Officers; 
and a Commissioner of Income-tax may assume generally or for particular 
cases the functions of an Appellate Assistant Commissioner (§ 5(5)). 
A Commissioner may issue instructions to any Income-tax Officer under 
him for the conduct of any assessment or inquiry, and has the same 
investigatory powers as an Income-tax Officer ($ 5(7B) ). 
The Central Board of Revenue is authorized to appoint Commissioners 
of Wealth-tax, Commissioners of Expenditure-tax, and Commissioners of 
Gift-tax; in practice, the functions of each of these officers have been 
assigned by notification to the Commissioners of Income-tax, 
‘

revenue (13/2.5), to rectify certain mistakes (18/4.6), to revise in favor 
of the taxpayer an order of an Income-tax Officer or an Appellate As-

1/8.4 
Directors of Inspection and Inspecting Assistant Commissioners of 
Income-tax 
The basic work of the assessment of income by the Income-tax Officers 
(1/8.5) 
is subject to control and inspection by Inspecting Assistant 
Commissioners (§5(7B)), who are appointed by the Central Govern- 
ment 
(§5(3))(1/8.1) 
and are under the general direction of the 
Commissioners of Income-tax (§§$5(5), 5(7)). 
The work of the In- 
specting Assistant Commissioners is in turn subject to examination and 
control by Directors of Inspection (§ 5(7)), who are appointed by the 
Central Government to perform, under the control of the Central Board 
of Revenue, such functions in income tax administration as the Central 
Government may assign to them ($5(1A)). 
Inspecting Assistant Com- 
missioners of Income-tax have generally been designated by the Central 
Board of Revenue to serve in a similar capacity under the wealth, ex- 
penditure, and gift taxes. 
In 1959 there were 3 Directors of Inspection 
and 67 Inspecting Assistant Commissioners. 
The principal function of an Inspecting Assistant Commissioner is to 
make periodical inspections of the work of the Income-tax Officers under 
his jurisdiction and ensure that the assessments are properly made. 
His 
consent is required for the imposition of certain penalties and for the 
~ initiation of certain prosecutions (13/7.1), and also for the imposition 
of additional supertax on the undistributed profits of a closely held 
corporation (12/2.7). 
The Directors of Inspection and the Inspecting 
Assistant Commissioners have the same powers as the Income-tax Officers 
in making inquiries under the Income-tax Act (13/2) and may issue 
instructions for the guidance of Income-tax Officers under their juris- 
diction in making assessments and inquiries (§ 5(7B) ). 
1/8.5 
 Income-tax Officers and Inspectors of Income-tax 
There are two classes of Income-tax Officers, appointed by the Central 
Government and by the Commissioners of Income-tax, respectively. 
Both 
classes perform the same functions, but as a rule those appointed by the 
Central Government are assigned the more important assessment wards.

The number of Income-tax Officers is determined by the Central Gov- 
ernment (§5(3)); in 1959, there were approximately 1,300. 
The field 
of responsibility of an Income-tax Officer, determined by the Commis- 
sioner of Income-tax to whom he is responsible (§ 5(5) ), usually covers 
a certain geographical area; but the Central Board of Revenue may by 
notification authorize Commissioners to assign Income-tax Officers to 
certain classes of taxpayers or certain classes of income (§5(6)). 
In 
making the assessment and conducting inquiries, an Income-tax Officer 
is subordinate to the Director of Inspection, the Commissioner of Income- 
tax, and the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner 
(§§5(7), 5(7B)). 
Income-tax Officers are ex officio Wealth-tax Officers, Expenditure-tax 
Officers, and Gift-tax Officers. 
An Income-tax Officer has the basic responsibility for assessing the 
income of taxpayers within his jurisdiction. 
His duties include issuing 
notices to file returns (13/1.1), examining returns and making assess- 
ments (13/1.3, 13/2), issuing notices requiring advance payment and 
notices of demand for payment of tax (13/1.4), issuing tax clearance 
certificates to persons leaving India (13/1.5), and initiating most types of 
proceedings for collection of delinquent taxes (13/1.6). 
An Income-tax 
Officer may modify an assessment in case of a mistake apparent from the 
record (13/2.4), and in some cases may be required to revise a “best 
judgment” assessment (13/4.2). 
He is entitled to be heard in an appeal 
by the taxpayer to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner (13/4.3), and 
upon direction from the Commissioner of Income-tax may appeal to the 
Appellate Tribunal an order issued by the Appellate Assistant Com- 
missioner (18/4.4). 
Claims for refunds are made to the Income-tax 
Officer (13/5.2). 
His powers in connection with interest, penalties, and 
prosecutions are discussed at 13/7. 
To supplement information acquired by direct investigation and evi- 
dence obtained from taxpayers themselves (13/2), the Income-tax Officer 
is assisted by a local staff of Inspectors of Income-tax appointed by the 
Commissioner of Income-tax (§§5(3), 5(5A)). The principal function 
of these officials, of whom there were about 1,000 in 1959, is to collect 
information about income-producing activities within the Income-tax 
Officer’s jurisdiction by compiling lists of houses, businesses, court cases, 
government contracts, and other data available from public sources. 
Under the control of each Commissioner of Income-tax there is also an 
Investigation Branch, consisting of similar Inspectors, whose function is 
to collect information on important transactions, price changes, con 
struction, purchases of property, contracts, new businesses, and other 
pertinent matters. 
This information is distributed to the Income-tax 
Officers concerned or sent to a Collation Branch at Madras for distribu- 
tion to Income-tax Officers throughout India.

1/8.6 
Taxpayer Remedies. 
Each taxing act prescribes administrative procedures for the considera- 
tion of a taxpayer's objections to his assessment. 
The Income-tax Act 
permits the modification or revision of income tax assessments at various 
points in the assessing procedure (13/1, 13/2). 
In addition, the Act 
provides for appeals by the taxpayer to Appellate Assistant Commis- 
sioners (13/4.3), for further appeals to an Appellate Tribunal (13/4.4), 
and for references to the High Courts (1/1.4c) of questions of law aris- 
ing out of orders of the Appellate Tribunal (13/4.7). 
A judgment of a 
High Court may be appealed to the Supreme Court (1/1.3c) if the High 
Court certifies the case for appeal or if the Supreme Court grants special 
leave to appeal (13/4.7). 
The Appellate Assistant Commissioners and 
the Appellate Tribunal serve also as appellate authorities, under similar 
procedures, for the wealth, expenditure, and gift taxes. 
Appeals under 
the estate tax are taken to Appellate Controllers and thence to the 
Appellate Tribunal (3/5.9e). 
Appellate Assistant Commissioners of Income-tax are appointed by the 
Central Government (§ 5(3) )(1/8.1). Although they are under the ad- 
ministrative control of the Central Board of Revenue (§ 5(4) ), the Board 
may not interfere with their discretion in the exercise of their appellate 
functions (§5(8)). 
A Commissioner of Income-tax may by general or 
special order assume the powers of an Appellate Assistant Commissioner 
with respect to any case or class of cases (§ 5(5) ). 
The Appellate Tribunal is a quasi-judicial body independent of the 
Central Board of Revenue and under the administrative control of the 
Ministry of Law. 
It is appointed by the Central Government (1/8.1) 
and consists of judicial members and accountant members (§ 5A). 
Its 
proceedings are governed by the Appellate Tribunal Rules of 1946. 
The Tribunal has several branches sitting in various parts of India. 
The Central Board of Revenue itself has no appellate functions under 
~ the income, wealth, expenditure, and gift taxes, but it is the principal 
appellate authority for the central excise tax (17/7.6), and for customs 
duties (4/5.4). 
The Central Government is the highest appellate au- 
thority for customs duties and for the central excise tax. 
The Income-tax Act (13/4.1) and the Wealth-tax, Expenditure-tax, 
Estate Duty, and Gift-tax Acts contain bars of jurisdiction which preclude 
the bringing of any suits in the courts to “set aside or modify any assess- 
ment” under any of those Acts. 
Such a provision has been held to bar 
a suit brought under the general jurisdiction of the civil courts for a 
refund of tax on the ground that assessment was made pursuant to an 
unconstitutional provision of law.!*° 
Such a provision does not bar a

The Constitution provides that no tax may be levied or collected except

Relief from unlawful imposition or collection of

general power to issue writs in the nature of mandamus, prohibition, quo

1/8.8 
Transfer of Cases and Changes of Personnel 
A case may be transferred by a Commissioner of Income-tax from one 
Income-tax Officer under his jurisdiction to another, or by the Central 
Board of Revenue from any Income-tax Officer to another, without en- 
tailing the reissue of any notice issued prior to the transfer (§ 5(7A) ). 
If any income tax authority having jurisdiction over a case is succeeded 
by another, the succeeding authority may continue any proceeding from 
the stage at which it was left by his predecessor unless the taxpayer 
demands a reopening of any part of the previous proceeding (§ 5(7C)). 
Time taken in reopening any part of the proceeding after a succession 
is excluded in the computation of the limitation period for assessment 
(13/6.1). 
1/8.9 
Disclosure of Information by Tax Authorities 
Returns, accounts, documents, or other evidence furnished in the course 
of income tax proceedings, and records of assessment and recovery pro- 
“ceedings, must be treated as confidential; and, with certain exceptions, 
a court cannot compel a public servant to disclose information from these 
sources (§§ 54(1), 54(3)). A public servant who discloses such informa-

_ be prosecuted and punished by imprisonment or a fine (§§ 54(2), 54(5) ).

tax proceedings, to certain proceedings involving the government, or to 
certain other proceedings involving the public interest (§ 54(3)).

2/1. 
Introduction 
2/1.1 
History of the Income Tax 
Although license taxes based on the profits of trades and professions 
have been known in India since before the advent of the British, the 
history of modern income taxation in India dates from 1860, when a 
schedular income tax patterned after the United Kingdom tax was intro- 
duced in an effort to end the budgetary deficits which followed the 
Sepoy Mutiny of 1857. 
The tax had not been intended to be permanent, 
and was repealed in 1865. 
Since budgetary deficits continued, the gov- 
ernment in 1867 resorted to a license tax on persons exercising trades or 
professions; the tax was in the form of a fixed fee determined by the 
taxpayer's income bracket, or, in the case of a corporation, by its paid-up 
capital. 
This was replaced in 1868 by a similar tax called a “certificate 
tax.” 
These measures did not yield the needed revenue, however, and 
the government again resorted to a general income tax from 1869 to 1873. 
The Indian Income-tax Act of 1886 was a general income tax which 
replaced the license taxes which had been levied on trades by some of 
the provinces beginning in 1878. 
The tax was levied as a percentage 
of salaries, interest on securities, profits of corporations, and other income 
if the other income exceeded Rs 2,000; if other income did not exceed 
Rs 2,000, the taxpayer was subject to a license tax in the form of a fee 
determined by his income bracket. 
This act continued in effect until 
superseded by the Indian Income-tax Act of 1918, which consolidated a 
number of wartime amendments. 
A graduated supertax on income over 
Rs 50,000 and on the undistributed profits of corporations and other 
entities had been introduced by the Super-tax Act of 1917, and con- 
tinued in effect with modifications by the Super-tax Act of 1920. 
The 
income tax and the supertax are now levied under a single act, the Indian 
Income-tax Act of 1922, as amended by various Finance Acts and Income- 
tax (Amendment) Acts. 
Capital gains were first subject to tax from 
31 March 1946 to 1 April 1948, and have been subject to tax since 
1 April 1956. 
Although throughout the history of the income tax, income below 
certain limits has been taxed at special rates, a graduated scale of income 
tax rates was not introduced until 1916. 
Since 1922, the rates of in- 
come tax and supertax have been prescribed in the annual Finance Acts 
instead of in the basic enactment. 
Administration of the tax was not 
centralized until 1922. 
Returns have been required from corporations 
since 1886, but until 1918 were required of other taxpayers only at the 
option of the local administration. 
Under the 1860, 1869, and 1886 Acts, 
an assessment of the taxpayer’s income in one year could be accepted for 
later years by prearrangement with the authorities. 
Tax was withheld

from salaries under the Act of 1869. 
Although the Act of 1886 required 
withholding of tax from public salaries and interest on securities, with- 
holding from private salaries was 
optional with the administrative 
authorities until 1918. 
Agricultural income was subject to the income taxes levied in 1860 
and 1869, but was exempted from tax under the Act of 1886 because 
agricultural producers were felt to be contributing their share toward 
the revenue in the form of land cesses which had been levied during the 
eighteen eighties. 
The Government of India Act of 1935 empowered 
the provinces to levy taxes on agricultural income; the states have re- 
tained this power under the Constitution, which also removes 
agri- 
cultural income from the tax jurisdiction of the central government. 
Several states now levy some form of agricultural income tax.1 
Except 
for a limited power to tax professions, trades, and employments (1/4.3), 
the states have no power to tax income other than agricultural income. 
An excess profits tax was levied during World War I. 
It was revived 
during World War II by the Excess Profits Tax Act of 1940, under which 
profits exceeding those of a standard prewar period were taxed at a 
flat rate. 
The Excess Profits Tax Act was repealed in 1946, but the 
Business Profits Tax Act of 1947 in effect continued the levy on excess 
profits, although it taxed the entire profits of a business at a lower flat 
rate. 
The Business Profits Tax Act remained in force until 31 March 
1949. 
From that date until the present, neither excess profits tax nor 
business profits tax has been levied. 
The only central income tax now in 
force is that levied under the Indian Income-tax Act of 1922. 
2/1.2 
Taxes Imposed 
The income of an individual is subject to two separate taxes: the 
income tax and the supertax (6/1.1). 
Both income tax (12/1.3a) and 
supertax (12/1.6) are levied at graduated rates; supertax becomes pay- 
able in the top income tax rate bracket and in effect adds a tax at more 
steeply graduated rates to the income tax computed at the maximum 
rate. 
The principal distinction between these two taxes is that certain 
exemptions or deductions are available for purposes of the one tax but 
not for purposes of the other (6/1.4, 6/1.5). 
There is no differentiation 
in the rate of tax applicable to different classes of income, although 
capital gains are, in effect, taxed at reduced rates as a result of a special 
provision (12/1.3c).

The rate of income tax is the same for all classes of corporations and for 
all categories of income (12/2.1).

on its dividends in excess of prescribed percentages of paid-up capital, 
and also to a special supertax on stock dividends and capitalization of 
earnings. 
A closely held corporation (“company in which the public 
are not substantially interested”) which fails to pay a dividend equal to 
a specified statutory percentage of profits is also subject to an additional 
flat rate supertax on its undistributed profits (12/2.7). 
2/1.3 
Tax Jurisdiction 
A resident taxpayer is subject to tax on his entire income regardless of 
geographical source (5/1.1). 
There is no exemption for any part of 
foreign income, except that a taxpayer who is resident but not ordinarily 
resident in India (5/1.2) is not taxable on income of certain types if it 
is neither received in nor brought into India (11/2.1). 
A nonresident is taxable only on income received in or accruing in 
India or deemed to be received in or to accrue in India (11/3.1). 
2/2. 
Income Tax Concepts 
2/2.1 
Income 
Income is divided into six “heads” or categories: income from salaries, 
interest on securities, income from property, profits and gains from a 
business, profession, or vocation, income from other sources, and capital 
gains (6/1.2). 
The function of this division is merely to permit the 
application of rules relevant to each particular type. 
Income of the sev- 
eral categories is lumped together, and tax thereon is assessed on a 
global basis. 
The rates of income tax and supertax are determined by reference to 
the taxpayer's “total income,” which is his net income under all categories,


<!-- page 113 of 600 -->

India 
2/2.2 
wa 
TAXES 
ON 
INCOME 
exclusive of certain exemptions (6/1.1). 
Income tax and supertax pay- 
able on total income at the applicable rates, however, is then reduced by 
those proportions of each which are attributable to certain other exemp- 
tions and certain deductions. 
Thus, some exemptions and deductions 
are made at the marginal rate, and these affect the rate of tax on the 
balance of total income; other exemptions and deductions are made at 
the average rate, and these reduce the proportion of total income which 
is subject to tax but do not affect the rates of tax applicable to the balance 
of total income. 
A nonresident may elect to compute the tax payable on his total income 
at the average rate applicable to his “total world income.” 
If he does 
not make this election, he is taxed on his Indian income at prescribed 
rates, higher than those applicable to residents, irrespective of the amount 
of his total world income (11/3.5). 
In general, total income includes any receipt or benefit in money, or 
capable of being turned into money, which is neither a capital receipt 
nor a receipt specifically exempted by law (6/1.1). 
Certain receipts 
are specifically included in total income, such as certain capital gains, as 
noted below, and certain distributions received by a shareholder from 
a corporation which are artificially treated and taxed as dividend income. 
On the other hand, certain receipts, such as gifts, legacies, and casual 
receipts, are excluded from total income as not within the ordinary con- 
cept of income (6/1.3). 
Apart from special treatment of intercorporate 
dividends (10/6.3) and the personal allowances granted to individuals 
" (12/1.2a), there are no significant differences between corporations and 
individuals in the determination of income. 
Capital gains arising from the sale, exchange, relinquishment, or trans- 
fer of capital assets are subject to tax at a reduced effective rate (9/8). 
Profit arising from the sale of property acquired for the purpose of profit 
making is taxed not as capital gains but as business income, on the 
_ ground that such a sale is not of a capital asset but of stock in trade 
(9/8.2). 
2/2.2 
Deductions 
Noncapital losses and expenditures incurred 
in producing taxable 
income are deductible in arriving at total income provided they are not 
of a private or domestic nature (6/1.5). 
Capital expenditures for busi- 
ness assets are deductible from business income in accordance with the 
depreciation rules (7/3). 
Deductible business expenses may be more 
remotely connected to the production of income than expenses deductible 
from nonbusiness income (6/1.5a, 7/2). 
Limited deductions from total income are permitted for charitable 
donations and for expenditures for life insurance, annuities, and em-

ployee benefits 
(6/1.5).

so deductible 
are

2/2.3 
Taxable Year 
Tax is levied for the “assessment year” on income derived during the 
“previous year” (6/3.1). 
The assessment year, herein referred to as 
the tax year, is the government financial year beginning 1 April of each 
calendar year and ending 31 March of the succeeding calendar year. 
The previous year, herein referred to as the base year, is the financial 
year immediately preceding the tax year. 
In lieu of the normal base 
year, any taxpayer may, at his option, adopt as his base year any other 
accounting period ending within the normal base year. 
If accounts are 
not kept for an accounting period different from the normal financial 
year, the normal base year must be used for computing taxable profits. 
Within the limits of the foregoing rules, a separate base year may be 
adopted for each separate income source, and total income for the tax 
year is the sum of the incomes for the several base years. 
2/3. 
Classes of Taxpayers 
2/3.1 
Individuals 
An individual, whether resident 
or nonresident, 
is subject to the 
income tax only if his total income exceeds 
a prescribed minimum. , 
The tax is imposed at progressive rates on income above a basic personal 
allowance (12/1.3a). 
The supertax is imposed at progressive rates on 
income above 
a prescribed minimum, 
with no personal allowance 
(12/1.6). 
As previously noted, a resident. individual is taxed on all 
income wherever received or accrued, with a limited exception for income 
accruing outside India to a taxpayer who is resident but not ordinarily 
resident (11/2.1); a nonresident individual is taxed only on income 
received or deemed to be received in India and on income accruing or 
deemed to accrue in India (11/3.1). 
Married persons are taxed as separate individuals, each being liable 
for tax on his or her own income and neither being liable for tax on the 
income of the other (5/1.3). 
There is no provision for joint returns of 
married couples, nor is there any provision for division of income between 
the spouses for income reporting purposes. 
However, any income arising 
to the wife from assets transferred to her without consideration by the 
husband is taxable to the husband 
(6/8.5). 
Likewise, any income 
arising to the wife from membership in a partnership of which the hus- 
band is a member is taxable to the husband (6/8.6). 
Personal allow- 
ances, which reduce income in the lowest rate bracket (12/1.2a), are 
increased for taxpayers whose total income exceeds Rs 20,000 and who

(12/1.3a). 
2/3.2 
Partnerships 
The tax liability of a partnership (5/3.1) depends on whether it is 
registered or not registered under the Income-tax Act. 
If it is un- 
registered, it is taxed as a separate entity at income tax and supertax 
rates applicable to an individual, and no assessment is made again on 
the individual partners. 
However, each individual partner must include 
in his total income his share of the profits of the firm in order to deter- 
mine the rate applicable to his own income. 
In the case of a registered firm, the partnership is taxed at a special 
low rate of income tax and is not subject to supertax. 
Each individual 
partner includes in his total income, and is taxed on, his proportionate 
share of the total income of the firm as reduced by the tax imposed on 
the partnership. 
2/3.3 
Trusts and Estates 
The income of a trust (5/3.7) or of an estate (5/3.8) is taxable either 
to the beneficiary or to the trustee or the administrator of the estate. 
Where the beneficiaries’ interests are fixed, the tax is levied on the trustee 
or the administrator at the rates applicable to the respective total incomes 
of the beneficiaries as though their trust incomes were included in their 
individual incomes. 
If the shares of the beneficiaries are indeterminate 
or unknown, income tax on the entire income is levied on the trustee at 
the maximum rate applicable to an individual and supertax is levied 
at the normal rate applicable to one individual. 
In specified situations, 
trust income may be taxed to the settlor in order to prevent tax avoidance 
by means of shifting income from one taxpayer to another. 
2/3.4 
Corporations 
The taxable income of a corporation (“company”) is determined in 
the same manner as that of an individual (5/2.1). 
However, a corpora- 
. 
tion is taxed at flat rates of income tax (12/2.1) and supertax (12/2.4) 
and there is no minimum taxable limit for corporations. 
A resident 
corporation is taxed on all income wherever received or accrued; a non- 
resident corporation is taxed only on income received or deemed to be 
received in India and on income accruing or deemed to accrue in India 
(11/3.1). 
A corporation is resident in India if its control and manage- 
ment are entirely situated in India or if it is incorporated under Indian 
law (5/2.3); a corporation cannot be resident but not ordinarily resident 
(5/2.1).

2/4. 
Income from Business 
Tax is imposed upon the amount of business profit remaining after 
subtracting allowable expense and depreciations deductions from gross 
receipts (7/1.2).. 
The most significant differences between the treat- 
ment of business income and the treatment of other classes of income 
are found in the special allowances in computing business profits, such 
as the depreciation allowance (7/3) and net operating loss deductions 
(7/4), and in the special rules for computing the profits of insurance 
businesses (10/3). 
There is a greater liberality in allowing deductions 
for business expenses than for expenses incurred in the production of 
other income (6/1.5a, 7/2). 
Inventories may be valued at the end of the base year on any regular 
method of accounting (6/5.1). 
Valuation at cost, or at market, or at 
cost or market whichever is lower, is permitted. 
Which of the per- 
missible methods is employed is optional with the taxpayer, and different 
methods may be applied to different categories of inventory items; but 
the method adopted cannot be varied from year to year, although a 
bona fide change of method may be allowed if it is intended to be 
permanent. 
Depreciation is allowed for buildings, machinery, plant, and furniture 
(7/3.1). 
Rates of depreciation for different types of assets are provided 
in the Rules issued under the Act by the Central Board of Revenue. 
Aggregate depreciation cannot exceed the original cost. 
However, in 
addition to depreciation, a “development rebate” is also allowed for the 
year in which certain assets are first acquired (10/6.4). 
The develop- 
ment rebate is not taken into account in determining whether the aggre- 
gate depreciation allowed exceeds the original cost; hence the total of 
allowable depreciation and the development rebate may ultimately 
exceed the actual cost of the asset. 
In general, depreciation is allowed 
on the declining balance method only, that is, each year’s depreciation 
is based on the original cost minus the depreciation actually allowed in 
prior years. 
The straight line method is allowed only for ships. 
Expenditure on scientific research related to the business (7/2.13), 
even if of a capital nature (7/3.12), is allowed to be written off over a 
period of five consecutive years. 
Business losses may be set off against the income arising under other 
categories or “heads” (7/4.1). 
If there is not sufficient income under 
other categories, the net loss can be carried forward and set off against 
business profits of succeeding years, not exceeding eight, until it is 
fully absorbed; however, it.cannot be set off against income under other 
categories for a subsequent year. 
All businesses are treated alike for the purposes of assessment except 
insurance businesses, for which, as stated above, special rules of com-

2/5. 
Income from Personal Services 
An employee is taxable not only on the remuneration received in 
cash (8/1.1) but on the value of anything given to him in connection 
with services rendered by him (8/1.6). 
Retirement benefits in the form 
of an annuity are taxable to the same extent as any other annuity, except 
that benefits derived from a recognized provident fund or an approved 
pension (“superannuation”) fund are accorded special treatment. 
Ex- 
penses, other than for entertainment, incurred by an employee in the 
course of earning income from employment are deductible, provided the 
conditions of his employment require the expenditures (8/1.9). 
Except 
in the case of vehicles, no depreciation is granted for property used in 
connection with the employment. 
Income from the performance of independent services or the practice 
of a profession is taxed as business or professional income (8/3.1). There 
is a provision for granting relief to authors of literary or artistic works 
by allocating their income over a period of years to obviate the higher 
rate of tax which would otherwise be charged if the income were treated 
as that of a single year (8/4.1). 
There is no provision for spreading over 
a period of years the income earned by an inventor or an owner of 
patents. 
Remuneration for employment is subject to withholding of tax at source 
(8/1.10). 
All employers, regardless of the number of their employees, 
are required to withhold tax from the remuneration of each employee 
whose remuneration exceeds a minimum taxable limit. 
The tax is to be 
withheld at the rate appropriate to the total yearly remuneration payable 
_.to the employee. 
The amount of tax withheld by an employer must be 
paid over to the government, and the employee receives credit for the 
tax so withheld in his individual assessment. 
Persons deriving income from independent or professional services are 
subject to advance payment of tax upon notice from the Income-tax 
~ Officer (13/1.4c).

2/6.1 
In General 
Total income includes 
all income from the investment of capital 
except income which is specially exempt under an express provision of 
law. 
Dividends from newly established undertakings (“new industries” ) 
are in certain circumstances exempt from tax for a period of five years

Intercorporate dividends are generally taxable in full to the 
recipient, but dividends from certain corporations qualifying for tax 
exemption as new industries are exempt from supertax (10/6.2). 
Divi- 
dends received by investment companies are also exempt from supertax, 
subject to prescribed conditions (10/5). 
Generally speaking, expenses incurred in earning income from capital 
are deductible provided they have been incurred solely for the purpose 
of earning such income (6/1.5a). 
In addition to expenses which are 
deductible under the general rule, a special provision is made for the 
deduction of commissions paid for the collection of taxable income, and 
for the deduction of expenses of borrowing money used for the produc- 
tion of taxable income from securities (9/1.2). 
If deductible expendi- 
tures exceed the income in that category, the resulting loss may be set 
off against income under other categories; but if the income under other 
categories is not enough to absorb the loss, it cannot be carried forward. 
Tax must be withheld at source from payments of interest on govern- 
ment securities, on securities of a local authority, and on securities of a 
corporation subject to tax in India. 
Starting with the tax year 1959- 
1960, tax must also be withheld from payments of dividends. 
Other 
payments of income from capital are subject to withholding of tax only 
if made to nonresidents. 
2/6.2 
Dividends 
The income of a corporation is taxable without regard to the amount 
distributed as dividends, although certain closely held corporations may 
be subject to additional supertax on the amount of their undistributed 
income (12/2.7). 
A dividend distributed by a corporation is taxable 
to the recipient even if paid out of tax-exempt profits of the corporation 
(9/2.2), unless the profits are exempt under the new industries exemp- 
tion (10/6.2). 
Distributions 
in liquidation are generally treated 
as 
taxable dividends to the extent of the earned surplus of the liquidating 
corporation. 
If stock dividends (“bonus shares”) are issued by a com- 
pany, the value of the shares issued is not taxable in the hands of the 
shareholder and is not treated as a dividend, but the company declaring 
the dividend has to pay a higher tax calculated by reference to the value 
of the bonus shares. 
Through the tax year 1959-1960, shareholders received a credit for 
the income tax, but not for the supertax, paid by the company on the 
profits out of which the dividend was declared; but starting with the tax 
year 1960-1961, shareholders will receive no credit or rebate for either 
income tax or supertax paid by the corporation. 
Intercorporate dividends 
are fully includible in the income of the corporate recipient, but exemp- 
tion from supertax is provided for dividends declared by certain newly

2/6.3 
Annuities 
Income in the form of an annuity is includible in income without any 
deduction for the capital consumed in the process of buying the annuity. 
2/6.4 
Rent 
Tax is not imposed on income actually received or accrued by the 
taxpayer on buildings or land appurtenant to buildings. 
Buildings and 
appurtenant land, except where the buildings are used for purposes of 
the taxpayer's business, are known as “house property” (9/4.2), and are 
subject to tax on their presumed income, that is, on their bona fide 
annual rental value as reduced by deductions for mortgage interest, 
taxes, ground rent, presumed repairs, and certain other expenses. 
No 
depreciation is allowed for buildings not used for purposes of the owner’s 
business 
or for structural improvements thereon. 
Presumed income 
from buildings used by the owner for purposes of his business or from 
lands appurtenant thereto is not subject to tax. 
2/7. 
Taxation of Nonresidents 
A nonresident is subject to Indian tax only on income which accrues 
or is received in India or is deemed to accrue or be received in India 
(11/3.1). 
In the case of the sale of goods, all or a part of the income 
accrues in India if the contract of sale is made in India or the sale takes 
place in India (11/1.2a). A sale may be treated as taking place in India 
if the contract is entered into there or if title to the goods passes there, 
although there is a conflict of authority as to the relative importance of 
these two factors. 
Remuneration for services is considered to accrue in 
“India if it is paid for services rendered in India (11/1.3). 
Dividends 
declared by an Indian company are deemed to accrue in India if they are 
paid out of profits which are taxable to the company in India (11/1.4). 
Generally speaking, dividends declared by non-Indian companies are not 
_. deemed to accrue in India, even if declared out of profits taxable in 
India, unless they are declared in India and are payable in India. 
All income arising through or from any “business connection in India” 
(11/1.2b), any property in India, any asset or source of income in 
India, any money lent at interest and brought into India, or any sale, 
exchange, or transfer of a capital asset situated in India (11/1.4), is 
deemed to accrue in India and is accordingly taxable to residents and 
nonresidents alike. 
Interest on a debt secured by a mortgage on property 
in India, or on a loan, where the money borrowed is brought into India,

is taxable to a nonresident even if it is paid outside India (11/1.4c). 
Royalties paid for the use of a patent, copyright, or trade-mark in India 
are treated as accruing in India (11/1.4d). 
Any payment to a nonresident may be subjected to the requirement of 
withholding at source if it represents income subject to tax under the 
Indian Income-tax Act (11/3.3). 
An employee of a nonresident, 
a 
person who has a business connection with a nonresident, or a person 
through whom a nonresident receives any income, may be designated 
by the Income-tax Officer as an agent of the nonresident and subjected 
to vicarious liability for taxation on income received by him on behalf 
of the nonresident (11/3.4). 
The person so designated and taxed as an 
agent of a nonresident need not be an agent in fact or under the general 
law. 
There is no similar provision for taxing anyone as the agent of a 
resident. 
International tax treaties have been entered into with certain dominions 
in the British Commonwealth, with Switzerland, and with Sweden. 
Tax 
treaties with Japan, the Federal Republic of Germany, and the United 
States have been negotiated but are not yet in effect. 
2/8. 
Tax on Undistributed Income 
A company in which the public are not substantially interested and 
which fails to distribute a prescribed statutory percentage of its dis- 
tributable profits as dividends is subject to an additional supertax on 
its undistributed income as reduced by income tax and other supertax 
(12/2.7). 
Both resident and nonresident corporations are subject to 
the tax. 
However, if the facts of a case are such that the payment of a 
dividend, or of a larger dividend than that declared, would not have 
resulted in a benefit to the revenue—for example, in the case of a foreign 
corporation whose shareholders are all foreigners—no such additional 
supertax is levied despite the insufficiency of the distribution. 
The per- 
centage of distribution required varies from 45% for manufacturing 
profits of domestic corporations to 100% for profits of investment com- 
panies. 
In general, a company in which the public are not substantially 
interested is one in which shares carrying less than 50% of the total work- 
ing capital are held by the public, or whose shares are not freely trans- 
ferable, or whose affairs are controlled by less than six persons, or in 
which shares carrying more than 50% of the total voting power were 
at any time during the base year held by less than six persons. 
For the 
purposes of the last two conditions, a person and his relatives are treated 
as one person. 
The rate of additional supertax on undistributed income is 50% for a 
company whose business consists wholly or principally in the dealing in 
or holding of investments; the rate is 837% for any other company.

2/9. 
Administration 
2/9.1 
Returns, Assessment, and Payment of Tax 
All taxpayers are normally required to file returns by 30 June following 
the end of the tax year (13/1.2). A public notice is issued before 1 May 
requiring every person whose total income exceeds the minimum taxable 
limit to file within 60 days a return of his total income. 
The returns are 
informational only, and the tax is assessed by the Income-tax Officer on 
the basis of information set forth in the return and any other information 
in his possession. 
Unless there is concealment or suppression of facts 
by the taxpayer, the assessment must be made within four years from 
the end of the relevant base year (13/6.1). 
The tax is payable within 
the time specified in the notice of demand which is issued after the assess- 
mnent is made. 
Usually a period of one month is specified. 
All taxpayers whose total income for the preceding base year, as shown 
in the files of the Department of Revenue, exceeded the minimum taxable 
limit by Rs 2,500 are served with notices requiring advance payment of 
tax during the current base year (18/1.4c). 
Advance payment must 
be made in accordance with the terms of the notice. 
Any person who 
has not been notified to make an advance payment of tax before 15 March 
of the base year must make advance payment of tax if his total income 
is likely to exceed the minimum taxable limit by Rs 2,500. 
The tax 
payable in advance is calculated at the rates in force for the tax year 
as applied to the income of the preceding base year or to taxpayer's 
estimate of income for the current base year. 
No advance payment of 
tax need be made in respect of income from salary or wages because tax 
on such income is withheld at source. 
The amount of tax due for the 
current year is normally specified in the notice of demand for advance 
payment of tax; the tax is payable in four installments, the last being 
due on 15 March of the base year. 
The amount of final tax demanded 
for any year is reduced by the amount of tax withheld or paid in advance 
for the year (13/1.4d). 
2/9.2 
Protests and Review Procedure 
A taxpayer who considers his assessment to be erroneous in law or in 
fact may file an appeal with the Appellate Assistant Commissioner 
(13/4.3). 
At his discretion, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner may 
allow the objection either wholly or in part, issue an amended assessment, 
and refund to the taxpayer any tax found to have been overpaid. 
The 
Appellate Assistant Commissioner also has the power to increase the 
assessment, even in respect of an item not appealed against, provided 
the item or subject matter was dealt with in the original assessment order. 
If the taxpayer 
is not satisfied with the Appellate Assistant Com-

missioner’s decision, he may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, which 
is entitled to hear appeals both on questions of fact and on questions of 
law (13/4.4). 
Similarly, the Income-tax Officer may appeal to the 
Appellate Tribunal on any point of fact or law if he is dissatisfied with 
the Appellate Assistant Commissioner’s decision in favor of the taxpayer. 
From the decision of the Tribunal, a reference can be made to the 
High Court of the state at the instance either of the taxpayer or of the 
income tax authorities (13/4.7). 
A further appeal lies to the Supreme 
Court of India from the decision of the High Court if the case is certified 
by the High Court to be fit for appeal or if special leave to appeal is 
granted by the Supreme Court. 
The reference to the High Court and 
the appeal to the Supreme Court lie only on points of law arising out 
of the Tribunal’s order. 
No reference can be made to the High Court 
on a question of fact. 
The Supreme Court has power under the Consti- 
tution to grant special leave to appeal to itself directly from any decision 
of the Tribunal, even on a point of fact; but this power is exercised most 
sparingly.

Description of Taxes on Capital 
> 
This chapter summarizes “land revenue,” 
“local taxes on land and 
buildings,” the net wealth tax, the “estate duty,” and the gift tax. 
Land revenue, a principal source of revenue before and during the 
colonial period, is levied by the states. 
In most of the states it is now 
based on the net produce of agricultural land, as estimated and “settled” 
for a period of years, and on the reasonable rental value, or “annual


<!-- page 125 of 600 -->

pesia 
3/2.1 
89

FOIN TGA

value,” of nonagricultural land. 
Local taxes on land and buildings are 
also based on the annual value. 
Although these state and local taxes 
on real property are measured by and are intended to fall on the 
income from the property and not the property itself, they must be 
distinguished from the income tax on presumed income from house 
property (9/4.2), which is also based on the annual value and fre- 
quently on the same annual value as the state and local taxes, but is an 
integral part of the structure of the income tax levied by the central 
government. 
The net wealth tax, the estate tax, and the gift tax are all levied by 
the central government and are all of recent origin. 
The net wealth 
tax is an annual levy on personal net wealth. 
The estate tax is levied 
on gratuitous transfers of property at death and on certain property 
which is “deemed to pass” at death, including gifts in contemplation of 
death or within two years of death. 
Gratuitous transfers inter vivos are 
subject to the gift tax, and gift taxes paid on transfers inter vivos which 
are also subject to the estate tax are allowed as a credit against the 
estate tax. 
As a result of constitutional provisions, agricultural land is 
exempt from the net wealth tax, and is subject to the estate tax only 
in those states which have delegated to the central government their 
power to levy estate taxes on agricultural land. 
For purposes of the 
taxes on net wealth, estates, and gifts, both real property and movables 
are valued at the current market price. 
3/2. 
Land Revenue 
3/2.1 
In General 
The power to impose “land revenue” is reserved exclusively to the 
states under the Constitution! 
The basis of the tax and the rates vary 
widely from state to state. 
In most of the states, the term “land revenue” 
applies only to the taxation of agricultural land, and nonagricultural 
“Jand is taxed under special provisions (3/2.5). 
Both agricultural land 
and nonagricultural land are also subject to municipal and local taxes, 
which are described at 3/3. 
The land revenue systems of the former provinces of British India, 
developed by the British from indigenous revenue systems and usages, 
may be classified into three types.” 
1. Zamindari. 
Under this system, the British gave proprietary rights to 
zamindars, officials who had collected land revenue under the Moghuls, 
in exchange for the annual payment of a fixed amount of revenue out of 
1 Const., Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 45. 
2 For the development of the various systems of land revenue, see 3 Report of the 
Taxation Enquiry Commission, 1953-54 182; Wald, Taxation of Agricultural Land in 
Underdeveloped Economies 18-20; Griffiths, The British Impact on India 879-890; 
and Thomas, The Growth of Federal Finance in India 17-29, 121-180,

90 
the rents to be collected from tenants and cultivators. 
The East India 
Company established this system in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa in the 
Permanent Settlement of 1793, and in later permanent settlements in 
Benares and in parts of Madras and Assam. 
2. Mahalwari. 
In areas where there was no established system of collection 
of land revenue through zamindars, the British made periodic settlements 
with village communities, under which the villagers were severally and 
jointly liable for payment of the tax. 
This system was established chiefly 
in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh) and in Punjab. 
3. Ryotwari. 
In some areas the British made settlements with individual 
farmers, who were recognized as proprietors and were solely responsible 
for payment of the tax in the form of a fixed annual assessment. 
This 
system was adopted in Bombay, parts of Madras, and in other western 
and southern provinces. 
Although the native Indian States (1/1.1) also levied land revenue, in 
many of these principalities there were no regular settlements and no 
systematic basis of levying the tax or collecting the proceeds. 
In some 
of the Indian States the rulers collected the tax from zamindars; in others, 
in recognition of services, the right to receive rents from the occupants 
of land had been granted to jagirdars or inamdars who had no rights 
of ownership or occupancy themselves and who were not required to 
pay any revenue to the state. 
Since the merger of former princely states with the states of India 
after independence, the state governments have undertaken a series of 
reforms to remove zamindars and other intermediaries, who are being 
compensated for their loss of proprietary rights; to protect the rights of 
tenants and occupiers; and to rationalize the imposition and collection 
of land revenue. 
As a result, rent formerly paid to intermediaries is 
now, pending further legislation, paid directly to the state 
as land 
revenue; and the land revenue system now in effect in the majority of 
states most closely resembles the ryotwari system. 
It is the owner of 
the land who is liable for land revenue, whether he occupies and culti- 
vates the land himself or collects rent from the actual occupant or 
cultivator.® 
In most of the states charges are made for irrigation in agricultural 
areas. 
The two principal types of charges are irrigation service charges 
payable by cultivators, either in addition to or as a part of land revenue, 
and betterment levies payable by the owners of lands whose value has 
been increased by the irrigation services.*
