produce, valued at the average price of the crop for a specified period 
(“commutation price”), and deducting the landlord’s estimated costs. 
In Madras the assessment is based directly on the value of the net 
_ produce, determined by deducting cultivation expenses and certain 
adjustments for bad seasons from gross produce valued at the commu- 
tation price. 
Originally, gross produce was the basis of assessment in 
all parts of India, and it is still the basis of assessment in Assam. 
In some states, the standards to be used by the assessing officers in 
determining the basis of assessment are fixed by law; in others, it is left 
to the judgment of the assessing officers to determine the assessment 
base. 
In determining the gross produce and its value, soil fertility, crop 
yield, climate and rainfall, proximity to markets, prices of agricultural 
produce, and the rental and sales value of the land are considered. 
Because of changes in the areas of land holdings, in the yields of 
agricultural produce, and in prices, assessments must be revised from 
time to time. 
In those parts of the former provinces of British India 
which were not subject to permanent settlements, periodic settlements 
at intervals of from 15 to 40 years are prescribed by law, although 
World War II disrupted the regular operation of the settlement pro- 
cedures. 
Regular settlement procedures have not yet been established 
for most of the former native Indian States. 
Most states provide, either by statute or by administrative order, for 
reduction or complete remission of land revenue in the event of exten- 
sive crop failure. 
Constant and severe price declines are grounds for 
reduction or remission of tax in some states. 
The state of Madras 
grants such relief only to landowners who cannot afford to set off losses 
in one year against the profits of other years.®

Rates of Tax 
~ Rates of tax are fixed by the assessing officers for the settlement 
period within limits prescribed by law. 
Where assessment is based on 
net assets or on net produce (3/2.2), the maximum limits on the rates

Where zamindari tenure has

3/2.4 
Administration and Procedure 
Except in areas subject to permanent settlement, land revenue 
is 
administered by the chief revenue authority of the state, which is usually 
known as the Board of Revenue (1/8.10). 
The Board exercises both 
administrative and appellate functions. 
In Bombay, however, appeals 
are decided by a revenue tribunal, and administrative questions are the 
responsibility of the state government itself. 
Most of the states are 
divided into divisions under Commissioners, and are further divided into 
districts administered by Collectors or Deputy Commissioners. 
The tax 
is collected by village officers who keep records and assist in carrying 
out inspections and surveys affecting the assessment of the tax. 
Taxes which are in default may be collected by distraint and sale of 
the taxpayer’s personal property, including growing crops, or by seizure 
and sale of the land itself. 
3/2.5 
Nonagricultural Land 
Uttar Pradesh and Orissa make no distinction between agricultural 
and nonagricultural land for purposes of assessment. 
In most of the 
states, however, special provision is made either in the land revenue 
code or by executive order for the separate assessment of nonagricul- 
tural land. 
West Bengal has a special enactment, the West Bengal 
Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act of 1949. 
Although in some areas rural 
or village residences connected with agricultural land are exempt from 
tax or are rent-free under long term revenue settlement, nonagricultural 
land whose value has been increased by community or commercial 
development is usually taxed at a higher rate or assessed at a higher 
value than agricultural land.® 
The taxation of nonagricultural land 
varies in some states according to whether the land is used for residen- 
tial or commercial purposes, in other states on whether the land is used 
for building, and in still other states on whether the land may be 
classified as rural, town, or urban. 
The basis of assessment and rates 
of tax also vary from state to state. 
In Assam, for example, rural 
nonagricultural land is assessed at up to 10 times the assessment for 
similar agricultural lands, while assessment of urban land is based on 
annual value. 
In Bombay, outside Bombay city, the maximum rates of 
tax in the two classes of towns are respectively Rs 50 and Rs 25 per acre;

3/3. 
Local Taxes on Real Property 
3/3.1 
In General 
The constitutional power of the states to levy taxes on improved land 
(“taxes on land and buildings”)!° has been delegated by state law to 
the local governments, for which such taxes are a principal source of 
revenue. 
In most states the levy of such taxes is optional for municipal 
corporations and municipalities, and compulsory for village panchayats 
(1/1.5). 
District local boards do not levy taxes on land and buildings. 
Local taxes on land and buildings are payable by the owners or occu- 
piers of the land. 
The cost of municipal services is charged either as a 
special “service rate” in addition to the “general rate” or is made part 
of a “consolidated rate.” 
In some states additional taxes or cesses for 
education, libraries, medical services, or health services are imposed as 
surcharges on the property tax. 
The principal source of revenue of the district local boards are land 
cesses (also called local fund cesses, local cesses, or local rates) which 
are usually collected by the state government as surcharges on land 
revenue and credited to the local boards. 
In some states the cess is 
based on the annual value of the property."? 
Improvement trusts in Calcutta, Nagpur, and Punjab, and local bodies 
in Madras, Andhra Pradesh, and Bombay are authorized to levy better- 
Ment taxes which are in effect levies on the increase in urban land values 
resulting from the execution of schemes for town planning or town 
improvement. 
Such levies are authorized only for land affected by 
major development projects, and in practice have been limited to the 
costs of the projects.”

Basis of Assessment 
Local taxes on land and buildings are assessed on the “annual value” 
or “ratable value,” although 
in some 
states 
village panchayats 
are 
allowed the option of using “capital value” (fair market value) as the 
basis of the tax.13 
The annual value is the reasonable rental value, 
which in practice is normally the actual rent. 
In some states, the annual 
value may not exceed the controlled rent. 
When the reasonable rental 
value cannot be ascertained, the annual value may be computed as a 
percentage of the estimated replacement cost of buildings, less depre- 
ciation, plus the fair market value of the land. 
This method of 
assessment 
is sometimes 
used 
for theaters, 
hospitals, 
and railroad 
properties. 
The annual value of places of entertainment is sometimes 
estimated as a percentage of gross receipts. 
In all states, the value of 
property is determined without regard to encumbrances. 
Annual value 
is usually fixed for periods of from three to five years, although, under 
the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, assessments may be revised 
annually,4 
3/3.3 
Rates of Tax 
The rates at which tax is imposed by village panchayats are relatively 
small and are generally subject to upper and lower limits fixed by the 
states. 
The rates of tax imposed by municipalities and municipal cor- 
porations are substantially higher; most of the rates fall between 10% 
and 30% of annual value. 
In those few instances in which the tax rate 
is applied to “capital value,” the rate is normally a fraction of 1%. 
In 
the state of Bombay, industrial and commercial property is taxed at 
higher rates than residential property. 
In some municipalities 
and 
municipal corporations, the rates are graduated according to the annual 
value of the property on scales running from 15% to 23%. 
Regressive 
rate scales in effect in some localities, under which the amount by 
which the annual value exceeds a designated figure is taxed at one half 
or one quarter of the regular rate, are being eliminated. 
Concessional 
rates which have been granted to property owners occupying their own 
property are also disappearing. 
3/3.4

Properties of the central government are exempt from local property 
taxes under the Constitution unless they were taxable before 1 April 
1937. 
However, the central government has undertaken to pay for

Although state governments are subject to local property taxes on

Some states exempt properties used for charitable,

Property whose annual value is less

In general, exemptions

Remission of tax is granted in most states for taxable properties

Generally, the period of vacancy must be no less than 30 days and more

The tax remission normally

the building alone, and frequently may not exceed one half the tax 
otherwise payable.

Administration and Procedure 
Although there is a trend toward the valuation of property by experts, 
such as state valuation boards whose decisions may not be overturned 
by local government administrative 
officials, most valuation work is 
performed either by municipal officers appointed for that purpose, by 
local government officials themselves, or by state officers from the state 
revenue boards who are loaned to local governments for the purposes 
of revaluing local property. 
Such revaluations generally take place 
every three years or every five years, although annual revaluations are 
permitted in some areas. 
Collection of tax is also handled by local 
officials. 
Appeals from tax assessments are generally taken to the local govern- 
ing body itself or to a committee of the local governing body.'* 
In 
some states, the decision of such a body or committee may be appealed 
‘to a magistrate or to an officer appointed for the purpose by the state 
government. 
In certain municipal corporations, appeal may be taken 
to the local courts; in Madras, questions of law may be further appealed 
to the High Court of the state.

3/5.1 
Introduction 
The estate duty (herein called “estate tax”) is levied by the central 
government under the Estate Duty Act of 195319 and rules issued there- 
under by the Central Board of Revenue.?° 
The tax is patterned after 
the estate duty in the United Kingdom.” 
In the amended version of 
the act, gift taxes (3/6) on property included in a decedent’s estate 
and one half of the court fees paid in connection with the administra- 
tion of the estate are allowed as credits against the estate tax (8/5.7e). 
The Constitution gives the central government the exclusive power 
to levy estate and succession taxes on any property except agricultural 
land.2?, 
The power to levy estate and succession taxes on agricultural 
land is reserved to the states.22 
However, most of the states have 
delegated the power to tax agricultural land within their respective 
borders to the central government (1/3.2, 1/4.2); and the value of such 
land located in any of these states, which are listed in the First Schedule 
to the Act, is taxable under the central government Act (EDA § 5(1)), 
subject to a rebate of 25% of the tax if the principal value of the 
estate does not exceed Rs 200,000 (3/5.7d). 
Agricultural land which 
is located in any of the other states is not taxed under the Estate 
Duty Act, but the value of such land is included in the aggregate

3/5.2 
Property, Interests, and Powers Held at Death 
__ 
Estate duty is payable on the principal value (3/5.5) of all property, 
whether “settled or not settled,” which passes on death (EDA §5(1)). 
The inclusion of settled property is important because it subjects to 
estate duty many interests in property which might otherwise be con- 
sidered to be outside the scope of tax. 
Property is settled if it is 
limited to, or limited in trust for, any persons by way of succession 
(EDA § 2(19)). 
Thus, where a trust is created to pay the income to A 
for life, then to B for the life of C, the principal to be distributed to D 
on the death of C, the property is settled; and estate tax will be payable 
on its principal value both upon the death of A and on the death of C 
unless C should predecease A. 
It appears that the principal value of 
the trust property is subject to tax even if payments to the decedent 
as a sole beneficiary were entirely discretionary with the trustees. 
An interest in expectancy is included in the estate at its value on the 
date of death (Rule 14(7)). 
At the option of the estate, however, 
payment of tax on that interest may be postponed until the interest 
becomes possessory; in that case, tax is computed on the value of the 
interest when it becomes possessory and at the rate applicable to the 
entire estate including that value (EDA § 38). 
Where property passes at death pursuant to a transaction effected 
for full consideration 
in money 
or money’s worth, it is not taxed 
(EDA § 26) except in the case of certain transactions involving the 
prior creation of a debt or encumbrance (EDA § 46). 
In the case of 
transactions 
with relatives, 
the burden 
of proving that they were 
effected for full consideration is on the estate (EDA § 27). 
If partial 
consideration has been received, its value is allowed as a deduction 
from the value of the property subject to estate tax (EDA § 26). 
Property which passes on death includes not only property whose 
ownership is transmitted from the deceased to another as the result of 
-death, but also property in which the beneficial interest changes as a 
result of the death, whether the change is certain or contingent, and 
whether the change takes place at the time of death or is to take place 
at some later date ascertainable only by reference to the date of death 
(EDA §2(16)). 
If the decedent's interest in property either termi- 
nates or passes to another as a result of his death, his estate includes 
that proportion of the property which the income payable to the 
decedent bears to the whole income from the property (EDA § 
40). 
Property in which the decedent or any other person had an interest

If the interest terminating on the death of the

a beneficial interest in the property, the tax on the property is computed 
separately, as if the property constituted 
a separate estate, and the 
property is not aggregated with the rest of the estate for rate purposes 
(3/5.7a). 
There are special provisions governing the cessation of the 
interest of a coparcener in a Hindu undivided family on his death. 
If the decedent had an interest in settled property which did not 
come into his possession during his lifetime, the termination of that 
interest by his death will not give rise to estate tax if subsequent 
limitations under the settlement continue to have effect (EDA § 
23). 
Thus, where property has been placed in trust for A for life, then to B 
for life, and remainder to C, the property will not be taxed on the 
death of B prior to that of A. 
Similarly, if there are subsequent limi- 
tations which continue in effect, a reversion retained by the donor is 
not included in his estate solely by reason of the termination of the 
reversion upon his death before it comes into possession. 
If property 
which has been settled upon the deceased reverts to the settlor, the 
property will not be included in the estate of the deceased provided the 
deceased did not have the power to dispose of such property (EDA 
§ 24). 
Where A has transferred property to B for life with remainder 
to C, but to revert to A if he survives B, the property will not be taxed 
on the death of B survived by A 
Any property of which the deceased was competent to dispose at 
the time of his death is deemed to pass on his death whether or not 
he actually disposed of it (EDA $6). 
A person is deemed competent 
to dispose of property if he has an estate, an interest, or a general 
power, which would enable him to dispose of the property if he were 
of full legal capacity (EDA § 3(1)(a)). 
Property held by the deceased as trustee for another person is not 
deemed to pass on his death unless the property was held under a 
disposition made by the decedent himself and the decedent was not 
excluded from any benefit for at least two years before his death if the 
decedent was the sole trustee, and for at least five years before his 
death if the decedent was the sole trustee (EDA § 22). 
A disposition which takes effect out of the interest of the decedent is 
deemed to have been made by him whether or not the concurrence = 
another person was required (EDA § 3(1)(b)).

death and conditional on death occurring (donationes mortis causa) are 
deemed to pass on the death of the donor (EDA § 8).

gifts not exceeding Rs 10,000 which are made in consideration of marriage, 
and gifts not exceeding Rs 10,000 which are proved to have been part of 
the “normal” or habitual expenditure of the decedent (EDA § 9).*4 Gifts

Thus, if A transferred property to B and C

unless brought into the estate by some cther provision. 
d. LIFE INSURANCE poLicies. 
The proceeds of insurance on the life of 
the decedent may be included in property passing on his death under 
any of the provisions discussed above. 
Thus, the proceeds of a policy 
which has been owned by the decedent and which was given away 
within two years of his death, or which was given away subject to 
benefits retained by the decedent, would be includible. 
In addition, if 
the decedent transfers a policy “effected” or taken out by him to a 
donee and continues to pay any of the premiums thereon, the propor- 
tion of the proceeds of the policy which premiums paid by the decedent 
after the transfer bear to total premiums paid after the transfer is deemed 
to pass on the decedent’s death (EDA $14(1)). 
The proceeds of 
policies purchased by the decedent are not deemed to pass on death 
under this provision if the donee pays all the premiums after the transfer. 
The proceeds of policies not taken out by the insured are not deemed 
to pass under this provision even if the insured pays the subsequent 
premiums. 
However, a policy taken out by virtue of a settlement made 
by the decedent is treated as having been taken out by him, and premiums 
paid by virtue of or in consequence of a settlement made by the 
decedent out of the property comprised in the settlement or the income 
therefrom are treated as having been paid by the decedent (EDA 
§ 14(2)).

'g. TRANSFERS TO CONTROLLED CORPORATIONS. 
If the deceased has trans- 
ferred property, other than property in which he had only a life interest, 
to a “controlled company,” that is, a corporation which was controlled 
by not more than five persons at any time between the date of transfer 
and the date of death, and has received any benefits from the corpora- 
_ tion within the three years preceding his death, a portion of the corpora- 
_tion’s assets are deemed to have passed at his death (EDA $17). 
The 
purpose of this provision is to prevent avoidance of estate tax by means 
of a variety of devices through which property could otherwise be 
removed from a person’s estate without relinquishment by him of the 
benefits from the property. 
The provision would apply, for example, 
if the decedent before his death had transferred property to a company 
controlled by members of his family, while retaining indirect enjoyment 
_of the property in the form of excessive salaries or dividends. 
Where 
property has been transferred to a controlled corporation, the net assets 
of the corporation are included in the transferor’s estate in the propor- 
tion which his aggregate benefits from the company within the three-year 
period preceding death bear to the aggregate net income of the corpora- 
tion during that period. 
The term “benefit” is given a broad meaning, 
-and there are numerous and intricate provisions, both in the Act (EDA 
$20) and in the Estate Duty (Controlled Companies) Rules of 1953, 
to prevent circumvention of the Jaw and to avoid inequity. 
The applica- 
tion of this provision is illustrated in Example 1.

took effect (3/5.8).

semiprecious stones or ornaments attached thereto (EDA § 33(1) (e)), 
are exempt without limitation.

An interest in expectancy is included in the estate at

b. SHARES AND sEcuRITIES. 
Shares and securities which are quoted on a 
public stock exchange are normally valued at the market price on the 
date of death except where unusual or abnormal circumstances 
are 
present. 
In general, shares and securities which are not traded on an exchange 
and which have not been subject to sufficient sales to provide an accurate 
basis for their valuation are valued by taking into account such items as 
the net market value of company assets in the event of liquidation on 
death, anticipated dividend yield, future earnings, prior earnings, and 
the nature and prospects of the business. 
If the shares or securities are 
subject to restrictions on transfer, such as a requirement that they first 
be offered to other shareholders at a designated price, and valuation 
of the shares is not feasible by reference to the company’s assets, then 
the price will not determine their value; but the existence of the restric- 
tion is taken into account in determining the price which would be 
paid by a purchaser acquiring them. The fact that a particular purchaser, 
for his own special reasons, might pay more than market price is dis- 
regarded (EDA § 87). 
Shares of a “controlled company” are subject to special provisions 
(3/5.3g). 
The shareholder's estate includes 
a proportion of the net 
assets of the company, including good will of a business, plus certain 
assets of the company which were distributed or disposed of in the three 
years preceding the shareholder’s death (EDA §$ 17).

Deductions 
Reasonable funeral expenses up to Rs 1,000 may be deducted from the 
value of the estate (EDA $44). 
Debts and encumbrances created in 
good faith for full consideration for the decedent’s own use and benefit 
and taking effect out of his interest are deductible if legally enforceable 
against the estate and legally payable out of property of the estate which 
is available to meet them (EDA § 44). 
If debts exceed the value of 
property actually passing at death, they cannot be deducted from property 
actually disposed of before death which is deemed to pass at death 
(3/5.3). 
Debts guaranteed for others can be deducted only if there is 
no possibility of reimbursement. Debts incurred by the decedent by 
way of dower to his wife are deductible only to the extent of Rs 5,000. 
Any part of a debt or encumbrance created for the purchase of an 
expectant interest in property is disallowed as a deduction to the extent 
of any interest in the property which accrues, as a result of the decedent’s 
death, to the person from whom he purchased the interest (EDA § 
45). 
Deduction for a debt is disallowed to the extent that consideration for 
it was or could have been derived from the decedent (EDA § 
46). 
Debts due to nonresidents 
are deductible only from the value of 
property located abroad unless such property is insufficient for payment 
thereof and the debts either were contracted to be paid in India or were 
charged, as by liens, on property located in India (EDA § 
47). 
No deduction is allowed for the cost of administration of the estate 
in India, but up to 5% of the value of property located abroad may be 
deducted for additional administration expenses incurred as the result of 
the foreign location of the property (EDA § 48). 
If property situated 
abroad is subject to death taxes in a country with which India does not 
have an estate tax treaty (3/5.8c), the amount of such taxes is deductible 
from the value of the foreign property included in the estate provided 
the property is not located in India under the Indian rules (EDA § 
49; 
Rule 16).

3/5.8 
International Aspects 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Real property located in India and movable property 
located in India are subject to Indian estate tax regardless of the citizen- 
ship, residence, or domicile of the decedent. 
Real property located 
outside India is exempt (EDA § 21(1)(a)). 
Movable property located 
outside India is subject to Indian estate tax if the decedent was domiciled 
in India at the time of death; in addition, settled movable property 
located outside India in which the decedent had a life estate is subject 
to Indian estate tax if the settlor was domiciled in India when the 
settlement took effect, even if the decedent was not domiciled in India 
at the time of his death. 
In all other cases, movable property located 
outside India is exempt 
(EDA §21(1)(b)). 
Domicile is determined 
in accordance with the principles set forth in the Indian Succession Act 
of 1925 (EDA § 3(1)(d)). 
If a nonresident decedent owned shares or debentures in a foreign 
corporation which is doing business in India and which was resident in 
India during two out of the three tax years preceding the shareholder's 
death, the shares or debentures are subject to special tax treatment 
~(8/5.7a). On learning of the shareholder's death, the corporation must 
report it to the Controller of Estate Duty; and the corporation 
is 
accountable for the tax (3/5.9b) if it is not otherwise paid (EDA § 20A). 
The deductions allowed for debts owed to nonresidents, for expenses 
of administration of property located abroad, and for death taxes payable 
in a foreign country on property located abroad are described at 3/5.6.

b. srrus oF property. 
The situs of interests in real or movable property 
is determined under rules issued by the Central Board of Revenue. 
Rights and interests in real property and benefits arising from real 
property are deemed to be located in India if the property itself is in 
India (Rule 9). In general, the situs of tangible personal property is 
determined by its location at the time of death (Rule 8). 
Securities 
issued by any government or local authority have their situs where 
located at the deceased’s death, if in bearer form, and at the place of 
registration, if registered. 
Shares or debentures in a company, whether 
held by a nominee or not, ordinarily have their situs at the place where 
the company is incorporated. 
Simple contract debts and debts under 
seal are situated at the place of the debtor’s residence; rights or interests 
in negotiable promissory notes or bills of exchange are situated where 
the instruments are located; money on deposit in a bank has its situs at 
the place where the account is kept. 
Patents, trade-marks, and designs 
have their situs where they are registered; rights or licenses to use such 
property are situated at the place where they are exercisable. 
C. ESTATE TAX TREATIES. 
The Central Government is authorized to make 
reciprocal agreements with other countries for the avoidance or relief 
of double taxation under Indian and foreign estate taxes (EDA § 80). 
The United Kingdom is the only country with which such an agreement 
has been made.** 
Under the United Kingdom treaty, each of the contracting countries 
agrees to exempt the estates of persons domiciled in the other country 
from tax on property which is not located in the taxing country under 
the treaty situs rules and whose devolution or disposition is not governed 
by the law of the taxing country. 
The situs rules provided by the treaty 
differ only slightly from those of the Estate Duty Act. 
However, India 
reserves the right to tax the estates of nonresidents on their shares in 
resident foreign companies doing business in India and the right to tax 
the estates of nonresidents on life interests created by settlors domiciled 
in India in settled property located outside India. 
If one of the 
countries taxes property which is not located in that country but is 
located in the other, it gives a credit equal to its own duty attributable 
to that property or the other country’s duty attributable to that property, 
whichever is less. 
If both countries tax property which is located in 
both or in neither, each country grants a credit equal to that proportion 
of its own duty attributable to the property or the other country’s duty 
attributable to the property, whichever is lower, that the lower duty 
bears to the sum of both duties.

Administration and Procedure 
a. IN GENERAL. 
The estate tax is administered and collected by Con- 
trollers of Estate Duty, who are appointed by the Central Government 
and who perform their functions under the general supervision of the 
Central Board of Revenue (EDA $4). 
Appellate authorities under the 
_ 
Act are Appellate Controllers, appointed by the Central Government, 
and the Appellate Tribunal (1/8.6, 3/5.9c).25 
The Appellate Tribunal 
may refer valuation problems arising on appeal to valuers appointed for 
that purpose by the Central Government (3/5.9c), but the valuation of 
property in the course of assessment is among the functions of the 
Controllers (EDA § 41). 
b. RETURNS. 
Legal representatives of the decedent to whom property 
passes on the decedent’s death, fiduciaries who manage or hold any 
interest in property passing on the decedent’s death, and other persons 
who hold interests in property passing on the decedent’s death are 
required to file “accounts” with the Controller of Estate Duty within six 
months of the decedent’s death (EDA §$53).3® 
Although each person 
“accountable” for estate tax is liable only for the tax on assets which he 
actually received or might have received but for his own default, each 
account must report all property of the decedent on which estate tax 
is payable. 
The filing of an account by an executor is a condition 
precedent to the grant of probate of the estate (EDA $56). 
Present 
or former trustees of settled property are accountable for estate tax 
on property subject to interests ceasing on the decedent’s death (EDA 
$54). 
Within three months after learning of the death of a shareholder 
or debenture holder, a corporation must file an account giving information 
relevant to the estate tax on its shares or debentures (EDA 8§ 20A, 84; 
Rules 28, 29).?7 
A controlled company (3/5.3g) 
is accountable for 
_estate tax payable on that portion of its assets which is includible in 
the decedent’s estate (EDA §$19(1)), and must furnish the relevant 
information to the Controller of Estate Duty within 45 days after the 
decedent’s death (EDA §18(1)). Persons who have received or dis- 
posed of assets of a controlled company on or after the death of the 
decedent and persons who have received assets of a controlled company 
on distribution are also accountable for all or part of the estate tax 
payable on the assets of the company (EDA $19(1)).

C. PAYMENT OF TAX. 
Estate tax is due on the date of the deceased's 
death (EDA § 57), but generally is not payable until the filing of an 
account.?8 
Any additional tax is due on assessment and demand therefor 
by the Controller of Estate Duty. The notice of demand may specify the 
time and place of payment; but if no time is specified, the tax must be 
paid on or before the first day of the second month following the date on 
which the notice is served (EDA §78). 
The tax is payable by check 
or cash at the office of the Controller or at various approved banks, or 
by adjustment of any refund of income taxes (EDA $51; Rule 18). 
Cash deposited by the decedent prior to his death for use in paying the 
tax bears interest at 2% (Rule 19). Government securities also may be 
used to pay the tax under rules provided by the Central Board of Revenue 
(EDA §52). 
The Controller may require payment of tax, or security 
therefor, on a provisional assessment (EDA § 57). 
If the tax cannot be raised by the due date without excessive sacrifice, 
the Controller may postpone payment on such terms as he thinks fit, 
at interest not exceeding 4% or at any higher interest which may be 
yielded by the property (EDA §70). 
At the option of the persons 
liable for the tax, estate tax on real property may be paid either in 
four equal annual installments or in eight equal semiannual installments at 
interest of not more than 4% or any higher yield actually realized on 
the property (EDA § 70(2) ).39

Unpaid tax constitutes a primary lien upon property included in the 
taxable estate, but the lien may be released at the Controller’s discretion 
(EDA §74). A person accountable for the tax is empowered to sell or 
mortgage taxable property to pay the tax, whether or not the property is 
vested in him (EDA $77). 
d. PERSONS LIABLE FoR TAX. Any person who is accountable for estate tax 
(3/5.9b) is liable for the estate tax payable on assets which he has 
received or which he might have received but for his own neglect 
(EDA §53). 
In general, the personal representative is liable for tax 
on all property which vests in the personal representative or which might 
have been disposed of by the deceased; a donee or a trustee is liable 
for tax on all property which is deemed to pass to him, such as gifts 
made within two years of death and trusts with reservation of benefits 
to the donor; tax on property in which the deceased had no interest is 
payable by those in whom such property is vested or is in possession. 
If a person accountable for estate tax pays the tax on property not in his 
possession and not passing to him, he is entitled to a lien on the property, 
against the trustees or beneficial owners for repayment of the amount 
of the tax on the property (EDA §8§ 76, 77). The determination of what 
property actually will bear the burden of tax is not considered here as 
it is a matter of the general law of property, estates and wills, rather than 
of tax law. 
e. APPEALS. 
Any person accountable for estate tax may appeal to the 
Appellate Controller, within 30 days after the issue of the notice of 
demand for payment of tax, any order of the Controller of Estate Duty 
valuing property, assessing 
or reassessing the estate, 
or imposing 
a 
penalty (EDA §62).4° 
Appeals to the Appellate Tribunal, the High 
Courts, and the Supreme Court are governed by provisions similar to 
__those of the Income-tax Act (1/8.6, 13/4). 
The Appellate Tribunal may 
refer questions regarding the valuation of property to valuers nominated 
by the parties to the appeal from among persons designated by the 
Central Government to serve in that capacity (EDA §§ 4(3), 63(6) ).

3/6.1 
Introduction 
A gift tax is imposed by the central government under the Gift-tax 
Act of 1958,41 which went into effect on 1 April 1958, applying to gifts 
made after 1 April 1957. 
Prior to the adoption of the Gift-tax Act there 
was no general tax on gifts, although gifts in contemplation of death and

fessor Kaldor of Cambridge University recommended the adoption of 
a single tax on property received by bequest or by inter vivos gift to 
replace the existing estate duty.*2 
As adopted by the government, how- 
ever, the gift tax is a separate tax levied on the donor and not on the 
recipient. 
Rules issued by the Central Board of Revenue under the Act prescribe 
methods of valuing certain types of property and forms and procedures 
for returns, assessment, appeals, and refunds.** 
3/6.2 
Classes of Taxpayers 
The gift tax is levied in each tax year on certain categories of gifts 
made during the base year (“previous year”) by individuals, Hindu 
undivided families, corporations, and associations of individuals (GTA 
8§ 2( xviii), 
3). 
The tax liability of an individual donor depends on his residence status, 
determined in the same manner as for the income tax (5/1.2), and on his 
citizenship (GTA § 5(1), $5, Explanation). 
1. Citizens who are ordinarily resident are taxed on their gifts of real 
property situated in India and on gifts of movable property wherever 
situated. 
2. Citizens who are not resident, or who are resident but not ordinarily 
resident, are taxed on gifts of real or movable property situated in India. 
8. Aliens, regardless of residence, are taxed on gifts of real or movable 
property situated in India. 
Hindu undivided families, associations, and corporations, if resident, 
are taxed on gifts of real property situated in India and on gifts of 
movable property wherever situated. 
If not resident, they are taxed on 
gifts of real or movable property situated in India. 
A corporation is resident if, during the base year, it is a company 
formed and registered under the Companies Act of 1956, or it is an exist- 
ing company within the meaning of that Act, or its control and manage- 
ment were situated within India (GTA $5, Explanation). 
However, a 
Hindu undivided family or other association is resident in India unless 
during the base year the control and management of its affairs were 
situated wholly outside India. 
The Act exempts from tax gifts made by “government companies” 
(1/3.3a), by corporations established by central, state, or provincial act, 
by charitable institutions and funds exempt from income tax (5/5.7), 
by public companies (1/3.3a) in which more than 50% of the voting

3/6.3 
Taxable Gifts 
a. IN GENERAL. 
A gift is defined as any voluntary transfer of existing 
property for less than full consideration in money or money’s worth 
(GTA § 2(xii)). 
If the donor receives consideration, tax is imposed only 
on the excess of the market value of the gift over the amount of the 
consideration (GTA § 4). 
“Property” includes any interest in property, real or movable (GTA 
§ 2(xxii)). 
“Transfer of property” is broadly defined and specifically 
includes the creation of a trust in property; the grant or creation of a lease, 
mortgage, charge, easement, license, power, partnership, or interest in 
property; the exercise of a power of appointment in favor of any person 
other than the donee of the power; and in general any transaction 
whereby a person intends to diminish the value of his own property and 
to increase the value of the property of any other person (GTA § 2(xxiv) ). 
The value of the release or abandonment of a debt, contract, or other 
actionable claim, or of any interest in property, is taxable as a gift to 
the extent that the release or abandonment is not made in good faith 
(GTA §4(c)). 
If a donor transfers property without adequate con- 
sideration to be held jointly by himself and another person, any appro- 
priation of the jointly held property by the other person is taxable as a 
gift of the donor (GTA § 4(d)). 
The base year for gift tax purposes is the taxpayer’s base year for 
income tax purposes (GTA § 2(xx)) (6/3). 
If the taxpayer has different 
base years for different classes of income, the one which expires last is 
the base year for gift tax purposes. 
If the taxpayer has no base year 
for income tax purposes, the preceding tax year is used for the gift tax. 
~ However, once the taxpayer has been assessed to gift tax for a particular 
base year, he must use a corresponding base period in any subsequent 
assessment unless the Gift-tax Officer consents to a change. 
_ b. exemptions. 
Each taxpayer is granted a basic allowance of Rs 10,000 
for gifts to all donees during the base year (GTA § 5(2)). 
In addition, 
the Act exempts gifts by certain taxpayers of property situated outside 
India (3/5.5); gifts to the central government, a state government, or 
a local authority; gifts to charitable institutions or funds to which contribu- 
tions are deductible under the income tax, and other charitable gifts not 
exceeding Rs 100 each and subject to a maximum of Rs 500 by one 
taxpayer to one donee in a year; marriage gifts to dependent relatives, 
subject to a maximum of Rs 10,000 for each marriage; gifts of insurance

Gifts to the taxpayer’s spouse are exempt up to an aggregate amount, 
after the effective date of the tax, of Rs 100,000. (GTA §5(1) (viii) ). 
Gifts made to third persons by a spouse out of gifts exempted under this 
provision, however, are subject to gift tax without regard to any other

Gifts made in the 
course of and for the purposes of a business, profession, or vocation, 
including the release or abandonment of a debt, contract, actionable

good faith (GTA §§4(c), 5(1) (xiv) ). 
Transfers by will and gifts in contemplation of death are exempt from 
the gift tax since they are subject to the estate tax (GTA §§5(1)(x), 
5(1)(xi)), but there is no provision exempting gifts within two years 
of death and gifts with interests reserved although such gifts are also 
subject to the estate tax (8/5.3). 
If a gift is irrevocable only for a 
specified period and is otherwise revocable, only the capitalized value 
of the income of the property for the period for which it is irrevocable 
is subject to tax (3/6.4). 
3/6.4 
Valuation 
A gift of property other than cash is valued at the price at which, in 
the opinion of the Gift-tax Officer, it could be sold in the open market 
on the date on which the gift was made (GTA $6). 
Special rules have 
been prescribed for the valuation of certain property which cannot be 
sold in the open market, such as insurance policies, shares of a private 
company, 
and interests 
in partnerships 
and associations 
of persons 
(Rule 10). 
The value of any other property not salable in the open 
market is determined by the Central Board of Revenue. 
The value of 
a gift which is irrevocable only for a specified period is the capitalized 
value of the income from the property during the period for which the 
gift is irrevocable (GTA § 6(2)).

Gifts made during the base year (3/6.3a), not including exempt gifts 
(3/6.3b), are aggregated, and the rates set forth in Table 17 are applied 
to the total.

3/6.6 
International Aspects 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Gifts of real or movable property situated in India are 
subject to gift tax unless otherwise exempt (3/6.3b), regardless of the 
residence or citizenship status of the donor. 
Gifts of movable property 
situated outside India are subject to gift tax if made by individuals who 
are citizens of India and are ordinarily resident in India, or by corpora- 
tions or other entities which are resident in India (3/5.2). 
Gifts of 
movable property situated outside India are exempt if made by non- 
resident entities or by individuals who are not citizens, or not resident, 
or resident but not ordinarily resident; all gifts of real property situ- 
ated outside India are exempt from tax (GTA §5(1)). 
Although no 
_rtules for the determination of situs of movable property have been pro- 
vided, it may be assumed that the Estate Duty Rules (3/5.8b) will 
govern. 
b. DOUBLE TAXATION. 
The Act empowers the Central Government to 
enter into reciprocal agreements with other countries for the avoidance 
or relief of double taxation of gifts (GTA § 44). No such agreements 
have as yet been concluded. 
The Act contains no provision for unilateral 
relief with respect to gifts taxable in other countries. 
3/6.7. 
Administration and Procedure 
The gift tax is administered by the income tax authorities (1/8) under 
procedures similar to those established for the income, wealth, and 
expenditure taxes.

Any person who during the previous year has made taxable gifts, after 
taking account of all applicable exemptions, is required to file a gift tax 
return not later than 30 June of the tax year (GTA $13). 
If the donor 
dies before filing a return, his legal representative is required to file 
instead (GTA §19). 
Under no circumstances is the donee required 
to file a return. 
The Gift-tax Officer may also issue a notice requiring 
any person whom he believes liable for gift tax to file a return within 
30 days of the notice (GTA §13). 
A penalty not exceeding 150% 
of the amount of tax may be imposed for failure to file a return when 
required, or for filing a fraudulent return (GTA $17). 
Gift tax is due upon receipt of a notice of demand from the Gift-tax 
Officer, following assessment based on the return and on any further 
information which the Gift-tax Officer may require (GTA §§ 15, 81). 
The procedures for the collection of delinquent taxes and the penalties 
which may be imposed are similar to those provided under the income 
tax (GTA $33) (13/7.3). 
If the Gift-tax Officer believes that payment 
cannot be obtained from the donor, tax may be recovered from the donee 
up to the amount of tax attributable to the value of the gift made to 
him (GTA § 29). 
If the donee is a trust, tax attributable to the gift may 
be recovered from either the trustee or the beneficiary. 
The tax is a 
first charge on gifts of real property except in the hands of a bona fide 
purchaser for value without notice (GTA § 30); movable property is not 
chargeable for nonpayment of tax. 
If an individual liable for gift tax dies before payment, his legal repre- 
sentative is liable for the tax to the extent of the decedent donor’s estate 
(GTA §19). 
On the dissolution of a partnership or association liable 
for gift tax, or on the partition of a Hindu undivided family liable for 
tax, the partners or members are jointly and severally liable for the tax 
(GTA 8§ 20, 21). 
The procedures for objections and appeals are similar to those under 
the income tax (18/4).

4/1. 
Description of Taxes on Transactions 
Taxes on transactions are imposed by the central government and by 
all of the states. 
The central government levies a sales tax on interstate 
sales, manufacturers’ and producers’ excise taxes, and import and export 
duties. 
The expenditure tax levied by the central government might also 
be classified as a tax on transactions, although its incidence is controlled 
by personal allowances and a minimum income limit. 
The states levy 
general sales or purchase taxes, excise taxes on alcoholic beverages and 
drugs, entertainment taxes, electricity duties, and taxes on sales or pur- 
chases of particular commodities, such as motor fuel, tobacco, sugar cane, 
and jute. Stamp taxes on nonjudicial documents are levied both by the 
central government and by the states, the central government determining 
the rates on some documents and the states determining the rates on 
others. 
Some of the states have special taxes on the registration or 
recording of documents. 
Many local authorities levy special taxes on 
transfers of immovable property, taxes, known as octroi, on the entry of 
goods into local areas for use, consumption, or sale therein, terminal taxes 
on goods or passengers carried by road or inland waterway, theater 
taxes (“show taxes”), and taxes on advertisements other than advertise- 
ments in newspapers. 
A substantial part of revenues from the central 
government taxes on transactions is distributed to the states. 
All commodities which are subject to excise tax if produced domesti- 
cally are subject to import duties if imported, but goods on which import 
duty has been paid are generally exempt from excise tax. 
However, the 
import duties on some goods are composed of a standard duty plus the 
excise tax which would have been payable if the commodities had been 
produced domestically. 
Transactions which occasion the import of goods 
into India are exempt from sales taxes, but subsequent transactions 
involving imported goods are subject to sales tax. 
Most exports are 
exempt from excise tax. 
Transactions which occasion the export of goods 
from India are not subject to sales tax. 
Goods may be subject to both excise and sales taxes. 
However, the 
central government has limited the rates at which sales taxes may be 
levied on certain goods declared to be of special importance to interstate 
trade (16/4.3), and goods which are subject to the central excise duty 
are exempted or taxed at concessional rates under some of the state sales

tax acts (16/4.1). 
Liability for stamp tax payable on a document is not 
affected by sales or other taxes previously imposed on the transaction 
evidenced by the document. 
4/2. 
Sales Taxes 
Under the Constitution in its present form, the states have exclusive 
power to tax intrastate sales and purchases of goods other than news- 
papers (16/1.2). 
The central government has exclusive power to tax 
sales and purchases of goods in the course of interstate trade, but the 
proceeds of any such tax must be assigned and distributed to the states 
in which they are collected (16/1.3). 
All of the states except Jammu 
and Kashmir levy general sales or purchase taxes on intrastate transac- 
tions. 
Some of the states levy special taxes on sales of certain commodi- 
ties, such as motor fuels, tobacco, sugar cane, and jute. 
By the Central Sales Tax Act of 1956 the central government imposed 
a tax at special rates on sales of goods in interstate trade (16/1.3). 
Sales of newspapers, actionable claims, stocks, shares, and securities are 
not subject to the tax (16/4.1). 
The proceeds of the tax are collected 
and retained by the state in which the movement of the goods in inter- 
state trade commences. 
The Central Sales Tax Act determines which 
dealers are liable to tax, determines what constitutes a taxable sale, and 
imposes limits on the rates of tax. 
The sales tax law of the state in 
which the movement in interstate trade commences determines which 
goods are taxable, determines the rates of tax within the limits set by 
the Central Sales Tax Act, and governs the administration of the tax. 
These taxes are analyzed in greater detail in Chapter 16. 
4/3.

4/3.1 
Introduction 
Under the Constitution the central government and the states have 
concurrent power to impose stamp duties, other than duties or fees on 
judicial documents.t| 
The central government, however, has exclusive 
power to prescribe the rates of stamp duty on bills of exchange, checks, 
promissory notes, bills of lading, letters of credit, insurance policies, 
transfers of shares, debentures, proxies, and receipts; ? the power to pre- 
scribe rates of duty on other nonjudicial documents is allocated exclu- 
sively to the states.* 
Stamp duties are levied by the central government under the Indian

The

and rules under the central Act are made by the state governments 
(ISA. §§ 74, 75, 76). 
In Madras and Andhra Pradesh local governments are required to levy

The taxes are imposed on the value

The rates are 5% for municipalities and

These taxes are in addition

Discussion in this volume is based on the central Act. 
State acts and

4/3.2 
Nature of the Stamp Tax 
The stamp tax is essentially a tax on documents rather than on trans- 
actions; in general, a transaction which is not consummated by a written 
instrument is not subject to tax. 
However, the Act expressly requires 
the giving of properly stamped receipts for payments exceeding Rs 20 
and for credits received for renewals of fire insurance policies (ISA § 80). 
Once an instrument has been executed and delivered, and the stamp tax 
has been paid, the instrument will not be subject to tax again unless it 
is amended or altered in such a manner as to have the effect of a new 
instrument. 
However, copies or duplicates of a taxable document are 
subject to additional stamp tax at modest rates. 
In general, an instrument is taxable if it creates, transfers, limits, 
extends, extinguishes, or records a right or liability (ISA § 2(14)). 
Ifa 
single instrument relates to several distinct matters, the instrument is 
taxed as if each matter were dealt with in an independent document 
(ISA §5). Thus, a conveyance of two pieces of property is taxed as two 
conveyances, and an instrument providing for the sale and mortgage of 
certain property is taxed both as an agreement of sale and as a mortgage. 
When several instruments are employed to effect a single sale, mortgage, 
or settlement, only the one selected by the parties as the “principal 
instrument” is taxed at the schedule rate; the remaining instruments aré 
taxed at a nominal fixed rate (ISA § 4). 
If a single instrument relating 
to only one matter performs a function which falls within more than one

5 Const. art. 268.

classification in the schedule, the instrument is taxed at the highest rate 
provided for any of the classifications (ISA § 6). 
Documents executed in India are subject to stamp duty regardless of 
the situs of the subject matter and regardless of where any acts which 
they call for are to be performed. 
Bills of exchange not payable on 
demand and promissory notes, even if executed outside India, are taxable 
if accepted, paid, presented for acceptance or payment, endorsed, trans- 
ferred, or otherwise negotiated in India. 
Other instruments executed 
outside India, but relating to property situated in India or to “any matter 
or thing done or to be done” in India, are taxable if received in India 
(ISA §8). 
Most of the state acts provide that documents executed outside the 
state but received in the state, and relating to property in the state or to 
acts to be performed within the state, are taxable at the rate provided 
by the state, after deduction of any tax which,may have been paid in the 
state of execution. 
Thus, documents relating to property located in the 
state or to acts to be performed in the state are taxed at uniform rates 
regardless of the place of execution. 
4/3.3 
Instruments Taxed at Specific Rates 
A large number of documents are required to bear stamps at specific 
rates per document regardless of the amount of consideration for their 
execution or the value of their subject matter (ISA, Schedule I). Many 
of the rates are nominal, varying in most instances from Rs 0.10 to Rs 5; 
and the tax itself is not generally a matter of serious concern to the 
taxpayer except for a few documents such as articles of clerkship, on 
which the rate is Rs 250. 
However, it is a matter of interest to the owner 
of a taxable document that it be properly stamped, since failure to stamp 
a document properly gives rise to penalties and fines not only against the 
__original parties but also against transferees, and renders the document 
inadmissible in civil legal proceedings (4/3.7). 
The most common commercial documents subject to a fixed rate of 
tax are receipts, bills of lading, and promissory notes payable on demand. 
In general, a receipt given for the payment of Rs 20 or more in money 
or money’s worth requires a Rs 0.10 stamp. 
Receipts are broadly defined 
as including any writing acknowledging receipt of money, bills of ex- 
change, notes, or movable property, or acknowledging the satisfaction or 
discharge of any debt, demand, or part thereof (ISA § 2(23)). 
Certain 
types of receipts are exempt, the principal ones being receipts for certain 
pensions and allowances, receipts for certain payments to or by the 
government, receipts for payment of money without consideration, and 
receipts contained in instruments otherwise bearing stamp tax. 
An 
unstamped receipt which is subject to stamp tax is admissible in evidence

lading executed outside India are exempt from tax even if relating to

Promissory notes payable on demand 
are subject to tax at rates of Rs 0.10, Rs0.15, or Rs 0.25, depending on

An agreement or a memorandum of agreement relating to the sale of 
a bill of exchange is subject to tax at a fixed rate of Rs 0.125. 
Agree-

goods or merchandise are exempt. Any other agreement or memorandum 
of agreement not otherwise provided for in the schedule is taxed at 
Rs 0.50. 
Other instruments subject to tax at fixed rates include acknowl- 
edgments, affidavits, appointments of trustees, articles and memoranda of 
association of companies, partnership instruments, articles of clerkship, 
apprenticeship deeds, delivery orders, letters of credit, powers of attorney, 
proxies, and copies or duplicates of taxable instruments. 
4/3.4 
Instruments Taxed at Ad Valorem Rates 
The rates of tax on many types of documents vary with the value of 
the property involved. 
However, the rate of tax on a document is not 
expressed as a percentage of the exact value, but as fixed amounts of tax 
payable on values falling within designated ranges and representing a 
constant percentage of the upper limit of each range (ISA, Schedule I). 
The more important types of documents taxed at ad valorem rates are 
discussed below. The rates for values under Rs 100, which usually repre- 
sent somewhat greater percentages of value than the rates for higher 
ranges, are omitted. 
a. SALES OR TRANSFERS OF PROPERTY. 
Although agreements exclusively 
for the sale of goods or merchandise are exempt from tax (4/3.5), stamp 
tax is payable on most other instruments conveying title to property. 
Thus, conveyances are subject to tax at Rs 1 for each Rs 100 of sale price 
up to Rs 1,000, and at Rs5 for each additional Rs 500 or fraction thereof. 
Transfers of marketable debentures, other than debentures 
of local 
authorities, are taxed on their face amounts at one half the rates appli- 
cable to conveyances. 
Transfers of corporate shares are taxed at the rate 
of Rs 0.75 for every Rs 100 of value or fraction thereof. 
Transfers by } 
endorsement of bills of exchange, checks, notes, bills of lading and other 
documents of title, insurance policies, and central government securities 
are exempt. 
An assignment of a lease is taxed in the same manner as a 
conveyance,

b. BILLS OF EXCHANGE. 
Bills of exchange payable in not more than three 
months are taxed at the rate of Rs 0.25 for each Rs 500 of face value up 
to Rs 1,000 and at Rs 0.50 for each additional Rs 1,000. 
These rates are 
multiplied by two for bills payable in between three and six months, 
by three for bills payable in from six to nine months, by four for bills 
payable in from nine months to one year, and by eight for bills payable 
in more than one year. 
Bills of exchange which are payable on demand, 
including checks, are exempt from tax. 
C. PROMISSORY NOTES NOT PAYABLE ON DEMAND. 
Promissory notes not 
payable on demand are taxable in the same manner as bills of exchange 
(4/3.4b). 
d. ISSUE OF BONDS OR DEBENTURES. 
Tax is payable on bonds at the rate 
of Rs 0.50 for each Rs 100 of the amount secured up to Rs 1,000, and 
Rs 2.50 for each additional Rs 500. 
The definition of “bond” includes 
any instrument which obliges the maker to pay money to another, and 
either is conditional, or is not payable to bearer and is attested by a 
witness. 
A marketable debenture which is transferable by endorsement or by a 
separate instrument of transfer is taxed at the rate of Rs 0.75 for each 
Rs 100 of value up to Rs 1,000, and at Rs 3.75 for each additional Rs 500 
of value. 
A marketable debenture transferable by delivery is taxed at 
the rate of Rs 1.50 for each Rs 100 of value up to Rs 1,000, and at Rs 7.50 
for each additional Rs 500 of value. 
Exemption is provided for deben- 
tures secured by specific property transferred to trustees under a mortgage 
which has been duly stamped for the full amount of the debentures. 
Bonds, debentures, and other securities of local authorities are subject 
to a tax at a special rate of 1% of their face amount, in lieu of ordinary 
stamp tax (ISA § 8). 
~ e. MorTGcAGES. 
If the mortgagor retains possession of the property, the 
mortgage is taxed in the same manner as a bond for the amount secured 
by the mortgage (4/3.4d). 
If the mortgagor gives or agrees to give 
possession of any part of the property to the mortgagee, the mortgage is 
_ taxed in the same manner as a conveyance for consideration equal to the 
amount secured by the mortgage (4/3.4a). 
An instrument which pro- 
vides additional or substituted security for a mortgage which has already 
been stamped is taxed at the rate of Rs 0.50 for each Rs 1,000 of value. 
f. girts. 
An instrument conveying or transferring property inter vivos 
as a gift is taxed in the same manner as a conveyance for consideration 
equal to the value of the property as set forth in the instrument (4/3.4a). 
A nontestamentary disposition of property under a “settlement” is taxed

An instrument which constitutes both a declaration of trust

A gift which is not effected or evidenced by a written

g. LEASES. 
A lease or agreement to lease for a term of less than one 
year is taxed in the same manner as a bond for the total rent (4/3.4d). 
A lease or agreement for from one to three years is taxed in the same 
manner as a bond for the amount of the average annual rent. 
A lease 
or agreement for a term in excess of three years is taxed as a conveyance 
for the amount of the average annual rent (4/3.4a). 
An indefinite lease 
or agreement is taxed as a conveyance for a consideration equal to the 
amount of the average annual rent over a hypothetical 10-year term. 
If 
the lease purports to run perpetually, it is taxed as a conveyance for a 
consideration equal to one fifth of the total rent payable in the first 50 
years of the lease. 
If the lease provides for the payment of a premium, 
either in addition to or instead of rent, it is subject to tax as a convey- 
ance for consideration equal to the amount of the premium, in addition 
to any tax based on the rent. 
If an agreement to lease has been duly 
stamped, the tax on a lease executed pursuant to the agreement is limited 
to Rs 0.50. 
A sublease or an agreement to sublet is taxable in the same 
manner as a lease. 
An assignment of a lease is taxed in the same manner 
as a conveyance for the consideration received for the assignment.

Workmen’s compensation policies are taxed at the rate of

Marine insurance may not be drawn

Exemptions 
Certain documents, such as wills and other testamentary dispositions, 
and bills of exchange payable on demand, are not taxed because they 
are not included in the schedule of taxable instruments. 
Sales, mortgages, 
and other transfers of registered ships are exempted from tax by an 
express provision of the Indian Stamp Act (ISA §3). 
Instruments exe- 
cuted by, on behalf of, or in favor of the government are exempt from 
tax if the government would be liable for the duty (ISA $3). 
Certain 
other types of documents, such as agreements for the sale of goods or 
merchandise, assignments of copyrights, certain leases to cultivators, and 
certain receipts, are expressly exempted from categories of taxable docu- 
ments listed in the schedule. 
A large variety of other limited special exemptions are provided by 
other enactments—for example, agreements under the Land Acquisition 
Act of 1894, and the Indian Works of Defense Act of 1903—or by central 
or state government notifications published in the Gazette of India or 
the state gazettes (ISA $9). 
Among the latter exemptions are those 
made by certain states for instruments transferring property between 
associated companies where 90% of the shares of the transferee company 
are beneficially owned by the transferor company. 
4/3.6 
Procedure for Stamping Documents 
a. TYPES OF STAMPS. 
Most types of documents require impressed stamps, 
which are engraved or embossed on the document by revenue officials. 
However, adhesive stamps, which are purchased from licensed stamp 
dealers and affixed to the document by the parties, may be used on the 
following instruments: instruments on which the tax does not exceed 
Rs 0.10; bills of exchange drawn in sets and payable otherwise than on 
demand; bills of exchange and promissory notes made outside India; 
~ entry of an advocate or attorney on court rolls; notarial acts; transfer of 
corporate shares by endorsement; transfer of public company debentures; 
certain agreements; proxies; letters of credit; letters of allotment of shares; 
and receipts. 
Special adhesive stamps denoting the nature of the trans- 
_ action are required for certain instruments such as transfers of shares 
and debentures. 
Adhesive stamps must be canceled by one of the parties 
to the instrument; the usual method is by marking them with the party’s 
name or initials and the date of cancellation (ISA § 12). Postage stamps 
are not used in lieu of adhesive stamps. 
b. TIME FOR STAMPING. 
The Indian Stamp Act requires that documents 
be stamped at or before the time of execution (ISA $17). 
However, 
any instrument subject to tax at a rate of more than Rs 0.10, except a bill

of exchange or a promissory note, may be stamped at any time upon 
payment of the proper tax plus a fine for late stamping (ISA § 35). The 
fine may be waived for good cause (ISA § 41). An unstamped receipt 
may be admitted in evidence upon payment of a fine of one rupee 
(ISA §85(b)). 
When an unstamped bill of exchange or a promissory 
note subject to tax of Rs 0.10 or less is presented for payment, the person 
to whom it is presented may stamp it and deduct the tax from the pay- 
ment on the bill or note (ISA § 47). 
A taxable bill of exchange or promissory note executed abroad must 
be stamped before presentation for payment, endorsement, transfer, or 
other negotiation in India (ISA $19). 
Any other taxable instrument 
executed outside India must be stamped within three months after receipt 
in India (ISA § 18). Under the state acts, taxable instruments executed 
outside the state must be stamped within three months after receipt 
within the state. 
C. PERSONS RESPONSIBLE FOR STAMPING. 
The parties to a document may 
designate by agreement the person responsible for stamping it. 
In the 
absence of such an agreement, the person who draws or issues the instru- 
ment is responsible for stamping it (ISA §§ 29, 30). Any other person 
paying the tax may recover it from the person who is responsible by 
agreement or under the law (ISA § 44). 
d. RULINGS AS TO LIABILITY. 
Upon payment of a nominal fee, an instru- 
ment may be presented to the Collector for his opinion as to its liability 
to stamp tax and as to the amount of tax payable (ISA $31). 
If the 
Collector determines that no tax is payable or that tax has been fully 
paid, the instrument is endorsed to that effect (ISA § 32). Such endorse- 
ment protects the instrument from further liability to tax or fine. 
The 
Collector is not permitted to endorse any instrument taxable at Rs 0.10 
or less, any bill of exchange, or any promissory note, which is executed 
but not stamped, and is not permitted to endorse any instrument more 
than one month after execution if it was executed in India, or more than 
three months after execution if it was executed outside India (ISA § 82). 
The Collector may refer any question regarding the taxability of an 
instrument to the chief revenue officer of the state for adjudication 
(ISA § 36), and the chief revenue officer may refer the question to the 
High Court (1/1.4c) of the state (ISA $57). 
Questions of liability to 
stamp tax or penalties may also be considered by the courts in ruling. 
on the admissibility of documents in evidence (ISA § 61) 
4/3.7 
Penalties, Fines, and Sanctions 
Late stamping of documents, when permitted, is conditioned on the 
payment of a penalty in addition to the amount of tax due. 
The penalty

India 
4/4. 
127 
TAXES 
ON TRANSACTIONS 
applicable to most documents, whether taxed at ad valorem or at specific 
rates, is Rs5 or 10 times the amount of tax due, whichever is greater 
(ISA §§ 35, 40). 
Since documents not properly stamped are not admis- 
sible in evidence in civil proceedings (ISA § 35), persons to whom they 
are issued have an interest in seeing that they are properly stamped. 
Payment of a penalty for late stamping does not relieve the maker 
or issuer from liability to a fine of up to Rs500 for failure to stamp 
the document properly (ISA § 62). A fine of up to Rs 500 is also imposed 
on any person who pays or in any manner negotiates an unstamped bill 
of exchange not payable on demand, or an unstamped promissory note, 
and on any person who votes or attempts to vote under an unstamped 
proxy. 
Penalties paid for late stamping are deducted from these fines, 
however. 
Substantial fines are also provided for failure to cancel a 
stamp, for failure to give a properly stamped receipt, for failure to 
issue an insurance policy on payment of a premium, for falsely stating 
the consideration received for an instrument, and for fraud. 
If an instrument has not been properly stamped, the Collector may 
recover the tax, together with any penalties, by distress and sale of 
movable property of the person liable therefor, or by any other procedure 
available for the recovery of arrears of land revenue (ISA § 48) (3/2). 
In some states, tax may be recovered from any person who tenders the 
instrument in evidence; in others, the tax may be recovered only from 
the person primarily liable. 
4/4. 
Excise Taxes 
The Constitution allocates to the state governments the power to levy 
excise taxes on alcoholic liquors and narcotics which are not used in 
medicinal or toilet preparations. 
The power to levy excise taxes on all 
other commodities is reserved to the central government (17/1). Alcohol 
and narcotics are subject to excise taxes in all the states which have not 
-prohibited their sale (17/4.5). 
Taxes levied by the central government 
on alcohol and narcotics for medicinal purposes are collected and retained 
by the states. 
The most important excise taxes are those levied under the Central 
Excises and Salt Act of 1944 (17/1). 
Tobacco, coffee, and a variety of 
manufactured goods are taxed at specific rates. 
Tires, woolen fabrics, 
footwear, and electric batteries and parts are taxed at ad valorem rates. 
Exported goods are in general exempt. 
The central government dis- 
tributes 25% of the proceeds among the states. 
The central government 
also levies special excise taxes on a number of designated goods, prin- 
cipally to defray the cost of government activities undertaken on behalf 
of the industries producing them (17/44). 
Cotton, certain fabrics, 
vegetable oils, salt, coal and coke, coffee, rubber, and copra are among 
the commodities subject to such taxes. 
The central government also

collects but distributes among the states additional excise duties on 
certain commodities of importance in interstate trade (17/4.4). 
The various excise duties, and in particular those levied under the 
Central Excises and Salt Act, are discussed in greater detail in Chapter 17. 
4/5. 
Customs Duties 
4/5.1 
In General 
The central government levies both import and export duties under 
its constitutional allocation of tax powers.® 
These duties supplement 
export and import controls as instruments of foreign trade policy, in 
addition to their revenue function. 
The procedural provisions of the 
customs law are set forth in the Sea Customs Act of 18787 and the 
Land Customs Act of 1924. 
The rates of duty are prescribed in the 
Indian Tariff Act of 1934.8 
Exemptions and rate changes made by the Central Government under 
the Indian Tariff Act are published in the Gazette of India. 
Twice each 
year the current rates and exemptions are published by the Department 
of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics in Indian Customs 
Tariff, 
which contains the import and export tariff schedules and schedules of 
rates for central excise taxes. 
The rate schedules 
are indexed for 
convenience. 
4/5.2 
Import Tariff 
Extensive development of the import tariff occurred in the early and 
middle nineteen twenties when revenue 
duties were increased and 
protective duties first imposed. 
Increased need for revenue stimulated 
this development thereafter, 
as did the necessity for protection of 
domestic industry. 
In 1952 a permanent Tariff Commission was created 
to conduct investigations and recommend future policy on the stimula- 
tion and protection of new and existing industrial enterprises. 
The Indian Tariff Act provides for entry of certain goods from the 
United Kingdom and from certain other British territories under the 
“Commonwealth preference” at favored rates set forth in the Indian 
Customs Tariff. 
Preferential rates are also accorded to certain goods 
imported from Burma. 
Since India is a member of the General Agree- 
ment on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), duties on some commodities are 
bound in the General Agreement and have been extended to nonsigna- 
tories of GATT as well since the Indian tariff contains no “most favored 
nation” rate other than the Commonwealth preference. 
These duties

bound in GATT, as well as all other duties of a nonpreferential nature, 
are termed the “standard rate of duty” and are the ordinary rates in 
force. 
Where preferential rates are imposed, either on goods imported 
from Burma or under the Commonwealth preference, they are stated 
separately in the tariff schedule. 
a. RATES. 
The First Schedule to the Indian Tariff Act of 1934 provides 
the rates of import duty for commodities in 22 classes. 
For each com- 
modity, the duty is listed as “protective,” “revenue,” or “preferential 
revenue. 
Most of the duties are now ad valorem, although some of 
the ad valorem duties are made specific by the fixing of the tariff values 
of the commodities to which they apply. 
Specific duties are provided, 
either alone or in addition to ad valorem duties, for some commodities, 
and in certain cases the duty is the higher of the ad valorem or the 
specific duty. 
Since imported goods are not subject to the central excise 
duty (17/6.1), the import duty on certain commodities may contain an 
additional levy based on the excise tax levied on similar commodities 
manufactured or produced in India. 
The ad valorem import tariff rates are generally between 30% and 
40%. 
However, the rates are higher on certain luxury or “non-essential” 
goods and on goods produced domestically in sufficient quantity to satisfy 
demand. 
Tobacco manufactures, wines and spirits, silk garments, certain 
fabrics, spices, and motor vehicles, for example, bear rates of from 
75% 
to 200%. 
Certain food products, raw materials 
for industry, 
agricultural implements, specified types of machinery, and fuel oils are 
exempt or taxed at lower rates. 
Protective duties, such as those on 
certain forms of aluminum and zinc, coal tar dies, and certain machinery 
and parts, are imposed for a limited period specified in the tariff schedule 
and at rates recommended by the Tariff Commission (ITA §3A). 
Most 
articles produced or manufactured in Burma either are totally exempt 
from duty or are subject to duty at rates lower than 20%. 
Preferential 
duties on a few commodities manufactured or produced in the United 
Kingdom or in certain of its territories differ by only 10 percentage points 
or less from the normal ad valorem duty.® 
~b. EXEMPTIONS AND REDUCTIONS. 
The Central Government is empowered 
to exempt any commodity from the import tariff in whole or in part, 
or to fix or revise the tariff values of any commodities, by notification 
in the Gazette of India (SCA §§ 22, 23). The most important notifica- 
tions of general application which have been issued under this power 
relate to the reimportation of goods previously imported, the reimporta- 
tion of goods exported less than three years previously, and goods im-

ported by a person on change of residence. 
Baggage in use is also 
exempt from duty (SCA § 75). With the approval of the Central Govern- 
ment (1/8.1), the Central Board of Revenue or its delegate may exempt 
particular goods from import duty by special order in exceptional cases 
(SCA § 23). 
c. VALUATION. 
An ad valorem duty on goods whose value is not pre- 
scribed in the tariff schedule is based on their “real value,” defined as 
the wholesale cash price for which goods of similar kind and quality 
are sold or are capable of being sold at the time and place of importa- 
tion (SCA §30). 
If the wholesale cash price is unascertainable, the 
goods are valued at the cost at which they could be delivered at the 
place of importation. 
In a large majority of cases, real value is deter- 
mined on the latter basis. 
The amount of import duty is excluded from 
the wholesale cash price, but normal trade discounts may be deducted; 
no other deductions are permitted. 
Real value determined from the 
wholesale cash price includes the wholesaler’s or importer’s profit. 
If the 
goods are warehoused before payment of duty, tariff is computed at 
the value and rate in force on the date of removal for consumption. 
Under certain circumstances, provisional assessment may be made if 
the goods cannot readily be valued (SCA § 29B). 
d. prawsacks. 
If imported goods are re-exported or shipped as ship’s 
stores within two years, seven eighths of the duty which has been paid 
on the goods is refunded under what is called “drawback” (SCA § 42). 
In the discretion of the customs authorities, drawback may be granted 
for goods which have been in the country up to three years. 
If, between 
import and re-export, the goods are used or become components or 
ingredients in products manufactured in India, as in the case of artificial 
silk fabrics, dry cell batteries, plasticware, electric fans, leather, and 
diesel engines, drawback is allowed in accordance with notifications and 
rules issued by the Central Government. 
4/5.3 
Export Duties 
Prior to 1946 export duties were imposed from time to time at modest 
rates on a small number of commodities, principally for revenue purposes. 
After 1946 heavier duties were imposed on a greater number of com- 
modities, in part to provide additional revenue but primarily to control 
inflation, stabilize prices in the internal market, and discourage the 
export of raw materials used in Indian manufacture.!° 
More recently 
most of these duties have been reduced or abolished in order to en- 
courage exports and thereby improve India’s balance of payments in 
international trade.
