The Second Schedule of the Indian Tariff Act of 1934, reproduced 
semiannually in the Indian Customs Tariff, at present lists 21 com- 
modities which are subject to export duties either at ad valorem or at 
specific rates. 
The value of goods for ad valorem export duties is 
determined in the same manner as for import duties (4/5.2c). 
The duty 
on tea, the most important in terms of revenue collected, is imposed at 
a specific rate. 
Other commodities subject to export duty are cotton 
and cotton waste (50%), cut cloth (25%), iron and steel (45%), 
manganese ore (25%), wool (80%), jute, rice, coffee, cigarettes, and 
certain vegetable oils. 
As in the case of import duties, the Central 
Government has the power to exempt goods or to reduce rates by 
notification; thus, black pepper, iron and steel products, manganese ore, 
and vegetable oils have been exempted. 
The Central Government has 
emergency powers to levy or increase export duties by notification, 
subject to the approval of Parliament (ITA § 4A). 
In addition to the export duties levied under the Indian Tariff Act, 
certain excise duties or “cesses” are levied on exports of tea, jute, certain 
unprocessed cotton, 
lac, coffee, bones, bristles, fiber, skins, tobacco, 
raw wool, and other commodities. 
Some of these duties apply to goods 
intended for domestic consumption as well as to exported goods. 
These 
duties are set forth in the Indian Customs Tariff. 
In general, exported 
goods are exempted from the tax levied by the Central Excises and Salt 
Act of 1944 (17/6.2). 
4/5.4 
Administration and Procedure 
The administrative and procedural provisions of all acts relating to 
customs duties have now been consolidated in the Sea Customs Act of 
1878 and the Land Customs Act of 1924. Customs duties are administered 
by the Central Board of Revenue (SCA § 3(a)), which has the power 
to make rules for that purpose (SCA § 9). Collectors of customs, assisted 
~ by deputy collectors, assistant collectors, and customs officers, are ap- 
pointed by the Central Government (SCA §6) and are assigned to 
the principal ports and foreign frontiers. 
Any order or decision of a customs officer may be appealed to the 
_. Central Board of Revenue or to a customs collector authorized by the 
Central Government to hear appeals (SCA §188). 
Both the Central 
Board of Revenue and the chief customs officer of a port have the power 
to revise a decision or order of a subordinate customs officer, provided 
that any person who would be prejudiced by such a revision is given 
an opportunity to be heard (SCA § 190A). 
The Central Government 
has the ultimate power, on application of an aggrieved person, to reverse 
or modify an order or decision of a customs authority (SCA § 191).

4/6. 
The Expenditure Tax 
Since 1958 the central government has levied a tax on the personal 
expenditure of individuals and Hindu undivided families. 
Expenditure 
above a standard allowance is taxed at sharply progressive rates, up to 
a rate of 100% on taxable expenditure over Rs 50,000. 
Nonpersonal 
expenditures and basic living expenses are exempt. 
Although the ex- 
penditure tax has been classified for purposes of this chapter as a tax 
on transactions, it is imposed only on taxpayers whose income from all 
sources exceeds Rs 36,000 and is more properly regarded as supple- 
mentary to the income tax (1/8.1, 15/2.4). 
The expenditure tax is described in detail in Chapter 15.

5/1. 
Resident Individuals 
5/1.1. 
Taxability 
In general, an individual who is resident in India is taxable on his 
entire income, wherever received or accrued; a nonresident individual 
is taxable on income which accrues or is deemed to accrue or is received 
or is deemed to be received in India (11/3.1). 
There are two categories 
of resident individuals: 
1, Resident and ordinarily resident. 
Individuals who are resident and 
ordinarily resident (5/1.2) are taxable in respect of their entire income, 
wherever received or accrued (11/2.1). 
Income which has accrued to 
the taxpayer outside India prior to the base year but after 1 April 1953 
and which was not taxed to him on accrual is taxed if it is brought into 
or received in India by him during the base year (11/1.5, 11/2.2). 
2. Resident but not ordinarily resident. 
Individuals who are resident but not 
ordinarily resident are subject to the same tax liability as those who are 
resident and ordinarily resident, except that income accruing outside 
India is not taxable unless derived from a business controlled in India of 
from a profession or vocation set up in India, or unless brought into or 
received in India during the base year (11/2.1) . 
Except for the purpose of the exemption of income of foreign tech- 
nicians (5/5.5), domicile and citizenship are immaterial in determining


<!-- page 173 of 600 -->

India 
5/1.3 
137 
CLASSES 
OF 
TAXPAYERS 
liability to tax. 
The taxable income of all individuals is subject both to 
the income tax (12/1.3) and to the supertax (12/1.7). 
5/1.2 
Determination of Residence 
Residence during the base year is determined exclusively on the basis 
of one or more statutory tests (§ 4A).1 
An individual is a resident in 
any base year in which he meets any of the tests listed below. 
1. He is in India in that year for an aggregate period of 182 days or more. 
2. He maintains or has maintained for him a dwelling place in India? for 
an aggregate period of 182 days or more in that year and is also in India 
at any time in that year. 
3. He has been in India for an aggregate period of 365 days or more within 
the four preceding base years and has been in India at any time in the 
base year other than for an occasional or casual visit. 
4. He has arrived in India during the base year and the Income-tax Officer 
(1/8.5) determines that he is likely to remain there for at least three 
years from the date of his arrival. 
Because the above tests are the sole determinants of residence, an 
individual cannot be treated as resident in India if he has not been in 
the country at any time during the year. 
If any of the above tests is 
satisfied in the base year, an individual is taxable as resident for the entire 
year notwithstanding the fact that he may have entered and left India 
during the year. 
An individual who is resident in India in any year is also “ordinarily 
resident” in that year unless he has been a resident in less than nine of 
the ten immediately preceding base years or has been in India for an 
aggregate period of not more than 730 days during the seven immediately 
preceding base years (§ 4B(a) ).? 
5/1.3 
Married Persons 
The incomes of husband and wife are not aggregated for tax purposes; 
each spouse is separately assessed on his or her own income. However, 
a husband is subject to tax on the income of his wife which arises from 
her membership in a firm of which her husband is a partner (6/8.6), 
and on income from assets transferred to or for the benefit of the wife

otherwise than for adequate consideration 
or in connection with a 
separation agreement (6/8.5). 
A wife who is resident in India may be 
taxed on remittances received by her out of any part of the income of 
her nonresident husband which is not included in his total income 
($ 4(2)). 
5/1.4 
Minors and Other Incapacitated Persons 
Individuals under 18 years of age and individuals of unsound mind 
are treated as incapacitated persons for tax purposes. 
The person or 
committee having the direction, control, or management of the property 
or affairs of an incapacitated person is assessable in the same manner 
as the incapacitated person would be assessed if he were of full capacity, 
and is responsible for the filing of returns and the payment of tax on 
behalf of the incapacitated person ($§ 40, 41). 
If two or more bene- 
ficiaries are entitled to share income from the same source, the guardian 
is subject to tax on each share at the rates applicable to each beneficiary.* 
The income of the incapacitated person and the tax thereon are cal- 
culated in the same manner as if he were not incapacitated. 
The income of a minor is not included in the total income of his 
parent except where such income results from a partnership of which 
his father is a member or from assets transferred to the minor by the 
father otherwise than for adequate consideration (6/8.5). 
5/2. 
Resident Corporations 
5/2.1 
Taxability 
A corporation (“company”) 
is subject to a flat rate of income tax 
(12/2.1) and a flat basic rate of supertax. 
However, the effective rates 
of supertax are reduced by certain rebates granted in the annual Finance 
Acts on dividends received by a corporation from a subsidiary and on 
the income of a corporation whose total income is less than Rs 25,000. 
Increased rates are applicable to foreign corporations which have not 
made arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends in 
India (12/2.4). 
Closely held corporations are subject to a special super- 
tax on undistributed profits (12/2.7). 
There is a special tax at graduated 
rates on dividends exceeding specified percentages of “paid up” capital, 
but the tax is expected to be discontinued as a separate tax in the year 
1960-1961, when the rates of income tax and supertax are to be adjusted 
so as to combine its net incidence with that of the income and wealth 
taxes on corporations.’

A resident corporation is taxable on its entire income 
wherever received or accrued; a nonresident corporation is taxable only 
on income received in India or derived from India (11/3.1). 
A corpora- 
tion which is resident in India is also treated as ordinarily resident 
there (§ 4B(c)); and a corporation therefore does not qualify for the 
special treatment of foreign income accorded to persons resident but not 
ordinarily resident in India (5/1.1). 
Corporate profits on which the corporation has paid income tax are 
not at present subjected to income tax again when distributed to the 
shareholders as dividends, since the shareholders receive a credit for 
the income tax which the corporation is deemed to have paid on their 
behalf (9/2.4a). 
Both the corporation and its shareholders must pay 
supertax. 
Under the new method of dividend taxation enacted in 1959, 
distributions of corporate profits which are assessed in the tax year 
1960-1961 or thereafter will be subjected to both income tax and super- 
tax in the hands of the shareholders, without any credit for taxes paid 
by the corporation; the corporation will continue to be liable, as now, 
for income tax and supertax on the distributed income (9/2.4b). 
5/2.2 
Entities Treated as Corporations for Tax Purposes 
The entities listed below are treated as corporations for tax purposes 
(§ 2(5A) ). 
1. A corporation formed and registered under Indian law and having its 
registered office in India (“Indian company”). 
2. Any association (5/3.3), whether or not incorporated, which was taxed 
or taxable as a corporation for the tax year 1947-1948. 
8. Any association, whether or not incorporated and whether or not carry- 
ing on business in India, which is declared by the Central Board of 
Revenue to be a corporation for income tax purposes. 
Under the above rules, a foreign corporation which was not taxed 
or taxable as a corporation for the tax year 1947-1948 is treated as an 
association, and is taxable in the same manner as an unregistered partner- 
ship (5/3.3), rather than as a corporation, unless the Central Board of 
Revenue declares it to be a corporation for tax purposes. 
The decision 
that a foreign company or an unincorporated association shall be taxed 
as a corporation is discretionary with the Central Board of Revenue, and 
is not a matter of right. 
A foreign corporation in which the public is 
substantially interested (12/2.7a) will generally be taxed as a corporation. 
The separate identity of affiliated corporations is recognized for tax 
purposes. 
Two affiliated corporations must file separate returns and 
cannot be taxed as one taxpayer even if one owns all the shares of the

Determination of Residence 
A corporation formed and registered under Indian law is resident in 
India. 
A foreign corporation is resident in India in any year if the 
control and management of its affairs are situated wholly in India in 
that year (§4A(c)).7 
Since the tests of residence are different for 
corporations and for unincorporated associations, the determination of 
residence of a foreign corporation may be affected by the fact that it 
is treated as an association.

5/3.1 
Partnerships 
A partnership is a taxable entity, although the method and quantum 
of taxation differ depending upon whether or not the firm is registered 
under the Income-tax Act. A firm will be registered if it complies with 
the conditions listed below (§ 26A; Rules 2-6B). 
1. There must be a valid partnership in existence, constituted under an 
instrument of partnership which specifies the individual shares of the 
partners. 
2. An application for registration under the Income-tax Act must be filed 
on the prescribed form within the time limit specified in the Rules.

4. The application must be signed by all partners (other than minors) and 
must furnish the name and address of each partner, the date of his ad- 
mission to the partnership, amounts paid him as interest on capital or 
loans, his salary or commissions from the firm, and the amount of his 
share of the profits of the firm. 
Registration is effective only for a single base year; to continue in force 
in subsequent years, it must be renewed annually on or before 30 June. 
If a partnership is subject to assessment on an estimated basis, the 
Income-tax Officer may refuse to register it or may cancel its registration 
if it is already registered (13/2.2). 
a. REGISTERED PARTNERSHIPS. 
A registered partnership, whether resident 
or nonresident, is subject to income tax on its profits at special low rates 
(12/3.1), and is not subject to supertax. 
The income of the partnership 
which is subject to the low rate of income tax is its income before deduc- 
tion of remuneration payable to the partners. 
Each partner is required 
to include in his taxable income remuneration payable to him by the firm 
in respect of the base year, plus his share of the profit of the firm as 
reduced by interest and remuneration payable to the partners in respect 
of that year (§ 16(1)(b)). 
Each partner’s pro rata share of the income 
tax payable by the firm is exempt from income tax (§ 14(2)(aa)) but 
must be included in total income (§ 16(1)(a)); for supertax purposes, 
the partner is exempt from tax only on that part of the firm’s income tax 
which is attributable to its nonbusiness income (§ 14(2)(aa), Proviso). 
If the firm has sustained a loss, a pro rata share of the loss is treated as a 
loss of each partner, to be set off against his other income or carried 
forward (7/4.1). 
The effect of this treatment of a registered firm is 
to tax the firm only at the special low rate of income tax and to treat 
each partner as if he had received his pro rata share of the firm’s income 
as reduced by his share of the tax borne by the firm. 
b. UNREGISTERED PARTNERSHIPS. 
An unregistered partnership is treated 
as a taxable entity, and income tax and supertax are levied upon the firm 
at the rates applicable to a single individual (§§ 3, 23(5), 55). A part- 
ner in an unregistered firm is not taxable on his share of profits of the 
firm on which the firm has paid tax, whether or not such profits have 
been distributed (§§ 14(2)(a), 55). 
However, each partner’s share of 
the profits must be included in his total income for the purpose of deter- 
mining the rates of income tax and supertax on his other income 
($§ 16(1)(a), 56). 
If the firm has been subjected to tax at a rate higher 
than that applicable to a partner’s individual income, the partner is not 
entitled to a refund. 
A partner in an unregistered firm is not entitled to 
the benefit of losses sustained by the firm (7/4.1). 
If taxing each partner

¢, RESIDENCE OF A PARTNERSHIP. 
Unlike a corporation, a partnership is 
resident in India unless the control and management of its affairs are situ- 
ated wholly outside India (§ 4A(b)). 
Hence, if any member of the firm 
is resident in India and actually manages and controls the firm’s business 
there, the firm will be resident in India notwithstanding the fact that the 
majority of the partners and the major portion of the partnership business 
are outside India.13 
However, a partnership will not be treated as resi- 
dent in India solely by virtue of the fact that a partner who has a legal 
right to participate in the control of the firm is resident in India; the 
control and management test requires that there be actual participation 
in the management of the firm’s business.'* 
As in the case of a corpora- 
tion, a partnership which is resident in India is also treated as ordinarily 
resident in India (§ 4B(c)), and a partnership therefore cannot take 
advantage of the special treatment of foreign income accorded to per- 
sons resident but not ordinarily resident in India (5/1.1). 
If a partnership, registered or unregistered, is resident in India, its total 
world income is subject to tax (11/2.1) notwithstanding the fact that 
some of the partners may be nonresident. 
A nonresident partner of a 
resident registered firm is required to include in his total income his 
proportionate share of the firm’s income without regard to the source 
of that income; 
the tax payable by him is assessed on the firm 
(§ 23(5) 
(a) (ii) ). 
A resident unregistered firm is taxed directly without regard to the 
residence status of its members. 
5/3.2 
Hindu Undivided Families 
The income of a Hindu undivided family (1/3.1) is assessed on the 
family as if it were the income of a married individual with the same 
number of dependent children as the number of minor members of the 
undivided family (12/3.2). 
The individual members of the family are 
not taxed on any of the family income which may be distributed to them 
(§ 14(1)), but only on income earned or received by them which does 
not belong to the joint family. On the total or partial partition of a Hindu 
undivided family, the share which each member receives is a capital 
receipt,!® the profit from which is not subject to tax as capital gain» 
(9/8.6).

A Hindu undivided family is resident in India unless the control and 
management of its affairs are situated wholly outside of India (§ 4A(b) ). 
If the control and management of its affairs are situated either wholly 
or partially in India, the Hindu undivided family is ordinarily resident 
if its manager is ordinarily resident; if its manager is either not resident 
or resident but not ordinarily resident, the family is resident but not ordi- 
narily resident (§ 4B(b)). The manager, called the “Karta,” is the father, 
or, if the father is dead, the eldest son. 
5/3.3 
Other Associations of Persons 
An “association of persons” is taxable as a separate entity (§ 3) and is 
subject to income tax and supertax under the same conditions and at 
the same rates as an unregistered partnership (5/3.1b). 
An association 
of persons is any combination of persons formed for the promotion of a 
joint enterprise and either not intended by the associates to constitute 
a partnership or not satisfying all the requirements of a valid partner- 
ship.17 
There must, however, be some community of action for the 
production of income. 
Thus, the ownership of property by tenants in 
common does not, of itself, give rise to an association 
of persons 
($9(3)),18 unless the interests of the cotenants are managed by an 
agent for all of them.'® 
Coheirs or colegatees joining together in a 
common income-producing purpose ?® are taxable as associations 
of 
persons. 
Cotrustees?! and coexecutors ** are taxable 
as associations 
of persons, with the result that a trust or estate is treated as a unit with- 
out regard to the number of fiduciaries. 
A partnership which is formed 
for an illegal object or which is otherwise in contravention of the law 
cannot be taxed as a partnership, since it is not a valid partnership, but 
is taxable as an association of persons.”? 
A member of an association is not taxable on his share of the profits of 
the association on which tax has already been paid by the association 
(§§ 14(2)(b), 55); but the amount of the share must be included in his 
total income (§§ 16(1)(a), 56). 
Losses of an association may be set 
off against profits of the association; but there is no provision, as in the 
case of a registered partnership, for setting them off against other income 
of the individual members. 
The residence of an association of persons 
is determined in the same manner as that of an unregistered partnership 
(§§4A(b), 4B(c) )(5/3.1c).

5/3.4 
Cooperatives 
Cooperative societies are taxable as associations of persons (5/ 3.3) and 
are subject to special rates of supertax (12/3.1). 
All cooperative societies 
except cooperative insurance societies are exempt on certain types of 
income (5/5.10). 
5/3.5 
Mutual Organizations 
In principle, no income is derived by a mutual concern which does 
business exclusively with its customer-members, as it is considered that 
the members of such a concern cannot derive a profit from “dealing with 
themselves.” 24 
In order for an organization to be exempt under this 
principle, there must be a complete identity between the contributors 
to the common fund and the persons who are entitled to participate 
in its surplus.?° 
Notwithstanding the general principle that no profit is derived from 
mutual trading, the income of a mutual insurance association is required 
to be computed in the same manner as is that of a nonmutual insurance 
business (10/3) and is taxable accordingly (§ 2(6C)); and the profits 
of a trade, professional, or similar association performing services for its 
members for remuneration related to those services are also taxable as 
business profits (§ 10(6)). 
For this purpose, a trade association is an 
association of businessmen for the protection or advancement of their 
common interests.2° 
Mutual insurance associations and trade associa- 
tions are taxable only because their liability to tax is specifically pre- 
scribed by statute. 
In view of the general principle discussed above, 
other mutual associations are not subject to tax on their mutual income. 
5/3.6 
Local Authorities 
A local authority is a person for purposes of taxation (§ 2(9)), but is 
taxable only on its income derived from the business of supplying a com- 
modity beyond its jurisdictional area (5/5.15). 
A local authority is any 
municipal committee, district board, body of port commissioners, or other 
authority legally entitled to, or entrusted by the government with, the 
control or management.of a municipal or local fund.27

5/3.7 
Trusts 
Except as noted below, the trustees of a trust are subject to tax on 
income receivable by them on behalf of the beneficiaries of the trust, 
and not attributed to the settlor (6/8), in the same manner and to the 
same amount as the beneficiaries would be taxed if the assessments were 
made directly on them (§ 41(1)). When the trustees are taxable under 
this provision, the measure of their liability is the liability of each bene- 
ficiary, even as to income assessable under section 10 from a business 
carried on by the trustees on behalf of the beneficiaries; 28 and the rates 
to be applied are the individual rates applicable separately to the total 
income of each beneficiary after taking into account the beneficiary’s 
exemptions, 
deductions, and personal allowances. 
No deduction 
is 
allowed for expenses of trust administration. 
When any part of the income of a trust is not specifically receivable 
on behalf of any one person, or when the individual shares of the 
beneficiaries are indeterminate or unknown, the trustee is taxable on that 
part of the income at the “maximum rate” of income tax (§ 41(1)) 
(12/1.3a) and at the normal rate of supertax applicable to one indi- 
vidual.”® 
In this event, the residence of the trustee would be relevant 
to the determination of his tax liability, whereas only the residence of 
each beneficiary is relevant in cases where the trustee is assessed in the 
same manner and to the same amount as the beneficiaries. 
Income is 
“not specifically receivable on behalf of any one person” if it is to be 
accumulated for a class of beneficiaries who have not been ascertained, 
or for designated beneficiaries subject to a contingency which has not 
yet occurred.*® 
The shares of the beneficiaries are “indeterminate or 
unknown” where the amounts or proportions of the income to be dis- 
tributed among the beneficiaries are discretionary with the trustee,*! 
even if the trustee actually distributes the income to the beneficiaries 
during the year in which it is earned. 
Notwithstanding the above provisions, the government has the option 
to assess tax upon the trust beneficiaries for the income which each 
receives or is entitled to receive from the trust, rather than upon the 
trustee (§ 41(2)); but if the trustee has been assessed and has paid tax 
on the trust income, that income cannot be taxed again to the beneficiary.

Decedents' Estates 
The executor, administrator, or other legal representative of a deceased 
person is liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased any tax payable 
by the deceased or which would have been payable by him if he had 
not died (§ 24B(1)). 
Coexecutors

5/4. 
Nonresidents 
5/4.1 
Individuals 
An individual is nonresident if he does not satisfy any of the four tests 
of residence set out at 5/1.2. The question of ordinary residence does not 
arise with respect to a nonresident inasmuch as a taxpayer must first be 
resident in order to be ordinarily resident.? 
A nonresident is taxable 
only in respect of income which accrues or is deemed to accrue in India 
or is received or deemed to be received in India (11/3.1). 
Income tax 
and supertax payable by a nonresident are computed at special rates, 
unless the taxpayer elects to be taxed at rates based on his total world 
income (11/3.5, 12/4), and must be withheld at source as described 
at 11/3.3. 
The Income-tax Officer may designate as agent for a non- 
resident any person who is employed by him or on his behalf, or who 
has a business connection with him, or through whom the nonresident 
is in receipt of income; the person so designated is personally liable to 
tax in respect of the nonresident’s income (11/3.4). 
A wife who is resident in India may be taxed on remittances received 
by her of any part of the income of her nonresident husband which is not 
included in his total income (§ 4(2)). 
5/4.2 
Change of Residence 
An individual who enters or leaves the country in the course of any 
base year during which he has met any of the tests of residence (5/1.2) 
is taxable as a resident in respect of his total income both from within 
and from without India for the whole year, without the benefit of appor- 
tionment on the basis of the part of the year for which he was actually 
resident in India. 
5/4.3

A temporary visitor is taxable as any other resident if he meets any 
of the tests of residence.

Corporations 
A corporation is nonresident if it does not meet any of the tests of 
residence set forth at 5/2.3. 
As in the case of nonresident individuals, a 
nonresident corporation 
is taxable only in respect of income which 
accrues or is deemed to accrue in India or is received or deemed to be 
received in India (11/3.1). 
Payments of income to a nonresident cor- 
poration are subject to deduction of tax at source as explained at 11/3.3, 
and a statutory agent may be made vicariously liable for the tax of a 
nonresident corporation as explained at 11/3.4. 
Dividends received by

practice nonresident shareholders 
are not subjected to tax on such

Instead, foreign corporations which have not made pre- 
scribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends in 
India are subject to supertax at a rate higher than the normal corporate 
rate (12/2.4). 
5/4.5 
Status of Branches 
A branch maintained in India by a foreign corporation is not a sepa- 
rate taxable entity distinct from the head office. 
A foreign corporation 
which is not controlled and managed in India does not become resident 
in India solely by virtue of the maintenance of a branch there. 
However, 
the maintenance of an Indian branch would normally constitute a “busi- 
ness connection” in India so that all profits arising directly or indirectly 
from that connection which could reasonably be attributed to the opera- 
tions carried on in India would be deemed to be from an Indian source 
(11/3.6a). The profits of a branch are accounted for as explained at 6/7. 
5/4.6 
Other Nonresidents 
Nonresident partnerships, associations, and other classes of taxpayers 
are taxable in the same manner as nonresident corporations (5/4.4). 
They are taxed at special rates, unless they elect to be taxed at rates 
based on their total world income (12/4).

of tax at source from income paid to nonresidents (11/3.3), for assess-

5/5.1 
Diplomatic Representatives and Employees of Foreign Governments 
Ambassadors of foreign states, envoys, ministers, chargés d affaires, 
secretaries, attachés, and foreign consular representatives (consuls gen- 
eral, consuls, vice-consuls, or consul agents) are exempt from tax on their 
official remuneration (§ 4(3) («) ). 
The official salary of any other official representative of a foreign 
government is exempt provided a reciprocal exemption is accorded rep- 
resentatives 
of the Indian government by the country represented 
(§ 4(3)(x)). 
The official salary of a member of the staff of any of 
the above officials is exempt if the staff member is a national of the 
country represented and is not engaged in any business, profession, voca- 
tion, or employment in India other than as a member of the staff. 
How- 
ever, the official salary of a member of the staff of a nondiplomatic 
representative is exempt only if, in addition, the country represented 
accords a reciprocal exemption to the staff members of similar represent- 
atives of the Indian government ($4(8)(x)). 
The official salaries of 
certain personnel of the United Nations and specialized agencies of the 
United Nations are also exempt.*® 
All of the above mentioned persons, and their wives, are exempt from 
the requirement of presenting tax clearance certificates on departure 
from India, except that members of the staffs of diplomatic envoys, con- 
sular officials, and trade commissioners are exempt from this requirement 
only if they are nationals of the country represented, are full-time em- 
ployees of the government of that country, and are not engaged in a 
private occupation for gain in India.*¢ 
The remuneration received from a foreign government by personnel 
of cooperative technical assistance programs or projects may be exempted 
by the agreement under which the service is rendered; the foreign income 
of such personnel, and of members of their families who accompany 
them to India, is exempt if it is not deemed to accrue in India and if 
it is subject to income tax or social security tax by the government em- 
ploying them (§ 4(3) (xv) ).

on in India.

mediately preceding the year of his arrival in India.

Pension Funds 
Income from the investments or deposits of a pension fund (“super-

Approval may be given only if all

1. The fund must be established under an irrevocable trust in connection

2. The sole purpose of the fund must be the provision of annuities for em- 
ployees of the business, or, upon the death of an employee or a former 
employee, for his widow, children, or dependents. 
3. The annuities must commence upon the death 
or retirement of the 
employees at or after a specified age, or upon their becoming incapacitated 
prior to retirement. 
4, The employer must be a contributor to the fund. 
In practice, the Central Board of Revenue also requires that the fund 
and the trustees be located in India, that all pensions be payable only 
in India, that there be no provision for commutation of pensions, ands 
that the employer's contribution not exceed 25% of the employee’s 
salary during the year.

withstanding the fact that contributions to it may be returned in certain 
contingencies; or that the provision of annuities is not the sole purpose

6/1. 
Concept of Taxable Income 
6/1.1 
Income Defined 
While the Income-tax Act enumerates sources of income and prescribes 
methods of computing income from the various sources, income as such 
is not defined. 
It has been said that “anything which can properly be 
described as income is taxable under the Act unless expressly exempted.” 1 
The Act also specifically includes in the term “income” certain items 
which might not otherwise be regarded 
as income. 
The most im+ 
portant of these items are capital gains (9/8), the profits of a mutual 
insurance association (5/3.5), benefits not convertible into money which 
are obtained from a company by a director or other person with a sub- 
1 Gopal Saran Narain Singh v. C.1.T. (1935) 3 L.T.R. 237 (P.C.).


<!-- page 193 of 600 -->

India 
6/1.1 
157 
DETERMINATION 
OF INCOME 
stantial interest in the company 
(8/1.6), cancellation of previously 
deducted indebtedness, and bad debt recoveries (7/6.1). 
A receipt may be taxable as income, even if it contains no element of 
profit or gain, if it has the quality of income. 
Thus, annuity installments 
are taxable as income even though part of the aggregate potential amount 
of the installments represents the price paid for the annuity, because the 
annuitant is considered to have relinquished his capital in exchange for 
an income right (9/3.2). 
In the case of income from a trade or business, 
only the “profits or gains” are taxable. 
While there is no provision for 
determination of gross income from business and deduction therefrom 
of cost of goods sold, the computation of business profits necessarily 
involves deduction of that cost (7/1.2). 
Generally, income must be in the form of money or something capable 
of being converted into money, although in certain instances specified 
by statute nonmonetary benefits may be taxed as income.2 
A check 
is the equivalent of cash,? but a promissory note of the debtor is not 
income when received unless the creditor employs the accrual method 
of accounting.* 
The Act requires that “income, profits, and gains” are to be taxed 
under one of six “heads” or categories (6/1.2). 
None of these categories 
provides any all-inclusive definition of what constitutes taxable income 
thereunder, and the categories are sufficiently broad to encompass any 
receipt or benefit which might fall within a generalized concept of 
income. 
Thus, with one exception, no item which is conceptually income 
would escape tax under one or another of the designated categories. 
The 
sole exception is rental income from improved real property, which is 
not taxable as such because the taxation of presumed income under the 
category “income from property” exhausts the taxability of that income 
(9/42). 
“Total income” is the sum of the taxpayer’s income under all the cate- 
gories, exclusive of certain exempt receipts which are not included in total 
income 
(6/1.4a), and reduced by deduction of certain expenditures 
incurred in earning total income (6/1.5). 
In effect, total income is 
used for determining the rates of income tax and supertax (12/1.8, 
12/1.6) and for the application of personal allowances (12/1.2a). 
In- 
come which is actually subject to tax is total income reduced by certain 
other exemptions (6/1.4b) and deductions (6/1.5). The term “taxable 
income,” although correctly applicable to this quantity, is not used in 
India because income tax and supertax are computed by applying the 
appropriate rates of tax to total income and then reducing the tax by 
that proportion of it which the exemptions and deductions to be sub-

tracted from total income bear to total income (12/1.4, 12/1.7). 
How- 
ever, the resulting tax is the same as if the rates were applied to “taxable 
income” as defined above. 
The term “gross income,” which would be 
correctly applicable to the amount from which expenditures incurred 
in earning total income are deducted in arriving at total income (6/1.5), 
is not used in India because income in each category is added to total 
income only after the expenditures allowable against that category have 
been deducted. 
“Total income” of a resident comprises all income wherever received 
or accrued; “total income” of a nonresident does not include incorne 
received and accrued outside India unless it is deemed to have been 
received or to have accrued in India (11/3.1). 
A nonresident is ordi- 
narily taxed on his taxable income at special rates, but a nonresident other 
than a corporation may elect to be taxed on his taxable income at rates 
determined by reference to his “total world income,” that is, his income 
wherever received or accrued (11/3.5). 
6/1.2 
Categories of Income 
Income is taxable under the “heads” or categories listed below (§ 6). 
. Salaries (8/1). 
. Interest on securities (9/1.2). 
. Income from property (9/4.2). 
. Profits and gains of business, profession, or vocation (7/1). 
. Income from other sources. 
. Capital gains (9/8). 
Owr 
ONE 
“Income from other sources” (item 5) is a residual category which 
includes dividends (9/2), income from miscellaneous services (8/3), 
annuities (9/3), nonagricultural rents and profits derived noncommer- 
cially from unimproved lands (9/4.5), interest, other than interest on 
securities, not received in the course of business (9/1.3), and royalties 
derived noncommercially from the leasing or licensing of income-pro- 
ducing assets (9/5). 
The function of the division of income into categories is merely to pre- 
scribe the rules applicable to the computation of taxable income of each 
particular type. 
Taxable income from all sources is reported on a single 
return, and only one assessment is made of income under all categories. 
6/1.3 
Exclusions 
The principal receipts which are nontaxable because they are not con- 
sidered to be income are gifts and bequests, the lump sum proceeds of 
endowment life insurance policies, death benefits under ordinary life 
policies, and amounts which represent a mere replacement of capital,

such as reimbursement of cost of goods sold or repayment of a debt, even 
if paid in installments (9/3.3). 
Although capital gains are not considered income under general prin- 
ciples, a specific provision of the Income-tax Act renders such gains tax- 
able if they arise from the sale, exchange, relinquishment, or transfer of a 
capital asset (9/8.1). 
However, as noted at 9/8.6, certain capital gains 
are specifically exempt from taxation. 
Casual and nonrecurring receipts are specifically excluded from income 
if they do not arise from a business or profession, are not by way of 
addition to the remuneration of an employee, and are not taxable as 
capital gains (§ 4(2)(vii)). 
This exclusion, available only in unusual 
circumstances, would apply to such receipts as lottery prizes, gambling 
winnings, and certain types of compensation for miscellaneous services 
(8/3.1). 
A benefit which is not convertible into money or money’s worth is 
not, conceptually, income, and is excluded from income except where 
rendered specifically taxable by the Income-tax Act, as in the case of 
“perquisites” in lieu of or in addition to salary (8/1.6), income of a mutual 
insurance business, and income of a professional or trade association 
(5/3.5). 
6/1.4 
Tax-exempt Income 
As explained in 5/5, certain classes of persons are exempt from tax 
on some or all types of income. 
In addition, certain types of income are 
specifically exempt from tax regardless of the classification of the tax- 
payer. 
Some types of exempt income are wholly excluded from the com- 
putation of the total income (6/1.1) which determines personal allow- 
ances and rates of tax. 
Other types of income, while exempt from tax 
themselves, are included in total income. 
Income which is exempted 
from tax by any provision of the Income-tax Act is normally not included 
in total income in the absence of an express requirement in the Act.® 
Most but not all of the exemptions in each category apply both to income 
tax and to supertax.

of employment (8/1.4).

Deductions 
In general, expenditures in producing gross income are deductible 
therefrom in determining total income. 
Losses under any of the cate- 
gories of income (6/1.2) may be set off against income in any other 
category which is taxable in the.same year (§ 24(1)) except that a loss 
sustained in speculative transactions in the nature of a business may be 
set off only against profits of a similar business, and capital losses may 
be set off only against capital gains (7/4.1). 
The amounts of deductible 
expenses, depreciation allowances, and losses are. deducted from gross 
income in determining total income for both income tax and supertax 
purposes. 
Certain expenditures which are not related to the production of income 
are deductible in determining income subject to tax, but are not deduct- 
ible in determining total income for rate purposes. 
Such deductions are 
made by reducing the tax payable on total income by that proportion 
which the deductible expenditure bears to total income (12/1.4, 12/1.6). 
Certain life insurance and annuity premiums, employee contributions to 
pension and provident funds, and charitable donations are deductible 
in this manner. 
a. EXPENSES. 
In determining total income, the taxpayer is permitted to 
deduct certain designated types of expenses incurred by him in earning 
salaries (8/1.9), business income (7/2), interest on securities (9/1.2), 
dividends (9/2.1), or presumed income from property (9/4.4). 
For each of the categories of income, there is also a general provision 
authorizing the deduction of expenses incurred in earning income of that 
category; but these provisions vary in their requirements as to the rela- 
tionship between the expense and the income earned. 
Thus, the taxpayer 
may deduct his “reasonable” expenses incurred in realizing interest on 
securities 
(9/1.2), expenditures “incurred solely in connection with” 
the disposition of a capital asset on which he realizes capital gain (9/8.7), 
and any noncapital and nonpersonal expenses “incurred solely for the 
purpose of” earning “income from other sources” (9/1.3). 
Under the

provision which permits the deduction from business or professional 
income of any expense “wholly and exclusively for the purpose of” his 
business or profession, he may deduct not only the cost of earning par- 
ticular business receipts but the cost of maintaining or improving the 
general earnings prospects of his business (7/2.14). 
The expenses which 
he may deduct from his salary, however, are limited to amounts which 
the terms of his employment require him to spend out of his remunera- 
tion and which are expended “wholly, necessarily and exclusively in 
the performance of his duties” (8/1.9).* 
In general, interest payable outside India is not deductible 
as an 
expense of earning interest on securities (9/1.2) or as an expense of bor- 
rowing capital for business purposes (7/2.5a), or as an annual charge 
on property whose presumed income is taxed (9/4.4), unless the tax 
on the interest has been withheld or paid in advance or can be collected 
from a statutory agent (11/3.4). 
Interest or salaries payable outside 
India are deductible from “income from other sources” only if the tax 
is withheld or paid in advance; the availability of a statutory agent is 
irrelevant (9/1.3). 
Except for a statutory allowance for repairs which is made against 
presumed income from buildings (9/4.4), the amounts deductible under 
the foregoing provisions are actual expenses so long as they are rea- 
sonable. 
b. DEPRECIATION. 
Depreciation is granted only for buildings, machinery, 
plant, or furniture owned by the taxpayer and used in his business 
(7/3.1b), for machinery, plant, or furniture which the taxpayer leases 
in return for “income from other sources” (9/4.5), or for an automobile 
owned by the taxpayer and used by him for purposes of his employ- 
ment (8/1.9). 
A “development rebate” of a percentage of the cost of 
certain new assets is also allowed as a business deduction in the year 
of acquisition (10/6.4). 
C. EXPENDITURES FOR LIFE INSURANCE, ANNUITIES, AND EMPLOYEE BENE- 
Fits. 
In determining income subject to income tax, the taxpayer may 
deduct insurance premiums paid by him for policies on his life or that 
of his spouse, up to 10% of the amount of the insurance; he may also 
deduct premiums paid by him for a deferred annuity for him or his 
spouse (§ 15). However, such amounts are not deductible in determin- 
ing total income for rate purposes and are not deductible in determining 
income subject to supertax (§$16(1)(a), 58). 
Contributions by an 
employee to an approved pension fund (8/1.5b) 
or to a recognized 
provident fund (8/1.5c) are treated in the same way.

d. CHARITABLE DONATIONS. 
In determining income subject to income 
tax, all taxpayers are permitted to deduct donations made to institutions 
or funds established in India for charitable purposes (§15B). 
Such 
donations are not deductible, however, in determining total income for 
rate purposes (§16(1)(a)). 
They are deductible in determining in-

17(3)). 
A donation is not deductible unless the institution or fund to which 
it is made is entitled to the exemption granted for the income of char-

(5/5.7), maintains regular accounts, and does not 
limit its purposes to those of any particular religious community, and 
in addition either (1) is a recognized charitable or educational institu- 
tion, (2) is registered under the Societies Registration Act of 1860 or 
under the Indian Companies Act, or (3) is financed wholly or in part 
by the central government, a state government, or a local authority 
($ 15B(2)). 
The aggregate of the taxpayer's donations must exceed Rs 250, and the 
amount deductible is limited to 5% of the taxpayer's total income, as 
reduced by other amounts exempt from tax, or Rs 100,000, whichever is 
less. 
The reduction of tax under this provision is limited to one half of 
the amount of the deduction allowed (§ 15B(8)). 
6/2. 
Books end Records 
6/2.1 
Laws Relating to Books and Records 
The Income-tax Act does not require that any books or records be 
maintained by a taxpayer, or if maintained, that they be in any particular 
form. 
However, the general law relating to corporations requires that 
a company incorporated in India keep proper books of account regarding 
its receipts and expenditures, sales and purchases, and assets and liabili- 
ties, and requires that the accounts be sufficient to give “a true and fair 
view” of the corporation’s affairs and to explain its transactions. 
The 
company law further sets forth in detail the principles and procedures 
to be followed in the preparation of a corporation’s annual balance sheet 
and profit and loss account.” 
The Income-tax Officer may require any taxpayer to deliver copies 
of any existing accounts relating to its business or to make available for 
inspection the books, accounts, and documents containing information 
as to transactions of the business (13/2.1). 
If such records do not exist,

Officer may estimate the taxpayer's liability, placing upon the taxpayer

6/2.2 
Weight to be Given to Book Entries 
While it is generally considered that the profits of a trade or profession 
are to be determined in accordance with “ordinary commercial prin- 
ciples,” nondeductible expenditures must be added back (7/5), and 
depreciation must be adjusted to conform to the statutory allowances 
(7/3). Accounts properly maintained in the ordinary course of business 
are generally accepted as evidence of the taxpayer’s transactions, but 
additional proof may be required if the accounts are incomplete or there 
is reason to suspect fraud (6/9.1). 
6/2.3 
Registration of Books 
There is no provision for the registration of books under the Indian 
Income-tax Act. 
But under section 125 of the Companies Act of 1956, 
companies are required to register with the Registrar of Companies all 
mortgages and charges on their assets. 
6/3. 
Accounting Periods 
6/3.1. 
Tax Year 
Each tax year (referred to as “financial year” or “assessment year” ) 
begins on 1 April and ends on the succeeding 31 March. 
Tax is levied 
for each tax year, at rates prescribed in the Finance Act for that tax year, 
upon income of the “previous year” (herein called “base year”). 
Thus, 
the tax assessment made in any tax year is upon the income of the base 
year; this income is both the measure and the subject of the tax.19 
How- 
ever, the annual Finance Acts provide for the application of the rates 
in force for the preceding tax year in determining income tax and super- 
tax on salaries, and in determining income tax on interest on securities 
and on dividends (12/1.3a). 
The law applicable to the assessment for any tax year is that in force 
at the beginning of that year, so that any changes brought into effect on 
or before 1 April operate retroactively as to income already earned in 
the base year; 
but any nonretrospective amendment which comes into 
effect after 1 April of a particular tax year cannot apply to that year,

unless the amendment is construed as procedural.!® 
Since the subject 
of the tax is the income of the base year, the assessment must be made 
in accordance with the facts as they existed during the base year, and 
not on the basis of the facts existing during the tax year. 
This system 
is in contrast to that under United Kingdom law, where the subject of 
the tax is the income of the tax year although the measure of the tax 
may be income of the preceding base year. 
6/3.2 
Base Year 
The base year is normally the 12-month period ending on the 31 March 
immediately preceding the tax year, or the 12-month accounting period 
ending within the preceding tax year (§ 2(11)(i)(a)). 
The use of an 
accounting period which ends on some date other than 31 March is op- 
tional with the taxpayer, except with respect to income from salaries 
(8/1), interest on securities (9/1.2), and presumed income from real 
property (9/4)(§$13). 
For example, if a taxpayer maintains his busi- 
ness accounts on a calendar year basis, his base year for the 1959-1960 
tax year would normally be the period from 1 April 1958 to 81 March 
1959, but the taxpayer may elect to use a base year beginning 1 January 
1958 and ending 31 December 1958. 
If the taxpayer keeps his accounts 
on a calendar year basis but uses the base year ending on 81 March, his 
income for the base year includes income of the current and prior calen- 
dar years in proportion to that part of each which falls within the base 
year. 
A taxpayer is entitled to use a different base year for each separate 
source of income. 
Thus, if the taxpayer operates two businesses, a dif- 
ferent base year may be employed for each; or if he operates a single 
business with a head office and a branch office, a different base year may 
be employed for each office; or if he has investments in the shares of 
several different companies, the income from each may be treated as a 
“separate source of income with a separate base year.'° Where a taxpayer 
uses different base years for different sources of income, the combined 
income from the different sources for the various base years must be 
added together to arrive at the total income taxable for any particular 
tax year. 
Notwithstanding the foregoing, the Central Board of Revenue or the 
Commissioner of Income-tax as the authorized delegate of the Board 
may designate any period as the appropriate base year for use by any 
person, business, or company or class of persons, businesses, or companies 
(§ 2(11)(i)(b)). 
In practice, this authority is seldom exercised, al-

began business on 18 April 1923 and kept his books on a fiscal year

would not have been taxable until the 1925-1926 tax year. 
However, 
the Commissioner required that the period ending 17 April 1924 be used

6/3.3 
Change of Accounting Period 
Once a taxpayer has chosen a particular period as his base year for 
any particular source of income, that base year cannot be changed except 
with the consent of the Income-tax Officer and upon such conditions as 
he may impose (§ 2(11)(i)(a), Proviso). 
In practice, such consent 
is not given unless the taxpayer keeps his accounts on the basis of the 
base year to which he wishes to change. 
If the change would result in 
duplicate taxation of the profits of a particular period, the duplication 
is eliminated. 
For example, if a taxpayer who has employed the normal 
base year ending on 31 March changes in 1959 to a base year correspond- 
ing with the calendar year, his assessment for the 1960-1961 tax year 
will be based upon profits of 1 January 1959 to 31 December 1959. 
Since 
the profits of the period 1 January 1959 to 31 March 1959 will already 
have been taxed in the 1959-1960 tax year, his 1960-1961 assessment will 
cover only the profits of the period from 1 April 1959 to 31 December 
1959. 
These profits would be determined as nine twelfths of the profits 
shown on the taxpayer’s books for the calendar year 1959. 
On the other hand, where there is a change from one accounting period 
to another or from a calendar year to an accounting year, a short account- 
ing period of less than 12 months may result, in which case this shorter 
period may nevertheless be used as the base year if consent is obtained. 
For example, if a taxpayer employing the calendar year as his base year 
changes to an accounting period ending 30 June, his assessment for the 
tax year following that in which the change occurs will be based upon 
the short accounting period of six months from 1 January to 30 June. 
6/3.4 
Commencement of Operations 
Where a business, profession, or vocation has been newly established 
in any tax year, no tax is assessed for that tax year, but the tax for the 
succeeding tax year will be either upon the profits from the date of 
establishment of the business, profession, or vocation to the succeeding

Example 1 
If a business is established on 1 June 1958, tax for the 1959-1960 tax 
year would normally be assessed on the profits from 1 June 1958 to 31 March 
1959. 
However, if the taxpayer adopts an accounting period ending 31 May 
1959, he may choose the 1 June to 31 May period as his base year, in which 
event there would be no base year for the 1959-1960 tax year and the profits 
for the period ending 31 May 1959 would not be taxed until the 1960-1961 
tax year. 
6/3.5 
Termination of Operations 
If a business, profession, or vocation is discontinued, its last base year 
ends on the date of discontinuance. 
Notwithstanding the fact that the 
assessment for any tax year is normally based upon the income of the 
preceding tax year, or of the accounting period ending in the preceding 
year (6/3.2), the profits of this final base period are taxable in the year 
of discontinuance at the rates of tax under the law in force for that year. 
Such assessment is in addition to the ordinary assessment in the current 
tax year upon the profits of the base year normally applicable to the 
business (§ 25(1)). 
The profits of the short period are the subject 
of a separate assessment, so that the profits of the two periods which 
are assessed in the tax year of discontinuance are not aggregated for 
rate purposes.!® 
The accelerated assessment of the profits of the year 
of discontinuance is discretionary with the Income-tax Officer who may, 
if he wishes, assess the profits of the final period in the succeeding tax 
year in the normal manner.’® 
A person carrying on a business, profession, or vocation is required 
to notify the Income-tax Officer of the discontinuance thereof within 15 
days of the discontinuance. 
A penalty not exceeding the amount of tax 
subsequently assessed on the taxpayer in respect of the profits of the 
final period may be imposed for failure to give such notice (§ 25(2)). 
If a business, profession, or vocation was at any time taxed under the 
Income-tax Act of 1918, and there has not been any succession to that 
business (6/3.6), profits of the period in which discontinuance occurs 
are not subject to income tax and are not included in total income 
(§ 25(3)).2°

Thus, upon discontinuance of such a business, 
omitting the profits of the final period from assessment makes the total 
number of taxable periods for which tax is assessed equal to the total

The tax-

assessment for that year, and if the tax has already been paid on income

The election 
must be made within one year of the date of the discontinuance of the

For purposes of the supertax, the exemption of the income of the period 
of discontinuance applies only if the income of the business, profession,

businesses would not have been subjected to supertax twice on the same 
income. 
Since under the Income-tax Act of 1886, a corporation was 
exempt from tax on income of the first year of its existence, corporations 
which received the benefit of that exemption do not receive any exemp-

Income received in the base year but attributable to a business dis- 
continued prior to the base year is not taxable, since the tax is imposed 
on the profits and gains of business “carried on” during the base year 
Ch). 
6/3.6 
Change of Ownership 
Where the ownership of a business, profession, or vocation changes 
hands, the transaction is treated as a “succession” and not as a discon- 
tinuance. 
In such a case, the old and new owners are each assessed on 
their respective shares of the profits of the base year in which the enter- 
prise has changed hands (§ 26(2)); the profits of the year in which the 
succession occurs are apportioned between the predecessor and the suc- 
cessor, and each is liable to tax at the rate applicable to him. 
However, 
where the predecessor cannot be found or where the tax assessed on him 
cannot be recovered from him, the successor is liable to pay the tax of 
the predecessor on profits apportioned to the predecessor for the base 
period of the succession and the profits of the preceding base period. 
If the business, profession, or vocation was at any time taxed under

the Income-tax Act of 1918, and the person succeeded was carrying on the 
business at the commencement of the Income-tax (Amendment) Act of 
1939, his income from the business from the end of the base year to the 
date of succession may be exempted from tax and from the income of 
the base year in the same manner and under the same conditions as are 
provided for the discontinuance of a business which was at any time 
taxed under the Income-tax Act of 1918 (§ 25(4) )(6/3.5). 
Assessment cannot be made under these provisions if there has been 
no effective change of ownership.2!. 
If the business carried on by the 
transferee is less than the whole business carried on by the transferor, 
or if it is in effect a different business than that which the transferor 
carried on, the transferee cannot be taxed under the succession provisions 
but must be treated as if he had commenced a new business (6/3.4). 
Hence, although a succession takes place if the transferee takes over 
and operates one of several distinct businesses of the transferor,22 the 
transfer of one of several branches of a single business does not give rise 
to a succession.” 
There is no succession when separate firms providing 
services under contract combine into a single firm to provide similar 
services under a new contract, using none of the assets of the original 
businesses.?* 
Although the fact that good will was sold along with other 
assets would strongly support a finding that a succession had taken place, 
it has been held that a parent corporation, on acquiring the assets and 
good will of a subsidiary which had sold its product exclusively to the 
parent, did not succeed to the wholesale business of the subsidiary.”° 
Where there has been a change in the constitution of a partnership, 
assessment is made on the partnership as constituted at the time of the 
assessment, and any tax which cannot be recovered from a partner may 
be assessed on the firm as constituted at the time of the assessment, even 
though for purposes of computing the incomes of the partners the income 
is apportioned among the partners who were entitled to receive it during 
the base year (§ 26(1)).

a period of 12 months, the taxpayer may treat the entire period from 
the date of commencement to the date of termination as his base year 
and include those profits in his income which is taxable in the tax year 
immediately following the date of termination.

6/4. 
Accounting Methods 
6/4.1_ 
In General 
Income which is taxable under the category “profits and gains of busi- 
ness, profession, or vocation,” and that which is taxable under the cate- 
gory “income from other sources,” is computed “in accordance with the 
method of accounting regularly employed” by the taxpayer ($13). 
As 
to all other categories of income, the method of accounting is prescribed 
(6/4.6, 6/4,7), and the method of accounting for dividends is also pre- 
scribed even though dividends are classified as “income from other 
sources.” 
Where the taxpayer is allowed a choice of accounting methods, he may 
use different methods of accounting for income from different sources, 
just as he may use different base years for income from different sources 
(6/3.2). 
But the taxpayer must apply consistently any method which 
he selects for a category or source of income.?° 
If the taxpayer has not 
regularly employed any method of accounting, or if the method which he 
has employed does not properly show his profits and gains, the Income- 
tax Officer may determine the manner in which the income is to be 
computed (§ 13, Proviso). 
Since even a recognized method of accounting which is regularly em- 
ployed will not be accepted if it does not properly show profits and gains 
in any particular tax year, it does not appear that either the last-in-first-out 
or base stock method of inventory accounting would be permitted.?7 
In the case of nonresidents, who are taxable only on income accruing 
or deemed to accrue in India and on income received or deemed to be 
received in India (11/3.1), the method of accounting employed may 
change the base year for which the income is taxed but cannot relieve 
the taxpayer of tax entirely. 
Thus, a nonresident cannot, by employing 
the accrual method of accounting, escape liability for tax on income 
received in India; ** the income must be included in income for the year 
of its accrual regardless of the place of accrual (11/1). 
Similarly, a 
nonresident who maintains his accounts on a cash basis is nevertheless 
taxable in the year of receipt on income accruing in India, even if such 
income is received outside India. 
On the other hand, if income accrues 
in India to a nonresident taxpayer in one year and is received by him in

6/4.2 
Change of Accounting Method 
A taxpayer is free to effect a bona fide change in his regular method 
of accounting. 
The taxing authorities are required to accept such change 
provided the taxpayer can establish that the new method is one regu- 
larly, and not casually, employed by him. 
However, the Income-tax 
Officer may require such adjustments in the taxpayer’s accounts as will 
prevent escape from taxation or will avoid double taxation.2® 
6/4.3 
Installment Sales 
If goods are sold for a price payable in installments, the tax treatment 
depends upon the method of accounting for such sales regularly employed 
by the taxpayer. 
For example, the entire sale price may be brought into 
income in the year of sale, or each installment may be brought into 
income when received, or the fair market value of the unpaid balance 
may be taken into income at the time of sale, or the proportion of the 
total profit on the sale which is applicable to each installment may be 
taken into income at the time of receipt of each installment. 
If the value 
of the unpaid balance were actuarially determined and included in income 
of the year of sale, the excess of the amount received over the amount 
of such value would be a nontaxable capital receipt. 
6/4.4 
Long-term Contracts 
The accrual of income from a contract whose performance is spread 
over several years may not be deferred until the work has been com- 
pleted. 
Even though the completed contract method of accounting is 
employed in the taxpayer’s books, the income attributable to the portion 
of the contract completed within each base year must be determined 
and included in taxable income of that year.*? 
In the case cited it was held that the completed contract method of 
accounting does not reflect the true profits of the base year, and, since 
the income tax is an annual tax, the profit that accrues on a contract 
which is partially completed during the year must be calculated and 
taxed for that year. 
Since the profits of the year could not be deduced 
from the taxpayer’s accounts kept on the completed contract method, 
taxable income under the contract was estimated by the Income-tax 
Officer in accordance with the provision for such an estimate where the

such a transaction or venture is taken into account upon its completion,** 
or, if the taxpayer has recovered his entire cost prior to completion, 
receipts in excess of cost are taken into account when received. 
If the 
taxpayer used the accrual method of accounting, the income from an 
isolated venture would begin to be taxed when the accrued income ex- 
ceeded the accrued costs and expenses. 
6/4.6 
Income from Employment 
Income which is taxable in the category “salaries” (8/1.1) is subject 
to tax either in the year of accrual or of receipt, whichever occurs first. 
Thus, salaries which are due but not paid, as well as salaries which are 
paid, whether due or not, are taxable as income (§ 7(1) ).°? Where salary 
has been taxed when due, it is not again subject to tax when paid. How- 
ever, if payment is made of salary which accrued in a prior year and was 
not taxed in that year, the salary is taxable in the year of payment.** 
Where an employer advances salary to an employee as a loan against 
salary to be earned in the future, the advance is treated as salary due 
on the date when the advance is received (§ 7(1)). 
As noted at 6/4.1, a taxpayer has no choice of the method of account- 
ing to be employed with respect to income from salaries. 
6/4.7 
Income from Capital 
A dividend is taxable as income of the year in which it is declared, 
regardless of the taxpayer’s method of accounting (9/2.1). 
A share- 
holder's right to a dividend arises upon its declaration,®4 so that if a 
dividend with respect to profits of several years is declared in a single 
base year, the entire amount is taxable as income of the year of declara-

Interest on government securities or on corporate debentures is taxable 
in the year in which it is received.** 
Such income may not be reported 
on the accrual method even though derived in the course of business. 
Interest on other forms of indebtedness is taxable either when accrued 
or when paid, depending upon the method of accounting employed by 
the taxpayer. 
Since income from improved real property is taxable solely on the 
basis of its presumed income (9/4.2), and since the actual amount of 
rental income therefrom is not subject to tax, the taxpayer has no choice 
of the method of accounting to be employed; he is deemed to have 
received each year an amount of income equal to the taxable annual 
value. 
In the case of property on which there are no buildings and which 
is not appurtenant to lands upon which buildings are situated, any rental 
income is taxable in the category “income from other sources” (9/4.5), 
and the taxpayer is free to choose his method of accounting therefor. 
6/5. 
Valuation of Assets 
6/5.1 
Inventories 
No inventory valuation method is prescribed by law, and the taxpayer 
is free to adopt any method of inventory accounting which meets the 
requirements of accounting methods discussed at 6/4.1. 
Inventories 
may be valued at cost, at market, or at cost or market whichever is lower, 
provided the particular method is employed consistently.*” 
Where inventory is valued at cost or market whichever is lower, either 
the inventory as a whole may be so valued or separate valuation of each 
item of inventory may be made and the aggregate of the lower figures 
_used.*8 
Whether the last-in-first-out method or the base stock method 
~ of inventory identification would be permitted does not appear to have 
been settled (6/4.1). 
There is no requirement that inventories be valued at market upon 
discontinuance of a business, upon dissolution of a partnership, or upon 
distribution of inventory among the partners unless the taxpayer has 
regularly valued its inventories at market.®

If a corporation with appreciated

If appreciated 
capital assets are converted into inventory, the appreciation is taxed

6/5.2 
Accounts Receivable 
Normally, accounts receivable arising out of transactions in the ordi- 
nary course of business are accounted for at their face value, but where 
the terms of payment are such that the right to collection is deferred sub- 
stantially beyond the period of ordinary commercial credit, the amount 
taken into account is the actuarial value of the receivable rather than 
its face value.*! 
6/5.3 
Securities 
In valuing securities, as in valuing other assets, the objective of the tax- 
ing authorities and the courts is to determine the amount of taxable 
income realized through the transactions in which the securities were 
involved. 
Shares held as inventory are ordinarily valued according to the 
principles governing valuation of inventory (6/5.1). 
When shares are 
held for purposes of investment, capital gain or loss thereon is determined 
by deducting cost from sale price, as in determining capital gain or loss 
realized on other assets (9/8.7). When a corporate taxpayer issues shares 
in exchange for assets, however, the nominal value of the shares is used 
as the cost of the assets to the corporation in computing its profit on the 
sale of the assets if that value represents what the corporation actually 
paid for them. 
The application of these principles may be illustrated in 
part by the three cases discussed below; although in these cases the 
income subjected to tax arose out of a receipt or transfer of inventory, 
the principles involved would also apply to gains realized on investments. 
Where the taxpayer received shares in newly formed corporations in 
exchange for transfers of mining concessions, it was held to have realized 
income measured by the market value of the shares rather than by their 
par value; but since the number of shares was such that they could not in 
fact be immediately converted into cash, the taxing authorities were 
required to estimate their actual value to the taxpayer in the year of 
acquisition.”

6/6. 
Reserves 
Because a liability is deemed to accrue for tax purposes only when it 
has become fixed, no deduction is allowed for reserves for contingent lia- 
bilities, for anticipated losses, or for future expenses.*® 
Thus, deductions 
have been disallowed for an unascertained liability to pay damages at a 
future date,** and for a liability claimed against the taxpayer but denied 
by him.4*7 
However, it is likely that deduction would be allowed for 
allocations to a reserve for future liabilities where the taxpayer incurs a 
large number of similar contingent obligations and the amount likely to 
mature can be calculated with reasonable accuracy.** 
A deduction is 
permitted for the estimated cost of a definite present liability to be dis- 
charged in the future, if incurred under a contract entered into in the 
normal course of business.*® 
While no reserves for depreciation are allowed for tax purposes, the 
system of depreciation deductions has a similar effect. 
In computing tax- 
able profit, all depreciation provisions made in the books during the base 
year are reversed, the income is computed without any deduction for 
_ depreciation, and the amount allowed for income tax purposes is then 
deducted (7/3.1).

While no deduction is permitted for a general reserve for bad or doubt- 
ful accounts receivable, the taxpayer may deduct amounts allocated to a 
reserve for specific accounts due him with respect to his business, pro- 
fession, or vocation which have become bad or doubtful during the base 
year and have been written off during that year (7/2.10). 
The only other type of reserve for which deduction is expressly pro- 
vided by law relates to the computation of the profits of insurance com- 
panies. 
Amounts written off or reserved by an insurance company for 
depreciation of securities or other assets are deductible; and any sums 
credited for appreciation of securities or other assets must be included 
in surplus in determining the taxable income of an insurance company 
(10/3.2a, 10/3.3). 
In practice, an insurance company which issues casu- 
alty policies is required to include in income its entire premium receipts 
during the base year but is permitted to deduct as a reserve a portion of 
such premiums for risks unexpired at the end of the year (10/3.3). 
6/7. 
Branch Accounting 
There are no special requirements concerning accounting for branch 
income. 
Since the branch and head office constitute a single entity, the 
profits of the branch are taxed as the profits of the principal organization 
of which it is a part. The branch need not, however, use the same base 
year (6/3.2). 
As noted at 11/3.6a, the maintenance of a branch in India 
by a foreign enterprise constitutes a “business connection” in India with 
the result that a part of the foreign income of the principal office may be 
deemed to accrue in India. 
The principal office may therefore be 
required to produce accounts or statements of its world income. 
Expenses 
paid by a branch to the principal office are disallowed as deductions; the 
income and overhead expenses of a branch may be computed under 
special rules (11/38.2). 
6/8. 
Attribution Rules 
6/8.1 
In General 
The Income-tax Act contains elaborate and complex provisions designed 
to counteract tax avoidance through transfers of income or property. 
The broad effect of these provisions is to tax the transferred income or 
the income from the transferred property as though it were the income of 
the transferor notwithstanding the fact that such income may actually 
belong to another. 
Sale of stock or securities with accrued interest is 
discussed at 9/1.6; sale of stock or securities before the dividend or 
interest date and repurchase under a collateral agreement shortly there- 
after (“bond-washing”) is discussed at 9/1.7. 
The remaining situations 
to which attribution rules apply are discussed below. 
The laws in this


<!-- page 213 of 600 -->

6/8.3

area are extremely intricate, and this summary will serve merely to define 
the major situations in which income of one person may be attributed 
to another. 
Where any of these attribution rules applies, the transferor of income 
or property is taxed as if the transfer had not taken place, even though 
the transfer may be effective for other purposes of the law, and even 
though the transferor has no right to recover the tax paid by him from 
the transferee. 
6/8.2 
Income of Nonresidents 
The transferor of assets to a person not resident or not ordinarily resi- 
dent in India is taxable on any income from the transferred assets which 
becomes payable to the transferee if the transferor has acquired rights 
whereunder he has the power to enjoy the income at any time (§ 44D). 
This provision does not apply if the transferor can establish that the 
avoidance of tax liability was not one of the purposes of the transfer. 
The 
provision is so designed as to bring within its ambit not only transactions 
which result in direct enjoyment of the transferred income by the trans- 
feror, but also a wide variety of transactions resulting in indirect benefits 
to him (§ 44D(5)). 
For example, if a resident transferred assets to a 
nonresident who agreed to pay expenses of the former's trips abroad, the 
income from the assets would be included in the resident’s income. 
In- 
come which is taxed to the transferor by virtue of this provision but which 
has not been received by him is not again subject to tax when actually 
received (§ 44D(9) ). 
Remittances received by a wife resident in India out of any part of 
the income of a nonresident husband which is not included in his total 
income for Indian tax purposes are deemed to be income accruing to 
the wife in India (§ 4(2)). 
6/8.3 
Transfers of Income 
Income arising by virtue of a “settlement or disposition” is taxable to 
the person by whom the settlement or disposition was made if the assets 
producing the income remain the property of that person (§ 16(1)(c) ). 
The term “settlement or disposition” is defined as including “any disposi- 
tion, trust, covenant, agreement, or arrangement.” 
The usual type of 
“covenant” encompassed by this definition consists of a promise given 
under seal, binding under Indian law, whereby one person agrees to 
pay to another a certain annual sum for a stated period. 
The rule does 
not apply, however, to a-settlement or disposition which is irrevocable 
for more than six years or which is irrevocable during the lifetime of the 
beneficiary, provided the settlor derives no direct or indirect benefit from 
the income. 
Income under such a settlement becomes taxable to the
