6/8.4 
Revocable Transfers of Assets 
If assets are transferred by means of a settlement, disposition, trust, 
or similar arrangement, the income therefrom is deemed to be that of the 
transferor if the transfer is revocable, or if it contains any provision for 
the direct or indirect retransfer of the assets to the transferor, or if the 
transferor has any right to reassume power directly or indirectly over 
those assets (§ 16(1)(c)). 
As in the case of transfers of income (6/8.3), 
this attribution rule does not apply to transfers which are irrevocable for 
a period exceeding six years or during the life of the beneficiary. 
The 
granting of a life estate would not be considered a revocable transfer 
of assets, but the income from the estate would be attributed to the 
transferor if the transferee agreed to pay any part of the income to him. 
6/8.5 
Transfers of Assets to Wife or Minor Child 
The income from assets transferred by an individual to his wife or 
minor child, or to a person or association of persons for the benefit of 
the wife or minor child, must be included in the taxable income of the 
transferor (§ 16(3)). 
This attribution rule does not apply to any transfer 
for adequate consideration, to a direct transfer to a wife in connection 
with an agreement to live apart, or to a direct transfer to a minor daughter 
who is married. 
It has been held that an individual who pays for property purchased 
in the name of his wife is subject to tax on the income from the property 
under this section.°° 
The Supreme Court has recently held that this 
attribution rule does not apply to transfers of assets by a mother to her 
minor child.64_ 
These provisions and those discussed at 6/8.3 are not 
mutually exclusive; the transferor may be taxed on income attributable 
to him under any one of them. 
6/8.6 
Family Partnerships 
If a wife is a member of a partnership of which her husband is also a 
partner, the wife’s share of the partnership income is included in the 
taxable income of her husband (§ 16(3)). 
Similarly, if a minor child 
of a partner is admitted to the benefits of the partnership, the partnership 
income of the child is included in the taxable income of the parent. 
An 
individual is not taxable in respect of the partnership income of his wife 
or minor child if he is not a member of the partnership ® unless such

6/9. 
Alternative Methods of Determining the Tax Base 
6/9.1 
Estimated Income 
The Income-tax Officer may estimate the taxpayer’s income if it cannot 
be accurately ascertained from the taxpayer’s accounts (6/4.1); an esti- 
mate is necessarily involved in a special assessment to prevent certain 
income from escaping tax (13/1.3). 
In addition, if the taxpayer fails 
to file a return or to comply with a notice to produce evidence, the 
Income-tax Officer may be required to make an assessment “to the best 
of his judgment” (13/2.2). 
The Income-tax Officer may also estimate 
the income accruing in India to a nonresident from business transactions 
carried out partly within and partly outside India if the actual amount 
attributable to operations in India cannot be ascertained (11/3.2). 
Reasonable methods may be employed in the making of estimates in 
any of these cases. 
Reasonable methods include Income-tax Officer’s 
observation of the taxpayer's business,°* use of the assessment for the 
last base year,’ and the application of a flat rate of profits to gross re- 
ceipts °* or to capital employed in a money-lending business.°* 
The flat 
rate of profits may be determined by considering the profits made by 
persons in similar businesses ** or the profits made by the taxpayer in 
past years.®® 
Recent investments, acquisitions, and expenditures made 
by the taxpayer,® and local knowledge and reports concerning him, 
may be taken into account.®! 
It has been held that an estimate neces- 
sarily involves guesswork; but the Income-tax Officer must not act dis- 
honestly, vindictively, or capriciously.*

similar to that governing the exercise of discretion by a trial judge, whose

faith.*8 
In considering any estimated assessment, the appellate authority 
must decide whether the Income-tax Officer made a fair and reasonable 
estimate on the basis of the materials available to him.

7/1. 
Gross Income 
7/\.1 
In General 
Business income is taxable under the category “profits and gains of 
business, profession or vocation” (§ 10(1)). 
The inclusion in the term 
“business” of any “trade, commerce, or manufacture or any adventure or 
concern in the nature of trade, commerce, or manufacture” (§ 2(4)) is 
of primary significance for the purpose of distinguishing between those 
isolated transactions which are taxable as capital transactions and those 
which are taxable as business transactions (9/8.2). 
Transactions which 
are not effected in the ordinary course of a business regularly carried 
on by the taxpayer but which are “in the nature of” business transactions 
are taxed in all respects as if effected in the course of a business. 
Since owners of improved real property are taxed only on presumed 
income therefrom (9/4.2), rents from leasing of property are not taxed 
as business income even if the renting of property constitutes one of the 
major activities of the taxpayer. 
However, the renting of machinery, 
plant, or furniture belonging to the taxpayer may constitute a business 
($12(8)). 
Dividends received are classified as “income from other 
sources,’ and not as business income, even if they are paid on shares 
held as part of the taxpayer’s stock in trade (§ 12(1A)). 
Capital gains, even though received by a taxpayer engaged in business, 
constitute a separate category of taxable income subject to special rules, 
but gains from an isolated venture may be fully taxable as business 
income under some circumstances (9/8.2). 
Although compensation for 
loss of office or cessation of business is in principle a capital receipt, such 
compensation is taxed as business income in certain cases 
(7/6.2). 
Proceeds received by an employer from an insurance policy purchased 
by him on the life of an employee are taxable as business income to the 
employer in the year of receipt.' 
The recovery of a debt previously written off as bad or doubtful 
(7/2.10), as well as any reduction of a liability or recoupment of a loss 
or expense previously allowed as a deduction, must be included in busi- 
ness income in the year in which the recovery, reduction, or recoupment 
occurs (7/6.1).

including insurance proceeds, are taxable as business income to the 
extent of depreciation previously allowed (7/3.6). 
Gains or insurance 
proceeds realized on nondepreciable assets are capital receipts. 
Since the tax is imposed upon the profits and gains of business “carried 
on” by the taxpayer (§ 10(1)), business profits may not be taxed in any 
tax year unless the business was carried on at some time during the 
relevant base year; but if the business was carried on during the base 
year, the income thereof may be taxed (6/3.5), notwithstanding the fact 
that the business is nonexistent during the tax year.? 
Thus, if a business 
employs the cash method of accounting and is discontinued during an 
accounting year, income received after discontinuance but during the 
remaining portion of the accounting year is subject to tax, but income 
received following the end of the accounting year of discontinuance is 
not taxable.? 
Similarly, a nonresident, who is taxable in India solely 
because his income is received there, would not be subject to tax if the 
receipt occurred in an accounting year after that in which the business 
was discontinued. 
Business income is determined in the same manner whether earned 
by an individual, a corporation, a partnership or other association of 
persons, a Hindu undivided family, or a local authority. 
The share of 
a member in the business income of a Hindu undivided family, partner- 
ship, or other association is classified as business income of the member. 
Resident taxpayers are taxed on business income regardless of the place 
where that income accrues or is received (11/2.1); nonresident taxpayers 
are taxed only on business income accruing or deemed to accrue in 
India or received or deemed to be received in India (11/38.1). 
Special rules for the taxation of business income from natural resource 
extraction, agriculture, insurance, shipping, investment companies and 
banks, and industrial operations in general, are discussed in Chapter 10. 
7/\.2 
Determination of Profits 
Income tax is not levied on gross receipts, but on “profits and gains” 
($10(1)). 
The term “profits” is used in its commercial sense. 
Profits 
are to be determined in accordance with the method of accounting regu- 
larly employed by the taxpayer and in accordance with standard account- 
ing rules, adjusted as may be necessary to reflect any difference between 
statutory and accounting principles as to taxable receipts and deductible 
expenses (6/4). 
The general principles governing the determination of income are

7/2. 
Deductions 
7/2.1_ 
General Principles 
The Income-tax Act makes specific provision for 14 types of deductions 
in computing income from a business, profession, or vocation. 
Each of 
them is allowable only within prescribed limitations 
or upon stated 
conditions (§ 10(2)). 
The types of deductions specifically provided for 
are listed below. 
1. Rent (7/2.2). 
2. Tenant’s repairs (7/2.6). 
8. Interest (7/2.5). 
4. Insurance premiums (7/2.9). 
5. Owner’s repairs (7/2.6). 
6. Depreciation (7/8). 
7. Loss on disposition or destruction of depreciable property (7/3.6). 
8. Loss because of death or uselessness of animals (7/2.7). 
9. Taxes (7/2.8). 
10. Bonus or commission paid to an employee (7/2.3c). 
11. Bad debts (7/2.10). 
12. Noncapital expenditures on scientific research (7/2.13). 
13. Contributions to a scientific research association (7/2.13). 
14. Capital expenditures on scientific research (7/3.12). 
In addition to the itemized deductions, the Act provides for deduction 
of any other expenditure which is made wholly and exclusively for the 
purpose of the business and which is neither a capital expenditure nor a 
personal expense of the taxpayer (§ 10(2)(xv)). 
Therefore, the list 
of allowances specifically enumerated above is not exhaustive. 
Since 
the tax is on profits, any loss or expenditure incidental to business may 
be deducted in computing those profits, subject to any statutory condi- 
tions or limitations imposed. 
Thus, a bad debt was allowed as a deduc- 
tion even when there was no special allowance for bad debts in the Act; ® 
loss of inventory through casualty ° and a loss through embezzlement by 
an employee have been allowed,” notwithstanding the fact that the Act 
does not specifically provide for their deductibility. 
However, a deduc- 
tion which is specifically provided for under one of the 14 clauses cannot 
be claimed under the residuary clause so as to nullify the express or 
implied conditions on which it is granted.*

A deduction may be taken only for expenditure incurred for the purpose 
of the taxpayer's own business. 
Hence, a parent company cannot claim 
a deduction in respect of a loss or expenditure incurred on behalf of a 
subsidiary.? 
However, if the taxpayer carries on several distinct busi- 
nesses, the losses or expenses of one business may be set off against the 
profits of another (7/4.1). 
Expenses and losses are deductible only to the extent incurred in the 
relevant base year; those incurred before the commencement of the year 
or after its close are not allowed as deductions.!° Thus, where the accounts 
are kept on the cash basis, a deduction for expenses is allowable only in 
the year in which the expenses are paid; where the accounts are kept on 
the accrual basis, the deduction is allowable only in the year in which the 
liability is incurred. 
Expenses incurred prior to the commencement of 
business are not allowable as deductions since the first base year of 
the business commences on the day when the business is established 
(6/3.4).11. 
Apparently, this rule is applied in practice even if the busi- 
ness is on the cash basis and payment is made after the commencement 
of business. 
As noted at 6/6, no deduction is allowed for anticipated future allow- 
ances or contingent liabilities except in a few limited situations. 
No deduction is allowable in respect of the diminution or exhaustion 
of capital except where specifically provided by law. 
Thus, there is no 
deduction for the exhaustion of wasting assets such as a mine, quarry, 
or oil well, or for the amount expended in the purchase of an annuity.” 
However, the law expressly provides for depreciation of buildings, ma- 
chinery, plant, and furniture (7/3.1b). 
As noted at 7/5, certain expenses which would be proper deductions 
under ordinary principles of commercial accounting are disallowed for 
tax purposes. 
7/2.2 
Rent 
Deduction is allowed for the amount of any rent paid or accrued for 
the premises in which a business is carried on (§ 10(2)(i)). 
If any 
substantial part of the premises is used as the taxpayer’s dwelling, the 
amount of the deductible rent is reduced by the proportion of the total 
annual value of the part used as the dwelling. 
If the taxpayer is the owner 
of the premises in which his business is carried on, the amount of the 
presumed income from the property is excluded from his total income 
(9/4.2) so that, in effect, the amount of the presumed rent received is 
allowed as a business expense deduction.

7/2.3 
Remuneration for Services Rendered 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Salaries, wages, and other remuneration of employees 
are deductible expenses if paid wholly and exclusively for the purposes 
of the business (§10(2)(xv)). 
Except in the case of bonuses and 
commissions (7/2.3c), or in the case of any remuneration paid by a 
corporation to a director or shareholder (7/2.3d), the reasonableness of 
remuneration is not material to its deductibility.1° 
However, if exces- 
sive remuneration is paid for extra-commercial reasons, such as a desire 
to benefit 
a member of the family of the taxpayer, the payment may be 
partially disallowed on the ground that it is not an expenditure “wholly 
and exclusively for the purpose of the business.” 17 
Remuneration volun- 
tarily paid without any legal obligation therefor is deductible if made for 
business purposes. 
Thus pensions, gratuities, and bonuses voluntarily 
granted to retain the services of employees or to increase their efficiency 
are deductible.4* 
Voluntary payments granted by a company to its 
employees upon cessation of business are not deductible; such payments 
are not for the purpose of the business, that is, for the purpose of keeping 
it in operation and making it profitable.’® 
Except in the case of remuner- 
ations payable outside India (7/2.3b), the deductibility of remuneration 
~ does not depend upon the taxpayer's having withheld tax therefrom or 
having performed any other act incident to enforcement of the tax lia- 
bility of the payee.

is taxable to the payee under the category “salaries” if it is payable outside

¢. BONUSES AND COMMISSIONS. 
Bonuses and commissions paid to em- 
ployees are allowable deductions provided the following conditions are 
met (§ 10(2)(x)): 
1. The amount paid to the employee must not have been what would have 
been payable to him as profits or as a dividend if it had not been paid 
as bonus or commission. 
This requirement is designed primarily to pre- 
vent distribution of the profits of a corporation to shareholders in the 
guise of a bonus or commission. 
2. The amount of the bonus or commission must be reasonable with reference 
to the employee’s pay and conditions of service, the profits of the business, 
and the general practice in similar businesses. 
If a bonus or commission exceeds a reasonable amount, it is only the 
excess which is disallowed as a deduction. 
The requirement that the 
amount be reasonable governs all payments of bonuses or commissions 
regardless of the relationship of the employee to the taxpayer. 
d. REMUNERATION OF PARTNERS, DIRECTORS, AND SHAREHOLDERS. 
No de- 
duction is allowed for any salary, commission, remuneration, or interest 
paid by a partnership to any of its partners ($ 10(4)(b)). 
A corpora- 
tion is not allowed a deduction for any expenditure which results directly 
or indirectly in the provision of any remuneration, benefit, or amenity to 
a director or to a person who has a “substantial interest” in the corporation 
(8/1.6) if, in the opinion of the Income-tax Officer, the amount thereof 
is excessive or unreasonable in view of the business needs of the com- 
pany and the benefit derived by it ($10(4A)). 
Similarly, a corporation 
may not deduct depreciation or any similar allowance for property used 
by any such person wholly or partly for his own purposes, if the allowance 
is excessive or unreasonable. 
€. PROFIT SHARING. 
Remuneration which is measured by a percentage 
of profits is deductible as an expense of earning the profits and is not 
treated as an appropriation of profits after they have been earned.2° 
f. BENEFITS IN KIND. 
The value of property given to an employee as 
remuneration is deductible. 
But if a corporation issues shares to its 
employees at a price which is below the market value, the difference 
between the issue price and the market value is not deductible.21

Pensions, Pension Plans, and Provident Funds 
Pensions and similar payments paid directly by an employer to a retired 
employee are deductible as business expenses whether the payments are 
made voluntarily or pursuant to a contractual obligation (§ 10(2) (xv) ).5 
Similarly, a lump sum paid for the purchase of an annuity for the benefit 
of a former employee, or paid to an employee in commutation of an annual 
pension due him, or paid in commutation of annual premiums payable 
under a group insurance policy, is deductible.*® 
A lump sum placed in trust for the purpose of funding a provident 
fund plan for the benefit of employees (5/5.18) is a capital disbursement 
and is nondeductible (§$ 58K ).27 However, where an employer maintains 
a provident fund which is not a trust fund, whether or not it is a “recog- 
nized provident fund” (5/5.13), and transfers the fund to trustees, the 
employer may deduct so much of any amount subsequently paid to an 
employee out of the fund as represents that employee’s share of the lump 
sum transfer to the trustee (§ 58K). 
The deduction is available in the 
year in which the amount is paid to the employee and is granted on 
condition that effective arrangements have been made to ensure with- 
holding of tax from the payment; this requirement is met if the trust 
provides for deduction of tax before making any disbursement to em- 
ployees.

7/2.5 
Interest 
Interest is deductible if paid on capital borrowed for the purposes of 
the business (§ 10(2) (iii) ). The use to which the borrowed funds are 
put is not material to the deductibility of interest thereon; interest is 
deductible whether the borrowed funds are used to meet current ex- 
penses, to purchase inventory, or to purchase a capital asset. 
However, 
because the law is strictly construed as requiring an actual borrowing, 
interest paid on the balance of the purchase price of assets used in the 
business is not deductible as interest on the borrowed moneys °8 although 
it may be deductible under the residual clause which provides for deduc- 
tion of expenses incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of 
business (§ 10(2)(xv)). 
Interest on money which is borrowed for the purposes of a business 
not taxable under the Indian Income-tax Act, such as the foreign business 
of a nonresident, is not deductible.?® 
There is a conflict of authority as to 
whether interest on money borrowed for the purposes of a single business, 
a part of whose profits are nontaxable, is deductible in its entirety,?° or

The cost of current repairs to machinery, plant, or furniture is allowed 
as a deduction to either the owner or the lessee thereof (§ 10(2)(v)), 
provided the repaired property is used for the purposes of the taxpayer's 
business at some time during the relevant base year (§ 10(3)). 
While 
the cited section refers only to the cost of “current repairs,” the cost of 
accumulated arrears of repairs may be deducted under the residual clause 
(§ 10(2)(xv)) allowing deduction for expenditures wholly and exclu- 
sively for the purpose of the business.**

Worthless Assets and Casualty Losses 
A deduction equal to the difference between the original cost and any 
amount realized is allowed for animals other than stock in trade which 
have died or become permanently useless for purposes of the business

against capital gains (9/8). 
A loss due to the damaging or destruction 
of business property by casualty is also nondeductible except where 
depreciable property or inventory is involved. 
A loss sustained with respect to depreciable property may give rise 
to a “balancing allowance” which has the effect of a loss deduction, the 
allowance being in the amount of the unrecovered depreciated cost of 
the property (7/3.4). 
A loss with respect to inventory property, while 
not directly allowable as a deduction, will have the effect of a deduction 
when reflected in the closing inventory value (6/5.1). 
A loss due to the 
partial or total worthlessness of a business account receivable is deduc- 
tible in accordance with the bad debt provisions discussed at 7/2.10. 
Any recoupment of a loss previously deducted is taxable as explained

Bad Debts 
No deduction is allowed for a general bad debt reserve (6/6). 
How- 
ever, a deduction is allowed for specific debts which have become bad 
or partially irrecoverable during the base year, provided all of the 
following conditions are met (§ 10(2) (xi) ): 
1. The debt must be in respect of a business carried on by the taxpayer in 
the base year. 
If a debt outstanding at the time a business was dis- 
continued subsequently becomes bad, the loss thereon is a capital loss. 
2. Except in the case of a banking or money-lending business, the accounts 
of that part of the business to which the debt relates must not be kept 
on the cash basis. 
It is not clear whether this requirement would preclude 
deduction by a taxpayer on the cash basis of an unrecovered loan, made 
in the ordinary course of business to a supplier or a customer, out of 
income previously received and taxed. Such a loan might be deductible 
under the residual clause (7/2.14). 
3. The debt must be in respect of and incidental to a business. 
If the debt 
did not arise in the ordinary course of a business in which the taxpayer 
was engaged, any loss thereon would be a capital loss. 
4. The debt must have become worthless or partially worthless in the relevant 
base year. 
A debt which in fact has become irrecoverable before the 
commencement of the year is not deductible.?® 
Whether, to what extent, 
and when a debt becomes bad are questions of fact.

If a debt

changed circumstances permit recovery in a later year, the recovery 
is not taxable. 
7/2.11 
Charitable Contributions 
As explained at 6/1.5d, contributions to designated classes of charitable 
institutions or funds are deductible within specified limits. 
The deduc- 
tion is available to all classes of taxpayers and regardless of any relation- 
ship between the contribution and the business purposes of the donor. 
Qualifying donations are deductible from income subject to income tax 
of all classes of taxpayers, including corporations, and from income subject 
to supertax of all classes of taxpayers other than corporations. 
However, 
the amount of income so deducted must be included in the taxpayer's 
total income for the purpose of determining the rate of tax applicable 
to the portion of income which is taxable. 
A charitable donation made by a business wholly and exclusively for 
business purposes would be allowed as a deduction under the general 
residuary provision for business expenses (7/2.14), and the allowance 
would not be subject to the limitation discussed at 6/1.5d. 
7/2.12 
Legal and Accounting Expenses 
Legal and accounting expenses are deductible provided they are in- 
curred for the purposes of the business and are not of a capital nature. 
Thus, the accounting expenses incurred in the normal operation of a 
business, such as the regular keeping of accounts, the preparation of an

In practice, however, legal and

with the determination of tax liability and not connected with appeals

Legal expenses incurred in acquiring a capital asset or in adjusting 
the capital structure of a corporation are nondeductible, while legal

The expenses of defending a suit for alleged

The cost of a successful defense against criminal

that the criminal action arose out of business activities of the defendant, 
when the purpose of the defense necessarily included protection of the 
defendant against conviction and imprisonment and the expenditure

It is doubtful, however, whether the same result would be 
reached in a criminal proceeding against a corporation, the only result of 
which could be the imposition of a fine or penalty or a prohibition against 
the conduct of business or against a particular manner of conducting 
business.

Deduction is allowed for any noncapital expenditure, made for scien-

research association carrying on scientific research related to the class 
of business of the taxpayer, or paid to a university, college, or other 
institution to be used for scientific research, research in social science, 
or statistical research related to the class of business carried on by the 
taxpayer (§ 10(2)(xiii)). 
The latter deduction is allowed only if the 
association, university, college, or institution is approved for this purpose 
by the Central Board of Revenue.

a. TYPES 
OF DEPRECIATION. 
The two types of depreciation currently 
allowed are normal depreciation, based on the useful life of the asset 
($ 10(2)(vi)), and extra-shift depreciation (“extra-allowance”) for the 
double shift working of machinery or plant, based on prescribed per- 
centages of the normal depreciation allowance (Rule 8). 
Additional depreciation in an amount equal to the normal depreciation 
was allowed, as a third type of depreciation, during the tax years falling 
between 1 April 1949 and 31 March 1959, limited to five tax years follow- 
ing the base year in which the asset was erected 
or constructed 
($ 10(2)(vi-a)). 
The granting of additional depreciation during the 
period when it was allowed is still material to the calculation of further 
depreciation on assets for which it was granted, since it was deductible 
for the purpose of determining the depreciated cost of the asset and was 
also taken into account for the purpose of the limitation of aggregate 
depreciation allowances to the taxpayer’s actual cost (7/3.1d). 
A fourth type of depreciation allowance, known as the “initial allow- 
ance, was given for buildings erected and new machinery or plant 
installed after 31 March 1945 and before 1 April 1956 (§ 10(2) (wi) ). 
This allowance was deductible from income of the base year of erection 
or installation. 
While it was not deductible for the purpose of deter- 
mining the depreciated cost of the asset (so that it did not reduce the 
amount of normal depreciation under the declining balance method) 
it was taken into account for the purpose of the limitation of aggregate 
depreciation allowances to the taxpayer's actual cost (7/3.1d). 
The 
granting of an initial allowance thus is still material to the calculation 
of further depreciation available with respect to assets which were the 
subject of the initial allowance. 
The amount of the initial allowance 
was 15% of the cost of buildings begun and completed within the pre- 
scribed period, 10% of the cost of other buildings, and 20% of the cost 
of machinery or plant. 
In addition to the depreciation allowances described above, a “de- 
velopment rebate” is granted in respect of new machinery and plant 
(7/3.11, 10/6.4). 
The development rebate is not, strictly speaking, a 
part of the depreciation allowance as its amount is not taken into account 
in calculating either normal depreciation, extra-shift depreciation, 
or 
additional depreciation, or in determining whether the aggregate of all 
allowances has exceeded the actual cost to the taxpayer. 
The term 
“depreciation” as hereinafter used does not include the development 
rebate.

b. PROPERTY WHICH IS DEPRECIABLE. 
Normal depreciation is granted in 
respect of buildings, machinery, plant, or furniture which is the property 
of the taxpayer and which is used for the purposes of the taxpayer's 
business (§ 10(2)(vi)). 
Extra-shift depreciation, as well as the expired 
initial depreciation, is granted for machinery and plant. 
The develop- 
ment rebate is applicable to machinery and plant only and is not 
applicable to buildings or furniture (§10(2)(vi-b)). 
The term “plant” 
is defined as including vehicles, books, scientific apparatus, and surgical 
equipment (§10(5)). 
It does not include animals (7/2.7). 
€. PERSONS ENTITLED TO DEPRECIATION. 
Depreciation is allowed only to 
the owner *4 of a depreciable asset who has used the property in his 
business during at least some part of the relevant base year. 
A lessee 
of a building is not entitled to any depreciation, regardless of the terms of 
the lease, although if he has undertaken to bear the cost of repairs, he 
may deduct the expense of such repairs when incurred (7/2.6). 
If the 
lease requires the lessee to erect a building of which he is to be the owner 
during the term of the lease, he is entitled to depreciation at the rate 
prescribed by Rule 8 even though the building is to revert to the lessor 
upon expiration of the lease. 
Where the owner of a building leases it to another, the rents are not 
taxable as such and the owner is taxed only on the basis of presumed 
income from the property (9/4.2); the rents are not taxed as business 
income even where the renting of property constitutes one of the major 
activities of the taxpayer.®> 
Therefore the lessor is not entitled to 
depreciation during the period of the lease. 
However, the renting of 
machinery, plant, or furniture belonging to the taxpayer may constitute 
a business, the income of which would be taxable as business income 
(9/4.7),°° so that depreciation would be allowed as a deduction from 
business income; if the activities do not constitute a business, the income 
is taxable as “income from other sources,” under which depreciation is 
specifically allowed to the owner of rented machinery, plant, or furniture, 
in accordance with the rules applicable to depreciation of business 
assets (9/4.7). 
d. ADDITIONAL CONDITIONS TO ALLOWANCE OF DEPRECIATION. 
In addition 
to the requirement that the assets to be depreciated be of the type 
described in the provision granting the particular type of depreciation 
(7/3.la) and the requirement that the property be owned by the tax- 
payer and used by him in his business during some part of the base 
year (7/3.1c), the following further conditions must be met:

2. The aggregate amount of all depreciation allowed with respect to a 
particular asset may not exceed the actual cost of that asset to the taxpayer 
($ 10(2) (vi), Proviso (c)).57 
In determining the aggregate amount of 
depreciation allowed, only depreciation allowed under current law or 
under prior law, and any initial allowance which has been made, are 
included. 
Hence, the taxpayer’s failure to take depreciation which was

7/3.2 
Real Property and Movable Property 
For the purposes of depreciation, no distinction is made between real 
property and movable property as such. 
Aside from differences in the 
applicable depreciation rates, and a possible difference in treatment be- 
tween the lessor of buildings and the lessor of other properties (7/3.1c), 
the depreciation rules are the same for buildings as for machinery and 
plant. 
However, buildings do not qualify for the development rebate 
(10/6.4). 
There are a number of distinctions between the treatment of machinery 
and plant and the treatment of furniture. 
Furniture does not qualify 
for extra-shift depreciation, or the development rebate, and did not 
qualify for the initial allowance or for additional depreciation. 
No bal- 
ancing allowance or balancing charge is made with respect to furniture, 
so that any profit or loss upon the sale of such property is treated as 
capital gain or capital loss (9/8). 
It should be noted that the depre- 
ciated cost of a building is specially calculated where the building was 
owned by the taxpayer prior to the time when it was first used for 
business purposes (7/3.4). 
7/3.3 
Methods Allowed 
Depreciation must be calculated on the declining balance method 
except in the case of ocean-going ships, which must be depreciated on 
the straight line method (§ 10(2)(vi)). 
Thus, in the case of ocean- 
going ships, the prescribed percentage of depreciation is applied to the 
actual cost of the asset to the taxpayer; in all other cases the prescribed 
percentage is applied to depreciated cost (“written down value” ) (7/34).

7/3.4 
Actual Cost and Depreciated Cost 
It is necessary to determine a taxpayer's “actual cost” of a depreciable 
asset because (1) the prescribed depreciation percentage is applied 
directly to the actual cost of an ocean-going ship, (2) the depreciated 
cost of other assets, to which the depreciation percentage is applied, is 
based upon actual cost, and (3) the aggregate of depreciation allowances 
is in all cases limited to actual cost. 
In general, the actual cost of an asset is the taxpayer's purchase price, 
increased by capital additions, including the installation cost of ma- 
chinery, and reduced by any portion of the price which has been met 
directly or indirectly by the government or by any public or local 
authority (§ 10(5)). 
Where a going business is purchased, the value 
at which the depreciable assets were taken over by the purchaser is 
treated as his actual cost; the actual cost to the seller is not taken into 
account.°? 
In general, depreciated cost is the actual cost reduced by all deprecia- 
tion “actually allowed” to the taxpayer (7/3.1d). 
However, for the 
purpose of determining the depreciated cost, actual cost is specially 
determined in the following circumstances (§ 10(5) 
): 
1. Where an asset was at any time used by another person prior to its 
acquisition by the taxpayer, and the Income-tax Officer is satisfied that 
the main purpose of the transfer to the taxpayer was the reduction of 
income tax liability, the Income-tax Officer, with the approval of the 
Inspecting Assistant Commissioner, may fix the cost figure to be used by 
the taxpayer. 
The purpose of this provision is to prevent claims for depre- 
ciation with reference to artificially enhanced costs. 
2. Where an asset previously belonging to the taxpayer and used by him in 
his business has been transferred by him and subsequently reacquired, 
his cost upon the reacquisition is deemed to be his cost on first acquisition 
as reduced by all depreciation actually allowed to him. 
3. Where a building previously belonging to the taxpayer is brought into 
use for the purposes of his business, the taxpayer’s cost is deemed to be 
his actual cost less depreciation which would have been allowable had 
the building been used for business purposes since the date of its acquisi- 
tion. 
Such hypothetical depreciation is computed as if the depreciation 
provisions currently in effect had been in effect since the date of acquisi- 
tion of the property. 
4, Where an asset has been acquired by the taxpayer by gift or inheritance, 
his cost of the property is deemed to be its depreciated cost in the hands 
of the previous owner or the market value at the time of acquisition, 
whichever is less. 
5. Where an asset has been acquired by a subsidiary corporation from a 
corporation which owns all of its shares, the subsidiary’s cost is deemed™

7/3.5 
Rates 
The rates of depreciation are prescribed by the Rules (§ 10(2) (vi); 
Rule 8). 
The prescribed rates are mandatory, and the taxpayer has 
no option to claim either a higher or lower rate. 
If an asset has been 
used throughout the base year, depreciation is allowed at the full rate; 
if the asset has been used for only a part of the base year, the deprecia- 
tion deduction is proportionate to the number of complete months of use 
for business purposes. 
If an asset is used partly for business purposes 
and partly for other purposes, the allowable depreciation is proportionate 
to the respective uses (§ 10(3) ). 
The Rules specify a percentage rate of depreciation for each type of 
asset and also prescribe the manner in which extra-shift depreciation is 
to be computed. The amount of extra-shift depreciation is 50% of normal 
depreciation where a double shift is worked and 100% of normal depre- 
ciation for triple-shift operation. 
Triple-shift allowances were available 
only for the tax years 1949-1950 through 1953-1954. 
The extra-shift allowances are calculated on the basis of the proportion 
of the number of days of extra-shift working to an assumed number of 
normal working days of 300 in the base year. 
Thus, if a business has 
worked double shift for 100 days, and triple shift for 100 days, the extra- 
shift allowance for double shift will be one third of 50% of the normal 
depreciation allowance. 
The extra allowance for the triple shift, when 
available, would have been one third of 100% of the normal allowance 
(Rule 8). Certain types of assets, designated in the Rules, do not qualify 
for the extra-shift allowance. 
Rule 8 sets forth depreciation rates for a large number of types of 
assets and provides for a general rate of 7% for machinery and plant for 
which no rate is specifically prescribed. 
With respect to buildings, 
separate rates are prescribed, each of which may be doubled in the case 
of factory buildings other than offices, warehouses, and officers’ and 
employees’ quarters. 
The prescribed rates, which may be doubled as 
indicated, are as follows: 
1. First class substantial buildings of selected materials: 2.5%. 
2. Second class buildings of less substantial construction: 5%. 
3. Third class buildings of construction 
inferior to that of second class 
buildings but not including purely temporary structures: 7.5%. 
Purely temporary buildings 
are 
not depreciable, but the cost ot 
replacement is allowed as an expense deduction.

8. Refinery process plant: 12%. 
4. Office machines: 15%.

Composite or group depreciation is not permitted except where all 
items in a particular class are acquired at the same time and are depre- 
ciable at the same rate. 
However, it is noteworthy that special rates 
are prescribed for certain industries, which are required to use a single 
prescribed rate for all machinery and plant used by them. 
Over 50 
industries qualify for this special treatment. 
For example, all machinery 
and plant of the iron and steel industry (other than rolling mill rolls, 
the cost of which is deductible on a replacement basis) is depreciable 
at the rate of 10%; all machinery and plant of shoe and other leather 
goods factories is depreciable at the rate of 9%; the general machinery 
and plant, other than molds, of the rubber and plastic goods industries 
is depreciable at the rate of 12%. 
Where a special rate is prescribed, 
the taxpayer may nevertheless elect to use the individual rate for certain 
assets, such as electrical machinery, office machinery, and motor vehicles. 
Special rates of depreciation in the petroleum industry are described 
at 10/1.5. 
7/3.6 
Disposition or Loss of Assets 
A deduction is allowed for a loss sustained on the sale, retirement from 
active use, demolition, or destruction of a depreciable asset other than 
furniture (§ 10(2)(vii)). 
The deduction, termed a “balancing allow- 
ance,’ is in the amount of the excess of the depreciated cost of the asset 
over the amount realized on the asset or its scrap value. 
If insurance or 
similar proceeds are received in respect of the property, the amount 
realized is taken to be the sum of the proceeds and the scrap value. 
If the amount realized on a depreciable asset other than furniture 
exceeds the depreciated cost of the asset, the excess, up to the amount 
of depreciation previously allowed, must be included in taxable business 
profits as a “balancing charge” (§ 10(2)(vii)). 
Thus, as much of the 
amount realized as exceeds depreciated cost but does not exceed actual 
cost is included in business profit, and any further amount realized is 
taxed as capital gain (9/8). 
No depreciation may be taken for an asset 
in the year in which it is sold, discarded, demolished, or destroyed 
(§ 10(4B) ). 
No balancing allowance is permitted unless the amount of the deduction 
is actually written off in the books of the taxpayer. 
If the property has

and any gain or loss realized thereon is capital gain or loss. 
If property 
is discarded and written off in one base year and sold in a subsequent 
year, any balancing allowance must be claimed in respect of the year 
in which the property is discarded. 
If property has been destroyed in 
one base year and insurance proceeds are recovered thereon in a later 
year, a balancing allowance measured by the excess of depreciated cost 
over scrap value must be claimed in respect of the earlier year and the 
insurance proceeds must be included in income of the year in which 
received. 
No balancing allowance is permitted and no balancing charge is made 
in respect of furniture. 
Gain or loss realized on the sale, discard, demo- 
lition, or destruction of furniture is not taken into account in the computa- 
tion of business profits but is treated as capital gain or loss (§ 10(2) (vii) ). 
7/3.7 
 Set-off and Carry-over of Unused Depreciation 
If the profits of a business in which depreciable assets are used are 
insufficient to absorb the depreciation allowable with respect to those 
assets, the taxpayer may set off the unused portion of the depreciation 
against the profits of any other business carried on by him which is 
taxable for the same tax year.*! 
While there is no express provision for 
the allowance of such a set-off, the profits of all businesses taxable under 
the category “income from business, profession, or vocation” are aggre- 
gated so that the losses of any one business may be set off against the 
profits of any other (7/4.1). 
If the taxpayer has no income which is 
taxable under this category, or if the income which is so taxable is insuffi- 
cient to absorb the allowable depreciation, the unabsorbed depreciation 
allowance can be set off against income which is taxable for the same 
tax year under any other category (§ 24(1)).” 
If full effect cannot be given to the allowable depreciation by setting 
it off against profits of the particular year, the portion of the allowable 
depreciation to which effect cannot be given is added to the amount 
of depreciation which 
is deductible 
in the following year and 
is 
treated in all respects as though it were depreciation of the follow- 
ing year (§ 10(2)(vi), Proviso (b)). 
Any depreciation which is not 
absorbed in this manner is carried forward to succeeding years until 
fully absorbed. 
Business 
losses 
(7/4.2) 
and development 
rebates 
(10/6.4) may be carried forward for only eight years.

of the right to carry forward unused depreciation without time limit is 
preserved, and those losses which are subject to a time limit are utilized 
first. 
As in the case of business losses generally, unused depreciation may 
be carried forward and set off against business profits of a subsequent 
year only if the business to which the depreciation relates continues to 
be carried on by the taxpayer who carried on the business at the time 
the depreciation became allowable. 
7/3.8 
Deduction for "Renewals" as Alternative to Depreciation 
For the assets listed below, no depreciation on a percentage basis is 
allowed, but the cost of renewal or replacement is allowed to be deducted 
as an expense (Rule 8). 
1. Buildings which are purely temporary (for example, temporary wooden 
structures). 
2. Rollers used in flour mills and sugar works. 
8. Wooden match frames used in match factories. 
4. Rolling mill rolls used in the iron and steel industry. 
5. Salt pans, reservoirs, and condensers made of impervious clay, used in 
salt works. 
6. Bulbs used in film studios and motion picture theatres. 
7. Coal tubs, winding ropes, haulage ropes, sand stowing pipes, and safety 
lamps used in mines and quarries. 
8. Wooden parts of plant and machinery used for the manufacture of 
artificial silk. 
9. Direct 
fire glass melting furnaces used in the glass manufacturing 
industry. 
10. Plant, machinery, buildings, and furniture of railway or nonelectric 
tramway businesses.®* 
7/3.9_ 
Amortization of Leasehold Improvements 
A lessee is entitled to depreciate a building which the terms of the 
lease require him to build on the premises and which he is to own 
during the term of the lease, even though the building is to revert to 
the lessor on the expiration of the lease (7/3.1c). 
Otherwise, there is 
no provision for depreciation or amortization of leasehold improvements. 
7/3.10 
Amortization of Intangibles 
Except in the case of insurance companies (10/3.2b), no amortization, 
depreciation, or other deduction is allowed for capital expenditure on 
the acquisition of intangible property or rights.

7/3.11 
Development Rebate 
As is explained at 10/6.4, a “development rebate” of 25% of the cost 
of new machinery and plant, and of 40% of the cost of new ships, is 
granted as a deduction from business profits of the base year in which 
the property is installed or acquired. 
Since the rebate is independent 
of any depreciation allowances granted for the same assets, the total 
amount deductible over the life of depreciable machinery or plant which 
qualifies for the development rebate is 125% of its cost, and the total 
amount deductible over the life of a new ship is 140% of its cost. 
7/3.12 
Capital Expenditure on Scientific Research Facilities 
Capital expenditure on scientific research related to the taxpayer’s 
business is deductible at the rate of 20% per year in each of the five 
consecutive base years beginning with that in which the expenditure 
was incurred (§ 10(2)(xiv)). 
If a qualifying expenditure is incurred 
within three years prior to the base year in which business is commenced, 
and the other requirements for the scientific research deduction are met, 
the deduction may be taken in each of the five base years beginning with 
that in which the business commenced. 
Scientific research and scientific 
research related to a business are defined as set forth at 7/2.13. 
The 
amount of any unused deduction for capital expenditure on scientific 
research is treated in all respects as though it were unused depreciation 
(§ 10(2) (xiv), Proviso (f) )(7/3.7). 
Where a scientific research facility 
ceases to be used for scientific research related to the business, no scien- 
tific research deduction is allowed in any base year after that in which 
the cessation takes place. In the base year of cessation of use, a balancing 
allowance is permitted in the amount of any excess of the actual cost over 
the sum of all amounts previously allowed plus the value of the asset 
immediately before the cessation. 
If the sum of such amounts is greater 
than the amount of the actual cost, no balancing charge is made. 
If the 
asset no longer used for scientific research related to the business con- 
tinues to be used in the business, ordinary depreciation is allowable 
thereafter; for this purpose, the, actual cost of such an asset is its original 
actual cost as reduced by all scientific research deductions already 
allowed. 
If a scientific research asset is sold without having been used for other 
purposes, a balancing allowance is granted in the amount of the difference 
between the sale proceeds and the actual cost as reduced by all other 
deductions made for the asset; if the proceeds of the sale plus the total 
amount of scientific research deductions exceed the taxpayer’s actual cost, 
a balancing charge is made up to the amount of such allowances. 
No depreciation may be taken with respect to an asset in a base year 
for which a scientific research deduction is allowed for that asset.

7/4. 
Net Losses from Operations 
7/4.1 
Current Year Set-off 
A net loss from the operations of a business in any base year may be 
set off against the profits of any other business, profession, or vocation 
carried on by the taxpayer which is taxable for the tax year following 
the base year in which the loss was sustained,®°* whether or not it is 
attributable to the same base year. 
While there are no special provisions 
of the Act which permit such set-off, income of a particular category, 
e.g., “business, profession, or vocation” (6/1.2), can be determined only 
by consolidating all profits and losses from various sources which fall 
_within that category. 
Consequently, a loss from a business, profession, 
or vocation carried on during the year may be set off against the profit 
of either a business, profession, or vocation; a loss sustained under any 
other income category may be set off against the profits which are taxable 
in that same category. 
If a net loss remains after setting off losses under a particular income 
category against profits under the same category, that loss may be set 
off against the taxpayer's income, profits, or gains under any other 
category which is taxable in the same tax year (§ 24(1)).°

1. A loss sustained in “speculative transactions which are in the nature of 
a business” may be set off only against the profits of a similar business 
(§24(1)). 
Thus, such a loss may be set off neither against other 
profits taxable under the business income category nor against profits 
taxable under any other category. 
A “speculative transaction” is defined 
as one “in which a contract for purchase and sale of any commodity, 
including stocks and shares, is periodically or ultimately settled otherwise 
than by the actual delivery or transfer of the commodity or scrips.” 
The 
principal types of transactions covered by this provision are commodity 
futures transactions 
and “short” sales of shares. 
However, hedging 
contracts entered into by a manufacturer, merchant, stock dealer, or 
stock investor to guard against loss through future price fluctuations are 
excluded from the definition of “speculative transactions,” and losses sus- 
tained under such contracts may be set off against other profits in 
accordance with the general rules discussed above.®® 
2. Capital losses may be set off only against capital gains (§ 24(2A)). 
Although the unabsorbed business loss of a business which changes hands 
or which is discontinued becomes a capital loss, such a loss does not 
arise from the sale, exchange, relinquishment, or transfer of a capital 
asset and therefore cannot be deducted either from income or from 
capital gains. 
Losses from different businesses or under different categories for which 
different base years are used may be set off against each other in the 
assessment for the common tax year in which income under the various 
categories is taxable. 
Thus, if the base year for the 1959-1960 tax year 
of a business is its accounting period ending 30 June 1958 and the base 
year for income under another category is the calendar year 1958, the 
income and losses under the two categories would be set off against each 
other in the 1959-1960 assessment.

is upon the members.

respective shares of the firm’s loss against their individual incomes 
(§ 24(1), 2nd Proviso). 
In the case of a registered partnership, the 
income of the firm is determined by setting off current losses against 
current gains in accordance with the above general rules and any net 
loss remaining is then apportioned among the partners; each partner may

7/4.2 
Loss Carry-over 
A business loss for which relief has not been obtained in the tax year 
with respect to which it is sustained may be carried forward and set off 
only against the profits of any business, profession, or vocation carried 
on by the taxpayer in a subsequent year or years (§ 24(2)). 
A capital 
loss may be carried forward and set off only against capital gains 
(§ 24(2B)). 
A loss sustained in a business consisting of speculative 
transactions may be carried forward and set off only against the profits 
of another such business (§ 24(2)(i)). 
Losses falling within any other 
category of income may not be carried forward. 
The right to carry forward a business loss is subject to the restrictions 
listed below. 
1. The loss must be set off against the profits of a business, profession, or 
vocation in the earliest year or years in which such profits are earned, 
until fully absorbed, and may not be carried forward in any event for 
more than eight years (§ 24(2) (iii) ). However, a loss may be carried 
forward before unused depreciation allowances, which can be carried 
forward without time limit (7/3.7). 
2. The business, profession, or vocation in which the loss was sustained 
must be carried on in the base year to which the loss is to be carried 
forward (§ 24(2) (ii)). 
3. The loss carried forward may be set off only against profits of the taxpayer 
who sustained the loss, with the sole exception that a person who carries 
on a business, profession, or vocation which he has acquired from another 
person by inheritance may carry forward the loss of his predecessor 
(§ 24(2), Proviso (e)). 
If there is a change in the constitution of a 
partnership, the firm may not carry forward that part of the loss remain- 
ing unabsorbed at the time of the change which is proportionate to the 
share of a retired or deceased partner (§ 24(2), Proviso (e)). 
However, 
a continuing partner in a registered firm would be entitled to carry 
forward so much of the loss as had been previously apportioned to him. 
If a partner in a registered firm retires, the requirement that the same 
business be carried on by him deprives him of his right to carry forward 
prior losses. 
4. A loss sustained under the category “business, profession, or vocation” 
may not be carried forward by any taxpayer unless he files a return 
showing the loss at the same time and in the same form as would have 
been required had there been a profit (§ 22(2A)). 
It is the duty of the 
Income-tax Officer to notify the taxpayer by order in writing of his de- 
termination of the amount of the loss. 
The taxpayer may appeal the 
order of the Officer, but only in that year, and not in a subsequent year 
to which he seeks to carry the loss forward.®

7/4.3 
Loss Carry-over by Branches of Resident Taxpayers 
As stated at 6/7, a branch is not a separate legal entity or a separate 
unit of assessment distinct from the principal office. 
The profit or loss 
of a branch of a resident taxpayer is consolidated with that of the 
principal office and any net loss resulting is governed by the principles 
set forth above. 
7/4.4_ 
Loss Carry-over by Branches of Nonresident Taxpayers 
A nonresident is taxable on his domestic income and not on his foreign 
income (11/3.1). 
Therefore, computation of a loss incurred by the 
domestic branch of a nonresident is made without reference to any profits 
earned abroad, and foreign losses cannot be set off against domestic 
income. A loss incurred by the domestic branch may be set off against 
its income of the same year and may be carried forward and set off 
against the business profits of the branch in a subsequent year in accord- 
ance with the provisions discussed at 7/4.1 and 7/4.2. 
7/4.5 
Loss Carry-back 
There is no provision for the carry-back of any loss to a year prior to 
that in which it has been sustained. 
7/4.6 
Losses on Foreign Exchange 
A loss on foreign exchange 
is deductible 
as 
a business expense 
(§ 10(2)(«v) ) if incurred in a business transaction and if not of a capital 
nature. 
Thus, a loss due to currency fluctuation would be deductible if 
incurred by a money lender loaning funds abroad,®* or if incurred with 
respect to foreign currency purchased so as to be available for payment 
for inventories, or if otherwise incurred in connection with the normal. 
operations of the business.*?

7/5. 
Nondeductible Expenses 
7/5.1 
Capital Expenditures 
No deduction is allowed for any expenditure which is “in the nature of 
capital expenditure,” notwithstanding the fact that it is made wholly and 
exclusively for the purposes of the business (§ 10(2)(xv)). 
The only 
exceptions to this rule are the allowances specifically provided for depre- 
ciation of fixed assets (7/3.1) and for depreciation of assets used in 
scientific research (7/8.12). 
The problem of distinguishing between nondeductible capital expendi- 
ture and deductible revenue expense is a difficult one; each case turns 
upon its own particular facts. 
While the courts have attempted to 
formulate a number of principles on which a distinction can be made, 
it is not possible to state any infallible rules which will permit prediction 
of the results in borderline situations. 
The nature of the payment, 
whether in a lump sum or periodic payments,” the source of the payment 
out of capital or income,” the treatment of the payment as capital or 
income of the recipient,’ and the manner in which the item is recorded. 
in the accounts of the taxpayer ™ are all immaterial in determining the 
capital or revenue nature of any particular expenditure. 
The test most frequently applied looks to the nature of the asset or 
benefit for which the expenditure is made. 
If the expenditure is made 
to bring into existence an asset or advantage “for the enduring benefit” 
- of the business, it is treated as capital.7* 
It has also been held that the 
question may depend on whether the expenditure is for “fixed” capital 
or “circulating” capital, circulating capital being that which is turned 
over in the course of the business for the purpose of earning profits.” 
However, an expenditure incurred in preserving or maintaining capital 
assets previously acquired is deductible since it does not bring into

The manner in which the foregoing principles have been applied in 
particular situations may be illustrated by the following cases in which 
expenditures were held to have been of a capital nature: a payment made 
by the taxpayer to free himself from an onerous lease,”® payments made to 
eliminate competition for an extended period,®® a payment for the pur- 
chase of good will of a business,®! payments made for growing crops 
acquired with land,*? expenses of an unsuccessful application for a license 
which would have been a capital asset if acquired,** the cost of capital 
improvements made by a lessee in lieu of rent,°* annual payments made

Further instances of expenditures which have been held to be 
of a capital nature are discussed at 7/2. 
Difficulty is frequently encountered in distinguishing between expendi- 
tures which are deductible 
as the cost of repairs to business assets 
(§ 10(2)(v)) and those which are not deductible because they represent 
the cost of replacement or renewal of those assets. 
The distinction is one 
of degree, renewal being the reconstruction of substantially the whole 
subject matter. 
If the work done substantially changes the identity of 
the subject matter, effects a substantial improvement in it, or results in 
a substantial extension of its useful life, its cost is a nondeductible capital 
expenditure.** 
Thus, although the cost of replacing old and worn-out 
machine parts with new parts has been held to be deductible,* the cost 
would not be deductible if the substitution were so extensive as to change 
the identity of the machine, alter its function, or materially extend its 
usability. 
As in distinguishing between capital and revenue expendi- 
tures generally, the question is entirely one of fact, and depending as it 
does on the degree of change, has given rise to considerable inconsistency 
in the decisions.

7/5.3 
Casualty Losses 
The mere fact that property has been lost or destroyed as the result 
of casualty does not justify deduction of the amount of the loss. 
How- 
ever, if the loss is in respect of an inventory asset, it will be reflected in 
the closing inventory value (6/5.1), and taxable income will thus be 
reduced by the amount of the loss; if the loss is in respect of a depreciable 
asset, it will give rise to a balancing allowance (7/3.6). 
A casualty loss 
in respect of any other asset would be treated as a capital loss, deductible 
only from capital gains as explained at 9/8.9. 
7/5.4 
Payments to Owners, Directors, and Partners 
No deduction is allowed for any payment of interest, salary, com- 
mission, or remuneration by a partnership, whether registered or un- 
registered, to any of its partners (7/2.3d), even though an unregistered 
firm is taxable as a separate entity. 
Other payments to partners, such 
as rent ®° and the purchase price of inventory,®® are deductible. 
A corporation is not allowed a deduction for payments and benefits 
to a director or to a person who has a substantial interest in the corpora- 
tion, nor for depreciation on property used by any such person for his 
own purposes, if in the opinion of the Income-tax Officer the allowance 
is excessive or unreasonable in view of the legitimate business needs of 
the company and benefit derived by it (7/2.3d). 
7/5.5 
Payments from Which Tax Has Not Been Withheld 
Interest which is payable outside India and which is taxable to the 
“payee is not deductible unless the requirements outlined at 7/2.5a are 
met. 
Payments to a fund established for the benefit of employees are 
nondeductible unless arrangements are made for withholding of tax at 
source (7/2.4). 
7/5.6 
Personal Expenses 
Amounts expended by the taxpayer for domestic or private purposes 
as distinct from the purposes of his business, profession, or vocation are 
not deductible even though they may have been made necessary by his 
business, profession, or vocation (§ 10(2)(xv)). 
Thus, where a person

Income and Other Taxes 
Income tax or any other tax levied or measured by profits is non-

Premiums Paid for Leases 
A premium paid by the lessee for the grant or renewal of a lease

Fines and Penalties 
Fines and penalties paid as a result of the commission of unlawful acts

Reserves 
Except for amounts reserved for specific bad or doubtful accounts

panies (10/3), no deductions are permitted for reserves, although deduc- 
tion has been permitted for the estimated cost of a present liability to be

business liability and the liability is remitted or extinguished in whole or 
in part, the value of the benefit thereby accruing to the taxpayer is

7/6.2 
Compensation for Loss of Office or Cessation of Business 
In principle, compensation for loss of office or cessation of business 
is a capital receipt. 
Thus, where it was the taxpayer's business to act as 
agent for other companies and the agency was terminated, compensation 
received by him was treated as capital receipt.” 
However, this principle 
has been modified with respect to certain managers or managing agents 
($ 10(5A)). 
Any compensation or other payment in connection with 
termination or modification of an agency or management agreement is 
taxable where the recipient is a manager or managing agent for an Indian 
company (1/3.3b, 5/2.2) or a person who manages the whole or substan- 
tially the whole affairs of a non-Indian company in India, or who holds an 
agency in India for any part of the activities relating to the business of 
any other person. 
Thus, compensation for loss of office or cessation 
of business is taxable as business income if it falls under any of the afore- 
said categories, but is otherwise a nontaxable capital receipt. 
At the 
taxpayer’s option, the tax on income falling within this provision may 
be computed at the average of the rates applicable to total income for 
the three base years immediately preceding that in which the payment 
is received. 
The deductibility of such a payment as a business expense of the payor 
is discussed at 7/2.3g.

8/1. 
Remuneration for Services as an Employee 
8/1.1_ 
In General 
Remuneration of an employee by an employer is taxable under the 
category “salaries” (§7). 
In addition to salary or wages, this category 
of income includes “any annuity, pension or gratuity, and any fees, 
commissions, perquisites or profits in lieu of, or in addition to, any salary 
or wages....” 
The principal types of remuneration falling within this 
broad definition are discussed in 8/1.5 to 8/1.8 below. 
No remuneration is taxable in this category unless the relationship of 
employer and employee exists between the payor and the payee. 
Income 
derived as the result of the rendition of services other than as an em- 
ployee is taxable either as “income from other sources” (8/3.1) or as 
income from a profession or vocation (8/2.1). 
Subject to the exemptions noted at 8/1.4, a resident is taxable on all 
salary income wherever received or accrued, except that a taxpayer who 
is resident but not ordinarily resident is not taxable on salaries accruing 
outside India which are neither received in nor brought into India unless 
they are derived from a business, profession, or vocation set up in India 
(11/2.1). 
The former exemption of up to Rs 4,500 of the income of a 
resident which was derived outside India and was not brought into or 
received in India applied to salaries derived outside India by a resident; 
the repeal of this exemption by the Finance Act of 1959 takes effect, so 
far as withholding of tax from salaries is concerned, in the tax year 
1959-1960 (11/2.1). 
A nonresident is taxable only on salaries received 
or deemed to be received in India (11/1.5), or accruing or deemed to 
accrue in India (11/1.3). 
8/1.2 
Employment and Independent Work Distinguished 
A director of a company is not a servant or an employee of the com- 
pany, and therefore directors’ fees are taxable as “income from other 
sources” and not as “salaries.” 1_ However, the articles of incorporation 
or the contract between the director and the corporation may make 
the director an employee, as where the director is vested with functions 
normally performed by employees.? 
A “managing agent” (1/8.8b) is 
considered to be engaged in business, so that remuneration received by 
a managing agent is taxable as business profit even if the services are 
rendered to only one company.* 
In general, a contract of service entered 
into as an incident to the practice of a profession produces professional

While there is no authority in point, it appears that neither a corpora-

remuneration for services performed either by a corporation or a partner- 
ship would be taxable as business income or as “income from other

As noted at 5/3.1b, the profits of an unregistered partnership 
are taxed to the firm; as noted at 7/2.3d, the profits of the firm are com- 
puted without deduction for any amount paid to a partner. 
Conse- 
quently, a partner in an unregistered firm is not taxed on salary or other 
remuneration paid to him by the firm, but he must include such pay- 
ments in his total income for rate purposes. 
In the case of a registered 
firm, the individual partners are taxable on their respective shares of 
the profits of the firm, and any salary, commission, 
or remuneration 
received by a partner from the firm is included in his share (5/3.1a). 
A partner's remuneration and his distributive share of the firm’s profits 
are both treated as business income. 
8/1.3 
Accounting Methods 
Employment income is taxable in any tax year to the extent allowed, 
due, or paid (§ 7(1)) in the base year. 
The base year is the 12-month 
period ending on 31 March immediately preceding the tax year. 
The 
taxpayer has no option to employ any other base year. 
Salaries 
are includible in income either when due or when paid. 
Salary which becomes due during the base year is includible in the 
income of that year whether or not paid, and salary which is paid during 
the base year is includible in income of that year, whether or not due.® 
Salaries are due only when the employee has an enforceable obligation 
for payment; hence if the terms of the employment provide for payment 
of salary in the year following that in which the work is performed, the 
salary is due and taxable only in the later year. 
Where the salaries or 
perquisites for several years are due or paid in one year, so that the 
applicable tax rate is increased, relief may be given as explained at 
8/4.2. 
Because of the fact that salaries are taxable when paid, advance pay- 
ments of salaries are taxable in the year in which paid, even though 
the services have not yet been performed or the obligation to aoe 
payment has not yet accrued.

Exemptions 
Benefits and payments specifically exempted from tax and not included 
in total income are listed below. 
1; Any special allowance or benefit specifically granted to meet expenses 
wholly and necessarily incurred in the performance of the duties of 
employment is exempt, to the extent that the expenses are actually in- 
curred for that purpose (§ 4(3) (vi)). 
This exemption does not extend 
to entertainment allowances, rent-free accommodations (8/1.6), insurance 
or annuity premiums which are taxable (8/1.5), benefits provided by an 
employer free of cost or at concessional rates which are taxable (8/1.6), 
or amounts paid by an employer in respect of an obligation which would 
otherwise have been payable by the employee (§§ 4(3) (vi) and 7(1), 
Explanation 1). 
. Remuneration received from an employer who has been disallowed a 
deduction therefor is exempt from income tax. 
Such remuneration is 
includible in the employee’s total income, and is exempt from super- 
tax only if paid by an employer other than a company and only if 
already subjected to supertax as the result of its nondeductibility by the 
payor.® 
. A limited amount granted to the taxpayer by his employer as an enter- 
tainment allowance is exempt, provided the taxpayer regularly received 
such an allowance from his present employer before the year beginning 
1 April 1955. 
The exemption 
is limited to 20% of the employee’s 
remuneration (exclusive of any special allowance, benefit, or other per- 
quisites) 
or Rs 7,500, whichever is less (§ 7(2)).7 
. Passage money paid to an employee for travel on leave to his home in 
India if he is a citizen, or outside India if he is not a citizen, is exempt 
($ 4(8) (vi-a)).8 
Passage money paid to an employee for passage to 
India at the commencement of employment or for passage home on its 
termination is not taxable in any event. 
. Salaries of diplomatic representatives, employees of foreign governments, 
rulers of Indian states, and employees of foreign enterprises and foreign 
missions are exempt as explained at 5/5.1, 5/5.4, and 5/5.5. 
. Allowances or perquisites paid or allowed outside India by the Indian 
government to a citizen of India for services outside India are exempt 
(§ 4(8) (x-a) ). 
Benefits derived by an employee under a pension fund or provident fund 
are exempt as explained at 8/1.5. 
Daily allowances paid to members of Parliament or members of state legis- 
latures are exempt (§ 4(3) (xix) ).

8/1.5 
Disability, Retirement, and Similar Benefits 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Annuities and pensions paid by an employer to or for 
the benefit of an employee are taxable to the employee as salary whether 
paid voluntarily or under a contractual obligation.? 
Premiums paid by 
an employer on a life insurance or annuity contract on the life of an 
employee for the employee’s benefit are similarly taxable, unless the 
premiums are paid through a recognized provident fund or an approved 
pension (“super-annuation”) fund (§7(1), Explanation 1(v)). 
A pen- 
sion voluntarily paid by an employer to the widow of an employee is 
taxable to her as “income from other sources” (6/1.2). 
The tax treat- 
ment of contributions to recognized provident funds or approved pension 
funds, of earnings of such funds, and of distributions from such funds 
is explained below. 
b. PENSION FUNDS. 
Contributions by an employee toward an approved 
pension fund (5/5.12) are treated as though they were insurance pre- 
miums on the life of the employee, provided the amount of the contribu- 
tion is either a fixed annual amount or an annual amount computed on 
a definite basis by reference to the earnings, the contributions, or the 
number of members of the fund ($$ 58N(c), 58R). As a result, so much 
of the employee’s “ordinary annual contribution” as does not exceed the 
applicable limitation is deductible from total income in determining his 
taxable income, but is not deductible in determining total income for rate 
purposes or in determining taxable income subject to supertax (6/1.5c). 
Contributions made by an employer to an approved fund are deductible 
from the employer’s income (7/2.4), and are not included in the income 
of the employee. 
If a fund is not approved, the employees are taxable on their respective 
shares of the employer’s contributions when the contributions are made, 
provided they are nonforfeitable. 
If the trust is irrevocable but the 
employee's interest is forfeitable upon termination of employment prior 
to death or retirement, the employee’s interest is taxable only when it 
becomes nonforfeitable or is paid to him. 
Income of an approved fund from investments or deposits, as well as 
capital gains arising from the sale, exchange, or transfer of capital assets 
of the fund, are exempt from income tax (5/5.12). 
Annuity or pension payments to an employee from an approved pension 
fund are taxable in the proportion which the employer's contributions, 
including interest thereon, bear to the total contributions, including total 
interest (§7(1), Explanation 2(ii)). 
If the employee’s contributions 
or interest on his contributions are repaid to him otherwise than as a 
pension or annuity, however, they are subject to income tax in the year

from an approved fund upon the death of the beneficiary, in lieu of or 
in commutation of an annuity, or as refund of contributions upon death 
or termination of service (§ 7(1), Explanation 2, Proviso). 
The provisions above discussed apply, with some modification, to 
payments made by various government-sponsored pension plans. 
C, RECOGNIZED PROVIDENT FUNDS. 
Contributions by an employer to a 
recognized provident fund (5/5.13) are excluded from the employee’s 
total income to the extent such contributions in any year do not exceed 
10% of the salary paid or due the employee in that year (§ 58E(a) ). 
Contributions by an employee to his individual account in the fund in 
any year, up to 20% of his salary in that year or Rs 8,000, whichever is 
less, are deductible for income tax purposes (§$58F), but are not de- 
ductible in determining total income and are not deductible for supertax 
_purposes ($58). 
The total amount deductible for contributions by an 
employee to a recognized provident fund or an approved pension fund 
and for the purchase of life insurance or deferred annuities (6/1.5c) 
may not exceed one fourth of the taxpayer’s total income or Rs 8,000, 
whichever is less, if the taxpayer is an individual; or one fourth of the 
total income or Rs 16,000, whichever is less, if the taxpayer is a Hindu 
undivided family (§15(8)). 
Interest credited by the fund to the ac- 
count of the employee is not taxable to the extent such interest does 
not exceed one third of the employee’s salary and is computed at a 
rate not exceeding 6% (§$58E(b)). 
Payments made from a recognized provident fund are accorded the 
same tax treatment as are payments from an approved pension fund, 
except that payment of the accumulated balance due an employee is 
exempt from income tax only if the employee has rendered five years 
continuous service with his employer, or if the Commissioner of Income- 
tax determines that service has been terminated for a cause beyond the 
control of the employee, such as ill health, or discontinuance or con- 
traction of the employer’s business (§58G(2)). 
If the payment of the 
accumulated balance is not exempted under this provision, the employee 
is liable for tax in the amount which would have been payable by him, 
had the fund not been recognized, since the commencement of his par- 
ticipation in it (§ 58G(3)). 
Such a payment is not exempt from super- 
tax in any case (§ 58(1) ).

Perquisites include the value of rent-free accommodation or the value

the taxpayer by his employer. 
The value of an unfurnished residence is

A furnished residence is

The actual rental value may be adopted 
if the employee can show that it is less than the percentage estimate.” 
Perquisites also include the value of any benefit or amenity granted or 
provided by a company free of cost or at a concessional rate to an 
employee who is a director of the company or who has a “substantial

A person has a substantial interest in a cor- 
poration if he is concerned in the management of its business and is the 
| 
beneficial owner of at least 20% of its voting shares which do not bear 
a fixed rate of dividend (§ 2(6C) (iii) ). Such benefits are taxable to 
any other employee whose salary, exclusive of the value of nonmonetary 
benefits, exceeds Rs 18,000. 
The word “perquisite” also includes sums 
paid by the employer in respect of any obligation which would other- 
wise have been payable by the taxpayer and the sums paid as insurance 
or annuity premiums otherwise than through a recognized provident 
fund or an approved pension fund (8/1.5). 
As a result of the broad definition of perquisites, free meals or living 
accommodations provided to an employee by his employer are taxable 
to the employee whether or not the nature of the employment requires 
him to occupy the accommodations. 
In addition, an option given to an 
employee to subscribe to shares at a price less than the market value 
is taxable to the extent that the market value exceeds the subscription 
price at the time the option is granted; apparently any further difference 
in price at the time the option is exercised would not be taxable. 
8/1.7. 
Termination Pay 
Taxable salary includes “the amount of any compensation due to or 
received by” a taxpayer from his employer or former employer at or in 
connection with, the termination of his employment, whether solely as 
compensation for loss of employment or for any other consideration 
(§7(1), Explanation 2(i)). 
Thus, while compensation for loss of em- 
ployment is in principle a capital receipt (7/6.2), such compensation 
is taxable as salary. 
It is immaterial whether the payment is made 
voluntarily or under claim of right, upon premature termination 
of 
employment or upon retirement; 
all such payments are taxable. 
In 
addition, a lump sum given in commutation of a right to future remu- 
neration, or in compromise or reduction of salary, is taxable as income.
