8/1.8 
Remuneration Paid Free of Tax 
Where an employer agrees to bear the burden of tax payable by an 
employee, the employee is credited with the tax paid on his behalf by 
the employer, but is required to include its amount in his total income 
along with the net salary received.!2 
If the employer pays the additional

8/1.9 
Deductions 
As noted at 8/1.4, exemptions are granted for certain expense allow- 
ances granted to an employee by his employer, passage money for home 
leave, and remuneration which has not been allowed as a deduction 
to the employer. 
The effect of each of these exemptions is the same as 
if the exempt amount were included in taxable income and allowed as a 
deduction. 
In addition, the Income-tax Act provides the deductions 
listed below for expenses 
arising out of the taxpayer's employment 
($7(2)). 
1. Amounts, up to Rs 500 per annum, expended by the taxpayer on the 
purchase of books and other publications necessary for the purpose of his 
duties. 
2. The cost of maintaining, and depreciation on, any conveyance owned by 
the taxpayer and used by him for the purposes of his employment. 
This 
deduction is not available where the taxpayer receives a conveyance 
allowance from his employer since such an allowance is exempt as noted 
at 8/1.4, item 1. 
3. Amounts actually expended wholly, necessarily, and exclusively in the 
performance of an employee’s duties, and required to be so spent by him 
by the conditions of his service, not including expenses for entertainment. 
Except for the depreciation allowance referred to in item 2 above, an 
employee is allowed no depreciation for property owned and used by 
him in connection with his employment. 
Any expenses which are not 
of a capital or personal nature and which meet the terms of item 3 above 
are deductible. 
If an employee receives an allowance for any such 
expenditures and that allowance is exempt as explained at 8/1.4, he 
may deduct any amounts actually expended by him which exceed the 
allowance.

8/1.10 
Withholding of Tax at Source 
a. RATES OF WITHHOLDING. 
An employer is required to withhold both 
income tax and supertax from any payment of income which is taxable 
as salary, whether the payee is resident or nonresident (§§ 18(2), 18(2A), 
18(2B)). 
In the case of payments to residents, the amount to be with- 
held is computed at the average effective rate of income tax and super- 
tax applicable under the Finance Act for the current tax year, to the 
taxpayer's estimated total income taxable as salaries for the year. 
The 
method of estimating such income and of computing the amount of tax 
to be withheld is not prescribed; but in practice the amount of any 
earned income allowance (12/1.2b) is deducted from the annual salary, 
any exempt items such as contributions 
to approved pension funds 
(8/1.5b) are excluded, and the progressive rates of income tax and 
supertax are applied to the amount remaining. 
The amount withheld 
from each payment is determined by dividing the total tax by the number 
of payments. 
If at the time of making any payment it appears that the 
amount withheld from previous salary payments has been either too 
great or too small, the excess or deficiency may be adjusted in the 
current deduction. 
Income tax and supertax must be withheld from salaries paid to non- 
residents, except Indian citizens employed abroad by the government, 
at the rates prescribed in the Finance Act for the year in which the 
payments are made (§ 18(2B)). 
A nonresident whose total income or 
total world income (11/3.5) will ultimately be subject to income tax 
and supertax at rates below those determined under the foregoing pro- 
visions may obtain a certificate from the Income-tax Officer authorizing 
his employer to withhold tax at lower rates, or if no tax will be payable, 
to withhold no tax (§ 18(2B), Proviso). 
If a nonresident has other 
income which is subject to tax in India, the Income-tax Officer may, 
on his own initiative, specify the rate at which tax is to be with- 
held from the salary, so that the applicable withholding rates may 
be increased beyond those which would normally apply to the salary 
alone. 
A person who fails to withhold the prescribed amount of tax from 
salaries paid to a nonresident is denied any expense deduction for such

Furthermore, any person who fails 
to make the proper withholding, whether from salaries paid to non- 
residents or from salaries paid to residents, or who withholds tax but 
fails to pay the tax to the government as required, is liable for the tax 
and, if such failure is willful, may be subjected to a penalty equal to the 
amount of the tax ($ 18(7)). 
Tax withheld at source is provisional, whether the taxpayer is resi- 
dent or nonresident. 
If the assessment on the employee for the tax 
year discloses that the amount of tax paid by withholding at source 
during the base year has been either greater or less than the amount of 
the assessed tax, the difference is adjusted either by refund or by assess- 
ment of a deficiency (§§ 18(5), 48). 
b. PROCEDURAL REQUIREMENTS. 
The three alternative procedures listed 
below are provided for payment to the government of sums withheld by 
an employer from salaries paid by him. 
1. Payment must normally be made within one week of date of withholding 
or from the date of receipt by the employer of the form which is to accom- 
pany the payment (Rule 10). 
2. With the permission of the Income-tax Officer, payments may be made 
quarterly on 15 June, 15 September, 15 December, and 15 March (Rule 
10, Proviso). 
8. With the permission of the Commissioner of Income-tax, payment may 
be made in a “lump-sum every month based on the average amount” of 
tax deductible every month from the total salaries paid to all employees 
(Rule 11A). 
The monthly payment is calculated by determining the 
total tax payable for the year on the salaries of all the employees and 
dividing by 12. 
No statement need be furnished an employee in explanation of the 
amount of tax withheld from salaries paid to him. 
The employer is 
required to file, for each employee, 
a monthly statement with the 
-Income-tax Officer setting forth detailed particulars as to the amounts 
and types of taxable salary paid to the employee, amounts due but not 
paid during the month, the cumulative amounts paid or due during the 
year up to the end of the month, and various particulars as to the com- 
putation of the amount of tax withheld.’ 
If the employer has obtained 
' permission to follow the alternative payment procedure in item 3 above, 
he need not file monthly returns, but instead must file a return for each 
employee at the end of the year setting forth the particulars as to pay- 
ments of salary and withholding of tax therefrom during the year (Rule 
11A).

8/2. 
Income from Professional Services and Independent Work 
8/2.1 
Gross Income 
Income from the exercise of a profession or vocation is taxed under 
the category “business, profession, or vocation” (§ 10), so that the prin- 
ciples discussed in Chapter 7 with respect to business income apply to 
the computation of income from the exercise of a profession or vocation. 
The rules applicable to the method of accounting for professional income 
and to the selection of a base year are the same as those applicable to 
business income. 
A person who is both resident and ordinarily resident 
in India is taxable on professional income regardless of its source 
(11/2.1); a nonresident is taxable on professional income which accrues 
or which is received in India, or which is deemed to accrue or be received 
in India (11/2.1). 
A person who is resident but not ordinarily resident 
in India is taxable on income from sources outside India and not received 
in India only if such income is derived from a profession “set up” in 
India (§ 4(1)). A profession “set up” in India is one having a fixed place 
in India in which the profession is exercised. 
8/2.2 
Deductions 
All of the rules governing the deductibility of business expenses are 
equally applicable to the deduction of expenses incurred by a person 
engaged in a profession, except that no development rebate (7/3.11) is 
available for assets used for the purpose of a profession (§ 10(2)(vi-b)). 
A loss sustained in a profession may be set off against income in other 
categories in the same year (7/4.1); and any portion of the loss which 
is not so absorbed may be carried forward and set off against the profits 
of any business, profession, or vocation of a subsequent year, provided 
the profession in which the loss was sustained is carried on by the 
taxpayer in the subsequent year (7/4.2). 
There is no provision for deduction by a professional or other self- 
employed person of the cost of purchasing retirement annuities or of 
other expenses of providing for retirement. 
8/3. 
Income from Miscellaneous Services 
8/3.1 
Gross Income 
Income from personal services not rendered in the course of employ- 
ment or in the exercise of a profession or vocation is taxable under the 
category “income from other sources” (§ 12)(6/1.2). 
Examples of per-

sonal service income falling under this category are directors’ fees,14 
sales commissions earned by one not regularly engaged in the profession 
or vocation of a broker,'® and fees received by a professional person for 
acting as a university examiner.'® Payments received by a nonprofessional 
writer or inventor for the use of a patent or copyright may also be taxable 
as “income from other sources” if they do not represent the sale price of a 
capital asset (9/5). 
While casual and nonrecurring receipts are excluded from income 
(§ 
4(3) (vii) ), the exclusion does not apply at all to transactions in 
property which are subject to the capital gains provisions discussed at 
9/8, to receipts from a business, profession, or vocation, 
or to any 
receipts which are by way of addition 
to the remuneration 
of an 
employee. 
Furthermore, a receipt is not considered to be casual and 
nonrecurring merely because it arises out of an activity not previously 
engaged in by the taxpayer and not likely to be engaged in by him 
again.’ 
In general, a receipt is casual only if it is not anticipated and 
not provided for under an agreement, and is nonrecurring only if the 
recipient has no claim of right to its recurrence. 
Thus, where the tax- 
payer received an annual allowance payable solely in the discretion of 
the payor, the receipt was held to be nonrecurring even though paid 
regularly over the period of a number of years,!® and a sum paid to a 
merchant who agreed to act as an arbitrator without stipulating for 
remuneration was held to be a casual and nonrecurring receipt.!® On the 
other hand, where a retired judge agreed to arbitrate a dispute for a 
fixed fee, the fee was held to be taxable.*° 
It appears that where isolated 
services are performed in consideration of a right to profits which are 
contingent or speculative, any profits actually received may be exempt, 
notwithstanding the fact that they were received under claim of right. 
Thus, where the taxpayer loaned a sum of money to a mining engineer 
to enable him to work certain mines and the engineer promised to pay 
the lender one third of any consideration received upon the sale of the 
~ mines, the lender’s share of the sale proceeds was held to be nontaxable.** 
Income from miscellaneous services is determined in accordance with 
the taxpayer’s regular method of accounting and the applicable base year 
is either the 12-month period ending on the 31 March immediately 
preceding the tax year or the 12-month accounting period ending within 
such preceding year (6/3.2).

8/3.2 
Deductions 
Expenses incurred solely for the purpose of earning income which is 
taxable as “income from other sources” are deductible therefrom, pro- 
vided such expenses are neither of a capital nor of a personal nature 
($ 12(2)). However, salaries payable outside India and interest payable 
outside India on a loan not issued for public subscription before 1 April 
1938 are not deductible, if the payments are taxable in India, unless tax 
has been withheld or paid in advance (§12(2)). 
There is no provision 
for depreciation, except where the taxpayer derives income from the 
rental of machinery, plant, or furniture (9/4.7). 
Losses may be set off 
against any income which is taxable for the same year but any loss which 
is not so absorbed cannot be carried forward, inasmuch as the carry-over 
provisions apply only to businesses, professions, or vocations (§ 24(2)). 
8/4. 
Income-spreading Provisions 
8/4.1 
Authors 
An author of a literary or artistic work who was engaged in the work 
for more than 12 months may elect to treat any lump sum consideration 
for the assignment or grant of any of his interests in the copyright of 
the work, as well as any royalties or copyright fees receivable in a lump 
sum or otherwise, in the following manner (§ 12AA). 
1. If the work required more than 12 but less than 24 months to complete, 
he may allocate one half of his receipts in any particular base year to that 
year and one half to the succeeding base year. 
2. If the work required more than 24 months to complete, he may allocate 
one third of his receipts to the base year in which received and one third 
to each of the two next succeeding base years. 
Apparently there is no limit of time within which a lump sum must be 
received in order to be covered by the above provisions, and a lump sum 
received for one type of right will not exhaust the benefits as to a lump 
sum received for another type. 
Thus, a lump sum received for serial 
rights to a novel, a lump sum later received for motion picture rights 
thereto, and a lump sum later received for reprint edition rights may 
be spread as though each were the only sum received. 
8/4.2 
Other Spreading Provisions 
The provision discussed at 8/4.1 is the only provision which entitles 
a taxpayer to spread the income of one year over a period of years.

However, the Central Government is empowered to grant “appropriate 
relief” where a taxpayer has received in a single year salary attributable 
to more than 12 months, or where he has received payment upon termina- 
tion of his employment, or where he has received a distribution from a 
provident or other fund (§ 60(2)). The granting of relief and the mode 
of relief are entirely discretionary with the Government. 
If the payment 
is a gratuity for past services, the present practice is to tax the entire 
payment in the year of receipt at a special rate determined by appor- 
tioning the payment between the base year and the two preceding base 
years and recomputing the tax for each of those years; the rate of tax 
applied to the payment is the lowest, the highest, or the average of the 
rates for the three years, depending on the duration of the taxpayer's 
employment. 
If the payment represents compensation for loss of em- 
ployment, the present practice is to tax the entire payment in the year 
of receipt at the average of the rates of tax actually applied to the 
taxpayer's income for the three immediately preceding base years.

An Indian resident generally is taxable on all interest received by or 
credited to him regardless of its source (11/2.1). 
A nonresident is 
taxable on interest accruing or deemed to accrue in India (11/1.4) or 
received or deemed to be received in India (11/1.5; 11/8.1). 
9/1.2 
Interest on Securities 
Interest on securities issued by the central government or by a state 
government, and interest on debentures or other securities issued by a 
local government authority or by a corporation subject to tax in India, 
are taxable under the special category “interest on securities” whether 
the securities are dealt with in the course of business, as inventory assets 
or otherwise, or are held as investments (§ 8).1 Interest in this category 
is taxable only if received by the taxpayer during his base year; interest 
accrued but not received is not included even though derived in the 
course of business (6/4.7). 
Income tax and supertax are withheld from 
payments of interest on securities as described at 9/7, and the amount 
withheld is includible in the recipient’s total income. 
The recipient of interest on securities is permitted to deduct therefrom 
reasonable amounts expended by him in collecting the interest, as well as 
any interest payable in India on money borrowed specifically for the 
purpose of purchasing the securities 
($8, Ist Proviso). 
Interest on 
money borrowed for general business purposes is deductible only from 
business income (7/2.5), and not from interest on securities, even if the 
funds are thereafter invested in securities.? 
Interest on money borrowed 
to invest in tax-free securities cannot be deducted.* 
Interest payable 
outside India which is taxable under the Indian Income-tax Act is deduct- 
ible by the payor only if tax is withheld from the interest payment or is 
otherwise paid, or if the lender has an agent in India on whom tax may 
be assessed, unless the loan was one issued for public subscription prior 
to 1 April 1938 (§ 8, Ist Proviso). 
Banks are entitled to treat a propor- 
tionate share of their general working expenses as costs of collecting 
interest and to treat a share of interest paid on deposits as interest on 
funds borrowed for the purchase of securities (§ 8, Explanation). 
9/1.3

Interest income which is not taxable as “interest on securities” is tax- 
able as “income from business” under section 10 of the Income-tax Act 
(7/1) if it is earned in the course of business operations, as by a bank

Where a loan is issued at a discount, or is repayable at a premium, the 
amount of the discount or premium recovered by the lender may be

The line of dis-

interest if it appears to be in lieu of interest and as capital if it appears to 
be in addition to interest. 
Where a company issued debentures bearing 
a reasonable rate of interest at a discount, and the notes were redeemable 
at a premium, the lender’s profit on redemption was held a nontaxable 
capital receipt.

9/1.5 
Capitalized Interest 
“Capitalization” of unpaid interest, that is, the addition of accrued 
interest to the amount of the loan so that it too bears interest, does not 
of itself constitute payment of interest.’ 
If the taxpayer keeps his 
accounts on the cash method, the capitalization of unpaid interest pay- 
able to him is taxed only when he receives the entire indebtedness, in- 
cluding capitalized interest. 
All sums paid in excess of the original 
amount loaned are treated as taxable interest. 
If a taxpayer is on the 
accrual or “mercantile” basis, all interest owing to him, other than inter- 
est on securities, is taxable when capitalized since that is the date of 
accrual.® 
9/1.6 
Sales of Obligations with Accrued Interest 
The sale of securities or other evidence of indebtedness “cum interest” 
prior to the interest due date normally does not cause any portion of the 
sale proceeds to be treated as income of the seller, even if the sale price 
includes an amount in payment for the accrued interest.1° 
The amount 
of interest when paid is taxable to the purchaser, without deduction for 
the portion of the purchase price which was attributable to accrued 
interest.'' 
It appears that the sale of securities or other forms of indebted- 
ness upon which interest is in arrears would have the same result even 
if a portion of the sales price were attributable to the arrearages. 
If the 
taxpayer engages 
in systematic sales of securities from interest and 
thereby avoids more than 10% of the income tax or supertax which 
would have been payable on the income from those securities if the 
income had been deemed to accrue from day to day, the interest may 
be deemed to have accrued from day to day and to have been received 
by the taxpayer when accrued (§ 44F).

Such particulars may be required

If the Income-tax Officer is not satisfied with a statement of

Failure to com-

9/1.7 
Sales of Interest and "Bond Washing" 
While there is no direct authority for the treatment of the sale of a 
right to receive interest or other income apart from the asset which pro- 
duces it, it appears that the buyer and not the seller would be liable 
for tax on the income when accrued following such a sale. 
The sale of a security before its interest date, followed by the repur- 
chase of the same or a similar security, does not relieve the original owner 
of any tax on the intervening interest if at the time of the original sale 
he agreed to the repurchase of the security or one similar to it or acquired 
an option to do so which he later exercised (§ 44E). 
The interest paid 
during the “bond washing” is treated as income of the original owner 
and not of the recipient of the interest. 
A dealer in securities is also pre- 
cluded from realizing a business loss for tax purposes on the resale of 
the securities to the original owner, while receiving interest which is 
taxed to the original owner (§ 44E(3)). 
The provision does not apply 
to “bond washing” which does not take place pursuant to a repurchase 
agreement or option although the provision governing sales of securities 
cum interest (9/1.6) may then operate to prevent any tax avoidance.

Interest on securities of the central government or a state government 
is fully taxable as “interest on securities” (9/1.2) unless the securities are 
issued or declared to be tax-free. 
The interest on tax-free issues is 
exempt from income tax only; it must be included in total income and is

A corporation is a distinct taxable entity subject to both income tax 
and supertax on its profits, and its payment of these taxes is in discharge 
of its own liability and not that of its shareholders.1* 
Under the scheme 
of dividend taxation in effect through the tax year 1959-1960, however, 
a corporation is deemed to have paid income tax on behalf of its share- 
holders on dividends declared out of income on which the corporation 
has paid Indian income tax, and the shareholder may claim a refund of 
the excess of the income tax deemed to have been paid at the corporate 
rate over the income tax payable by him at his individual rate (9/2.4a). 
Thus, as regards income tax, there is at present no double taxation of 
corporate earnings; for supertax purposes, however, both the corporation 
and the shareholder, whether an individual or a corporation, are assessed 
on the income represented by the dividend unless the income is other- 
wise exempt (9/2.5). 
Dividends declared for a base year whose profits will be taxed to the 
corporation in the tax year 1960-1961 or thereafter will be subjected to 
both income tax and supertax in the hands of the shareholder, with no 
credit for the income tax already paid by the corporation on the profits 
out of which the dividends are declared. 
The corporate rate of income 
tax will be lower than under the present system. 
Before paying the 
dividend, the corporation will be required to withhold income tax and 
supertax payable by the shareholder (9/7).

Corporate Distributions Treated as Income 
Any dividend declared by a corporation is taxable as income to the 
shareholders regardless of the fund out of which the dividend is paid. 
In addition, any distribution by a corporation out of “accumulated 
profits,” whether capitalized or not, is taxable as income if it entails a 
release of part or all of the corporate assets (§ 2(6A)(a)). 
“Accumu- 
lated profits” do not include capital gains realized before 1 April 1946 
or between 81 March 1948 and 1 April 1956, periods during which capi- 
tal gains were not taxable (§ 2(6A), Explanation) (9/8.1). 
With this 
one exception, distributions of accumulated corporate profits are treated 
in the same manner as ordinary dividends, and are taxed as income to 
the shareholder even if declared out of capital gains ‘* or out of other

b. TAX YEAR 1960-1961 AND arreR. 
The method of taxing dividends 
described above requires complicated calculations whenever a corpora- 
tion declares dividends out of tax-exempt income. 
It also makes it 
impossible to determine the amount of the dividend to be included in 
the shareholder’s total income, and therefore to grant any credit or 
refund to which the shareholder may be entitled, until after the assess- 
ment of the corporation’s income has been completed. 
To eliminate these difficulties a new method of dividend taxation has 
been enacted, to become effective for the taxation of dividends declared 
for base years whose profits will be taxed to the corporation in the tax 
year 1960-1961 or thereafter. 
Under the new system the corporation 
pays income tax and supertax on its taxable profits, but the income tax 
is computed at a lower rate designed to yield the net amount of income tax

Dividends paid by a corporation entitled to the new industries exemp-

company which have borne or will bear supertax (10/5), are exempt 
from supertax but not from income tax.

Annuities—In General 
An annuity paid by an employer to an employee or for his benefit 
is taxable as “income from salaries,” whether paid voluntarily or under 
a contractual obligation (8/1.5a). 
Payments from approved pension 
funds and from recognized provident funds are taxable as income from

All other annuity payments

(6/8.3), are fully taxable as income of the 
recipient, whether paid out of income or out of capital.*>

ments made under a trust to a beneficiary pursuant to the exercise of 
discretion conferred upon the trustee are taxable.?6 
Periodic payments 
to a wife under a deed of separation *’ or a decree of alimony,** and 
periodic payments to a widow under a consent decree arising out of a 
will contest,*® are taxable as income. 
Annuities received by the taxpayer in return for a payment of money 
(9/3.2) or for a transfer of an interest in property (9/3.3) are fully 
taxable as income to the extent that they represent payments of income 
unless the contract calls for the repayment of the original capital price. 
If the contract calls for the repayment of a capital sum, the capital 
payments are exempt even if paid in installments. 
Where the taxpayer 
purchases a right to appropriate the income of certain properties, on the 
other hand, the amounts appropriated are taxed as income.’ 
A voluntary allowance, such as that by parent to child, even though 
made regularly, is not taxable as annuity income but is treated as a 
series of casual gifts or windfalls (6/1.3),** unless it is payable under 
some legal contract or agreement, binding custom or usage, or court 
order,” and is not regarded as a return of capital.

9/4.1 
In General 
Buildings, and their appurtenant lands, which are owned by the tax- 
payer and not occupied by him for purposes of his business, are presumed 
to give rise to income in the amount of their reasonable rental value 
(9/4.3). 
The owner of the buildings is taxed only on this presumed 
income (9/4.2), which may be reduced by certain deductions (9/4.4), 
rather than on any actual income which he may derive from the build-

purposes of his business is not taxed provided the income of the business 
is subject to tax. 
Actual income from the renting of buildings and appurtenant land 
not owned by the taxpayer himself, from the renting of vacant land, 
of furniture, machinery, or equipment, or from the furnishing of services 
or fuel, is taxed either as income from business (7/1) or as “income from 
other sources” (9/4.5). 
Residents are taxable on income from real property situated in India 
and with limited exemptions are taxed on income from real property 
situated abroad (11/2.1). 
Nonresidents are taxable on income from real

9/4.2 
Presumed Income from Buildings and Appurtenant Land 
Buildings, and their appurtenant lands, which are owned by the tax- 
payer and not occupied by him for the purposes of his business, profes- 
sion, Or vocation, are known as “house property.” 
The owner of such 
property is subject to tax on its presumed income under the category 
“income from property” ($9(1)). 
Subject to special limitations in the 
case of the owner’s residence, the measure of the presumed income is 
the reasonable rental value of the property (9/4.3). 
Tax is not imposed 
on the actual rental income from the property, even if the taxpayer rents 
the property as a business.®® 
A resident may be taxed on the presumed 
income from property situated abroad even if he has acquired and holds 
the property in the course of business.®® 
Whether a structure on land 
is a “building” for purposes of the tax on presumed income, and how 
much of the land surrounding a building may be said to be “appurtenant” 
to it are questions of fact in every case. 
Tax on presumed income 
is assessed only on the owner 
of the 
property. 
An occupier or possessor other than the owner is subject to 
tax on any actual income which he derives from a sublease of the 
property (9/4.5) but not on its presumed income. 
Ownership is deter- 
mined with respect to the taxpayer’s base year and regardless of his 
ownership in the tax year.®! 
If the property is held in trust, tax may be 
imposed either on the trustee or on the beneficiary. 
If the property 
is mortgaged, the tax is levied on the mortgagor, regardless of which 
party holds the legal title.®* 
A lessee who erects and owns buildings on 
land leased from another is taxable on the presumed income from the 
buildings even if they are to revert to the lessor at the expiration of the 
term.®* 
If property is owned jointly or in common by more than one 
person, the share of each co-owner is assessed individually if the shares 
are definite and ascertainable ($9(3)). 
If the shares of co-owners are 
not fixed or not clear, all the owners are assessed as an association of 
persons (5/3.3). 
If residential property consisting only of a residential dwelling is not 
rented and is unoccupied by the owner because his business, profession, 
or employment requires that he reside elsewhere, and as a result the 
owner actually resides in a dwelling or portion thereof which he does 
not own, the presumed income from his own property during his absence 
from it is exempt from tax (§ 9(2), 2nd Proviso).

Presumed income from the ownership of buildings used for agricul- 
tural purposes is “agricultural income” and is therefore exempt from tax 
(10/2.2). 
Any portion of buildings or appurtenant lands owned by the taxpayer 
which is occupied by him for his business, profession, or vocation is 
excluded in determining the bona fide annual value of the property 
provided the income of the business is subject to tax, with the result 
that the rental value of the property is in effect allowed as a business 
expense deduction. 
Presumed income from a building which was begun and completed 
between 1 April 1946 and 31 March 1956 was exempt from tax for two 
years from the date of completion (§ 4(3) (xii) ). The exemption was 
originally applicable to construction between 1 April 1946 and 31 March 
1950 and was extended successively to 1952, 1954, and 1956 by subse- 
quent enactments. 
There has been no extension beyond 1956. 
9/4.3 
Bona Fide Annual Value 
The “bona fide annual value” of house property is the amount of gross 
annual rent which might reasonably be expected to be derived from it 
(§$ 9(2)) under the conditions existing where the property is situated. 
Whether the property owner actually derives or could derive rent from 
the property is irrelevant,®* although the amount of total rent actually 
paid for use of the property, the actual rents paid for similar property,*®* 
and the valuation placed upon the property by a local government for 
property tax purposes ® constitute evidence of the annual value of the 
property. 
The bona fide annual value does not include the rental value 
of machinery, plant, or furniture, even when affixed to the realty, since 
any part of the rent actually received which is attributable to such assets 
is taxed separately (9/4.7). 
The assessment of the bona fide annual value of a property exhausts 
the owner's tax liability on income from it. Rent actually received from 
the property is not taxable, whether or not it exceeds the bona fide 
annual value.”° 
Where residential property is occupied by the owner as a residence, 
the annual value is reduced by one half, or by Rs 1,800, whichever is 
less. The resulting figure or 10% of the owner’s total income, whichever

9/4.4 
Allowances and Deductions 
The deductions which may be made from the bona fide annual value 
in determining the net taxable amount of presumed income are listed 
below (§9(1)). 
1. An automatic statutory repair allowance of one sixth of the bona fide 
annual value, regardless of actual repair expenses. 
This fixed deduction 
is available when the property is occupied by the owner, is temporarily 
vacant, or is rented to a tenant who is not obligated to bear the cost of 
repairs. 
If the tenant is required to pay for repairs, the owner’s deduc- 
tion is limited to the difference between the annual value and the actual 
rent paid, not exceeding one sixth of the annual value, in order that the 
landlord will not benefit by a deduction for expenses the burden of which 
has been shifted to his tenant. 
2. Annual insurance premiums paid to insure the property against damage 
or destruction by any cause. 
8. Interest paid on a mortgage or debt secured by the property, regardless 
of the purpose for which the money is borrowed, and interest paid on 
money borrowed for the purpose of acquiring, constructing, or main- 
taining the property, regardless of whether the debt is secured by a 
mortgage. 
4, Any “annual charge” legally enforceable against the property. 
An annual 
charge is an amount payable periodically pursuant to a recurring non- 
capital liability. 
A promise to pay an annual stipend, even though the 
promise was made voluntarily and without consideration, or a voluntary 
promise to pay alimony to a wife, are deductible annual charges if 
legally enforceable and secured by the property. 
While an unsecured 
debt payable in installments is a “capital charge,” the interest on the 
debt is an annual charge if payment of it is secured by the property. 
Interest on an annual charge payable abroad is generally not deductible 
unless the tax on such income has been paid or deducted at source 
(9/1.8). 
5. Rent paid by the owner of a building for a lease of the underlying land 
(“ground rent”). 
6. Property taxes 
(“land revenue”) 
paid to a state government 
(3/2). 
If the property is occupied by a tenant, the owner may deduct any 
municipal or local property taxes (3/3) which he is required to pay, in 
excess of one half the total amount of those taxes (§ 9(2), 3rd Proviso). 
7. Collection costs, including legal expenses, paid by a property owner in 
collecting rents from tenants, not exceeding 6% of the gross annual value 
of the property (Rule 7). 
8. That part of the gross annual value of vacant property or of a vacant 
portion of property which is proportionate to the period of vacancy.

9/4.5 
Actual Rental Income from Real Property 
Profits earned from the rental of vacant land by anyone including the 
owner, profits earned from the rental of improved real property by any- 
one other than the owner, and profits from the rental of mining or grazing 
rights, are taxed as business income if the taxpayer carries on the rental 
activities on a commercial basis. 
If the owner of improved real property 
leases it in the course of business, any portion of the rent which is 
attributable to the furnishing of utilities or services, or to the use of 
machinery, plant, or furniture, must be separated from the portion 
attributable to the buildings and appurtenant land and taxed as business 
income. 
All expenses normally deductible from business income (7/2) 
are allowed. 
If the parties have agreed on an apportionment of the 
rent which attributes a higher rent to the buildings and land than the 
bona fide annual value, their agreement controls.74 
Where the various rental activities discussed above are not pursued 
on a commercial basis, their profits are assessed as “income from other 
sources’ ($12). 
In computing the profits subject to tax, deductions 
normally allowable from “income from other sources” (9/1.3) are per- 
mitted. 
Insurance premiums (7/2.9), repair expenses (7/2.6), depre- 
ciation (7/3), and balancing allowances (7/3.6) are also deductible from 
rental income attributable to machinery, plant, or furniture owned by 
the lessor ($ 12(3)). 
Furthermore, where the taxpayer rents machin- 
ery, plant, or furniture belonging to him, as well as buildings, and the 
renting of the two classes of assets is inseparable, deductions of the 
types allowed for the machinery, plant, or furniture are allowed for 
income attributable to the buildings (§$ 12(4)). 
However, it is not clear 
whether these deductions can be made only from income from buildings 
not owned by the taxpayer and therefore taxed as “income from other 
sources” or whether they may also be made against rent received from 
buildings owned by the taxpayer which would otherwise be subject to 
tax on their presumed income.*®

9/4.6 
Premiums for Leases 
A premium (“salami”) received in consideration of the grant or assign- 
ment of a lease is a capital receipt 7° subject to tax as capital gain. How- 
ever, where the circumstances indicate that the premium is, in fact, an 
advance payment of rent rather than the sale price of a leasehold, it is 
treated as income. 
In general, a premium paid for the grant of an 
indefinite 
or exceedingly long-term 
lease, indicating permanency, 
is 
treated as capital, while recurrent payments at short intervals, as at the 
time of lease renewals, may be taxable as income. 
The burden of proving 
that a premium is income rather than capital rests with the income tax 
authorities.** 
Premiums received by a taxpayer who engages in leasing 
in the course of business, such as a land development company, are 
treated as income in all cases. 
9/4.7. 
Rental Income from Movables 
Rental income from leasing of movables is taxable as business income 
(7/1) if carried on in the course of business and as “income from other 
sources’ (6/1.2) if received through noncommercial transactions. 
The 
rules governing deductions for expenses under those categories of income 
- are applicable (7/2, 9/1.3). 
In the case of rental income from the 
leasing of machinery, plant, or furniture assessable as “income from 
other sources,” specific statutory deductions also are permitted for certain 
expenses, such as depreciation, allowable in computing taxable business 
income (§ 12(3))(9/4.5). 
9/5. 
Royalties 
When the owner of an asset leases it to another or licenses another to 
use it in return for periodic royalties measured by the use of the asset or 
by the licensee’s profits from its use, the payments are taxable as income.”® 
This rule applies to profits from the leasing of mineral rights (10/1.6) 
and to profits from the licensing or assignment of patents, copyrights, 
trade-marks, processes, designs, and formulas. 
Periodic payments of a 
fixed sum for the right to use an asset are taxable as income, even if not 
measured by the use of the asset or by the licensee’s profits,” unless they 
are clearly to be regarded as installments of the sale price of a capital 
asset.

9/8.2 
Business Income Distinguished 
The definition of “capital asset” expressly excludes “any stock-in-trade, 
consumable stores or raw materials held for the purposes of [the tax- 
payer’s] business, profession, or vocation” (§ 2(4A)); hence if the prop- 
erty transferred is of the type normally dealt with in the taxpayer’s 
business, the proceeds of the sale are taxed as income and not as capital 
gains.*7 
The problem of determining whether the profits from a trans- 
action outside the scope of the taxpayer’s normal business are capital 
receipts or income is more difficult and has given rise to frequent litiga- 
tion, much of it antedating the enactment of the capital gains provisions. 
The criteria set forth below are those on which the courts rely most 
frequently. 
However, since the trading or investment nature of a trans- 
action is primarily a question of fact for determination by the administra- 
tive authorities,*8 the list cannot be exhaustive, and it is impossible to 
predict the relative weight to be given to each criterion in any particular 
case.59 
1. Subject matter of the transaction. 
Property which does not yield income 
or personal enjoyment to its owner merely by virtue of its ownership, 
and which is normally the subject of trading and rarely the subject of 
investment, is more likely to have been acquired for the purpose of trad- 
ing than property which does yield such income or enjoyment.°° 
2. Period of ownership. 
The fact that property is held for but a short time 
after its acquisition may tend to indicate that the purpose of acquisition 
was to deal in it for a business profit, rather than to hold it as an 
investment.®! 
3. Frequency of transactions. 
If there have been a number of transactions 
in the same kinds of property, it may be presumed, although not conclu- 
sively, that the taxpayer’s purpose in purchasing the particular property 
was its resale in a trading transaction.92 
The exemption of casual and 
nonrecurring receipts does not apply to business profits (§ 4(3) (vii) 
),

4, Alteration of property to render it more salable. 
The fact that material 
alterations or improvements have been made to property, or that its 
character or quality has been changed so as to render it more marketable, 
would tend to indicate that the profit was derived from an adventure- 
in-trade rather than from realization of an investment.® 
The acquisition, 
improvement, subdivision, and sale of land is illustrative,®® although if 
lots are subdivided and sold by a landowner rather than a land speculator, 
the profits may be treated as capital gains.%” 
5. Methods employed in disposing of property. 
Special exertion made to 
find or attract purchasers, as by opening an office or by advertising ex- 
tensively, may tend to indicate that the property is being dealt with in 
a business fashion.?® 
The manner of arranging the transaction, as well 
as of completing it, may point to its business nature. 
Thus, the use of 
borrowed money to finance the purchase of property to be sold may be 
indicative of the business nature of the transaction.®® 
6. Circumstances responsible for sale. 
The fact that the sale of property is 
occasioned by sudden emergency or unanticipated need for funds may 
tend to indicate that the property was not dealt with in a business fashion. 
Thus, where a company discontinues its normal business operations and 
goes into liquidation, transactions incident to the liquidation, or a lump 
sum sale of machinery and plant, may result in capital gains, un- 
less the liquidators go beyond what is reasonably necessary to dispose 
of the assets so that it can be said that the business has actually been 
continued,191 
7. Motive. 
The mere fact that an investment is made in the hope and 
expectation that it will be resold at a profit at a later date is not, of itself, 
sufficient to cause the income from it to be taxable as business income 
rather than as capital gains.!°2_ 
However, where the purpose of acquisi- 
tion is resale at a profit, that fact, together with other indicia of com-

9/8.3 
Speculation and Transactions in Securities 
Whether a taxpayer who purchases and sells securities is merely real- 
izing on his investments by the disposition of capital assets, or is carrying 
on a business or trading venture in securities, depends upon the circum- 
stances of the individual case.'°* 
In theory, gain from the disposition of 
securities held as investments would represent capital gain, whereas gains 
from purely speculative operations would be taxable income; and the 
criteria for distinguishing between the two would be those used to dis- 
tinguish the disposition of any other capital asset from the sale of inven- 
tory in any business (9/8.2). 
However, in the case of individuals, the 
difficulty of distinguishing between a change of investment and a specu- 
lation is such that security transactions are generally treated as giving 
rise to capital gain or loss unless they are so frequent and so large as to 
justify the conclusion that the taxpayer is carrying on business as a 
dealer or broker.1° 
Where a broker speculates frequently in shares on 
his own account, the resulting gains are treated as business income.!% 
Whether a corporation is dealing in securities with a view to earning 
a profit on disposal, or whether any profit realized is merely incidental 
to holding the securities for investment, is a question of fact. Thus, where 
a corporation sells securities which have been acquired with the intent 
of securing a management agency or directorship, the resulting gains or 
losses are treated as capital,'°’ even if the corporation regularly deals in 
securities in the course of business.1°° 
Gains realized on the disposition 
of shares in speculative transactions by companies not primarily engaged 
in securities transactions have been treated as taxable income where the 
companies’ charters permitted purchase and sale of shares and the com- 
panies’ activities in that respect were frequent and part of their normal 
business operations.'° 
Gains from the purchase and sale of securities by banks, loan and 
finance companies, insurance companies, investment 
companies, 
and 
similar institutions normally are taxable as business income, since the 
investment and reinvestment of funds is regarded as an ordinary incident 
of the business activities of such companies (10/5).1%° 
However, gains 
realized by such companies from particular transactions involving assets

Sales of Patents and Copyrights 
Lump sum or installment payments received from the sale of patents 
or copyrights are taxed as business income if the recipient is a professional 
author or a professional inventor, or deals in patents and copyrights as 
a business.11_ 
If the taxpayer is not professionally engaged in writing 
or inventing or in dealing in patents or copyrights, receipts from the sale 
of patents or copyrights, or of exclusive licenses or rights to use such 
assets,!!” are treated as capital gains arising from the sale of capital assets. 
The price received for a grant of a nonexclusive license or right to use 
a patent or copyright is generally taxed as income whether paid in 
installments or in a lump sum (9/5), since such a grant does not entail 
the complete transfer of the asset. 
An author, whether professional or amateur, may spread the income 
or capital gain received by him for an interest in his literary or artistic 
work (8/4.1). 
9/8.5 
Dealings in Other Assets 
Gain or loss resulting from the purchase and sale of foreign exchange 
is treated as business income if it arises out of the ordinary course of 
business, and as a capital gain if the transaction represents an isolated 
investment.'!® 
The treatment of the following receipts as capital gain or 
ordinary income is discussed elsewhere: sums received upon termination 
of employment or upon retirement (8/1.5, 8/1.7); loan discounts and 
premiums (9/1.4); annuities (9/3); proceeds of life and accident in- 
surance policies (9/3.4); compensation for loss of office or cessation of 
business (7/6.2).

Distributions of capital assets 
by gift or by will, or on the total or partial partition of a Hindu undivided 
family, are nevertheless specifically excluded from transfers whose gains 
are subject to tax (§ 12B(1)). 
Any unrealized gain or loss is taken into 
account for tax purposes when the transferee disposes of the asset, since 
in determining his gain he must deduct the cost which would have been 
deductible by the prior owner (9/8.7). 
However, if the taxpayer does 
not distribute the assets themselves, but sells them and distributes the 
proceeds, gain or loss for tax purposes is realized at the time of the sale.1!4 
Transfers of capital assets by a parent corporation to its wholly owned 
resident subsidiary, registered under the Indian Companies Act of 1956, 
are also excluded from transfers whose gains are subject to tax. 
The 
cost or written-down value of the assets transferred to the subsidiary is 
deemed to be the same as it was in the hands of the parent for depre- 
ciation and for the application of balancing allowances and charges 
(§ 12B(1))(7/38.6). 
The provision which defines “capital asset” expressly excludes land 
from which agricultural income (10/2) is derived at the time of its 
disposition, and personal effects which are held for personal use by an 
individual taxpayer or his dependents, including clothing, furniture, and 
jewelry (§ 2(4A)). 
Gains realized from the disposition of such assets 
are as a result exempt from tax. 
In addition, gains realized on the disposition of the types of residential 
property listed below are excluded from total income and exempt from 
tax. 
1. Improved real property which is subject to tax on its presumed income 
(9/4.1), provided the sale price does not exceed Rs 25,000 and the 
aggregate fair market value of all such real property owned by the tax- 
payer does not exceed Rs 50,000 (§ 12B(4) (a)). 
2. A personal residence used as such by the taxpayer or his parents for two 
years prior to disposition which is taxed on its presumed income and 
which is not subject to the exemption discussed in item 1 above, provided 
the taxpayer purchases a new residence within one year before or after 
the disposition of the old property. 
The exemption is limited to the cost 
of the new residence. 
Any portion of the capital gain realized which 
exceeds the cost of the new residence is taxable (§ 12B(4) (b)).

Determination of Gain 
In computing the amount of capital gains subject to tax, the taxpayer 
may deduct the cost of the assets involved, determined as explained 
below, and any expenses incurred solely in connection with the disposition 
of the assets (§ 12B(2)).

are deductible. 
The taxpayer is permitted to include, as part of the actual cost of a 
capital asset, any expenditure of a capital nature incurred by him in 
making additions or alterations to it, but not any expenditure which has 
been allowed as a deduction for income tax purposes (§ 12B(2)). 
If the 
taxpayer has taken a depreciation allowance on the asset, its actual cost 
is its depreciated cost (7/3.4), increased by any balancing charge, or 
decreased by any balancing allowance, actually made on the disposition 
of the asset (7/3.6). 
The result of this adjustment is that any excess of 
the selling price over the depreciated cost, up to the amount of depre- 
ciation actually allowed, is taxed as business income by means of the 
balancing charge, and only the excess of the selling price over actual 
cost is taxed as capital gain. 
Any excess of depreciated cost over the 
selling price is deductible from business income through the balancing 
allowance, and is not treated as a capital loss. 
Where the asset was the subject of prior negotiations for its disposition, 
the taxpayer must reduce his cost by any sums received by him in con- 
nection with the negotiations. 
Thus, if the taxpayer received any amount 
in return for an option, thereafter unexercised, to purchase the property, 
that amount, which is not subject to tax as income, must be subtracted 
from the actual or depreciated cost of the asset. 
If a capital asset was acquired by the taxpayer before 1 January 1954, 
he is entitled to substitute its fair market value on that date as his 
deductible cost, if he can establish the value to the satisfaction of the 
Income-tax Officer. 
Any depreciation deductions allowed to the tax- 
payer after 1 January 1954 must be taken into account, as must any 
balancing allowances or charges on the disposition of the asset. 
Any 
excess of the depreciated market value over selling price which is not 
absorbed by the balancing allowance is capital loss (9/8.9). 
If the taxpayer acquired the asset by gift, succession, inheritance, or 
irrevocable trust, or upon the dissolution of a firm, the liquidation of a 
company, or the partition of a Hindu undivided family, his cost of the 
asset is deemed to be the cost which the prior owner could have deducted 
under the foregoing provisions ($12B(3)). 
If the actual cost to the 
prior owner cannot be ascertained, and if the taxpayer does not or cannot 
elect to use the fair market value on 1 January 1954 as his own cost, he 
must use the fair market value of the asset on the date of its acquisition by 
the prior owner. 
If the taxpayer acquired the asset before 1 April 1956 
by gift or on partition of a Hindu undivided family, the fair market value. 
of the asset on the date of the gift or partition must be taken as its cost 
if that value is greater than the cost computed in accordance with the 
foregoing provisions. 
The cost of an asset acquired after 1 April 1956

Since the transfer of a capital asset by a parent corporation to its

transfer, the cost used by the subsidiary in computing its gains on later

(9/8.6). 
If the Income-tax Officer believes that the disposition of a capital asset 
between related taxpayers is designed to avoid tax, he may, with his 
superiors approval, compute the taxable capital gain after substituting 
the fair market value of the asset for the price actually paid for it 
(§ 12B(2)). 
If the taxpayer later sells the asset, the cost which he may 
deduct is the price he actually paid for the asset. 
9/8.8 
Computation and Rates of Tax 
In the case of a noncorporate taxpayer, income other than capital gains 
is subjected to income tax and supertax at rates determined as if capital 
gains were not included in total income ($17(6)). 
If capital gains 
exceed Rs 5,000 and total income exceeds Rs 10,000, the capital gains 
are subject to income tax at the rate applicable to total income less 
two thirds of capital gains (12/1.3c); they are not subject to supertax 
(§ 17(6)). 
If the taxpayer is a corporation, its capital gains are included in total 
income and subjected to income tax at the corporate rate ($$ 12B(1), 
17(6), 17(7)). 
Through the tax year 1959-1960, capital gains are 
excluded from the total income of a corporation for supertax purposes 
and are exempt from supertax. 
Beginning with the tax year 1960-1961, 
the capital gains of a corporation will be subject to supertax at the rate 
of 10%, and the rate of supertax on the balance of its income will be 
determined as if no capital gains were included in total income (§ 17(7) ). 
All taxpayers realizing taxable capital gains are required to complete 
a separate schedule of the income tax return, demonstrating their com- 
putations of the tax payable (Rule 19). Examples of such computations 
are given at 12/1.11 and 12/2.11. 
9/8.9 
Capital Losses 
A loss under the category “capital gains” is deductible, but only against 
taxable capital gains (§24(2A)). 
The loss is set off against the full 
amount of the gains, and not against the amount which is included in 
total income for rate purposes 
(9/8.8). 
Any net capital loss which 
remains after setting off capital losses against capital gains for the base 
year may be carried forward and set off against capital gains of later

other than a corporation cannot carry forward a net capital loss which

A loss sustained on a transaction 
in the nature of trade (9/8.2) is deductible in the same manner as any

Losses sustained on depreciable capital assets of a business are generally 
deductible from business income, because unless the taxpayer substitutes 
fair market value for actual cost (9/8.7), any excess of depreciated cost 
over the amount realized is absorbed by a balancing allowance (7/3.6). 
While capital losses are not deductible from income arising under any 
other category, it has been held that business losses may be set off against 
capital gains realized in the same tax year.’

Organization, Reorganization, and Dissolution of Business 
Gq 
9/9.1_ 
In General 
In only three instances does the Indian Income-tax Act make special 
provision regarding the taxation of transfers or distributions on the organ- 
ization, reorganization, or dissolution of a business. 
First, amounts dis- 
tributed 
to the shareholders 
on the liquidation 
or dissolution of a 
corporation are taxable to the shareholders as dividend income to the 
extent of the accumulated profits of the corporation immediately before 
liquidation (9/2.2b). 
Secondly, no capital gain or loss for tax purposes 
is incurred when a parent corporation transfers capital assets to a wholly 
owned resident Indian subsidiary, and the subsidiary receives the same 
depreciation allowances and balancing charges or allowances as would 
have been made to the parent (9/8.6). 
Thirdly, when a taxpayer sells 
assets distributed to him on the dissolution of a partnership, the liqui- 
dation of a corporation, or the partition of a Hindu undivided family, the 
cost which he deducts in computing his gain or loss is that which would 
have been deductible by the prior owner; no gain is considered to have 
been realized on the prior distribution of the assets (9/8.7). 
In all other 
respects, the principal tax consequences of corporate organizational trans- 
actions flow entirely from application of the general rules governing 
transfers of property, discontinuance of business, payment of dividends, 
and issuance of shares or debentures. 
These general rules are outlined 
below. 
1. Transfers of capital assets (except as noted above) give rise to capital 
gain or loss in the amount of the difference between the taxpayer’s de-» 
ductible cost of the property and the consideration received or deemed 
to be received in the transfer, reduced by any expenses incurred by the 
taxpayer in disposing of the property (9/8.7). 
In the case of depreciable

. Sales of depreciable property give rise to income or loss (by means of the

in the amount of the dif- 
ference between the depreciated value of the property and the con- 
sideration received or deemed to have been received in the transfer. Such 
taxable income is limited to the amount of depreciation previously al- 
lowed or allowable (7/3.6), and any further profit realized is taxed as 
a capital gain (9/8.7). 
The basis for further depreciation of the assets 
in the hands of the purchaser is the purchaser’s cost, except in the case 
of transfers effected for tax avoidance purposes, acquisitions by gift or 
inheritance, acquisitions by a wholly owned resident subsidiary from 
its parent corporation, and in certain other instances (7/3.4). 
. Transfers of inventories, whether or not in the ordinary course of business, 
are brought into account at the price stated therefor or at the proportion 
of the total consideration for the entire business properly allocable to 
inventories. 
There is no requirement that closing inventory of the trans- 
feror be valued at market in the event of a “succession” or discontinuance 
(6/5.1), although if the transferor normally uses market value as his 
basis of valuation, he must do so with respect to closing inventory. 
A 
purchaser of inventory is entitled to value it at cost, at market, or at cost 
or market whichever is lower. 
However, if a taxpayer converts capital 
assets to inventory, the inventory cost is deemed to be the fair market 
value at the date of conversion (6/5.1). 
. A loss sustained in one year is deductible in a later year only from 
income of the taxpayer by whom the loss was sustained except that, in 
the case of business succeeded to by inheritance, the heir may carry 
forward his predecessor’s loss from the business for set-off against future 
income of the business (7/4.2). 
Thus, if there is a change in the owner- 
ship of a business (“succession”) (6/3.6), the new owner may not carry 
forward any losses sustained prior to the change. 
Such losses generally 
are not available to the old owner either, since the business in which the 
losses were incurred is no longer carried on by the same taxpayer. 
While 
unabsorbed business losses of a business which is discontinued or changes 
hands become capital losses, they are not deductible against capital gains 
because they do not arise from the sale, exchange, relinquishment, or 
transfer of capital assets (7/4.1). 
Losses apportioned to a continuing 
partner in a registered firm continue to be available to him even though 
there is a change in the constitution of the partnership (7/4.2). 
In 
the case of a business carried on by a corporation, a mere change in the 
shareholders has no effect on the corporation’s right to deduct any losses 
it may have incurred in earlier years. 
. Shares of one corporation distributed by another corporation are taxable 
as dividends (9/2.2). 
. Although there are no cases on the point, it appears that a taxpayer who 
purchases accounts receivable with a going business is permitted to de- 
duct debts which later become worthless under the rules explained at 
7/2.10; any excess of the amount actually recovered over the price paid 
is taxable as business income in the year of receipt.

9/9.2 Exchange of Assets or Business for Shares 
_ 
Where the assets of a business carried on by a sole proprietorship or 
partnership are transferred to a corporation in exchange for shares in 
order that the business may be carried on in corporate form, a “succession” 
takes place (6/3.6), and the transaction is treated as is any other transfer 
of assets. 
Inventory is deemed to have been disposed of at the selling 
price attributable to it, and the basis normally used by the seller in 
valuing his closing inventory is retained in determining his profits of the 
base year in which the transfer takes place. 
The profits of the year are 
apportioned between the predecessor and the successor, each being liable 
to tax at the rate applicable to him (6/3.6). 
The fact that the consider- 
ation received for inventory is less than its market value is irrelevant in 
determining the transferor’s tax, and the Income-tax Officer must accept 
the price stated unless he can show that the transaction was a sham."® 
If the sale price of depreciable assets is not specified in the transfer 
agreement, a suitable proportion of the price paid for the entire trans- 
fer will be allocated to the assets. 
If the price specified or allocable is 
less than the depreciated cost of the assets, the difference between the 
price and the depreciated value is deductible from the transferor’s busi- 
ness income as a balancing allowance. 
If the price exceeds the depre- 
ciated cost, that amount of the excess which represents depreciation 
allowed in the past is taxable as business income through the balancing 
charge, while any remaining amount is treated as capital gain (7/3.6). 
The basis for depreciation of the asset in the hands of the transferee is its 
cost to him (7/3.4). 
If the accounts receivable are retained by the sole 
proprietor or partnership after the succession or discontinuance, any loss 
thereon is a nondeductible capital loss (9/9.1).. 
Gains or losses realized 
on nondepreciable capital assets, including good will, patents, trade- 
marks, and similar properties transferred with the business, are treated 
as capital gains or losses under the general rules explained at 9/8. 
Losses sustained by the business prior to its transfer to the corporation 
cease to be available to the transferor after the succession (7/4.2).

Creation of Subsidiaries 
If a corporation creates a subsidiary by transferring to a newly formed 
corporation a business or branch formerly operated by it, the transaction 
generally is treated in the same way as is the transfer of a business to a 
corporation by a sole proprietor or a partnership (9/9.2). 
However, 
the transfer of capital assets by a parent corporation to its wholly owned 
resident subsidiary which is registered under the Indian Companies Act 
is not treated as a transfer of capital assets for capital gains tax purposes 
(9/8.6).

9/9.4 
Exchange of Shares for Shares 
When persons owning shares in different companies exchange their 
respective holdings, each party realizes a gain or loss on his original 
investment and makes a new investment. 
If a party to such a transaction 
deals in investments as a business, as in the case of a bank or an invest- 
ment company (10/5), any gain or loss which it realizes on the sale is 
taxable as business income. 
Otherwise, any gain or loss is taxed as capital 
gain or loss (9/8). 
However, if a shareholder in one corporation ex- 
changes his shares for newly issued shares of another corporation which 
has acquired the assets of the first, no gain or loss is considered to have 
been realized by either of the corporations or by the shareholder (9/9.6). 
9/9.5 
Exchange of Shares for Assets 
If a corporation increases its authorized capital and issues fully paid 
shares in consideration for particular assets or an entire business, the par 
value of the shares will ordinarily be taken as the purchase price of the 
assets (6/5.3) and as the cost of the assets for purposes of depreciation 
(7/3.4) and for the determination of capital gain (9/8.7). 
If accounts 
receivable are transferred to the corporation, any profit or loss on collec- 
tion by the corporation is taxable income or deductible loss (9/9.1). 
Transferred inventories are brought into account at the price stated 
therefor or attributable thereto, and thereafter may be valued according 
to the corporation’s regular method of accounting (6/5.1). 
Losses. sus- 
tained by a business prior to its transfer to the corporation cannot be 
carried forward by the corporation against its own income (7/4.2). 
9/9.6 
Mergers 
A corporation transferring its assets or business to another corporation 
in exchange for shares of the other corporation is taxed under the pro- 
visions applicable to an exchange of assets for shares (9/9.2), and the 
consequences to the corporation receiving the assets are the same as 
under any exchange of shares for assets (9/9.5). 
However, if the A Co., 
Ltd., acquiring the assets of the B Co., Ltd., increases its capital and issues 
new shares to the shareholders of B in exchange for their shares of B, B 
incurs no gain provided the new shares of A are allotted to B’s share- 
holders in their own right and not as the nominees of B. On the exchange 
of their shares of B for the new shares of A, the shareholders of B incur 
no gain; their shareholding in B is extinguished and replaced by their

9/9.7 
Division of Corporate Assets Among Several Corporations 
If a corporation operating several distinct businesses desires to have 
one of the businesses carried on by a separate corporation owned directly 
by the shareholders of the original corporation, the transaction may be 
accomplished by transferring the business to a new corporation in ex- 
change for its shares and distributing those shares to the shareholders 
of the old corporation. 
The formation of the new corporation and the 
transfer of the business in exchange for its shares would result in the tax 
consequences described at 9/9.3. 
The distribution of shares to the old 
corporation’s shareholders may be handled as a dividend in kind, taxable 
as any other dividend. 
Alternatively, the old corporation may reduce 
its capital and distribute to its shareholders, in extinguishment of part 
of their shares in the old corporation, the shares it acquired in the new 
corporation. 
In that event, also, the value of such shares is taxable to 
the shareholders as a dividend to the extent of the old corporation’s 
accumulated profits arising after the end of its last base year preceding 
1 April 1933 (9/2.2b). 
9/9.8 
Sale of Partnership Interests 
The sale by a partner of his interest in the firm or the retirement or 
death of a partner does not cause a discontinuance or succession so long 
as the firm continues in existence, but the firm is assessed as constituted 
at the time of assessment (6/3.6). 
Adjustments to the income of a 
withdrawing partner (5/3.1) are computed on his share of firm profits 
as of the date of withdrawal. 
If the firm is registered and does continue 
in existence, payment of the outgoing partner's share of firm profits, 
whether of the year of withdrawal or of earlier years, is taxable as 
income to him.’ 
Inventory is valued at the date of withdrawal accord- 
ing to the regular accounting method of the partnership (6/5.1). 
Gain 
or loss realized by a partner on his interest in the capital assets of the 
partnership is treated as capital gain or loss.’ 
Neither the retiring 
partner nor the remaining partners can carry forward losses allocated 
to the retiring partner by a registered partnership. 
The retiring partner’s 
successor can carry such losses forward only if he succeeds to the part- 
ners share by inheritance. 
Losses incurred by an unregistered firm are 
carried forward by the firm itself, and not by its members (7/4.2).

by him on the dissolution of a partnership is determined by reference

9/9.9 
Distribution of Corporate Assets on Liquidation 
When a corporation is liquidated, the accounting rules applicable to 
a discontinuance of business (6/3.5) take effect unless the shareholders 
continue the same business in another form (6/3.6). 
Inventory disposed 
of on liquidation is valued according to the corporation’s regular account- 
ing method (6/5.1), and any difference between the value so determined 
and the price attributable to inventory is treated as business income or 
loss. 
Gain or loss on the sale of nondepreciable capital assets is treated 
as capital gain or loss; but if the business was being carried on during 
the base year in which depreciable assets are sold, the corporation’s 
business income of that year may be subject to a balancing charge or 
balancing allowance representing the difference between the depreciated 
cost of the assets and the price received for them (7/3.6). 
Amounts distributed to the shareholders on liquidation are taxable to 
them as dividends to the extent of accumulated profits of the corporation 
immediately before liquidation (9/2.2b). 
If the corporation sells its 
assets before liquidation, gains realized thereon by the corporation are 
included in the accumulated profits. whose distribution is taxed as a 
dividend. 
If the corporation is liquidated before the assets are sold, 
however, the distribution of any gain realized on the sale of the assets is 
not taxable as a dividend to the shareholders since it is not a part of the 
accumulated profits of the corporation immediately before liquidation, 
and is not taxable as a capital gain since it does not involve the sale, 
exchange, relinquishment, or a transfer of a capital asset by the share- 
holders. 
Liquidation itself does not involve the sale, exchange, relin- 
quishment, or transfer of capital assets by the shareholders, and any 
amount distributed which does not represent accumulated profits of 
the corporation is a nontaxable distribution of capital. Unabsorbed losses

10/1. 
Natural Resource Extraction 
10/1.1 
In General 
Income from the extraction of minerals and the production of oil is 
determined in the same manner as is that of any other business (Chap- 
ter 7), with no special tax concessions other than those granted to other 
industrial undertakings which are newly established (10/6.2). 
Income 
resulting from mining activity which does not constitute the carrying on 
of a business is taxable as “income from other sources” (6/1.2). 
Ex- 
penditures peculiar to these activities are treated as discussed below. 
Where the central government is associated with the taxpayer in the 
extraction or production of petroleum (“mineral oils”) (10/1.7), special 
arrangements as to the expenses which are deductible are authorized. 
For purposes of the tax on undistributed profits, Indian companies 
engaged in mining or certain other industries are permitted to retain a 
higher proportion of profits than companies not engaged in those indus- 
tries (12/2.7b). 
10/1.2 
Exploration, Extraction, and Development Expenses 
The problem of distinguishing between a nondeductible capital ex- 
penditure and a deductible revenue expense is as difficult for natural 
resources activities as for business enterprises in general (7/5.1). 
Expenditures on exploration or prospecting are not deductible if in- 
curred prior to the commencement of a business (7/2.1), unless made 
under a government participation agreement on petroleum (10/1.7). 
Exploration expenditures incurred after the commencement of business 
are generally treated as nondeductible capital outlays designed to bring 
an asset, such as a mine, into existence. 
However, exploration expenses 
involving scientific research, even if of a capital nature, are deductible 
at the rate of 20% per year for five years under the provisions described 
at 7/9,12. 
Expenditures incurred in sinking a pit or shaft are usually treated as 
nondeductible capital expenditures since they serve to bring an asset 
into existence." 
Where it is necessary to extract minerals from a single 
« 
deposit lying at depths close to the surface by the frequent sinking of 
shafts at shallow depths, however, the expenditures incurred thereby are 
deductible. 
The costs incurred in keeping a mine free from water and thereby

The cost of acquiring mineral properties or the right to work such

10/1.4 
Depletion 
No depletion allowances are granted except under government partici- 
pation agreements on petroleum (10/1.7). 
Thus, when a mine or mining 
rights or nitrate grounds are purchased, the cost thereof cannot be treated 
as a cost of the minerals subsequently produced, despite the wasting 
nature of the asset.1?

10/1.6 
Royalties 
Royalties paid for the right to extract natural resources are taxable to 
the recipient in the same manner as are royalties from patents and other 
intangibles (9/5). 
A mining royalty under a license may be taxable as 
income whether paid in a lump sum, in fixed annual amounts, or in 
amounts predicated upon production.!2, 
Where payments are made in 
consideration for an outright sale or for an exclusive license to work the 
mineral property, however, such payments may represent capital sums 
subject to capital gains tax.18 
Royalties paid for the right to extract natural resources are deductible 
expenses of the payor, subject to the general limitations applicable to 
deductible expenses (7/2.1); installment payments of the purchase price 
of property are nondeductible capital expenditures. 
A payment which is taxed to the recipient as an income receipt is not 
necessarily a deductible expense of the payor. 
For example, even though 
a royalty paid for the total assignment of a patent is taxable as income to 
a recipient whose business is the buying and selling of patents or the sale 
of patents on his own inventions, the payment of the royalty may be 
regarded as a nondeductible capital expenditure on the part of the payor. 
for the purchase of a capital asset.

Agreements for Government Participation in Oil Production 
Beginning with the tax -year 1959-1960, agreements entered into by 
the central government for association or participation with the taxpayer 
in petroleum exploration, extraction, or production may authorize, with 
respect to the properties involved in the agreement, more liberal expense 
deductions than the provisions discussed above. 
Subject to approval and 
modification by Parliament, the following arrangements will be given 
effect (§ 10(2AA)): 
1. Deduction of expenses of unsuccessful exploration of any area surrendered 
prior to the beginning of commercial production by the taxpayer. 
2. Deduction, after the beginning of commercial production, of expenses, 
whenever incurred, of exploration, of drilling, or of services, and the cost 
of nondepreciable assets used in those activities. 
8. Allowance for depletion of petroleum in the mining area for the base 
year in which commercial production is begun and for as many years 
thereafter as are specified in the agreement. 
These deductions may be taken instead of or in addition to the standard 
business deductions (7/2). 
10/2. 
Agriculture 
10/2.1 
In General 
Under the Constitution, the central government has no power to tax 
“agricultural income” as that term is defined by the Income-tax Act.’ 
Such income, however, is subject to tax by several of the Indian states 
pursuant to a constitutional authorization (2/1.1).*° 
The Income-tax Act exempts “agricultural income” from tax by exclud- 
ing it from the total income of the recipient (§ 4(3) (viii) ). The Act 
defines agricultural income in terms broad enough to encompass not only 
profits from the production of food and commercial agricultural goods, 
but income realized by a landowner from the rental of land for the grow- 
ing of such goods during the base year, whether he is engaged in the 
~ business of renting farm land or not (§ 2(1)). 
Agricultural income, whether derived from cultivation or from rental 
of farm property, qualifies for exemption only if it meets the three condi- 
tions set forth below. 
1. The agricultural product must be the result of basic operations of culti- 
vation of the land itself, such as planting or tilling the soil, prior to 
germination.17 
Proceeds from the sale of trees grown naturally are not 
exempt, even if activities for further growth and for conservation are 
pursued,!8 although profits from the sale of trees actually planted by the

10/3. 
Insurance 
10/3.1 
In General 
The income of an insurance business, whether derived from the sale of 
insurance premiums, from interest on securities, from property, or from 
other investments, is taxed under special rules contained in the Schedule 
to the Income-tax Act (§ 10(7)). 
Mutual organizations and cooperative 
societies, although exempt from tax on their other income, are subject to 
tax on income from insurance business (§ 14(3); Schedule, Rule 9). 
Since the ordinary methods of accounting for business income do not 
accurately reflect the real income of insurance businesses,*® special com- 
putations, varying with the type of insurance, are prescribed to estab- 
lish the tax base artificially. 
While investment profits of an insurance 
company are treated as insurance income, the income from an industrial 
undertaking carried on by an insurance company is computed in the 
same manner as all other business income (7/1.2). 
Although the tax- 
payer's insurance income must be computed independently of all other 
business income, losses in either activity carried on by the same taxpayer 
may be set off against gains of the other in the same or future years under 
' the rules applicable to other business losses (7/4). The base year for all 
insurance businesses is always the calendar year. 
10/3.2 
Life Insurance 
The Life Insurance Corporation of India, established by the Life 
Insurance Corporation Act of 1956, is completely owned and controlled 
by the government and is now the only corporation permitted to carry on 
life insurance business in India. 
It is taxed at special rates prescribed in 
the annual Finance Acts. 
Income from a life insurance business must be computed separately 
from income from any other business carried on by the taxpayer (Sched-
