ule, Rule 1). The tax base for income from a life insurance business is 
an artificial figure determined by taking either the “gross external incom- 
ings” (gross receipts) of the base year, less certain management expenses 
(10/3.2a), or the annual average surplus of the life insurance business, 
subject to prescribed adjustments (10/3.2b), whichever is greater. 
If 
both methods reveal a deficit or loss, the method which results in the 
smaller deficit must be adopted. 
Neither method gives the actual net 
profit from the entire life insurance operation during the base year, 
although the annual average surplus method more nearly approximates 
actual net profits. The gross external incomings method takes investment 
income less expenses as the tax base although it excludes from computa- 
tion profits on the sale of investment assets. 
If the taxpayer has not 
engaged in business long enough to have required the filing of the valua- 
tion reports, upon which the annual average surplus method is based, 
assessment will be made by the gross external incomings method. 
a. GROSS EXTERNAL INCOMINGS METHOD. 
Under this method, the amount 
of the gross receipts of the life insurance business less management 
expenses for the base year is taken as the tax base if it is larger than the 
annual average surplus of the business. 
Receipts of an income nature, 
such as interest, dividends, fines, profits from reversions or the sale of 
annuities, as well as presumed income from house property (less the statu- 
tory deductions attributable thereto (9/4.4)), are included in the com- 
putation; but premiums from policyholders, 
interest 
and dividends 
earned on any annuity funds, and gains on the sale of securities or other 
assets are specifically excluded (Schedule, Rule 5). 
Management expenses are defined to include, in general, all those 
expenses which, if incurred by an ordinary business, would be proper 
expense deductions (7/2.1); these include commissions paid to agents, 
remuneration of officers, directors, and employees, and general office 
overhead (Schedule, Rule 5). Where the taxpayer company carries on 
other types of business as well as that of life insurance, a fair proportion 
of general management expenses incurred in the operation of the other 
business activities may also be deducted. 
No deduction is allowed for 
bonuses paid to or reserved for policyholders, for depreciation of securi- 
ties or other assets or losses realized on their sale, or for any expense not 
allowable as an ordinary business deduction. 
It is important to note that the deductibility of management expenses 
is limited to a maximum amount computed on the basis of certain per- 
centages of the life insurance premium receipts of the taxpayer for thé 
base year (Schedule, Rule 2). Thus the amount of a business loss which 
could result from the use of this method of computing profits or losses of 
a life insurance company is severely limited.

If this method of computing the tax base results in greater income than 
that of the annual average surplus method, the tax assessed thereon will 
be credited with the amount of all taxes deducted at source on the gross 
receipts during the base year (§ 18(5) ). 
b. ANNUAL AVERAGE SURPLUS METHOD. 
Under this method, the profits of 
the life insurance business are computed actuarially on the basis of peri- 
odic valuation reports which insurance companies are required to file at 
least once every three years under the Insurance Act of 1938.. Where 
valuation reports are filed once every three years, the profits (“annual 
average surplus”) for the base year are taken to be the average (in this 
case one third) of the difference between the net worth or surplus as 
shown on the beginning and ending valuation reports of the last triennium 
reported prior to the tax year. 
If valuation reports are prepared annu- 
ally, the increase in surplus as shown by those reports is taken as the 
basis for assessment of income for the year (Schedule, Rule 2). Reports 
are generally made once every three years. 
The surplus disclosed by the valuation report is computed in accordance 
with the rules listed below. 
1. Any surplus or deficit carried forward from a prior intervaluation period 
must be excluded (Schedule, Rule 2(b)). 
2. Expenditures written off or reserved in the report but not deductible 
from ordinary business income must be added back (Schedule, Rule 2(b)). 
It has been held that this rule does apply to depreciation of furniture, 
automobiles, and books, and that therefore the amount of depreciation 
debited in the accounts for such assets must be allowed in full.®4 
8. Four fifths of any amounts paid to policyholders, 
or reserved for or 
expended on behalf of them, is deductible whether a surplus or a deficit 
exists prior to such deduction (Schedule, Rule 3(qa) 
). 
4, Losses occasioned by sale or other realization, or by the decline in value, 
of securities and other investment assets must be deducted if actually 
written off or depreciated in the accounts or in the valuation surplus 
balance sheet (Schedule, Rule 8(b)). 
Thus, these deductible losses 
need not be realized so long as an actual depreciation of value has 
occurred. 
Gains of a similar nature, whether realized or not, must be 
included in or added to the valuation surplus. 
If this method results in a greater tax base than that of the gross exter- 
nal incomings method, the tax imposed on the annual average surplus is 
credited with the annual average of taxes deducted at source during the 
intervaluation period and not with the taxes deducted at source in the 
base year (Schedule, Rule 4). 
Insurance companies taxed under this 
method are exempt from income tax (but not supertax) on interest on 
tax-free securities of the central government (Schedule, Rule 3(c)). 
Such interest is not exempt from tax if the gross receipts method is used.

10/3.3 
Other Insurance 
The income for tax purposes from an insurance business other than a 
life insurance business is determined from the annual accounts which 
insurers are required to file with the Controller of Insurance under the 
Insurance Act of 1938 (Schedule, Rule 6). 
The accounts must be 
adjusted by adding back any expenditure which would not have been 
deductible from ordinary business income. 
The determination of income 
from a non-life insurance business differs from the determination of 
ordinary business income in two respects, however. 
First, the accounts 
are adjusted for profits and losses realized on the sale of securities and 
other investment assets and for unrealized changes in the value of such 
assets (Schedule, Rule 6). This provision corresponds to the adjustment 
which life insurance companies are required to make in computing annual 
average surplus. 
Secondly, a portion of the premiums received during 
the year is deductible, in practice, as a reserve for unexpired risks. 
The 
percentage deductible is 100% in marine insurance businesses and 50% 
in other insurance businesses. 
10/3.4 
Indian Income of Nonresident Insurers 
If sufficient reliable data are available, a nonresident insurer doing 
business in India must be assessed in the same manner as a domestic 
insurer furnishing the same type of insurance. 
Thus, the income of an 
Indian branch of a nonresident life insurance company is the greater of 
the amounts determined under the gross external incomings and annual 
average surplus methods if the accounts of the branch permit the required 
computations to be made.*? 
Interest earned by a nonresident insurer 
from the investment abroad of premiums received in India is deemed to 
accrue 
in India through the insurers business connection 
in India

In the absence of reliable data sufficient for the determination of 
income under the rules applicable to domestic insurance companies, a 
nonresident insurer doing business in India may be taxed on that propor- 
tion of its world-wide income which Indian premium receipts bear to 
total premium receipts in the base year (Schedule, Rule 8). World-wide 
income of a life insurance company is computed according to the gross 
external incomings method, with the result that deduction of management 
expenses is permitted (10/3.2a). 
Indian premium income consists of all 
premiums paid to the branch in India, but does not include premiums 
payable by an Indian resident on policies taken out abroad. 
This method 
of determining the income of nonresident insurer is not applicable if 
“more reliable data” are available.

10/4. 
Shipping 
Income from the transportation by water of passengers or cargo to or 
from India, or from place to place in India, is taxable as business income 
if the contract of carriage was entered into in India or if the price or fare 
was received in India (11/1.2). 
If a nonresident carries on a shipping business in India, and there is no 
resident agent from whom taxes can be collected (11/3.4), the master of 
any ship owned or chartered by the nonresident must, before leaving an 
Indian port, furnish a return showing the gross receipts paid or payable 
to the nonresident for the transportation of passengers or cargo from that 
port since the last arrival of the ship there (§$ 44A, 44B(1)). 
The 
Income-tax Officer then assesses one sixth of this amount as income and 
collects the income tax and supertax thereon at the rates applicable to a 
company doing business in India (§ 44B(2) )(12/2.1, 12/2.4). 
A port 
clearance will not be granted until the tax has been paid. 
This summary 
assessment becomes final unless the taxpayer, in the year following pay- 
ment of the tax, elects to have his tax reassessed on the basis of ordinary 
business profits for the base year. 
In the event of such an election, the 
tax is recalculated, and a refund is made or additional tax is paid, as the 
reassessment requires (§ 44C). 
A portion of the cost of a new ship may be deducted from business 
income as a “development rebate” in the year of acquisition (10/6.4). 
10/5. 
Investment Companies and Banks 
The income of an investment company which is derived from transac- 
tions in investments is taxed as business income in the usual manner 
(7/1).%> 
It is therefore subject to all the general rules relative to com- 
mencement and termination of business (6/3) and other accounting 
techniques (6/4), deductions (7/2), and inventory valuations (6/5.1). 
At the taxpayer’s option, investment assets may be, and usually are, 
treated as inventory and valued accordingly; and profits or losses made on 
the sale of such assets, as well as on the unrealized appreciation or depre- 
ciation in value of the assets at the end of the base period, are thereby 
taken into account as business income or losses. 
However, profits realized

Industrial Incentives 
10/6.1 
In General 
In order to encourage industrial development, there is a special exemp- 
tion for the income of new industries and a further exemption for divi- 
dends paid by corporations operating new industries 
(10/6.2). 
An

dividends (10/6.3). 
Moreover, all businesses are permitted to deduct a 
percentage of the cost of new machinery or plant, or of a new ship, as a 
“development rebate,” in addition to depreciation, in the year in which 
such assets are acquired or installed (10/6.4). 
Apart from the development rebate and the extra-shift depreciation 
allowances available for machinery and plant (7/8.la), there are no 
longer any provisions for accelerated depreciation.

10/6.2 
New Industries Tax Exemption 
Certain industrial enterprises established after 31 March 1948 are 
exempt from income tax and supertax on so much of their income as does 
not exceed 6% of “the capital employed in the undertaking” (§§ 15C, 
17(3) ). However, the amount of such exempt income is included in total 
income for the purpose of determining the tax rate applicable to the 
taxpayer's taxable income (§ 16(1)(a)). 
The exemption is available for 
the base year in which production commences and for the four succeeding 
base years. 
In order to qualify for the exemption, an industrial enterprise 
must have begun to manufacture or produce articles in India within 18 
years after 1 April 1948; must employ 10 or more workers in a manufac- 
turing process carried on with the aid of power, or 20 or more workers in 
~ one carried on without the aid of power; and must not have been formed 
by the splitting up or reconstruction of an existing business or by the 
acquisition of property previously used in any other business (§ 15C(2) ). 
The capital employed in an enterprise is to be determined in accord- 
ance with rules issued by the Central Board of Revenue. 
In general, 
these rules prescribe that the capital employed shall be the sum of the 
cost of nondepreciable assets, the written-down value of depreciable 
assets, and half the total profits of the base year, reduced by outstanding 
liabilities.*° 
Dividends paid by an industrial enterprise out of profits which have 
been exempted under the foregoing provisions are exempt from income

While the object of these exemptions is to encourage the establishment

of cases. 
Depreciation allowances (7/3) and the development rebate 
(10/6.4) are ordinarily sufficient to provide full exemption for the income

It is noteworthy that the exemption of profits 
equal to 6% of capital employed by new industries may have an anoma-

through the tax years 1959-1960 (9/2.4a). 
If the enterprise has no

development rebate, any dividend declared out of its actual profits is 
taxable to the shareholders; but if taxable profits remain after the depre- 
ciation allowances and the development rebate, and a dividend is declared 
out of that portion of the remaining profits which is exempt under the 
provisions here discussed, the shareholder is exempt from tax on the 
dividend. 
10/6.3 
Intercorporate Dividend Exemption 
Dividends received by any company are exempt from supertax (but not 
income tax) if received from an Indian company which has been formed 
and registered after 31 March 1952 and which meets the conditions set 
forth below (§ 56A). 
1. The company declaring the dividends must be qualified for exemption 
of its own income under the new industries tax exemption discussed at 
10/6.2. 
However, the language of the provision does not seem to limit 
the intercorporate dividend to five-year period for which the new indus- 
tries exemption is available. 
2. The company must be wholly or mainly engaged in the manufacture or 
production of one or more of the commodities listed below. 
(a) Coal, including coke and other derivatives. 
(b) Iron and steel. 
(c) Motor and aviation fuel, kerosene, crude oils, and synthetic oils 
(not including exploration for petroleum deposits). 
(d) Heavy chemicals, including fertilizers. 
(e) Heavy machinery used in industry, including ball bearings, roller 
bearings, gear wheels, and parts thereof, boilers, and steam gener- 
ating equipment. 
(f£) Machinery and equipment for the generation, transmission, and dis- 
tribution of electric energy.

Development Rebate 
A “development rebate” of 25% of the cost of new machinery and plant 
installed after 31 March 1954 is granted to the taxpayer as a deduction 
from business profits of the base year in which the property is acquired 
~or installed (§ 10(2)(vi-b)). 
A development rebate of 25% of cost was 
also granted for new ships acquired after 31 March 1954 and before 1 Jan- 
uary 1958, but for new ships acquired after 31 December 1957 a develop- 
ment rebate of 40% of cost is granted. 
The amount of the development 
rebate is treated in all respects as if it were an expense paid or incurred 
for the purposes of the business. 
The development rebate is allowed only 
if the relevant property is used wholly for the purpose of the taxpayer's 
business. 
With respect to ships acquired and plant and machinery 
installed after 31 December 1957, the allowance of the rebate is condi- 
tioned upon the requirements listed below. 
1. The taxpayer must furnish the particulars prescribed for the depreciation 
allowance (7/3.1d). 
2. Seventy-five percent of the amount 
of development rebate must be 
debited to the taxpayer’s profit and loss account and credited to a

During this period it

remitted outside India either as profits or for the creation of an asset 
outside India. 
3. The property involved must not be sold or otherwise transferred by the 
taxpayer to any person other than the government within 10 years from 
the end of the year in which the property was acquired or installed. 
Although the practice of the Department of Revenue has been to 
allow the development rebate only for industrial plant and machinery, 
which are used for manufacture and production, and not for equipment, 
such as automobiles, trucks, and typewriters, there has been a recent 
High Court decision that the allowance of the development rebate cannot 
be restricted in this manner.*° 
If within 10 years after a development rebate is taken the relevant asset 
is sold or transferred to anyone except the government, or if any portion 
of the special reserve account is distributed as dividends, used to create 
an asset outside India (other than an asset intended for shipment to 
India), or used for any purpose other than the taxpayer's business, the 
Income-tax Officer may disallow the rebate for the year in which it was 
taken and make a reassessment for that year as if rectifying a mistake 
apparent from the record (§ 35(11))(13/2.4). 
A transfer to a new 
corporation in the course of a corporate reorganization would cause the 
withdrawal of the rebate. 
The development rebate is not treated as a depreciation allowance; 
hence it does not enter into the computation of the total depreciation 
allowable to the taxpayer, does not affect depreciated cost, and is disre- 
garded in the computation of a balancing allowance or balancing charge. 
As a result, the total amount deductible over the life of a depreciable 
asset which qualifies for the development rebate is 125% of the cost to 
the taxpayer of new machinery and plant, and 140% of the cost of a 
new ship. 
If the taxpayer's total income from all sources during the base year is 
insufficient to absorb the development rebate, any unused portion of the 
rebate may be carried forward and set off against the taxpayer's total 
income in succeeding years for a maximum of eight years. 
Rebates car- 
ried forward from earlier years must be deducted before those of later 
years, and any rebates carried forward must be deducted first before 
setting off a development rebate for the current year (§ 10(2) (vi-a)). 
The development rebate may be carried forward before unused deprecia- 
tion allowances, which can be carried forward without time limit (7/3.7).

11/1. 
Introduction 
11/1.1 
General Principles 
The total income of any taxpayer includes all income received or 
deemed to be received by him in India (11/1.5) and all income which 
accrues to him or is deemed to accrue to him in India during the base 
year (§4(1)). 
The total income of a resident taxpayer includes, in 
addition, all income accruing or arising to him outside India during the 
base year; but a taxpayer who is resident but not ordinarily resident is 
not taxed on income accruing or arising outside India and not derived 
from a business or profession in India, provided the income is neither 
received in nor brought into India (11/2.1). A resident taxpayer receives


<!-- page 326 of 600 -->

a credit for foreign taxes paid on income neither accruing nor deemed to 
accrue in India (11/2.4). 
Apart from this credit and the limited exemp- 
tion available to persons resident but not ordinarily resident, where in- 
come is received or deemed to be received and where income accrues or is 
deemed to accrue is material only to the tax liability of nonresidents 
(11/8). 
Domicile and citizenship do not affect tax liability except in 
the case of foreign technicians (5/5.5). The effects of income tax treaties 
are described at 11/4. 
The place where income accrues or arises under the Income-tax Act 
— 
is, in effect, its “geographical source,” the place where the income from 
a transaction is considered to originate. 
This is not necessarily the same 
as its “generating source,” the location of the property or activity which 
produces it. The generating source of income from the sale of goods, 
for example, is the seller’s place of business; but if the place where title 
to the goods passes is regarded as the geographical source of the income, 
then the place where title to the goods passes is the place where the 
income accrues or arises under the Income-tax Act (11/1.2a). 
Hence 
the meaning of “accrual” in the phrase “place of accrual” must be dis- 
tinguished from the accounting use of the word in connection with the 
problem of when income not yet received should be shown in the tax- 
payer's books; the relevance of time of “accrual” of income in the latter 
sense is discussed at 6/4. Throughout the following discussion “accrues” 
will be used in place of “accrues or arises.” 
Income which does not actually accrue in India may nonetheless be 
deemed to accrue in India if it is derived from a business connection in 
India (11/1.2b), from the performance of services in India (11/1.3), 
as a dividend paid out of profits taxable in India (11/1.4b), from any 
property, asset, or source of income located in India, as interest from 
money brought into India, or from the sale, exchange, or transfer of a 
capital asset located in India (11/1.4). 
The determination of residence status of various taxable entities is 
explained in Chapter 5 as indicated: individuals (5/1.2, 5/4.1), corpo- 
rations (5/2.3, 5/4.4), partnerships (5/3.1c), Hindu undivided families 
(5/3.2), associations (5/3.3), trusts (5/3.6). 
The pattern of taxation 
is the same for all taxable entities; but provisions which apply to tax- 
payers “resident but not ordinarily resident” cannot apply to corpo- 
rations, since a resident corporation is deemed to be ordinarily resident 
(5/2.1). 
The statutory provision which provides the basis for taxation refers to 
residents and income received or accrued in or outside the “taxable 
territories” (§ 4(1)).

11/1.2 
Place of Accrual of Business Income 
a. ACTUAL PLACE OF ACCRUAL. 
There are no rigid criteria which can be 
applied for determining the actual place of accrual of business income; 
each case is decided on its particular facts. 
In general, income is con- 
sidered to accrue at the place where business transactions are “effected,” 
that is, the place where they are actually carried out, rather than at the 
place from which the business is controlled or directed.? 
It appears that income from the sale in India of goods purchased out- 
side India accrues entirely in India if the contract of sale is entered into 
in India and the title to the goods passes to the buyer in India; and con- 
versely, if goods are purchased in India and title is passed abroad to a 
foreign buyer under contracts executed abroad, the entire income from 
the sale accrues outside India.* 
The courts are uniform in holding that 
income from the purchase and sale of goods accrues either at the place 
of contract or at the place where title passes to the buyer, but there is 
a divergence of views as to the proper treatment where these two places 
are different. 
Thus, where an offer for the sale of goods produced out- 
side India was accepted in India by an Indian buyer, but title to the 
goods passed outside India and the sale price was received outside India, 
it was held that the entire profits accrued outside India; * but in another 
case, the execution of contracts of sale in India with respect to goods 
produced abroad was held to give rise to Indian income, without any 
teference to the place where title passed.? 
In a third case, in which the 
operation of a business involved entering into contracts of sale in India 
and the purchase abroad of goods which were delivered outside India 
to an Indian buyer, it was held that the profit had to be apportioned 
between the place of contract and the place where title passed, that is, 
where the sale was eftected.°®

If the proceeds of the sale are 
received in India, however, the entire proceeds are taxable without 
apportionment (11/1.5). 
In the case of a business which involves the rendition of services, 
rather than the sale of goods, the profit is attributed to the place where 
the services are rendered. 
Thus, if technical services are rendered partly 
in India and partly outside India, as where plans and designs are pre- 
pared outside the country and construction is supervised in the country, 
income is apportioned between the domestic and foreign activities. 
The 
installation of goods by a nonresident for a customer in India does not 
give rise to income accruing in India merely because installation is 
included in the selling price of the goods, unless other elements of the 
transaction also take place in India. 
However, if the installation services 
are provided under a separate contract, the price received for the serv- 
ices accrues in India. 
b, DEEMED PLACE OF ACCRUAL. 
Income is deemed to accrue or arise in 
India if it is derived, directly or indirectly, “through or from any business 
connection in India” (§ 42(1)). 
The effect of this provision is to cause 
some income to be attributed to an Indian origin regardless of its actual 
origin, and thus to tax income which would not otherwise be taxable. 
However, unlike income received in India, which is taxable in its entirety 
regardless of where it accrues or is deemed to accrue, income which is 
derived through a business connection is taxable only to the extent that 
it is reasonably attributable to operations carried out in India (§ 42(3) ). 
It will be seen that there is a certain overlapping between income 
deemed to accrue in India because of the business connection doctrine 
and income which actually accrues in India. 
Thus, if goods are manu- 
factured outside India and sold in India under a contract of sale entered 
into there, it is immaterial whether there is a business connection in 
India; in either event, the manufacturing and selling profits will be segre- 
gated, and only the portion of the profit attributable to the selling activity 
will be taxed. 
It is important to note that the existence of a business 
connection in India does not, of itself, subject to tax the income from all

Income from business transactions entered into inde- 
pendently of the business connection becomes taxable only if it actually 
accrues in India under the rules discussed above. 
A business connection in India may be found if there is a business in 
India, there is a connection between a nonresident and that business, and 
the nonresident has earned some income through that connection.?. 
But 
there must be some continuity of relationship between the nonresident 
and the Indian connection; the business connection doctrine does not 
apply where there is merely an isolated transaction or several discontinu- 
ous transactions between the nonresident and his Indian counterpart.® 
Listed below are examples of relationship which would constitute a

1. Maintenance in India of a branch office, or appointment of an agent in 
India, for the purchase of goods.® 
2. Maintenance of a factory in India for the processing of raw materials ex- 
clusively for export.1° 
3. Establishment of an Indian subsidiary corporation to purchase products 
of the foreign parent and resell them in India. 
4. Maintenance of close financial association between a resident company 
and a nonresident company.!? 
5. The grant to a resident of a continuing license to exploit in India an 
asset of a nonresident.1* 
A business connection does not exist unless the profits of the nonresi- 
dent are in some way affected by the activities carried on in India.

Place of Accrual of Income from Services 
Income which is taxable under the category “salaries” is deemed to 
accrue in India if the services for which it is paid are rendered in India 
($4(1), Explanation 2). 
Starting in the tax year 1959-1960 for pur-

Explanation 2A). With this exception, the Act is silent as to the place of 
accrual of remuneration for work performed abroad. 
If remuneration 
for work performed outside India is received in India, it is taxable in 
India regardless of where it accrues (11/1.5).

11/1.4 
Place of Accrual of Income from Capital 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Income arising directly or indirectly through or from 
any property, asset, or source of income in India is deemed to accrue in 
India (§ 42(1)). 
The phrase “source of income,” as used in the Act, 
refers to the location of the property or asset which gives rise to the 
income, the “generating source” of the income, and not to the “geograph- 
ical source” of the income (11/1.1). 
Therefore, income derived from

accrue in India.

’ could be deemed to accrue in India,?° in practice nonresident share-

company, even if the dividends are paid wholly or partly out of profits

Interest on securities issued by the government of India,

Royalties from the use of tangible property in India are

Royalties for the use of intangible properties not

€. CAPITAL GAINS. 
Income from the sale, exchange, or transfer of a capital 
asset situated in India is deemed to accrue in India (§ 42(1)). 
11/1.5 
Income Received in India 
All taxpayers, whatever their residence status, are taxed on income 
received in India during the base year (§ 4(1)(a)). 
Income is received 
in India only if it is received there on the first occasion when the recipi- 
ent obtains control over the funds.”* 
If income is received outside India 
by the party entitled to it, any subsequent remittance of that income to 
India is not a receipt of income in India, since the receipt of the amount 
as income took place abroad.?4 
Income which is exempt from tax when 
received because received abroad cannot be taxed when it is later remit- 
ted to India unless the taxpayer is resident in India in the year of remit- 
tance 
(11/2.2).

11/2. 
Income of Residents from Outside India 
11/2.1 
In General 
A resident taxpayer is taxable on 
all income from outside India 
($4(1)(a@)). 
Prior to the Finance Act of 1959, income of a resident 
which was derived outside India and which was not brought into or 
received in India was exempt from tax up to a maximum limit of 
Rs 4,500 per year. 
This exemption has been withdrawn for income, 
including salaries subject to withholding, taxable in the tax year 1960- 
1961 or thereafter. 
A person resident but not ordinarily resident in India is not taxable on 
foreign income which is neither brought into nor received in India unless 
that income is derived from a business controlled in India or from a pro- 
- 
fession or vocation set up in India (§ 4(1), 2nd Proviso). 
The exemp- 
tion is not available to a corporation since a corporation cannot be 
resident but not ordinarily resident. 
The exemption applies to income 
which accrues abroad notwithstanding the fact that it may be deemed to 
accrue in India. 
If exempt income is brought into India in a subsequent 
year, it may become taxable at that time (11/2.2). 
If a person who is not ordinarily resident in India carries on business 
with a resident and, as a result of artificial arrangements between the 
parties, the profits of the business are less than the ordinary profits which 
might be expected therefrom, the income of the resident may be esti- 
mated on the basis of that which might reasonably be expected to be 
derived but for the artificial arrangement (§ 42(2)). 
Such an estimate 
may be based on a percentage of turnover, or on that proportion of the 
total profits of the business which the receipts attributable to Indian 
activities bear to total receipts, or “in such other manner as the Income- 
tax Officer may deem suitable” (Rule 34). 
Remittances received by a wife resident in India out of any part of 
the income of a nonresident husband which is not included in his total 
income are deemed to be income accruing to the wife in India (§ 4(2) ).

As explained at 6/8.2, a resident may be taxed on the income from assets 
transferred by him to a person not ordinarily resident or to a nonresident 
if he acquires any rights to the enjoyment of that income. 
11/2.2 
Income Brought into India 
A resident is subject to tax on income brought into India during the 
base year which accrued to him outside India in an earlier base year 
when it was exempt from tax (§ 4(1)(b) (iii) ). This provision operates 
only to tax income of a resident which was not taxable in the year of 
accrual because it was neither received in nor brought into India in that 
year (11/2.1), because the taxpayer was not resident in India in that 
year, or because the income accrued prior to 1 April 1933. 
Income of a 
nonresident which is not otherwise taxable is not rendered taxable merely 
because it is brought into India. 
Income accruing outside India prior to the base year will nonetheless 
be exempt from tax when brought into India by a resident if the taxpayer 
was not resident in India in two of the three years immediately preceding 
the base year ($ 4(1), 4th Proviso). 
This provision permits a person 
who establishes residence in India to bring into the country, during the 
first two years of continuous residence, income earned by him abroad in 
prior years. 
Income accruing outside India prior to the base year will also be 
exempt when brought into India if, within three months after the receipt 
in India of the foreign income, the taxpayer has paid all income tax, 
interest, or penalty otherwise owing by him under the Income-tax Act 
(§ 4(1), 5th Proviso). 
This provision is applicable only to income which 
would not have been taxable unless brought into or received in India. 
Hence it would benefit a taxpayer who was ordinarily resident when 
the income was originally earned only to the extent that the income had 
qualified for exemption up to Rs 4,500 because not brought into India at 
that time. 
It would benefit a taxpayer who was resident but not ordinar- 
ily resident when the income was earned only to the extent that the 
income was subject at that time to either of the exemptions described at 
11/2.1. 
Its chief purpose is to enable persons who have established 
ordinary residence in India to continue to bring into India income earned 
by them in prior years when they did not occupy that status. 
Income initially received abroad by the taxpayer is “brought into” 
India if it is remitted to India out of the taxpayer’s foreign profits. 
There 
is a presumption that a remittance to India is out of foreign profits, and 
not out of foreign capital, if foreign profits are sufficient to cover the 
remittance.*? 
However, this presumption may be rebutted. 
Thus, where 
a taxpayer borrowed money in India, transmitted it abroad for use in his

If foreign income is converted into capital 
and the capital is transferred thereafter to India, the transfer is treated 
as the remittance of capital and not as income brought into India. 
Thus, where foreign income was used to purchase machinery which was 
brought into India for use in domestic manufacture, and not for the 
purpose of resale, it was held that what was brought into India was capi- 
tal and not income.2*? 
However, it appears that if income were not 
genuinely converted into capital, as where foreign income was used 
abroad to purchase capital assets which were then brought into India 
and resold without any intention of ever using the assets as capital, there 
would be no effective capitalization of income and the foreign income 
would be deemed to have been brought into India.?8 
Whether a particular remittance from abroad is out of income, and 
whether foreign income has been effectively converted into capital before 
remittance to India, are difficult questions which must be resolved on the 
basis of the particular facts of each case. 
11/2.3 
Blocked Foreign Income 
When prohibitions or restrictions in the laws of a foreign country pre- 
vent income derived there from being brought into India in any form, 
whether capitalized or not, and from being used abroad, the income is 
assessed in the normal manner in the year in which it is earned, but the 
taxpayers liability for payment of the tax thereon, computed at his 
average rate for that year, is deferred until the prohibitions or restric- 
tions have been removed (§ 45, Proviso). 
11/2.4 
Credit for Foreign Taxes 
a. NONTREATY CREDIT. 
A resident in India who has paid income tax in 
any country with which India does not have a treaty for the relief or 
avoidance of double taxation is entitled to credit against his Indian 
income tax for an amount equal to the Indian average rate or the foreign 
average rate, whichever is lower, applied to the “doubly taxed income” 
~(§49D(1)). 
No credit is allowed for foreign tax paid on any income 
which, under the Indian rules as to place of accrual (11/1), either 
accrues in India or is deemed to accrue in India. 
However, so long as 
the income did not accrue and was not deemed to accrue in India, the 
fact that it arose in a country other than that in which the foreign tax 
was paid would not prevent the granting of a credit.

The amount of the foreign tax credit is computed in the manner 
described below. 
1. Determine the Indian average rate of tax by dividing the amount of 
Indian income tax and supertax by the total income for Indian tax. 
2, Determine the foreign average rate of tax by dividing the amount of 
income tax and supertax actually paid to the foreign country by the 
amount of income subjected to tax in the foreign country. 
3. Multiply the doubly taxed income by the lower of the two rates found 
above. 
Creditable foreign income taxes include excess profits taxes and busi- 
ness profits taxes levied by the government of a foreign country, but do 
not include any taxes levied by any governmental subdivision or local 
authority. 
Special provision is made for credit against Indian tax of either the 
amount of tax paid to Pakistan on agricultural income, or an amount of 
tax on Pakistan agricultural income computed at the average rate of 
Indian tax, whichever is less (§ 49D(3) ).

11/3.1 
In General 
A nonresident, whether an individual, a corporation, or

All of the rules governing the determination

Moreover, special provisions for determination of the

Income tax and

his total world-wide income 
(11/3.5, 12/4). 
Foreign corporations, 
whether resident or nonresident, are subject to special rates of supertax 
if they have not made prescribed arrangements for the declaration and 
payment of dividends in India (12/2.4). 
The rules governing the determination of the place of accrual of 
income are discussed at 11/1. 
Of particular interest to nonresidents are

11/3.2 
Apportionment of Income from International Transactions 
Where income of a nonresident from business transactions carried out 
partly within and partly outside India is taxable in India either because 
it actually accrues there or because it is deemed to accrue there through 
a business connection or otherwise (11/1), only that portion of the 
income which is attributable to the operations in India is taken into 
account; any portion of the income which is attributable to operations 
carried out abroad is nontaxable (§ 42(3)). 
Thus, if a nonresident 
manufactures goods abroad and sells them in India, his total profit is 
apportioned between the manufacturing profit and the selling profit and 
only the latter is subject to tax.2® 
Similarly, where raw materials are 
purchased in India and exported for processing abroad, and the nature 
of the operation is such as to constitute a business connection in India, 
the portion of the total profit which is attributable to the activities per- 
formed in India must be determined, and only that portion is taxable.®° 
Conversely, if goods are purchased abroad and sold in India, the portion 
of the profit attributable to the foreign purchasing activities may be 
allocated to the foreign source so as not to be taxable in India. 
However, 
it appears that the mere act of buying would not itself be considered as 
producing a profit unless conducted systematically with considerable 
effort and expense.*!

The withholding requirements apply only to payments of income which 
are taxable under the provisions of the Income-tax Act. 
A payment of 
the purchase price for property is not, of itself, income, since the income 
of the seller can only be determined after deducting his cost of goods 
sold and other expenses from his receipts; but the payor may none the 
less be required to withhold tax on the estimated profit to be realized 
from the payment. 
Tax also would have to be withheld from fees paid 
to a nonresident for technical services rendered in India. 
Tax need not 
_ be withheld from gross trading receipts.?* 
In cases of doubt the payor 
would ordinarily protect himself by consultation with the Income-tax 
Officer. 
b. RATE OF wITHHOLDING. 
Where withholding is required, tax is with- 
held at rates prescribed for that purpose in the Finance Act for the tax 
year in which the payments are made (§ 18). A nonresident may obtain 
from the Income-tax Officer a certificate requiring payments of interest 
on securities to be made with income tax withheld at a reduced rate 
or with no income tax withheld, or a certificate requiring payment of 
dividends with no income tax or supertax withheld, as explained at 9/7. 
For purposes of withholding of income tax and supertax from payments 
of salaries, withholding of supertax from payments of interest on securi- 
ties, and withholding of income tax and supertax from payments other 
than salaries, interest on securities, or dividends, a nonresident taxpayer 
other than a corporation may obtain a certificate requiring payment with 
tax withheld at a reduced rate or without withholding of tax; in these 
cases, the Income-tax Officer may also on his own initiative require the 
withholding of income tax and supertax from payments to a nonresident 
at rates higher than those prescribed in the Finance Act (§§ 18(2B), 
18(3), 18(3B)). 
In order to obtain a certificate, the taxpayer must 
show that his potential tax liability for the year will be less than the 
amount which would be withheld at the prescribed rates because his 
~ total income or total world income will be taxable at lower rates than 
those provided for withholding. 
In addition, if any payment to a nonresident, other than a payment 
of interest, appears to be only partly taxable, the payor may obtain from 
the Income-tax Officer a determination as to the proportion which is to 
be regarded as taxable, and may withhold tax accordingly (§ 18(8C) ). 
The income of a nonresident payee of income from which tax is with- 
held at source includes the amount of the tax withheld (§ 18(4)). 
The 
withholding system is provisional in nature since all amounts withheld 
are treated as payments on account of the taxpayer’s final liability for 
the year. 
Consequently, if the tax finally assessed for the year is more

11/3.4 
Other Methods of Recovering Tax Owed by Nonresidents 
The tax on any income receivable on behalf of a nonresident by a 
trustee or agent may be recovered from the trustee or agent if not levied 
on the beneficiary directly (§ 40(2)). 
Tax owed by a nonresident on 
income taxable because it is deemed to accrue or arise in India is not 
only subject to withholding, but may be assessed on an agent of the 
taxpayer or recovered from any assets of the taxpayer in India (§ 42(1), 
1st Proviso). 
Moreover, any person employed by or on behalf of a non- 
resident, or having a business connection with him, or through whom the 
nonresident receives any income, may be designated by the Income-tax 
Officer as agent of the nonresident for income tax purposes, provided the 
person so appointed is given an opportunity to be heard (§ 48), even if 
he is not in fact an agent of the nonresident,®° and even if he is himself 
a nonresident.?6 
However, a person designated as an agent under this 
provision may be required to pay tax only on income of the nonresident 
with which he has had some connection.** 
A person designated as a statutory agent is authorized to retain out 
of any money payable by him to the nonresident an amount equal to the 
agent’s estimated liability on behalf of the nonresident (§ 42(1)). 
If 
there is a disagreement between a nonresident and his statutory agent, 
the agent may obtain‘a 
certificate from the Income-tax Officer stating the 
amount to be retained. 
If such a certificate is obtained, the agent may 
not thereafter be held accountable for any amount in excess of that 
specified in the certificate unless he has in his hands additional funds of 
the nonresident. 
Since the appointment of a person as an agent may 
be made even after the income on which the tax is imposed has arisen 
and has been paid to the nonresident, the agent may have to pay the 
tax out of his own pocket if he has retained no funds of the nonresident 
out of which he can reimburse himself. 
However, proceedings may not 
be commenced against a statutory agent if more than two years have 
elapsed after the end of the tax year in which the income of the non- 
resident was taxable (§ 34(1), 2nd Proviso). 
No one who is not in fact an agent or trustee may be required to 
pay the tax owing by a nonresident unless specifically designated as 
agent of the nonresident for tax purposes.

11/3.5 
Rates of Tax Applicable to Nonresidents 
The rates of income tax and supertax applicable to nonresident cor- 
porations do not differ from those applicable to resident corporations, 
but higher rates of supertax are provided for foreign corporations which 
have not made prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment 
of dividends in India (12/2.4, 12/2.9). 
For other nonresident taxpayers, 
two alternative methods of determining the rates of tax are provided 
($17(1)): 
1. Under the normal method, a nonresident is subject to income tax on his 
total income at the maximum rate 
(12/1.3a) without benefit of the 
graduated rates. 
Supertax is payable on total income either at the rate 
of 19% or at the graduated rate (12/1.6), whichever produces the higher 
tax. 
2. In lieu of paying income tax and supertax on the foregoing basis, the tax- 
payer may elect to compute tax on his “total world income” (6/1.1) in 
the same manner as if he were a resident and to pay that proportion of 
the tax so computed which his total income (Indian income) bears to 
his total world income. 
The election of this method of computing the 
tax may reduce the taxpayer's liability if, as a result of foreign losses 
or for some other reason, the graduated rates of income tax and supertax 
determined by reference to total world income result in a lower effective 
rate of tax on Indian income than the special rates provided for non- 
residents. 
An election to be taxed on the second basis must be made prior to 
30 June of the first tax year in which the taxpayer becomes taxable. 
Once the election has been made, it is binding for all subsequent tax 
years. 
Starting with the tax year 1960-1961, the second basis of compu- 
tation will be the only one available to a nonresident citizen of India 
receiving a salary from the Indian government for services performed 
abroad (§ 17(1A)). 
11/3.6 
Effect of Form of Business Organization 
a. DOMESTIC BRANCH OF A FOREIGN CORPORATION. 
A branch is not a 
taxable entity separate and distinct from the principal office. 
If a foreign 
corporation maintains a branch in India, it is the corporation which is 
the taxpayer, and not the branch. 
As noted at 11/1.2b, a branch consti- 
tutes a business connection in India, with the result that income derived 
by the corporation through transactions with the branch is deemed to 
accrue in India; and the maintenance of a branch in India may result in 
taxation not only of those profits which are directly attributable to the 
branch activities in India, but also of those profits which are earned by

In order to determine whether a nonresident corporation has

the Income-tax Officer may require the branch or the principal office to 
furnish financial statements relating to the corporation’s activities outside 
India. 
If the income of the branch cannot be readily ascertained from 
the information furnished, its income may be estimated as explained 
at 11/38.2. 
Losses incurred by the corporation outside India may not be set off 
against the branch profits. 
Losses incurred by a domestic branch may be

foreign profits of the nonresident corporation (7/4.4). 
Interest paid by

as a deduction. 
However, a portion of the overhead expenses of the principal office may

domestic corporation unless the foreign corporation has made prescribed 
arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends in India 
(12/2.4, 12/2.9). 
b. RESIDENT SUBSIDIARY OF A FOREIGN CORPORATION. A resident subsidiary 
of a foreign corporation is taxable on its entire income wherever received 
or accrued. 
It is taxed at the same rates as an Indian company unless 
it is a foreign corporation which has not made the prescribed arrange- 
ments for the declaration and payment of dividends in India (12/2.4, 
12/2.9). 
A foreign parent corporation is exempt from tax on dividends declared 
by a resident subsidiary out of income entitled to the new industries 
exemption (10/6.2). 
If the subsidiary is an Indian company meeting 
certain conditions, all dividends which the parent receives from it are 
exempt from supertax (10/6.3); if the subsidiary is an Indian company 
which does not meet those conditions, dividends received from it by the 
parent are subject to supertax at a preferential rate (12/2.4, 12/2.9). 
In addition, since a resident subsidiary carrying on a business in India 
constitutes a business connection of the parent in India, the parent may 
be taxed on income deemed to accrue in India through the business con- 
nection (11/1.2b); and the subsidiary may be taxed as agent of the 
parent in respect of such income (11/3.4).

11/4. 
Tax Treaties 
11/4.1 
Treaties in Force 
Treaties for the avoidance of double taxation have been entered into 
with Pakistan, Ceylon, Sweden, and Switzerland, pursuant to authoriza- 
tion in the Income-tax Act to enter into such agreements.3® 
Treaties 
with the United States, West Germany, and Japan were negotiated in 
1959 but are not yet in effect. 
In addition, rules have been issued to 
provide for relief against double taxation in respect of income on which 
tax has been paid both in India and in Aden or one of several African 
members of the British Commonwealth. 
The rules with respect to Aden and the African countries confine relief 
to the granting of a credit against the tax payable to India for tax paid 
to the other country, and does not extend to any other matters (11/4.8c). 
The treaties with Pakistan and Ceylon are designed to avoid double 
taxation by allocating the taxing authority between the respective 
parties, and providing for an abatement of the tax imposed by either 
country on any income allocated to and taxed by the other (11/4.8b). 
These two agreements contain no provision for a foreign tax credit 
except for taxes paid to a third country (11/4.3c). 
Although the Pak- 
istan and Ceylon treaties and the Aden and African relief rules are 
principally applicable to residents of the respective countries, it should 
be noted that their provisions are equally available to any person who 
derives income which, under the treaty provisions, is reserved for tax- 
ation either to India or to the other country. 
The Swedish and Swiss treaties, on the other hand, both avoid double 
taxation by exempting certain classes of income from tax in one of the 
contracting countries (11/4.3a). 
Except for the treatment of income 
from shipping under the Swedish treaty (11/4.6), these treaties contain 
no provisions for credit for foreign taxes paid. 
The draft United States 
treaty operates in part by exempting a few classes of income from tax 
in one of the contracting countries, but also provides for the granting

11/4.2 
Taxes Covered 
The treaties and the Aden and African relief rules apply to Indian 
income tax and supertax, including surcharges.*® At the time the Pakistan 
agreement was adopted, it applied also to a business profits tax then in 
effect (2/1.1); and the Ceylon and Sweden treaties apply to any profits 
tax or other tax similar to an income tax which may be enacted. 
In each 
case, the treaty covers similar taxes in the other contracting state. 
The 
Swiss treaty covers Swiss cantonal and communal, as well as federal, 
taxes on income and profits. 
The Swedish treaty covers the Swedish 
income tax, including the coupon tax; the tax on corporations reducing 
share capital; the tax on undistributed profits of corporations; the tax 
on public entertainers; the local income tax; and the seamen’s tax.4° 
The 
draft United States treaty covers federal income taxes, including surtaxes. 
11/4.3 
Methods of Avoiding Double Taxation 
a. EXEMPTION. 
Under the Swedish and Swiss treaties and the draft 
United States treaty, each country exempts from tax entirely certain 
classes of income which would otherwise be taxable under its law, 
regardless of whether the other party imposes tax on the income so 
exempted. 
Thus, the Swedish treaty provides exemption from Indian 
tax for specified classes of income received in or derived from India by 
persons resident in Sweden and not resident in India, and for specified 
classes of income derived by Indian residents from Sweden; and corre- 
sponding exemptions from Swedish tax are provided for the Indian 
income of Swedish residents and for Swedish income of Indian residents. 
The Swiss treaty covers only income from the operation of aircraft by 
foreign enterprises (11/46). 
The draft United States treaty provides 
exemption only for commercial or industrial profits not derived through 
a permanent establishment 
(11/4.4), income from the operation of 
aircraft by foreign enterprises (11/4.6), payments received for technical 
services by foreign enterprises 
(11/4.15), salaries paid by a foreign 
government to its citizens (11/4.12), pensions and annuities received 
by residents from foreign governments (11/4.12), and certain classes of 
income received by temporary visitors (11/4.13). 
Under the treaty with 
Sweden, the taxing country may require that amounts exempt from its

The effects of the Swedish and Swiss treaties and the potential effect

11/4.4 through 11/4.15. 
Since this volume is limited to Indian taxation,

could affect the operation of the credit against Indian tax (11/4.3c). 
b, ABATEMENT OF LOWER TAX ON DOUBLY TAXED INCOME. 
The Pakistan 
and Ceylon agreements provide for avoidance of double taxation by the 
grant of an abatement of tax by each country on income which it is 
agreed shall be taxable only by the other. 
The procedures are set forth 
in schedules annexed to the treaties, and are summarized below. 
While 
these schedules set forth the percentages of the various types of income 
which each party is “entitled to charge,” the abatement is not made simply 
by excluding from income taxable by one party the income which is 
reserved for taxation by the other. 
Since differences between the re- 
spective tax systems may result in differences in the amounts allocated 
to the respective jurisdictions by the two countries, the abatement calcu- 
lations are made in such a manner that each country gives abatement 
only on the amount of income which it allocates to the other, or on the 
amount which the other allocates to itself, whichever is lower. 
This 
lower figure represents the amount which is actually subjected to double 
tax; no abatement is granted by a party to either of these treaties on 
income which, although allocated to the other party, is not actually taxed 
by it. Abatement is given by applying the lower of the average rates of 
tax applicable in the two countries to the amount actually subjected to 
double tax. 
Since at the time of assessment neither country normally has any 
information as to the manner in which the other will tax the income from 
intercountry transactions, the tax payable to each country is determined 
as if there were no treaty; and each country tentatively gives the taxpayer 
an abatement of that proportion of its tax which is attributable to the 
income allocable to the other country under the terms of the treaty. 
If 
within one year the taxpayer produces a certificate of assessment from 
the other country, the following calculations are made. 
1. The amount allocable to the other country under the treaty and the 
amount which the other country allocates to itself are compared, and the 
lower amount is treated as doubly taxed income. 
2. The tax payable to the first country on the doubly taxed income is de- 
termined by applying to the tax payable in the absence of treaty the 
proportion which the doubly taxed income bears to income taxable in 
the absence of treaty. 
3. The tax payable to the other country on the doubly taxed income is

If the taxpayer does not produce a certificate of assessment from the

for the full tax on the income from the intercountry transactions just 
as if there had been no treaty. 
Annexed to each of these treaties is a schedule prescribing the per-

The allocations are summarized in sections 11/4.5

The agreements provide that if any question arises as to whether income 
falls within any of the classes specified in the schedule, and if so, under 
which one, the question shall be decided by each country under its own 
law without reference to the treatment of the income by the other country. 
Any income which is derived from a source or category of transaction 
which is not included in any of the classes specified in the schedules is 
allocable entirely to the country in which the income actually accrues 
or arises. 
C. CREDIT FOR FOREIGN TAXES. 
Special rules provide for the relief of 
double taxation of income on which tax has been paid both in India and 
in Aden, Kenya, Tanganyika, Uganda, Zanzibar, Gold Coast, Nigeria, 
Sierra Leone, Gambia, or Mauritius. 
These rules, although unilateral in 
form, were issued pursuant to statutory authorization to provide such 
relief in respect of tax imposed in any part of the British dominions whose 
laws, in the opinion of the Central Board of Revenue, provided for 
corresponding relief.‘ 
Under the rules relative to each country, any person, whether or not 
resident in India, is entitled to credit, against his Indian income tax for 
any year “on any part of his income,” for income tax paid for that year 
in the other country on “the same part of his income.” 
The quoted 
phrases make it clear that credit is to be given only for tax on income 
which has actually been subjected to tax in both countries; any portion 
of the Aden tax which is attributable to income not subjected to Indian 
tax is not creditable. 
This particular type of credit is given only where

11/4.4 
Definitions 
The Indian treaties with Pakistan and Ceylon operate by reducing 
taxes computed in the normal manner for one or both of the countries 
involved and therefore present no occasion for defining classes of tax- 
payers or sources of income for purposes of exemption from tax. 
How- 
ever, the Indian treaties and draft treaties which operate by means of 
exemption contain definitions of certain terms; the important definitions 
of the Swedish treaty are discussed below, with references to the draft 
United States treaty when its provisions differ from those of the Swedish 
treaty. 
1. Swedish enterprise or Indian enterprise. 
A “Swedish enterprise” is defined 
as “an industrial or commercial enterprise or undertaking carried on by a 
resident of Sweden.” 
“Indian enterprise” is defined in a similar manner. 
2. Resident. 
Under the Swedish treaty, a person is a “resident” of one of 
the contracting countries if he is resident in that country under its tax 
laws and is not resident in the other country under the tax laws of 
that country. 
As a result, a person who would be classified as a resident 
of both countries under their respective tax laws is a resident of neither 
for purposes of the treaty, and is taxed without reference to the treaty 
provisions. 
A corporation is regarded as resident in one of the contracting 
countries if it is incorporated in that country or its business is wholly 
managed and controlled in that country. 
Under the draft United States 
treaty, a corporation or partnership organized in the United States or 
under the laws of the United States is regarded as resident in the United 
States if it is not resident in India for purposes of Indian tax, but a 
corporation whose business is managed and controlled in India is regarded 
as resident in India. 
No resident of India or Indian company is entitled 
to the protection from Indian taxation afforded by the treaty to residents 
of the United States, and no United States citizen or United States 
corporation is entitled to the protection from United States taxation 
afforded by the treaty to residents of India. 
_8. Permanent establishment. 
A “permanent establishment” is a fixed place 
of business, such as a place of management, branch, office, factory, work- 
shop, warehouse, mine, or construction project. The use of storage facilities, 
or the maintenance of a place of business exclusively for the purchase of 
goods and not for processing, does not amount to having a permanent 
establishment. 
A corporation resident in one of the countries does not 
necessarily have a permanent establishment in the other merely because it 
has a subsidiary which either is a resident of the other country or carries 
on business in that country, through a permanent establishment or other- 
wise. However, a person acting in one of the countries on behalf of an en- 
paid to it by the Indian company on money borrowed for the purchase outside India 
of capital plant and machinery under a loan approved by the government (9/1.3). 
The tax which may be deemed to have been paid under any of these provisions is 
limited to the tax payable on the amount exempted or deductible under the Indian 
Income-tax Act as in effect on 10 November 1959, the date on which the agreement 
was signed,

Under the Swedish treaty, industrial or commercial profits derived in 
India by a Swedish enterprise are exempt from Indian tax unless they 
are derived from a permanent establishment (11/4.4) in India (art. 
III(1)). 
Indian tax may be imposed only on profits attributable to the 
permanent establishment, which are to be determined as if the perma- 
nent establishment were an independent enterprise dealing with the 
principal enterprise at arm’s length (art. III(2)). 
The treaty permits 
the Indian taxing authorities to estimate the profits to be attributed to the 
permanent establishment in accordance with Indian law (11/3.2), if 
the amount actually derived from the permanent establishment cannot 
be determined 
(art. III(2)). 
Where artificial arrangements between 
an Indian enterprise and a Swedish enterprise have resulted in lower 
profits to either enterprise than it could have been expected to derive 
from its business with the other, the taxing authorities may include in 
the income of that enterprise the profits which would have accrued to 
it in the absence of the artificial arrangements, making a compensating 
adjustment in the income of the other enterprise (art. IV). 
“Industrial or commercial profits” under the Swedish treaty do not 
include interest, dividends, management charges, remuneration for labor 
or personal services, income from the operation of ships or aircraft, or

The schedules of the Pakistan and Ceylon agreements allocate profits 
from the sale of goods between the country of manufacture or purchase 
and the country of sale in various proportions depending on the place of 
delivery of the goods and on whether or not the sale is made through a 
branch or regular agency in the country of sale. 
Separate but similar 
allocation formulas are provided for profits from the sale of minerals, 
petroleum, and forest products. 
The Ceylon treaty allocates income 
from motion picture films in varying proportions between the country in

which they are produced or distributed and the country in which they 
are exhibited. 
Under the draft United States treaty, industrial or commercial profits 
of a United States enterprise are exempt from Indian tax unless the enter- 
prise is engaged in trade or business in India through a permanent 
establishment in India; but if the United States enterprise does business 
in India through a permanent establishment in India, Indian tax may be 
imposed on the entire income of the enterprise from sources within India, 
and not merely on the income derived from the permanent establishment 
(art. III(1)(b)). 
The profits attributable to the permanent establish- 
ment are determined as if the permanent establishment were an inde- 
pendent enterprise, but may be estimated (art. III(2)). 
All expenses 
reasonably allocable to the permanent establishment, including executive 
and general administrative expenses, are allowed as deductions from the 
commercial profits of the permanent establishment regardless of where 
they are incurred (art. III(2)). 
If an enterprise of one of the countries 
participates in the management, control, or capital of an enterprise of the 
other or the same persons participate in the management, control, or 
capital of enterprises of each of the countries, and the commercial or 
financial relations of the two enterprises differ from those which would 
exist between independent enterprises, either of the enterprises may be 
taxed on profits which have not accrued to it but which would have 
accrued to it in the absence of the special relations (art. IV). 
Income 
derived by a person in one of the countries from the sale of goods pro- 
duced by him in the other country wholly or in part are to be treated 
as derived partly in the country of production and partly in the country 
of sale (art. XI(2)(b)). 
11/4.6 
Shipping and Air Transport 
The Swedish treaty provides that profits derived by a resident of 
Sweden from shipping operations carried on in India are subject to tax 
both in Sweden and in India, but the Indian tax is reduced by two 
thirds, and the remaining Indian tax is allowed as a credit against the 
Swedish tax (art. VI). 
An Indian resident is similarly taxed in both 
countries on profits derived from shipping operations in Sweden, and his 
Swedish tax is similarly reduced and credited against his Indian tax. 
These reductions and credits do not apply to profits arising from coastal 
traffic in either country. 
Income derived from the operation of aircraft or from participation in 
an air transport pool by a Swedish enterprise is exempt from Indian tax 
under the terms of the Swedish treaty, unless the aircraft is operated 
wholly or mainly between places within India (art. V). 
The Swiss 
treaty similarly exempts from Indian tax income derived from air trans-

port by Swiss enterprises other than income arising from traffic originating 
and terminating in India (art. IT). 
Profits from sea or air transport operations are allocated under the 
Pakistan and Ceylon treaties to the country in which the traffic originates. 
Under the draft United States treaty, income derived by an enterprise 
of one of the countries from the operation of aircraft registered therein is 
exempt from tax in the other country (art. V). The treaty contains no 
allocation of income from shipping. 
11/4.7 
Dividends 
Dividends received by a resident of India from a corporation which 
is a resident of Sweden are exempt from Indian tax under the treaty 
with Sweden (art. VIII). 
Conversely, dividends received by a resident 
of Sweden from a corporation which is a resident of India may be taxed 
in India but not in Sweden. 
The Pakistan treaty allocates dividends to each country according to 
the proportion of the corporate profits which is taxable by the two coun- 
tries under the terms of the treaty. 
The Ceylon treaty makes no separate 
allocation of dividend income, which therefore is allocated under the 
residuary provision of the schedule to the country in which it accrues 
or arises. 
11/4.8 
Interest 
Under the Swedish treaty, interest on any form of indebtedness derived 
by a Swedish resident from sources in India may be taxed in India, but not 
in Sweden, and a resident of India is exempt from Indian tax on interest 
derived from Swedish sources (art. IX). 
The Pakistan agreement allocates interest on government securities 
to the place where the securities are payable and interest on other securi- 
ties to the country where the investment is used. 
Under the Ceylon 
agreement, interest on government securities is allocated to the issuing 
government, and interest on other securities is allocated to the country 
in which the entity issuing them is situated. 
Both agreements allocate 
interest on other obligations to the country in which the money is used. 
Under the draft United States treaty, interest on any form of indebted- 
ness received by a creditor. of one of the countries from a debtor in the 
other is treated as income from sources in the debtor’s country (art. 
XI(2)(a)). 
11/4.9 
Royalties 
Under the terms of the Swedish treaty, a Swedish resident may be 
taxed in India, but not in Sweden, on royalties derived from sources in 
India for the right to use copyrights, artistic or scientific works, patents,

Royalties on similar properties derived by Indian 
residents from Swedish sources are exempt from Indian tax. The Pakistan 
and Ceylon treaties allocate royalties from such properties to the country 
in which the asset is used. 
Royalties from motion picture films are treated as commercial profits 
(11/4.5); royalties from mines, quarries, or other natural resources are 
treated as income from real property (11/4.10). 
Under the draft United States treaty, royalties from the use of copy- 
rights, artistic or scientific works, patents, models, designs, trade-marks, 
plans, secret processes, formulas, and similar property are to be treated as 
income from sources within the country in which the properties are used 
(art; S12) ey): 
11/4.10 
Income from Real Property 
Under the terms of the Swedish treaty, income from real property, 
including rents, royalties, or other income derived from the extraction of 
natural resources, may be taxed in India only if the property is situated in 
India (art. X). 
Although the Pakistan and Ceylon treaties treat income from the sale 
of minerals, petroleum, and forest produce as business income and 
allocate it between the country of production and the country of sale 
(11/4.5), the taxation of royalties paid out of such income is allocable 
entirely to the country in which the property is situated. 
Under the draft United States treaty, income from real property, includ- 
ing rents, royalties, and other income derived from the extraction of 
natural resources, is to be treated as income arising in the country in 
which the property is situated (art. XI(2)(c)). 
11/4.11 
Capital Gains 
Under the Swedish treaty, capital gains derived from the sale, exchange, 
or transfer of a movable or immovable capital asset are taxable in India 
only if the asset is situated in India at the time of the transfer (art. XI). 
The Pakistan treaty allocates capital gains derived from the sale of an 
immovable asset to the country in which the asset is located and capital 
gains derived from the sale of a movable asset to the country in which 
the transfer takes place. 
No specific allocation of capital gains is made 
under the Ceylon treaty; under the residuary provision, such gains are 
allocated to the country in which they accrue or arise. 
Under the draft United States treaty, gains derived from the sale or 
exchange of real property are treated as income arising in the country 
in which the property is situated 
(art. XI(2)(c)), and capital gains 
derived from a contribution of capital in kind by a resident of one country

toward the formation of a new company incorporated in the other are 
to be treated as arising in the first country (art. XI(2)(g)). 
11/4.12 
Public Salaries 
Salaries and wages paid in India by the government of Sweden for 
services rendered in India are exempt from Indian tax unless paid to an 
Indian citizen (art. XII). The exemption does not apply to payments for 
services in connection with any trade or business carried on by the Swed- 
ish government, or a political subdivision thereof, for purposes of profit. 
The Pakistan and Ceylon treaties allocate public salaries to the govern- 
ment which pays them. Under the draft United States treaty, salaries and 
wages paid by the government or a governmental subdivision of one of 
the countries to a citizen for services not connected with a trade or 
business carried on for profit are exempt from tax in the other country 
(art. VII(1)). 
Government pensions and annuities are treated in the 
same manner, but pensions and annuities received by residents of one 
of the countries from funds administered by the government of the other 
are not taxable in the latter country unless they are allocable to services 
for which remuneration was taxable in the country (art. VII(2)). 
11/4.13 
Private Salaries and Remuneration for Professional Services 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Under the Swedish treaty, salaries, wages, directors’ fees, 
and professional fees received by a resident of Sweden for services per- 
formed in India are taxable only in India; and an Indian resident is 
exempt from Indian tax on remuneration for services performed in Sweden 
(art. XIV(1)). 
Remuneration exempt from tax in the country in 
which the services are performed by virtue of one of the provisions 
described below may be taxed in the country of residence. 
The Pakistan and Ceylon treaties allocate private salaries and income 
from a profession or vocation to the country in which the service is ren- 
dered. 
The draft United States treaty provides that remuneration for 
personal services is to be treated as income from sources within the 
country in which the services are rendered (art. XI(2)(d) ). 
Remuneration received by a Swedish resident for services performed in 
India is not taxable in India if the total duration of his stay in India during 
the base year did not exceed 183 days, the services were performed for 
a resident of Sweden, the remuneration is subject to Swedish tax, and the 
remuneration is not deducted in computing the profits of an enterprise 
subject to Swedish tax (art. XIV). 
The draft United States treaty pro- 
vides that remuneration received by a resident of one of the countries 
for personal services shall not be taxed by the other country if the taxpayer 
is temporarily present in the other country for a period not exceeding 180 
days during the base year, the services are rendered for a resident of the

b. SERVICES ON SHIPS OR AIRCRAFT. 
Under the Swedish treaty, where an 
individual permanently or predominantly performs services on ships or

C. VISITING PROFESSORS OR TEACHERS. 
The remuneration of a professor or 
a teacher who visits India from Sweden for the purpose of teaching at a 
university or other educational institution in India is exempt from Indian 
tax for a period of two years (art. XV). The draft United States treaty 
grants a similar exemption and extends it to remuneration for research 
whose results are freely available to the general public (art. IX). 
d. STUDENTS OR APPRENTICES. 
An individual from Sweden who is tempo- 
rarily present in India solely as a student or business apprentice, or 
under a grant or award for the purposes of study or research, is exempt 
from Indian tax on remittances received from abroad for purposes of 
maintenance, education, or training, or for a scholarship (art. XVI). 
A 
student or business apprentice from Sweden is exempt from Indian tax 
for a period of three years on salaries received for services performed in 
India, provided the remuneration is necessary for his maintenance and 
education and does not exceed the equivalent of 4,000 Swedish crowns 
in the year of assessment. 
The corresponding provision in the draft United States treaty omits 
the scholarship exemption and substitutes an exemption for remuneration 
for employment (art. X(1)). 
Under this treaty an individual from one 
of the countries who is present in the other for not more than one year 
as an employee of, or under contract with, an enterprise or religious, 
charitable, scientific, or educational organization of the first country, 
solely to acquire technical, professional, or business experience from 
a person other than the enterprise or organization employing him, is 
exempt in the second country from tax on his remuneration provided the 
remuneration does not exceed the equivalent of US$5,000 (art. X(2). es 
An individual from one of the countries who is temporarily present in 
the other under an arrangement with its government solely for the 
purpose of training, research, or study is exempt from tax in that country 
on remuneration received therefor provided the remuneration does not 
exceed the equivalent of US$10,000 (art. X(3)).

Pensions and Annuities 
Under the Swedish treaty, a pension or annuity is taxable in India only 
if it arises from an Indian source (art. XIII). 
The Pakistan and Ceylon 
agreements allocate pensions paid by private employers to the country 
in which the services were performed and government pensions to the 
country which pays them. 
Under the draft United States treaty, a 
pension or annuity paid by an enterprise of one country to a resident of 
the other is to be treated as income from sources within the first country 
(art. XI(2)(f)). 
11/4.15 
Payment for Technical Services 
Under the draft United States treaty, amounts received by an enter- 
prise of one of the countries for technical services furnished to an 
enterprise of the other country are not subject to tax in the latter country 
unless the services are actually performed there (art. VI). 
Expenses 
incurred in that country must be allowed as deductions from amounts 
which are subject to tax.
