12/1.1 
Determination of Income for Income Tax 
Total income (6/1.1) of an individual for income tax purposes is the 
sum of his income under the six categories (6/1.2), including attributed 
income (6/8), but exclusive of exempt receipts which are not included 
in total income (6/1.4a) and reduced by deduction of certain expendi- 
tures incurred in earning total income (6/1.5). 
Total income less capital 
gains determines the applicable personal allowance (12/1.2a) and the 
rates of tax payable on income other than capital gains (12/1.3a). When 
an earned income allowance was granted, total income as reduced by 
the allowance was used instead of total income (12/1.2b). 
A regular 
surcharge, a surcharge on earned income over Rs 100,000, and a sur- 
charge on unearned income are applied to the tax on total income less 
capital gains (12/1.3b). 
The tax on capital gains is computed separately


<!-- page 358 of 600 -->

12/1.2 
India 
ANALYSIS. OF INCOME 
TAX 
322 
from the tax on the rest of total income (12/1.3c). 
The total tax and 
surcharges are reduced by that proportion which is attributable to those 
exempt receipts (6/1.4b) and deductible expenditures (6/15) which 
are included in total income (12/1.4). 
Husband and wife are separate taxpayers, and the liability of one 
spouse is determined independently of the income of the other, except 
in regard to personal allowances (12/1.2a) and certain income of one 
spouse which may be attributed to the other (5/1.3). 
The author of a literary or artistic work may spread his income there- 
from over two or three years as described at 8/4.1, thereby reducing his 
total income in the year of actual receipt. 
12/1.2 
Allowances for Income Tax 
a. PERSONAL ALLOWANCES. 
Personal allowances are provided for in the 
annual Finance Acts. 
The applicable allowance is determined by the 
taxpayers family status at the close of the base year. 
The allowance 
is subtracted from the first Rs 5,000 of the taxpayer’s income and there- 
fore affects the total tax payable but does not affect the application of 
the rate schedule to the balance of total income. 
The personal allow- 
ances granted for the tax year 1959-1960 are as follows: ? 
1. A taxpayer whose total income does not exceed Rs 20,000 is granted a 
personal allowance of Rs 1,000 if he is unmarried, Rs 3,000 if he is 
married with no children, Rs 3,300 if he is married with one dependent 
child, or Rs 3,600 if he is married with more than one dependent child. 
2. A taxpayer whose total income exceeds Rs 20,000 is granted a personal 
allowance of Rs 1,000. 
b. EARNED INCOME ALLOWANCE. 
The following items of income of an 
individual are earned income (§ 2(6AA) ): 
1. Income from salaries or on account of past services of the taxpayer or any 
deceased person. 
2. Income from profits and gains of a business, profession, or vocation carried 
on by the taxpayer. 
3. Income from profits and gains of a business, profession, or vocation on 
account of a share in a registered partnership or an unregistered partner- 
ship assessed as a registered partnership, if the taxpayer is actively en- 
gaged in the conduct of the partnership business. 
4. Income from “other sources” 
(6/1.2, 8/3.1) 
if immediately derived 
from personal exertion. 
A portion of the taxpayer’s earned income, to be specified in the 
annual Finance Act, may be allowed as an exemption from income tax, 
but not from supertax, and subtracted from total income for determining 
the rates of income tax, but not the rates of supertax (§ 15A). The last

have been applicable to the amount of total income less capital gains 
under the Finance Act for the preceding tax year. The rate applied to 
all other income less capital gains is that applicable to total income less 
capital gains under the Finance Act for the current tax year. 
Under the rate schedule for the tax year 1959-1960, no tax is payable 
if total income less capital gains does not exceed Rs 3,000; if total income 
less capital gains exceeds Rs 3,000, income tax is computed at the rates

Capital gains are subject to tax only if their amount 
exceeds

The tax payable on capital gains is that proportion of total taxable 
capital gains which the tax payable on total income less two thirds 
of capital gains, under the Finance Act for the tax year, bears to total 
income less two thirds of capital gains (§ 17(6)). 
Since if capital gains 
exceed Rs 5,000 the entire amount becomes taxable, and not merely the 
excess over Rs 5,000, relief against the high effective marginal rate of tax 
on income just above Rs 5,000 is obtained by limiting the tax to one half 
the amount by which capital gains exceed Rs 5,000.

The adjustments reduce the supertax and surcharges by that 
proportion which the exempt or deductible income bears to total income 
(§ 17(8)). 
12/1.8 
Credits 
In the tax year 1959-1960 a credit against tax is allowed for the amount 
by which dividends received by a shareholder have been increased on 
account of income tax deemed to have been paid by the corporation 
(9/2.4a). 
Starting with the tax year 1960-1961, this credit will no longer 
be given with respect to dividends declared out of profits assessed in 
that tax year or thereafter. 
Credits granted for foreign taxes 
are 
described at 11/2.4 and 11/4.8c. 
Taxes withheld at source or paid in 
advance during the base year are also credited against the taxpayer's 
tax liability (13/1.4). 
12/1.9 
Withholding at Source 
Income tax and supertax are withheld from salaries payable to a 
resident at the average rates of tax applicable under the Finance Act of 
the current tax year to the taxpayer’s estimated total income taxable as 
salaries (8/1.10). 
Starting in the tax year 1959-1960, tax is withheld 
from payments of dividends and of interest on securities, other than 
tax-free central government securities, at rates prescribed in the annual 
Finance Act for the year of withholding (13/1.4b) unless the taxpayer 
obtains a certificate modifying the rates as explained at 9/7. 
The rate 
prescribed for the withholding of income tax on interest and dividends 
in the tax year 1959-1960 for taxpayers other than corporations is 25% 
plus a surcharge of 5% of the tax. 
Supertax is withheld only from pay- 
ments to persons whom the payor of the income has no reason to believe 
— 
to be resident in India; the rate of withholding is 19% or the rate appro- 
priate to the taxpayer’s total income, whichever is greater.’

12/2. 
Corporations 
12/2.1 
Income Tax 
Total income (6/1.1) of a corporation for income tax purposes is the 
sum of all income under the six categories (6/1.2), exclusive of exempt 
receipts which are not included in total income (6/1.4a) and reduced 
by deduction of certain expenditures incurred in earning total income 
(6/1.5). 
The rate of income tax applicable to total income under the 
Finance Act for the tax year is applied to total income under all cate- 
gories, including capital gains (9/8.8). 
The corporate income tax rate 
for the tax year 1959-1960 is 30%, plus a surcharge of 5% of the tax.® 
The total tax and surcharge is reduced by that proportion which is 
attributable to those exempt receipts (6/1.4b) and deductible expendi- 
tures (6/1.5) which are included in total income (§§17(2), 17(3); 
Rule 20). 
12/2.2 
Structure of the Supertax 
Under recent Finance Acts, the supertax on corporations (sometimes 
called “corporation tax”) has been levied in the form of a standard rate of 
tax and a series of rebates applicable at different percentages to different 
classes of corporations. 
The amounts of the rebates are reduced by an 
additional supertax on stock dividends, capitalized earnings, and dividend 
distributions 
exceeding 
certain 
percentages 
of paid-up 
capital. 
<A 
further supertax is imposed on the undistributed profits of closely held 
corporations exceeding. certain percentages of profits for the base year. 
The tax is levied at a flat rate (12/2.7). 
12/2.3 
Determination of Income for Supertax 
Total income of a corporation for supertax purposes is determined in 
the same manner as the total income of an individual (12/15). 
The 
rate of supertax applicable to the corporation for the tax year is applied 
to total income for the base year, less capital gains. 
The basic supertax 
is reduced by that proportion which is attributable to income exempt 
from tax though included in total income (6/1.4b). 
Capital gains of a corporation are not subject to supertax in the tax 
year 1959-1960, but beginning with the tax year 1960-1961, they will 
be subject to supertax separately at the rate of 10% (§17(7)). 
12/2.4 
Rates of Basic Supertax 
The basic supertax on corporations is levied at a rate of 50%, modified 
by rebates of different percentages for different types of income and

For convenience the application of the 50% 
rate and the percentages of rebates have been converted throughout this 
chapter to “rates of basic supertax,” each of which represents 50% less 
the applicable percentage of rebate. 
Dividends received by a corporation from a domestic subsidiary 1° are

On the balance of income 
less capital gains, a domestic corporation, or a foreign corporation which 
has made the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment 
of dividends in India and for the withholding of supertax from dividend

However, if

is one in which the public is substantially interested or is a subsidiary of

The rate of basic supertax on the

India and for the deduction of supertax from dividend payments is 
30%.1* 
The reason for the imposition of this special rate is that non- 
resident shareholders in a foreign corporation are not subject to tax on 
dividends paid by the corporation outside India, even if the dividends 
are declared out of profits subject to tax in India (11/1.4b). 
The arrangements prescribed for the declaration and payment of 
dividends in India and for the deduction of supertax from dividends are 
listed below (Rule 13D). 
1. The register of all shareholders of the corporation must be regularly 
maintained from 1 April of the base year at the corporation’s principal 
place of business in India. 
2. The general meeting for approving the accounts of the base year and 
for declaring any dividends in respect of the base year must be held 
in India. 
3. Any dividends declared must be payable only in India to all shareholders. 
Since a corporation becomes liable to supertax at a higher rate on its 
entire taxable income when its total income exceeds Rs 25,000, the tax 
on income over Rs 25,000 is limited by a marginal relief provision to

Adjustments to Basic Supertax for Exemptions and Deductions 
With the exception of charitable donations, the adjustments to super- 
tax listed at 12/1.7 are allowed to corporations. 
In addition, an adjust- 
ment is allowed for dividends received from certain corporations engaged 
in the manufacture or production of products considered essential to 
economic development (§ 56A)(10/6.3). 
12/2.6 
Additional Supertax on Excess Dividends, Stock Dividends, and 
Capitalization of Earnings 
a. TAXABLE DISTRIBUTIONS. 
Domestic corporations and foreign corpora- 
tions which have income subject to supertax and have made the pre- 
scribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends in 
India and for the deduction of supertax from dividends (12/2.4) are 
subject to additional supertax on the following amounts: 1+ 
1. The amount of any stock dividends (“bonus shares”) or bonus issued 
during the base year to increase paid-up capital, unless issued out of 
premiums received in cash on the issue of the shares of the corporation.15 
The objectives of the tax on stock dividends and capitalization of earnings 
appear to be (1) to prevent avoidance of the present tax on excess 
dividends and (2) to compensate for the loss of revenue from the tax 
which would have been payable by the shareholders if the earnings had 
been distributed as a dividend. 
2. Dividends distributed in the base year, other than dividends payable at 
a fixed rate, in excess of 6% of paid-up equity capital not entitled to 
dividends at a fixed rate.1® 
Foreign corporations which have not made the prescribed arrange- 
ments for the declaration and payment of dividends in India and for the 
deduction of supertax from dividends are not subject to the additional 
supertax, but are subject to a higher rate of basic supertax (12/2.4). 
b. COMPUTATION AND RATES OF TAX. 
The rate of additional supertax on 
stock dividends and capitalization of earnings is 30%.

are taxed at the rate of 30%, and all other corporations

Of the total tax computed at the above rates, however, the corporation 
is required to pay only that proportion which total income bears to total 
income plus exempt income not included in total income, less allowances 
made for income tax purposes but not shown in the corporation’s profit 
and loss account for the year (as, for example, a development rebate, 
or depreciation allowed although not claimed by the taxpayer). 
The additional supertax is applied against the amount of the rebate 
which determines the rate of basic supertax (12/2.4), and there is no 
additional supertax if no basic supertax is payable. 
If basic supertax 
is payable, the total effective rate of the basic supertax and the additional 
supertax on excess dividends, stock dividends, and bonuses may not 
exceed 50%; any additional supertax which because of this limitation is 
not payable in any tax year is carried forward and added (subject to the 
same limitation ) to supertax for the following year. 
12/2.7. 
Additional 
Supertax on 
Undistributed 
Profits of Closely Held 
Corporations 
Since the rates of supertax on corporations are considerably lower than 
those applicable to other taxpayers, an individual in the higher income 
brackets could avoid a substantial part of the supertax on his income by 
transferring the source of his income to a corporation which, instead of 
declaring dividends, would accumulate the income and distribute it later 
in capital form. 
From 1941 until 1955, if any corporation distributed 
less than a prescribed percentage of its profits for the base year, as 
reduced by income tax and supertax, the undistributed portion was 
deemed to have been distributed as dividends among the shareholders, 
and each shareholder’s proportionate share of the undistributed profits 
was then included in his total income and subjected to tax. 
Under 
changes introduced by the Finance Act of 1955, however, the share- 
holder is no longer taxed on his share of the undistributed profits, but a 
closely held corporation which fails to distribute a prescribed percentage 
of its profits after taxes is itself subject to an additional penalty supertax 
on the entire undistributed balance. 
a. CORPORATIONS SUBJECT TO THE TAX. A corporation is subject to super- 
tax on its undistributed profits unless, at the end of the base year, it is a

A corporation is one in which the public is substantially 
interested if (1) 40% or more of its stock is held by the central govern- 
ment or a state government, or if (2) it is not a “private company” for 
purposes of general corporate law,!* and in addition meets the following 
conditions (§ 23A, Explanation 1). 
1. At no time during the base year have the corporation’s affairs been con- 
trolled by fewer than six persons, exclusive of the central government, 
state governments, corporations established by central, state, or provincial 
acts, and corporations which are not subject to the undistributed profits 
tax provisions. 
A corporation necessarily satisfies this condition if it is 
controlled by the central government, a state government, a corporation 
established by a central, state, or provincial act, or a corporation not 
subject to the undistributed profits tax provisions. 
In determining the 
number of persons controlling a corporation’s affairs, 
a nominee or a 
shareholder who is a spouse, sibling, ancestor, or lineal descendant of 
another shareholder is not counted. 
The control requirement relates to 
actual control by the shareholders, not to the day-to-day overseeing of 
management by the directors, and therefore does not make it necessary 
for a corporation to have six or more directors.!9 
2. At no time during the base year have shares carrying more than 50% of 
the corporation’s total voting power (more than 60% in the case of a 
domestic corporation engaged solely in manufacturing, processing, mining, 
or the generation or distribution of power) been owned by fewer than 
six persons, exclusive of the central government, state governments, corpo- 
rations established by central, state, or provincial acts, and corporations 
which are not subject to the undistributed profit tax provisions. 
The 
determination of the number of shareholders required and of the number 
who are actually to be counted is governed by the rules applicable to the 
control test in item 1 listed above. 
8. Throughout the base year, shares, other than shares entitled to a fixed 
rate of dividend, carrying not less than 50% of the total voting power 
(not less than 40% in the case of a domestic corporation engaged solely 
in manufacturing, processing, mining, or the generation or distribution 
of power) have been owned by the central government, a state govern- 
ment, a corporation established by a central or state act, or by the 
public (not including a corporation subject to the undistributed profit tax 
provisions). 
4. The corporation’s shares, other than shares entitled to a fixed rate of 
dividend, were at some time during the base year traded on a recognized 
stock exchange in India, or were freely transferable throughout the base 
year. 
By the terms of the Act, domestic and foreign and resident and non- 
resident corporations are equally subject to the supertax on undistributed 
profits. 
However, the tax would not be assessed against a foreign

b, DISTRIBUTION REQUIRED TO AVOID THE TAX. 
In order to avoid the 
additional supertax on its undistributed profits, a corporation subject to 
the tax must distribute as dividends a prescribed percentage of its profits 
for the base year within 12 months following the end of the base year. 
Stock dividends and capitalization of earnings are not counted as distri- 
butions for the purpose of determining whether the corporation has 
distributed the prescribed percentage of its profits. 
For this purpose, 
profits are the total income less income tax, supertax other than the tax 
on undistributed profits, and any central, state, or local taxes which 
have not been deducted in determining total income. 
The total income 
of a banking company may also be reduced by the amount actually 
transferred to a reserve fund under section 17 of the Banking Companies 
Act of 1949. 
The percentages of profits prescribed for distribution are listed below 
(§ 238A, Explanation 2). 
1. Profits of a corporation whose business consists wholly or mainly in the 
dealing in or holding of investments: 100%. 
2. Profits derived by a domestic corporation from manufacture, processing, 
mining, or the generation or distribution of power: 45%, to be increased 
to 50% as of 1 April 1960. 
8. Other profits of a domestic corporation, and all profits of a foreign corpo- 
ration, whose accumulated earnings which have not been subjected to 
the undistributed profits supertax exceed either (1) the paid-up equity 
capital of the company created out of profits which have been subjected 
to the undistributed profits supertax, plus loans advanced by shareholders, 
or (2) the actual cost of the fixed assets of the corporation: 90%. 
4, Other profits of any other domestic corporation, and all profits of a foreign 
corporation, not fulfilling the condition set forth in item 3 above: 60%, 
to be increased to 65% as of 1 April 1960. 
C. COMPUTATION AND RATES OF TAX. 
If the distribution by a corporation 
subject to the tax falls short of the prescribed percentage of profits, the 
appropriate rate of tax is applied to the entire undistributed balance of 
the profits as determined at 12/2.7b, and not merely to the amount by 
which the distribution falls short of the prescribed percentage. 
The rates applicable to the undistributed balance are 50% for a 
corporation whose business consists wholly or mainly in the dealing in 
or holding of investments, and 37% for any other corporation (§ 23A(1) ).

d. RELIEF PRovistons. 
In certain cases the taxpayer must be permitted 
to make a special distribution within three months of receipt of an 
appropriate notice from the Income-tax Officer. 
The special distribution 
will then be treated as if made during the twelve months following the 
end of the base year (§ 23A(2)). 
A special distribution must be per- 
mitted under any of the following conditions: 
1. The amount by which the distribution of profits by an investment cor- 
poration falls short of the specified percentage does not exceed 10% 
of its profits. 
2. The amount by which the distribution of profits by a corporation other 
than an investment corporation falls short of the prescribed percentage 
does not exceed 5% of its profits. 
3. The difference between the prescribed percentage and the distribution 
of profits results from the assessment of a higher total income than was 
reported by the taxpayer, provided the corporation has maintained 
proper accounts and disclosed its income fully and truly, and the assess- 
ment is not a “best judgment” assessment (13/2.2). 
Moreover, supertax on undistributed profits is not payable if the 
Income-tax Officer finds that, in view of losses incurred by the corporation 
prior to the base year, or in view of the corporation’s small profits in the 
base year, distribution of a larger dividend than was actually declared 
would have been unreasonable 
(§ 23A(1)). 
Thus, relief has been 
granted when the application of a balancing charge (7/8.6) made 
profits for tax purposes substantially larger than profits for commercial 
accounting purposes,”® and when the annual value of property held by 
the taxpayer (9/4.2) exceeded the actual income from such property.”4 
Taxable capital gains are included in total income for the purposes of 
determining whether the taxpayer is entitled to this relief. 
The need to 
retain profits to meet the reasonable requirements of business is not a 
ground for relief. 
Relief from the supertax on undistributed profits may also be given 
if the Income-tax Officer finds that a larger distribution than was actually 
made would not have resulted in any benefit to the revenue (§ 23A(1) ). 
For this reason, the tax is not payable by a foreign corporation all of 
whose shareholders are foreigners, or by a corporation whose entire 
profits are entitled to the new industries exemption (10/6.2). 
e. PROCEDURE. 
The Income-tax Officer must issue an order requiring 
the payment of supertax on undistributed profits in every case in which the 
prescribed percentage of profits has not been distributed and no relief* 
provision is applicable. 
However, he may not issue such an order with- 
out the approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner.

12/2.8 
Credits 
The credits available to a corporation against its tax are the same as 
those available to an individual (12/1.8). 
12/2.9 
Withholding at Source 
Starting with the tax year 1959-1960, income tax and supertax must 
be withheld from interest on securities and from dividends payable to 
corporations at rates prescribed in the annual Finance Act for the year 
of withholding (13/1.4b). 
Tax is withheld from payments other than 
dividends or interest on securities made to a corporation only if the 
corporation is nonresident or is a foreign corporation which has not made 
the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of divi- 
dends in India (12/2.4). 
The rates of withholding of income tax and supertax from payments to 
corporations for the tax year 1959-1960 are listed below.?? 
1. Income tax is withheld at the rate of 20% from all payments except 
payments of interest on tax-free securities of the central government. 
2. Supertax is withheld at the rate of 10% from those dividends of a sub- 
sidiary Indian company which are not entitled to the intercorporate 
dividend exemption (10/6.3). 
8. Supertax is withheld from all other payments to a corporation, except 
dividends entitled to the intercorporate dividend exemption (10/6.3), 
at the rate of 43% if the recipient is a foreign corporation which has 
not made the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of 
dividends in India (12/2.4), and at the rate of 25% in other cases. 
12/2.10 
Prepayment of Tax 
A corporation may be required to. make advance payment of tax on 
income not subject to withholding (13/1.4c). 
The rates of advance 
payment are those of the tax year in which the payments are made.

12/3. 
Other Taxpayers 
12/3.1 
Partnerships and Associations of Persons 
In determining income from profits and gains of a business, profession, 
or vocation, a partnership is not allowed to deduct interest or salaries, 
commissions, or other remuneration paid to a partner (7/2.3d). 
It would 
seem, however, that an association of persons can deduct similar pay- 
ments to its members. 
An association of persons or unregistered partner- 
ship is granted a standard allowance of Rs 1,000 for income tax purposes. 
The schedule of rates set out in Table C in effect grants a registered 
partnership a standard allowance of Rs 40,000. 
It would appear that 
the total income of a partnership cannot include income from salaries 
(8/1.2). 
Income from profits and gains of a business, profession, or 
vocation carried on by a partnership or association of persons is within 
the statutory definition of earned income but no allowance for any class 
of earned income is made by the Finance Act of 1959 (12/1.2b). 
It has been held that a partnership cannot itself be a member of 
another partnership.?*

On similar principles, the adjustment to tax on 
account of income which has been subject to income tax in the hands of 
an association of persons may be inapplicable to a partnership or asso- 
ciation of persons. 
Those adjustments to the tax of an individual relating 
to the death or retirement of the taxpayer are applicable only to indi-

All other adjustments to the tax of an individual 
apply to the tax of a partnership. 
Unregistered partnerships and associations of persons are subject to

An association of persons constituting a cooperative society (5/3.4) is 
subject to income tax at individual rates, but is subject to supertax, after 
exemption of Rs 25,000 of total income, at a special rate of 16% plus a 
surcharge of 12.5% of the supertax.”®

12/3.2 
Hindu Undivided Families 
Except as explained below, the income tax and supertax of a Hindu 
undivided family are determined in the same manner, and in accordance 
with the same rate schedules, as in the case of an individual (12/1.3, 
12/1.6). 
There is no prohibition of the deduction of interest or remuneration 
paid by a Hindu undivided family to a member. 
Such a payment may 
therefore be deducted, if reasonable in amount, in determining profits and 
gains of a business, profession, or vocation carried on by the Hindu 
undivided family. 
If total income does not exceed Rs 20,000, a Hindu un- 
divided family is granted the following allowances 
for income

the family has one minor coparcener; Rs 3,600 if the family has more 
than one minor coparcener. 
A Hindu undivided family with a total 
income in excess of Rs 20,000 is granted a standard allowance for income 
tax purposes of Rs 1,000. 
The total income of a Hindu undivided family cannot include income 
from salaries (8/1.2). 
Income from profits and gains of a business, 
profession, or vocation carried on by a Hindu undivided family is within 
the statutory definition of earned income (§ 2(6AA) ), but no allowance 
for any class of earned income is made by the Finance Act of 1959. 
Certain adjustments to the tax of individuals relate to provisions for 
the death or retirement of the taxpayer and are by definition applicable 
only to individuals (6/3.5, 6/3.6). 
All other adjustments to the tax of 
an individual apply in the case of a Hindu undivided family (6/1.4b, 
6/1.5). 
In the case of a Hindu undivided family having at least two members 
entitled to claim partition who are not less than 18 years of age and not 
lineally descended from a living member of the family, and neither of 
whom is descended from the other, the limit at which surcharges become 
payable (12/1.3b) is increased from Rs7,500 plus the amount of divi- 
dends on common stock, or Rs 9,000, as the case may be, to Rs 15,000 
plus the amount of dividends on common stock, or Rs 16,500. 
Marginal 
relief applies with respect to these increased limits -(12/1.8b). 
12/3.3 
Trusts 
A trust is assessed as an entity for income tax and supertax to the 
extent to which income is not specifically receivable on behalf of a 
particular beneficiary, or to which the individual shares of the bene- 
ficiaries are indeterminate or unknown (5/3.6). 
The rate of income 
tax is the rate established as the “maximum” rate in the annual Finance 
Act. 
In the Finance Act of 1959, the maximum rate is 25%, plus a 
surcharge of 20% of the tax.?° The trust is not entitled to any personal or 
standard allowances. 
The rates of supertax are those applicable to 
individuals.?” 
12/3.4 
Local Authorities 
A local authority is taxed on income from profits and gains of the 
business of supplying a commodity or service outside its own jurisdictional 
area (5/3.3, 5/5.15).

12/4. 
Nonresident Taxpayers 
The computation and rates of tax for a nonresident corporation do not 
differ from computation and rates for a resident corporation, but a foreign 
corporation which has not made arrangements for the declaration and 
payment of dividends in India is subject to higher rates of supertax 
(12/2.4, 12/2.9). 
Special rates of income tax and supertax apply to 
nonresident persons other than corporations, but in all other respects 
the tax of a nonresident is computed in the same manner as that of a 
resident. 
If a nonresident other than a corporation elects to be taxed at rates 
based on his total income as determined under the principles described 
at 11/3.1, his income tax is computed at the “maximum” rate established 
by the annual Finance Act (11/3.5). 
For the tax year 1959-1960, the 
maximum rate is 25%, plus a surcharge of 20% of the tax.?8 
Supertax 
is payable either at the rate of 19% or at the rate applicable to resident 
individuals (12/1.6), whichever is higher. However, a nonresident other 
than a corporation may elect to be taxed on his total income at rates 
determined by applying the rate schedules for resident taxpayers to his 
total world income (11/3.5). 
Total world income is income from what- 
ever sources and wherever arising except income attributable to mem- 
bership in a Hindu undivided family (5/8.2), income which is exempt 
in connection with the termination of a business, profession, or vocation 
(6/3.5), and capital gains not included in the taxpayer's total income 
(§ 2(15)). 
If the taxpayer has made such an election, income tax and supertax 
before adjustments to tax and credits are computed on total world 
income. 
The tax so computed is multiplied by total income and divided 
by total world income. 
Adjustments to tax are made (12/1.4), and 
credits against tax are taken (12/1.8). 
The rates at which tax is withheld from payments to a nonresident are 
those prescribed for the purpose in the annual Finance Act unless the 
rates are modified as explained at 11/3.3. 
In the tax year 1959-1960, 
the rate of withholding of income tax from any income payments to 
noncorporate taxpayers other than interest on tax-free government securi- 
ties is 25% plus a surcharge of 5% of the tax; supertax is withheld from 
payments to nonresidents other than corporations at the standard rates

Description

tax Officer.

(18/1.4d).

13/1.1 
Notices to File Returns 
Between 1 April and 1 May of each tax year, a general notice to file 
returns for regular assessment is published by the Income-tax Officers 
(1/8.5) in all leading English and regional language newspapers. 
The 
notice requires all persons who during the previous year had income in 
excess of the standard allowances (12/1.2a, 12/3.1, 12/3.2) to file a re- 
turn within a specified period. 
The time allowed for filmg must not 
be less than 60 days and is usually 65 days.

general notice may also be made by posting in certain public places 
(§ 22(1); Rule 18). 
In addition, the Income-tax Officers may at any time during the tax 
year issue individual notices to file returns for regular assessment to 
persons whom they believe to have had income in excess of the allowances 
during the base year. 
Such notices must allow at least 30 days for the 
filing of a return (§ 22(2)). 
They usually require filing within 35 days 
and as a matter of practice are sent with return forms to persons who 
have filed returns in past years. 
A notice may be served abroad on a 
nonresident.’ 
Similar notices to file returns for additional assessment may 
be issued after the end of the tax year (§ 34) (13/2.3). 
Special individual notices may be sent to persons about to leave India 
permanently. 
Such notices require the filing of a return showing esti- 
mated income for the tax year up to the probable date of departure and 
income for all base years which have not yet been assessed and are not 
barred by the time limit on assessments (13/6.1). 
At least seven days 
must be allowed for the filing of these returns (§ 24A). When a business 
is discontinued, its income for the base period ending on the date of 
discontinuance may be assessed either during the current tax year or 
in the following tax year in the discretion of the Income-tax Officer 
(6/3.5). 
If assessment is to be made in the current tax year, the Income- 
tax Officer may issue a notice allowing not less than 30 days in which to 
file a return (§ 25(6)). 
13/1.2 
Returns 
Information and particulars are reported by the taxpayer on return 
forms; the computation of tax is made by the Income-tax Officer on 
separate assessment forms (Rule 20). 
A person served with an individual notice must file a return within 
the time specified in the notice, whether or not he has income subject to 
tax. 
Any person not served with an individual notice who has sustained 
a loss in the previous year must file a return setting forth the prescribed 
particulars relating to the loss, within the time specified in the general 
notice. 
The filing of a return is a condition of obtaining the benefit of 
a loss carry-forward (§ 22(2A))(7/4.2). 
The master of a ship about 
to leave an Indian port must file a special return if the ship is owned or 
chartered by a nonresident who has no resident agent (10/4). 
Persons 
who have not been individually notified to file and have not sustained a 
loss or received taxable income during the previous year need not file 
returns. 
Returns must be made on one of the three forms which are described 
at 12/5. An individual must sign his return personally; it has been held

that the signature of an authorized agent will not suffice.’ 
The return 
of a corporation must be signed by its principal officer. 
Both a partner- 
ship and its members are required to file returns covering partnership 
income. 
A taxpayer carrying on a business, profession, or vocation should nor- 
mally file a return with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction over 
the taxpayer’s principal place of business (§64(1)). 
Partners should 
file with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction over the principal 
place of business of the partnership. 
In all other cases, returns should 
normally be filed with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction over 
the taxpayer’s place of residence (§64(2)). 
The Central Board of 
Revenue may authorize the appointment of Income-tax Officers having 
jurisdiction over certain classes of persons or of income in place of the 
usual territorial jurisdiction (1/8.5). Taxpayers falling under such special 
grants of jurisdiction should file their returns with the officers so named. 
The Income-tax Officer may in his discretion extend the filing date of 
any return (§§ 22(1), 22(2)). 
Although returns may be filed late or 
may be revised at any time before an assessment is made (§ 22(8)), 
such revision or late filing does not preclude the imposition of appro- 
priate penalties (§ 28) (13/7.4). 
13/1.3 
Assessment 
It is the duty of the Income-tax Officer to assess the taxpayer’s income 
and determine the amount of the tax payable. 
If the Income-tax Officer 
is satisfied that the return is correct and complete he assesses the tax on 
the basis of the return alone (§ 23(1)). 
Ordinarily this is done only 
where the taxpayer has a more or less constant annual income derived 
from salaries, interest on securities, and house properties, and where the 
figures shown in the return can be verified from the employer's annual 
return, from certificates of tax deducted at source, or from municipal 
registers. 
In other cases, the Income-tax Officer will usually seek further 
information and make a regular assessment as described in 18/2.1 or 
an estimated assessment as described in 13/2.2. 
Persons about to leave India permanently may be assessed before 
departure on all income liable to assessment which has not been pre- 
viously assessed. 
Income attributable 
to any base year is assessed 
promptly at the rates applicable to that year. 
In addition, income for 
the period from the commencement of the current tax year to the probable 
date of departure is estimated and assessed at the rates applicable in® 
the current tax year (§ 24A), 
When a business is discontinued, its income for the base period ending 
on the date of discontinuance may be assessed either during the current

Officer (6/3.5). 
There is no provision for the subsequent revision of 
taxes so assessed at the rates which would have been applicable had 
assessment been made in the following tax year in the normal manner. 
If a business, profession, or vocation carried on by a partnership or other 
association of persons has been discontinued, or if a partnership or asso- 
ciation is dissolved, assessment is nevertheless made on the partnership 
or association. 
In addition, the members of the partnership or association 
are jointly and severally liable for taxes and penalties payable by the 
partnership or association (§ 44). 
Income of a ship about to leave an Indian port is assessed under a 
special summary procedure if the ship is owned or chartered by a non- 
resident who has no resident agent (10/4). 
At any time after the receipt of a return, a provisional assessment may 
be made on the basis of the return and any accounts and documents 
accompanying it. 
The provisional assessment must be followed by a 
regular assessment (§ 23B).8 
13/1.4 
Payment 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Payments of tax are made through withholding 
or 
deduction of tax at source, by advance payment, or by payment on 
notice of demand following final assessment. 
Advance payment of tax 
is not required with respect to income which is subject to withholding. 
Taxes withheld or paid in advance are credited on later notices of 
demand. 
b. WITHHOLDING. 
Payments of income taxable as salaries are subject to 
the withholding of both income tax and supertax whether made to resi- 
dents or to nonresidents. 
Different methods of determining the amount 
of tax to be deducted are, however, prescribed for residents and non- 
residents (8/1.10). 
The trustees of a recognized provident fund (5/5.13, 
8/1.5c) are responsible for deducting the tax payable by an employee 
on receipt of the accumulated balance due him from the fund (§ 58H); 
the trustees of a pension fund (5/5.12, 8/1.5b) are required to deduct the 
tax payable by an employee on contributions which are repaid to him 
during his lifetime but not at or in connection with the termination of 
his employment (§ 58S). 
Payments of dividends or of interest on securities are subject to the 
withholding of income tax and supertax whether made to residents or 
to nonresidents (§§ 18(3), 18(3D)). 
For the tax year 1959-1960 rates 
have been prescribed for the withholding of income tax and supertax 
from payments to corporations (12/2.9) and payments to nonresidents

All

ject to withholding of income tax and supertax if made to a nonresident 
or to a foreign corporation which has not made the prescribed arrange- 
ments for the declaration and payment of dividends in India (§ 18(3B) ) 
(12/2.4). 
No tax is withheld from any interest or dividend payable to 
the government or to the Reserve Bank of India in respect of any 
securities or shares which the government owns or in which it has a 
beneficial interest (§ 18(10) ). 
Although prior to the Finance Act of 1959 tax was withheld at the

tax year, the rates at which tax is to be withheld during the current tax 
year are now prescribed for that purpose in the annual Finance Acts 
(§ 18(11) )(12/1.9, 
12/2.9). 
The rates of withholding from payments 
of interest on securities and from payments of dividends may be varied 
as described at 9/7. Methods of varying the rates of withholding of tax 
from payments made to nonresidents are described at 11/3.8. 
Sums withheld from payments to a taxpayer are paid to the central 
government and credited against the taxpayer’s tax liability (§§ 18(5), 
18(6); Rule 10). 
Persons withholding tax from payments other than 
salaries must furnish the payees with certificates specifying the amount 
deducted and the rates of tax at which the amount deducted was com- 
puted (§ 18(9); Rules 13-18C, 14). 
Cc. ADVANCE PAYMENT. 
Advance payment of income tax and supertax 
may be required on income not subject to withholding. 
The Income-tax 
Officer may serve a notice, requiring advance payment of tax during the 
base year, on a taxpayer whose assessed income for his last previous base 
year exceeded the applicable standard allowance by Rs 2,500 (§ 18A(1); 
Rule 20A).* A taxpayer who has been previously assessed is not required 
to make advance payments unless he is served with a notice. 
In practice, 
notices are sent to all taxpayers whose income in the last previous base 
year exceeded the required amount. 
A taxpayer who has not been 
previously assessed but whose income for the base year is likely to exceed 
the applicable statutory allowance by Rs 2,500 is required to file an 
estimate on or before 15 March of the base year and to make advance 
payments of tax based thereon (§ 18A(3) ). 
The rates of advance payment are those of the current tax year

($ 18A(1)); if different rates are in force in the year of assessment, 
adjustment is made at the time of assessment (§ 18A(11)).

The payments are due in equal installments on 15 June, 15 September, 
15 December, and 15 March of the base year, or on such of those dates 
as follow the date of the notice or estimate. 
The taxpayer, whether 
assessed or not, may revise his estimate before any one of the dates 
specified for payment (§18A(2)). 
The advance payment of tax in 
respect of commissions may be deferred until the commissions are re- 
ceived (§ 18A(4)). 
If the advance payments exceed the amount ulti- 
mately assessed, interest is paid the taxpayer at the rate of 4% from the 
beginning of the tax year to the date of regular assessment (§ 18A(5)). 
d. NOTICE OF DEMAND. 
On making a provisional or regular assessment, 
the Income-tax Officer serves the taxpayer with a notice of demand 
(§ 29). A notice of demand is also issued if an assessment is increased 
on modification (§ 35(4) )(13/2.4). 
Forms of assessment showing the 
computation of tax are attached to the notice except in the case of notices 
following provisional assessments (Rules 20, 20B). 
The notice specifies 
the time and place of payment and the person to whom payment must 
be made. 
Usually one month is allowed for payment. 
If a due date is 
not specified, payment must be made on or before the first day of the 
second month following service (§ 45). 
Payment is normally made to 
a Treasury or Sub-Treasury Officer, the Reserve Bank of India, or an 
agent of the State Bank of India. 
In the notice of demand the taxpayer 
is credited with tax withheld at source, with tax paid in advance and 
interest thereon, and with tax paid upon provisional assessment. 
Special treatment is accorded to taxpayers assessed on foreign income 
which cannot be remitted to India or used abroad because of prohi- 
bitions or restrictions of the country in which the income arises. 
Taxes 
attributable to such income are not in default until the income can be 
brought into India or expended abroad (11/2.3).

In order to leave India, any person who is not domiciled in India, or 
who “even if domiciled in India at the time of .

. departure” has no 
intention of returning, must obtain a tax clearance certificate (§ 46A). 
Such a certificate can be obtained from any of the Income-tax Officers 
in certain designated areas.® 
It must state either that the person intend- 
ing to depart has made satisfactory arrangements for the payment of any 
liabilities under the Income-tax Act of 1922, the Excess-Profits Tax Act 
of 1940, and the Business Profits Tax Act of 1947, or that he has no such

13/1.6 
Collection of Delinquent Taxes 
Delinquent taxes, interest, and penalties may be recovered by means 
of the following procedures (§§ 46, 47). 
1. The District Collector (1/8.10), upon the receipt of a certificate from 
an Income-tax Officer, may collect the amount certified under the pro- 
cedure provided by state law for the collection of delinquent land revenue 
(§ 46 (2) ) (3/2). 
2. The Income-tax Officer may employ any procedure available under state 
law for the collection of delinquent municipal taxes or local rates (3/3) 
provided that the Commissioner of Income-tax has authorized the use of 
such procedures in the local area (§§ 46(3), 46(4) ). 
8. The Income-tax Officer may require an employer to deduct the amount 
due from payments of salary (§ 46(5)). 
4. The Income-tax Officer may require any person who owes or may owe 
money to the taxpayer, or who holds or may hold money for or on account 
of the taxpayer, to withhold payment (§ 46(5A) ). 
5. The amount due may be set off against the payment of any refund to 
which the taxpayer may be entitled (§ 49E). 
6. Procedures available under general law for the collection of sums due 
the government, including the filing of suit in the civil courts of India, 
may be employed.® 
The foregoing procedures are not mutually exclusive and may be 
employed cumulatively (§ 46(7), Explanation). 
The applicable time 
limits are discussed at 13/6.3 and 13/6.4. 
Special provisions regarding 
the collection of tax from nonresidents are discussed at 11/3.4.

The taxpayer may comply with the notice by appearing

to permit the production of further evidence.

The Income-tax Officer may make a regular assessment based on an 
estimate of the taxpayer’s income if reliable evidence of the actual 
amount of the income is lacking (6/4.1, 6/9.1). 
There is a provision 
for estimating income arising from systematic dealings in securities 
(9/1.6), and the special assessments which are made to prevent certain 
income from escaping taxation necessarily involve an estimate of income 
for the current year (18/1.3). 
In certain cases the Income-tax Officer is required to make an assess-« 
ment “to the best of his judgment.” 
Such an assessment must be made 
if the taxpayer is delinquent in any of the following respects (§ 23(4) ):

Additional Assessments 
An individual notice to file a return for regular assessment may be 
issued only during the tax year (18/1.1). 
A taxpayer who has not been 
served with an individual notice but who files a return voluntarily after 
the end of the tax year may be assessed under the regular assessment 
procedure (§ 23). 
If the taxpayer does not file a return voluntarily, 
however, any assessment after the end of the tax year must be made 
pursuant to notice under the additional assessment procedure (§ 34). 
An additional assessment may also be made if the taxpayer did not 
file a return or did not disclose fully and truly all material facts necessary 
for his assessment, and the Income-tax Officer has reason to believe that 
as a result the taxpayer’s income has escaped assessment, has been under- 
assessed, or has been taxed at too low a rate, or that the taxpayer has 
been allowed excessive relief, loss or expense deductions, or depreciation. 
Production of account books or other evidence from which the Income- 
tax Officer could have discovered material facts is not necessarily a full 
disclosure of the material facts necessary for assessment (§ 34(1), Ex- 
planation). 
Even if the taxpayer has filed a return fully disclosing all 
material facts necessary for his assessment, the Income-tax Officer may 
order an additional assessment if, as a result of information 
in his

Modification of Assessments by the Income-tax Officer 
The Income-tax Officer may on his own motion rectify any mistake 
which is apparent from the record of an assessment or refund order which 
he has issued (§ 85). 
The record includes the order and all materials 
and proceedings upon which it is based.‘ 
An error in the application 
of a point of law is a mistake apparent from the record only if there is 
no doubt concerning the point of law.!® 
An Income-tax Officer may 
modify on his own motion the assessment of a partner, 
a member of an 
association of persons, and in certain cases a corporate shareholder, in 
order to account for changes in the assessment of the partnership, asso- 
ciation, or corporation, as the case may be. The Income-tax Officer may 
on his own motion withdraw a development rebate if the taxpayer 
subsequently makes an unauthorized use of the amount credited or makes 
an unauthorized disposition of the asset with respect to which the rebate 
was granted (10/6.4). 
Modification of an assessment by an Income-tax 
Officer on his own motion may either reduce or increase the amount 
of tax due.

13/3. 
Withholding Returns and Information Returns and 
Statements 
13/3.1 
Withholding Returns 
Employers withholding tax on payments taxable as salaries are nor- 
mally required to file monthly statements showing the particulars of 
such deductions; the Commissioner of Income-tax is authorized to permit 
the filing of a yearly statement in lieu of the usual monthly statements 
(8/1.11). 
Persons deducting tax from payments taxable otherwise than 
as salaries are required to file statements of particulars upon making the 
deductions (Rules 12, 12A). 
13/3.2 
Information Returns and Statements 
The following persons must file returns of information relating to the 
possible tax liability of others; the returns must be filed regularly on 
the specified dates, and no notice to file is required. 
1. Employers are required to file a return within 30 days after 31 March of 
each year showing the names and addresses of persons to whom they have 
paid or owe salaries during the year ending on 31 March, the amounts 
paid or due, and the amounts of tax deducted (§ 21; Rule 17). The return 
need only report payments and amounts due to persons for whom tax 
has been deducted at the source or who received or were owed more 
than a minimum of Rs 600 less than the personal allowance (12/1.2a) 
applicable to them (Rule 16). 
Returns are filed with the Income-tax 
Officer having jurisdiction over the employer. 
2. Persons paying interest other than interest on securities are required to 
file a return on or before 15 June of each year showing the names and 
addresses of all persons to whom payments of such interest were made 
during the year ending on 31 March in a total amount exceeding Rs 400, 
and the dates and amounts 
of payment 
(§ 20A; Rules 42A, 43A). 
Corporations file with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction to assess 
them. 
Other persons file with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction 
over their places of residence. 
8. Corporations declaring dividends in India are required to file returns on 
or before 15 June of each year listing the name and address of any 
corporation to which dividends were paid during the year ending on the 
preceding 31 March in a total amount exceeding one rupee and the name 
and address of any other person to whom dividends were paid during 
that period in a total amount exceeding Rs 5,000 (§ 19A; Rules 42, 43). 
Returns are filed with the Income-tax Officer having jurisdiction over the 
corporation.

The statements listed below relating to the possible tax liability of 
other persons must be filed upon notice from the Income-tax Officer 
(§ 38). 
Persons other than corporations who report taxable income 
are regularly required to file these statements as parts of their own 
return forms (Rule 19, Forms A and B). 
1. A statement to be filed by partnerships listing the names and addresses 
of the partners. 
2. A statement to be filed by Hindu undivided families listing the names 
and addresses of the manager and the adult male members. 
3. A statement to be filed by trustees, guardians, and agents showing the 
names and addresses of the persons for whom they are trustees, guardians, 
or agents, as the case may be. 
4, A statement to be filed by any taxpayer giving the names and addresses 
of all persons to whom during a specified year he has made aggregate 
payments of rent, interest, commissions, royalties, brokerage, and annui- 
ties not taxable as salaries, amounting to more than Rs 400, together with 
particulars of all such payments. 
5. A statement to be filed by dealers, brokers, agents, or other persons 
concerned in the management of a stock or commodity exchange showing 
the particulars, including the names and addresses of payees or payors, 
as the case may be, of all payments and receipts on account of the sale, 
exchange, or transfer of capital assets. 
Form A, which regularly requires 
the filing of this statement as a part of the annual return of such persons, 
requires only that the taxpayer report total payments exceeding Rs 2,000 
during the base year to any person, representing “differences” paid in 
settlement of contracts without actual delivery of shares or commodities, 
and total payments to or receipts from any person during the base year 
in excess of Rs 10,000 on account of the sale, exchange, or transfer of 
capital assets. 
The form states that the taxpayer should treat all pay- 
ments and receipts as pertaining to capital assets for reporting purposes, 
because the Income-tax Officer is responsible-for the ultimate decision as 
to whether capital assets are involved in any particular transaction. 
13/4. 
Protests and Appeals 
13/4.1 
In General 
The Income-tax Act establishes 
a number of procedures by which a 
taxpayer may obtain administrative and judicial review of action taken 
by the income tax authorities (13/4.2-18/4.7). 
The Act contains a bar 
of jurisdiction which provides that no suit shall be brought in any civil 
court “to set aside or modify any assessment” (§ 67). 
Although this 
provision bars a suit for a refund under the general jurisdiction of the 
courts after assessment, it does not bar a suit for specific relief to enjoin 
assessment. 
Relief may also be available under the jurisdiction conferred 
on the courts by special constitutional provisions, but this jurisdiction 
will usually not be exercised if an adequate remedy is otherwise available 
or if the action of the tax authorities has a reasonable basis and is within 
their jurisdiction (1/8.6).

13/4.2 
Application for New Assessment 
A taxpayer may apply to the Income-tax Officer to set aside a best 
judgment assessment (18/2.2) and make a new assessment. 
The applica- 
tion must be on the ground that the taxpayer was prevented by sufficient 
cause from making a return, or that his failure to comply with a notice 
to produce accounts, documents, or information or a notice to attend or 
to produce evidence (18/2.1) was due to the fact that he did not receive 
the notice, did not have a reasonable opportunity to comply, or was 
prevented by sufficient cause from complying. 
The application must 
be made within one month from the service of the notice of demand. 
If the taxpayer satisfies the Income-tax Officer of the validity of the 
application, the Income-tax Officer must set aside the assessment and 
make a new assessment (§ 27).

The Appellate Assistant Commissioner has broad powers of review. 
He may make further inquiry into the facts himself or may direct that 
further inquiry be made by the Income-tax Officer (§ 31(2)). 
He may 
allow points not specified in the grounds of appeal to be raised by the 
taxpayer (§ 31(2A)) and may raise such points on his own motion.”* 
He may confirm or set aside an order from which an appeal is taken 
or may modify such an order whether the effect is to reduce or to 
increase the liability of the taxpayer (§$31(3)). 
However, the tax- 
payer’s liability may not be increased unless he has had an opportunity 
to be heard (§ 31(3), Proviso), and the power to increase liability does 
not include the power to assess income not previously assessed.28 
The 
Income-tax Officer has the right to be heard by the Appellate Assistant 
Commissioner.

Appeal to the Appellate Tribunal 
An order issued by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner in the exer- 
cise of his appellate authority (13/4.3) may be appealed to the Appellate 
Tribunal (1/8.6) both by the taxpayer and, upon direction from the 
Commissioner of Income-tax, by the Income-tax Officer. 
In addition, the

missioner of an order of an Income-tax Officer found prejudicial to the

ADMINISTRATION 
A person who has withheld tax pursuant to section 18(3B) may appeal 
the question of his liability to do so (§ 30(1A)). 
The Appellate Tribunal has power to review both questions of fact 
and questions of law. Allegations made on appeal to the Tribunal which 
are not established by the record or are contrary to it must be supported 
by affidavits.*® 
Although the parties are not entitled as a matter of 
right to produce additional evidence before the Tribunal, the Tribunal 
may direct that oral or written evidence be taken before it, before the 
Appellate Assistant Commissioner, or before the Income-tax Officer.?° 
In addition, the Tribunal may in the exercise of reasonable discretion 
allow an appellant to argue grounds not specified in the prescribed form 
of appeal.*!_ 
The Tribunal may not increase the taxpayer’s assessment 
on any ground not raised by the Commissioner of Income-tax on appeal.” 
The decision of the Appellate Tribunal on questions of fact is final 
(§ 33(6) ); questions of law may be further referred to the High Court 
(13/4.7). 
13/4.5 
Revision by the Commissioner in Favor of the Taxpayer 
The Commissioner of Income-tax (1/8.3) may revise, in favor of the 
taxpayer, an order of the Income-tax Officer or of the Appellate Assistant 
Commissioner either on his own motion or on application by the taxpayer 
($ 834A). He may grant or refuse revision within the limits of reasonable 
discretion.** 
An application by the taxpayer for revision must be made within one 
year from the date of the order or within such further time as the Com- 
missioner of Income-tax may for sufficient cause allow. 
Revision on the 
Commissioner's own motion must be made within a year from the date 
of the order. 
If an order is appealable to the Appellate Assistant Com- 
missioner or the Appellate Tribunal, revision may not be made until the 
time for appeal has expired unless the taxpayer has waived his right of 
appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. 
Revision may not be made while 
an appeal is pending before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but 
may be made after the disposition of the appeal. 
The Commissioner 
cannot revise 
an order which has been appealed to the Appellate 
Tribunal even if the appeal is later disposed of or waived by the taxpayer 
(§ 383A).

13/4.6 
Rectification of Mistakes 
The Appellate Assistant Commissioner (1/8.6) may rectify a mistake 
apparent from the record of an order issued by him. 
Similarly, the 
Appellate Tribunal (1/8.6) may rectify a mistake apparent from the 
record of an order issued by it. 
The Commissioner of Income-tax 
(1/8.3) may rectify a mistake apparent from the record of an order of 
revision in favor of the taxpayer issued by him. 
The rectification of all 
such mistakes must be made within four years from the date of the 
order (§§ 35(1), 35(2)). 
The power of the Income-tax Officer to rectify 
mistakes is discussed at 13/2.4. 
13/4.7. 
References to the Courts 
The taxpayer or the Commissioner of Income-tax may apply for the 
reference to the High Court of questions of law arising out of an order 
of the Appellate Tribunal (§ 66(1); Rule 22A). The application must be 
made to the Appellate Tribunal within 60 days of notification of an order 
of the Tribunal. 
The Tribunal must state the case and refer the ques- 
tions of law unless it finds that a question of law does not arise or that 
the application is not timely. 
If the Tribunal denies the application 
for reference, application may be made to the High Court to require 
the Tribunal to make a statement of the case and reference of questions 
of law (§§ 66(2), 66(3)). 
The statement of the case should contain 
the relevant findings of fact and conclusions of law made by the Ap- 
pellate Tribunal, the order of the Tribunal, and other relevant papers 
and documents.*4 
The High Court can decide only questions of law 
referred to it and cannot raise new questions.*> 
However, the High 
Court has considerable latitude in reframing questions of law referred 
to it? 
A case referred to the High Court is heard by a bench of at 
least two judges (§ 66A(1) ). 
An appeal may be taken to the Supreme Court from a judgment of the 
High Court which the High Court certifies to be fit for appeal (§ 66A). 
A case is considered fit for appeal if an important question of law is 
involved.*"

13/4.8 
Payment of Tax Pending Review 
The Income-tax Officer is authorized in his discretion to treat taxes 
otherwise due as not in default while an appeal is pending before the 
Appellate Assistant Commissioner (§ 45). 
Administrative instructions 
require the Income-tax Officer or his superiors to stay collection under 
this provision if satisfied that the appeal is not frivolous and that grant- 
ing the stay will not jeopardize collection of the tax if the appeal should 
be unsuccessful. 
There is no other statutory provision for a stay of 
collection pending review. 
Refunds are directed when it is determined 
on review that there has been an overpayment of tax (13/5.1). 
13/5. 
Claims for Refund 
13/5.1 
Circumstances in Which Refund Claims May Be Filed 
A refund may be obtained on application to an authorized Income-tax 
Officer if the payment of tax in excess of the amount properly due can 
be shown 
without reviewing 
a previous 
determination 
of the tax 
authorities 
(§§ 48(1), 48(4)). 
Circumstances 
in which claims 
for 
refund may be filed include those listed below. 
1. Income tax or supertax has been withheld from payments of salary at a 
higher rate than is applicable to the taxpayer (8/1.10). 
2. Income tax or supertax has been withheld from payments of interest on 
securities at a higher rate than is applicable to the taxpayer (9/7). 
8. Income tax or supertax has been withheld from payments to a nonresident 
at a higher rate than is applicable to the taxpayer (11/3.3b). 
4. Income tax with respect to dividends has been paid at the source and 
the rate of tax actually applicable to the recipient of the dividends is 
less than the maximum (9/7). 
5. The taxpayer is entitled to relief because he has been subject to double 
taxation (11/2.4, 11/6). 
Any other overpayment of tax is ground for a refund claim if the 
claim does not involve the review of an assessment or other determina- 
tion of the tax authorities. 
A refund may be granted, notwithstanding 
this condition, when a mistake apparent from the record is rectified 
(13/2.4, 13/4.6) or when an order is revised by the Commissioner of 
Income-tax (13/4.5). 
A refund is due without the filing of a claim by the taxpayer when it 
is determined on review that there has been an overpayment of tax

13/5.2 
Procedure for Filing Claims 
An application for refund must be made in the prescribed form (Rule 
36) within four years from the close of the tax year ($50). 
The 
application should be accompanied by a return of world-wide income, if 
such a return has not already been filed (Rule 37), and by the certifi- 
cates which must be given to the payees of dividends 
(9/2.4a) 
or 
payments other than salary from which tax has been withheld (Rule 38) 
(13/1.4b). 
Residents file their application with the Income-tax Officers 
having jurisdiction over their places of residence unless they fall within 
a particular class for which other officers have been authorized to re- 
ceive applications. 
Nonresidents file their applications with specially 
authorized Income-tax Officers (Rule 39).

13/6.1 
Assessment of Residents 
Time limits are imposed on action by the Income-tax Officer at two 
different points in the procedure for assessment of residents. 
Except 
when a voluntary return has been filed or the assessment follows a 
reconsideration of a previous assessment (13/2.5, 18/4.2-13/4.5, 13/ 4.7), 
assessment may not be made unless an individual notice to file a return 
for regular assessment (13/1.1) or notice to file a return for additional 
assessment (13/2.3) has been served on the taxpayer. 
The issuance* 
of these notices is subject to time limits, as is the issuance of assessment 
orders. 
An individual notice to file a return for regular assessment may be

In the case of an

file a return must be served on the taxpayer within four years from 
the end of the tax year. 
In the case of an additional assessment which 
is based upon reasonable belief that a proper assessment has not been 
made by reason of the omission or failure of the taxpayer to file a return 
or to disclose fully all material facts (13/2.3), the time limit on service 
of the notice depends upon the amount involved. 
In such cases, the 
notice may be served at any time if the aggregate additional assessment 
on account of the base year and any prior years equals or exceeds 
Rs 100,000. 
If the additional assessment is less than Rs 100,000, the 
notice must be served within eight years from the end of the tax year 
(§ 34(1)). 
If the taxpayer has concealed the particulars of his income or de- 
liberately furnished inaccurate particulars of his income, there is no time 
limit during which a regular assessment must be made, provided the 
taxpayer has been served during the tax year with an individual notice 
to file a return for regular assessment or has voluntarily filed a return 
during or after the tax year ($ 34(3)). 
A new assessment following the 
setting aside of a best judgment assessment (13/4.2) and an assessment 
following the determination of an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Com- 
missioner (13/4.3) or the Appellate Tribunal (18/4.4), a reference to 
the courts (13/4.7), or revision by the Commissioner (13/2.5, 18/4.5) 
may also be made at any time (§ 34(3)). 
All other regular, special, or 
provisional assessments must be made within four years from the end 
of the base year (§ 34(8)). 
Additional assessments based upon reasonable belief in consequence 
of information in the possession of the Income-tax Officer (13/2.8) 
must be made within four years from the end of the base year or one 
year from the service of notice to file a return for additional assessment, 
whichever is later. 
There is no time limit on additional assessments 
based upon reasonable belief that a proper assessment has not been 
made by reason of the omission or failure on the part of the taxpayer 
to file a return or to disclose fully or truly all material facts (§ 34(3) ). 
Modification or rectification of an assessment (13/2.4) must ordinarily 
be made within four years from the date of the original assessment order 
(§ 35(1)). 
However, when it is necessary to modify a taxpayer's assess- 
ment because of certain changes in the assessment of a corporation in 
which he owns shares or in the assessment of a partnership or association 
of which he is a member, the four-year period runs from the date of the 
final order assessing the corporation, partnership, or association (§§ 35(5), 
35(7)-35(9)). 
When the taxpayer has made an unauthorized use of

or

(§ 45) (11/2.3).

In General 
The procedures listed below may be employed in connection with the

1. When tax is assessed, interest may be added if the taxpayer has failed 
to make proper advance payments of tax (13/7.2) .41

formation (13/7.5), and the making of false statements (13/7.6).

alties under this section may be imposed by the Income-tax Officer (with

of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner (1/8.4).

Interest and Penalties Relating to Advance Payments 
Where the taxpayer makes or should make advance payments on the

by which the advance payment, if any, is less than 80% of the tax 
determined on regular assessment. 
Such interest may be reduced or 
waived by the Income-tax Officer in certain cases prescribed by rule 
and in other cases where the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner con- 
siders reduction or waiver justified (§ 18A(6); Rule 48). 
If an estimate

payment of tax on commissions is deferred improperly or for too long

number of installments, and interest may be charged at the rate of 6% 
on the amount by which the resulting figure exceeds each of the install- 
ments actually paid. 
If the rates of tax in effect during the base year 
are lower than those in effect during the tax year (and applicable to the 
base year), the tax is computed for this purpose at the lower rate.

13/7.3 
Late Payment of Tax 
‘There is no provision for the addition of interest to taxes which are 
not paid within the time specified in the notice of demand (13/2.4d). 
However, the practice of the Department of Revenue is to charge interest 
at reasonable rates where the taxpayer delays payment of tax or pays tax 
in installments over a long period. 
The Income-tax Officer may at his 
discretion impose a penalty for late payment in an amount which does 
not exceed the amount of tax due (§ 46(1)). 
The amount of any such 
penalty may be increased from time to time up to the maximum as long 
as the tax is in default (§ 46(1A)). 
Penalties which may be imposed for 
late payment of advance payments of tax due, under a notice requiring 
advance payment or an estimate filed by the taxpayer, are discussed at 
18/7.2. 
13/7.4 
Failure to File Returns; Late Returns; and Invalid Returns 
A penalty may be imposed for failure without reasonable cause to file 
a return for regular assessment as required by a general or individual 
notice (13/1.1), or for failure to file a return for additional assessment 
as required by individual notice (§ 28(1))(18/2.3). 
In practice, penal- 
ties are not imposed for failure to file a return pursuant to a general 
notice except in the case of taxpayers who have not been previously 
assessed. 
A penalty may also be imposed if a return is filed late or is 
invalid because it is incomplete or otherwise not in the prescribed form. 
The penalty for such failure to file or for late or invalid filing may be 
in an amount up to one and one half times the tax which is assessed for 
the relevant base year (§ 28). 
For the computation of this penalty, a 
registered partnership is treated as if it were an unregistered partnership 
(§ 28(1), Proviso (d)). 
In the case of a failure to file a return for 
regular assessment required by an individual notice, the taxpayer may 
alternatively be prosecuted before a magistrate and on conviction fined 
Rs 10 per day until a return is filed (§ 51(c)).

13/7.5 
Failure to Furnish Information 
A penalty may be imposed for failure without reasonable cause to 
comply with a notice to produce accounts, documents, or information, 
or a notice to attend or to produce evidence (13/3.1). 
In practice, such 
penalties are imposed only in cases in which a best judgment assessment 
is made (13/3.2). 
The maximum penalty is one and one half times any 
difference between the tax assessed and the tax which would have been 
assessed if the return filed by the taxpayer had been accepted as correct 
(§ 28(1)). 
For the computation of this penalty, a registered partnership 
is treated as if it were an unregistered partnership (§ 28(1), Proviso (d) ). 
A taxpayer who fails without reasonable cause to comply with a notice 
to produce accounts, documents, or information may alternatively be 
prosecuted before a magistrate and on conviction fined Rs 10 per day 
until he complies with the notice (§$51(d)). 
The Income-tax Officer may impose a penalty on a taxpayer who fails 
without reasonable excuse to comply with a notice requiring him to 
furnish particulars relevant to the provisions concerning the sale of 
securities cum interest or under an agreement to buy back (9/1.6). 
The 
penalty may be in an amount up to Rs 500 per day for each day in which 
the default continues 
(§§ 44E(6), 44F(5)). 
The Income-tax Officer 
may impose a penalty on a taxpayer who, on the discontinuance of a 
business, fails to file a notice which is required for the purpose of a 
special assessment (13/1.3). 
The maximum penalty is an amount equal 
to the tax specially assessed on the business (§ 25(2) ). 
Failure to file information returns or statements (13/3.2) or to allow 
the inspection or copying of corporate records (13/2.1) is grounds for 
prosecution before a magistrate and the imposition of a fine of Rs 10 
per day as long as the default continues (§§ 51(c), 51(e) ). 
An agent for a nonresident (11/3.4) cannot be subjected to a penalty 
for failure to file a return on behalf of a nonresident unless he has been 
served with a notice to file a return (13/1.1) for regular or additional 
assessment (§ 28(1), Proviso (c) ). 
13/7.6 
False Statements and Representations 
A penalty may be imposed on a taxpayer who has concealed the par- 
ticulars of his income or deliberately furnished inaccurate particulars 
of his income. 
The maximum penalty is one and one half times the 
difference between the tax assessed and the tax which would have been 
assessed if the return filed by the taxpayer had been accepted as correct 
(§ 28(1)). 
For the computation of this penalty, a registered partner- 
ship is treated as if it were an unregistered partnership 
(§ 28(1), 
Proviso (d) ).

A person who knowingly makes a false statement in the verification 
of a return of income for regular assessment (13/1.2), a statement re- 
quired by the Income-tax Officer in the course of assessment (13/2.1), 
an information return regularly required to be filed (13/3.2), an appli- 
cation for the registration of a partnership (5/3.1), or an appeal to the 
Appellate Assistant Commissioner (13/4.3) or the Appellate Tribunal 
(13/4.4), is subject to prosecution. 
On conviction before a magistrate, 
the maximum penalty is six months imprisonment, a fine of Rs 1,000, 
or both ($52). 
Persons who furnish false evidence to the income tax 
authorities may also be prosecuted under the Indian Penal Code. 
The 
maximum penalty is six months imprisonment, a fine of Rs 1,000, or 
both.*® 
Persons who give or use false evidence in a proceeding before 
the income tax authorities may be prosecuted under the Indian Penal 
Code. 
The maximum penalty is seven years imprisonment, a fine for 
which no maximum is specified, or both (§ 37(4) ).* 
A penalty may be imposed on a partner in a registered partnership 
if his income is understated because shares of profit are not distributed 
in accordance with the partnership agreement. 
The maximum penalty 
is one and one half times the difference between the tax assessed and 
the tax which would have been assessed if the income of the partner had 
not been understated (§ 28(2)). 
In such cases, the other partners are 
not allowed to reduce their tax by showing that the share distributed 
to them was less than the share distributable to them under the partner- 
ship agreement. 
13/7.7 
Withholding Agents 
Persons who fail to withhold taxes when withholding is required during 
the base year or to furnish the payees with the required certificates 
stating the amounts withheld (18/1.4b), employers who fail to with- 
hold delinquent taxes from payments of salary when required to do so 
(18/1.6), and corporations which fail to furnish shareholders with the 
required certificates relating to the payment of taxes on distributed 
profits (9/2.4a) are subject to prosecution under the Act. 
On conviction 
before a magistrate, the maximum penalty is a fine of Rs 10 per day as 
long as the default continues (§ 51(a)).
