14/1. 
Introduction 
A tax on net wealth has been in effect in India since 1 April 1957.1 
The enactment of a net wealth tax was among the proposals for an inte- 
1The Wealth-tax Act of 1957 (cited herein as WTA) was introduced in the 
lower house of the Indian Parliament on 15 May 1957 (Gaz. of India, Extra., Pt. IL,


<!-- page 437 of 600 -->

India 
14/2.14a 
401 
NET 
WEALTH 
TAX 
grated direct tax system which were made in a study conducted at the 
request of the Indian government by Nicholas Kaldor of Cambridge 
University.” 
The tax is levied annually on the taxable net wealth (14/3) owned 
by the taxpayer on “the valuation date” (14/4.1). 
Individuals and Hindu 
undivided families are taxed at progessive rates, while corporations are 
taxed at a uniform rate (14/7.2). 
Net wealth located outside India is 
taken into account in the case of ordinarily resident taxpayers other than 
aliens. 
Other taxpayers are taxed only on net wealth located in India. 
14/2. 
Classes of Taxpayers 
14/2.1 
Individuals 
a. IN GENERAL. 
Liability of an individual to the wealth tax, like liability 
to the income tax, depends on whether he is ordinarily resident, resident 
but not ordinarily resident (5/1.1), or not resident (5/4.1), but, in addi- 
tion, is based in part on citizenship. 
Residence status during the year 
ending on the valuation date is determined in accordance with the stand- 
ards applicable under the Income-tax Act (WTA §6, Explanation 1) 
(5/1.2). 
There are three classifications of liability to tax on domestic and 
foreign net wealth. 
1. Citizens who are ordinarily resident are taxed on the value of their 
world-wide net wealth, but are granted a reduction of 50% of the tax 
attributable 
to net wealth located outside 
India (WTA §3; WTA, 
Schedule, Rule 4) (14/7.3a). 
2. Citizens who are either resident but not ordinarily resident or not resident, 
and aliens who are resident are taxed only on net wealth located in India 
(WTA §§ 3, 6(i)). 
8. Aliens who are not resident are taxed on net wealth located in India, but 
are granted a reduction of 50% of the tax (WTA §8§3, 6(i); WTA, 
Schedule, Rule 3) (14/7.3b). 
Sec. 2, No. 8, 15 May 1957, p. 110). 
It was reported favorably, with amendments, 
by a Select Committee (Gaz. of India, Extra., Pt. II, Sec. 2, No. 25A, 17 August 
1957) and was enacted 12 September 1957. 
2 Kaldor, Indian Tax Reform, Report of a Survey 19-28, 130-136. 
Kaldor sug- 
gested that under the proper conditions a wealth tax would contribute to a fairer 
measure of taxable capacity and a more effective administration of direct taxes, and 
would produce additional revenue without the disincentive effects of an income tax 
on risky undertakings. 
Annual taxes on net wealth are levied by Sweden, the Netherlands, Norway, 
Colombia, the Federal Republic of Germany, Ceylon, and other countries. 
The 
Swedish net wealth tax is described in WTS: Sweden, Chapter 14. 
The net wealth 
tax in Ceylon is part of an integrated direct tax system enacted in 1959 pursuant to 
a study made by Kaldor for the government of that country. 
3 The basic principles governing citizenship are to be found in articles 5 through 
11 of the Constitution of India, and in the Citizenship Act of 1955.

b. MARRIED PERSONS, MINORS, AND INCAPACITATED PERSONS. 
No provision 
is made for the aggregation of the assets of husband and wife. However, 
certain assets transferred by a husband to his wife or minor child are 
treated as assets of the husband (14/3.3). 
Guardians or trustees holding 
assets for minors or incapacitated persons are assessed for the tax which 
would be payable by their wards if the latter held the asssets directly 
(WTA §21(3)). 
If the beneficiaries under a trust and the shares to 
which they are entitled are ascertained, the fiduciaries 
are similarly 
charged with the tax which would be payable by each beneficiary on the 
assets held in trust, at the average rate applicable to each beneficiary 
(WTA §21(1)). 
Since guardians, trustees, or fiduciaries are taxed by 
reference to the hypothetical liability of their wards or beneficiaries, the 
amount of tax is determined in accordance with the residence and 
citizenship status of the wards or beneficiaries. 
14/2.2 
Corporations 
Corporations organized under Indian law and corporations organized 
under foreign law which have a place of business in India are subject 
to the wealth tax (WTA 8§ 2(h), 3). 
However, certain corporations 
are exempt (14/2.4); and it is expected that corporations will be ex- 
empted entirely from the wealth tax in 1960, when the rate structure of 
the corporate income tax will be revised. 
A corporation organized 
under foreign law which does not have a place of business in India is 
not subject to the tax, regardless whether it has a business connection or 
owns assets in India. No provision is made for the taxation of associations 
as corporations (5/2.2). 
Corporations subject to tax are taxed as resident or not resident, the 
classification “resident but not ordinarily resident” having no application 
to them. 
All corporations organized under Indian law are resident 
(WTA § 
6, Explanation 2(a)). 
A corporation organized under foreign 
law is resident only if the control and management of its affairs were 
situated wholly in India during the year ending on the valuation date 
(WTA § 6, Explanation 2(b) ).5 
Resident corporations are taxed annually on the value of their world- 
wide net wealth. 
The allowance of 50% of the tax attributable to net 
wealth located outside India, granted to individuals and Hindu undivided 
families (14/2.1, 14/2.3a), is not available to resident corporations. How- 
ever, the flat rate of tax applicable to corporate net wealth is lower than 
the progressive rates applicable to the net wealth of individuals and® 
Hindu undivided families (14/7.2). 
In addition, corporations are ac-

corded special treatment in connection with losses or low profit margins 
(14/7.3e). 
A limited form of relief from double taxation of corporate 
shareholders is provided (14/7.3d). 
Nonresident corporations which are subject to the Act are taxed in 
full on the value of their net wealth located in India. 
14/2.3, 
Other Taxpayers 
a. HINDU UNDIVIDED FAMILIES. 
The liability of a Hindu undivided family 
to the wealth tax depends on its residence status (5/3.2) during the year 
ending on the valuation date, as determined according to the standards 
applicable under the Income-tax Act (WTA § 
6, Explanation 1). 
1. Hindu undivided families which are ordinarily resident are taxed on their 
world-wide net wealth. 
The allowance of 50% of the tax attributable to 
net wealth located outside India (14/7.3a), granted to ordinarily resident 
citizens, extends to such families (WTA § 3; WTA, Schedule, Rule 4). 
2. Hindu undivided families which are resident but not ordinarily resident 
or not resident are taxed only on their net wealth located within India 
(WTA §§ 8, 6(i)). 
The allowance of 50% of the tax attributable to net 
wealth located within India, granted to nonresident aliens, does not 
extend to such families. 
The rate schedule for Hindu undivided families, slightly lower than 
the individual rate schedule, applies uniformly without regard to the 
number of members participating in the family (14/7.2). 
Double tax- 
ation of such families and their members is avoided by excluding a 
coparcener’s interest in the property of the family from his individual 
taxable wealth (WTA § 5(1)(ii)). 
b. TRUSTS AND DECEDENTS ESTATES. 
To the extent that the beneficiaries 
of a trust or their shares are unascertained, the trust is, in effect, taxed 
as an entity at the rates applicable to individuals (WTA § 21(4)). 
The 
residence and citizenship status of such a trust is considered to be that 
of the trustee. 
If the beneficiaries are ascertained, the trustee is liable 
as described at 14/2.1b for the tax on their interests. 
The executor, administrator, or other legal representative of a deceased 
person is liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased any tax which 
is payable by the deceased or which would have been payable by him 
if he had not died (WTA § 19(1)). The tax liability of the representative 
is determined by the residence status of the decedent. 
It would seem 
that legal representatives of an estate would also be liable to tax on 
property acquired by the estate after the death of the deceased. 
C. LOCAL AUTHORITIES, PARTNERSHIPS, AND ASSOCIATIONS. 
Local authorities 
(5/3.6), partnerships (5/3.1), and associations (5/3.3) are not taxable 
entities under the Wealth-tax Act (WTA § 3).

d. RULERS OF INDIAN STATES. 
Rulers of former native Indian States are 
subject to the net wealth tax, but are granted special exemptions for their 
official residences (WTA § 5(1)(iii)) and for heirloom jewelry (WTA 
§ 5(1) (xiv) ). 
14/2.4 
Tax-exempt Entities 
The entities listed below are specifically exempted from liability to 
the wealth tax. 
1. Banking corporations falling within the definition of “company” contained 
in section 5 of the Banking Companies Act of 1949 (WTA § 45(a)).® 
2. Corporations which are insurers within the meaning of the Insurance Act 
of 1988 (WTA § 45(b)). 
3. New corporations organized to carry on industrial undertakings in India 
(WTA § 45(d)).7 
Corporations established on or after 1 April 1957, 
the effective date of the wealth tax, are exempt for the five years follow- 
ing the year in which the corporation is established; corporations organized 
before that date are exempt for the balance, if any, of the five-year period 
following the year in which they were organized. 
Although “establish- 
ment” probably means the date of incorporation, there is a possibility 
that it could refer either to the date on which construction of the plant 
was commenced or to the date on which trading began. 
An “industrial 
undertaking” is defined as an enterprise engaged in the manufacture, 
production, or processing of goods or articles, in mining, or in the genera- 
tion or distribution of power (WTA § 45(d), Explanation). 
The exemp- 
tion does not apply to a corporation formed by the splitting up or 
reconstruction of a business already in existence or by the transfer to a 
new business 
of buildings, machinery, 
or plant used in a business 
previously carried on. 
4. Corporations, established to finance private industrial enterprises in India, 
to which the central government has made or agreed to make a special 
advance or for which it has guaranteed or agreed to guarantee a loan 
from a foreign institution 
(WTA § 45(c)). 
5. Shipping corporations which do not engage in any business other than 
shipping (WTA § 45(e)). 
6. Nonprofit corporations registered under section 25 of the Companies Act 
of 1956 for promoting “commerce, art, science, religion, charity, or any 
other useful object” (WTA § 45(f)). 
The purposes or objects of such 
corporations need not be located in India.8 
6 The Banking Companies Act of 1949 (§5(d)) defines “company” as any com- 
pany which may be wound up under the Indian Companies Act of 1956. 
A branch 
of a foreign banking company, since it may not be wound up under the Act, would 
not be exempted.

It is expected that all corporations will be exempted from the wealth

14/3. 
Taxable Wealth 
1473.1 
In General 
The tax is imposed on “net wealth” (WTA §3). 
Net wealth is basi- 
cally the aggregate value of all assets owned by the taxpayer on the 
valuation date less his debts on that date (WTA § 2(m))(14/7.1). 
Certain assets which have been transferred by the taxpayer are treated 
as though still owned by him (14/3.3). 
Various classes of assets are 
exempt (14/3.4). 
World-wide net wealth is taxable in the case of 
ordinarily resident 
citizens, Hindu undivided 
families, and resident 
corporations. 
Other taxpayers are taxed only on net wealth located in 
India (14/5.1). 
Certain debts which are identified with exempt assets

Assets Included 
“Assets” are defined as including “property of every description, mova- 
ble or immovable” (WTA § 2(e)). 
However, certain classes of assets 
are expressly excluded from the definition of “assets,” and others are 
excluded from taxable wealth (14/3.4). 
It is not clear whether contractual rights which are not property rights 
in the conventional legal sense, or contingent rights, would be treated 
as assets for wealth tax purposes. 
An exclusion from assets of any 
interest in property vested in the assessee but not yet in his possession 
or enjoyment, was proposed by the Select Committee,® but was omitted 
from the law as passed; hence it seems clear that future interests are to 
be included in net wealth. 
The value of a taxpayer’s interest in a partnership or association is 
expressly required to be included 
as part of his net wealth (WTA 
§ 
4(1)(b))(14/4.2). 
An interest 
in the coparcenary property of a 
Hindu undivided family is expressly excluded from net wealth because 
the family itself is a taxable entity under the law (WTA §$5(1)(ii)). 
Except in the case of shares in certain industrial corporations and shares 
held by other corporations (14/3.4f), corporate shares are included in 
net wealth even though corporations themselves are taxable entities; 
however, a limited form of relief against the double taxation of corporate 
shareholders is provided (14/7.3d).

Deductible Debts 
Total debts are deducted from total assets in arriving at net wealth 
(WTA § 2(m)). “Debt” is not defined. 
It does not seem that deduction 
would be allowed for liabilities which are either contingent or uncertain 
in amount. 
The law provides that debts “secured on” or “incurred in relation to” 
assets on which wealth tax is not payable are not deductible (WTA 
§2(m)). 
The phrase “incurred in relation to” is evidently intended to 
have a wider meaning than the expression “secured on” in order to cover 
debts incurred in acquiring exempt assets and loans obtained by credit 
founded on the ownership of such assets. 
The forms issued by the Cen- 
tral Board of Revenue refer to “debts which have been incurred for 
acquiring assets which are exempted from wealth tax, or for utilization

International Aspects 
14/5.1 
Foreign Net Wealth 
While net wealth located in India is taxed in full to all taxpayers 
except nonresident alien individuals, net wealth located outside India 
is taxed in full only to resident corporations (including domestic corpora- 
tions and foreign corporations whose control and management are situ- 
ated wholly in India) (14/2). 
Citizens who are ordinarily resident and 
Hindu undivided families which are ordinarily resident (5/1.2) 
are 
taxed on foreign net wealth, but are granted a reduction of 50% of the 
tax attributable thereto (14/2.la, 14/2.3a). 
Nonresident corporations, 
citizens or Hindu undivided families which are either resident but not 
ordinarily resident or not resident, and aliens are not taxed on foreign 
net wealth (14/2). 
Instructions issued by the Central Board of Revenue provide that the 
following classes of assets are located in India.?* 
1. Real property situated in India, rights and interests in and over such 
property other than security interests, and benefits arising out of such 
property. 
2. Debts, secured or unsecured, for which repayment in India is contracted 
or which, although no place of repayment is specified, are owed by a 
debtor residing in India. 
8. Bank deposits, if the branch where the account is kept is situated in 
India. 
4. Securities issued by the central government, a state government, or a local 
authority, unless inscribed for payment outside India. 
5. Shares, stocks, debentures, or debenture stocks, issued by a corporation 
organized under Indian law. 
6. Ships or aircraft registered in India. 
7. Copyrights or copyright licenses exercisable in India. 
8. Patents, trade-marks, 
or designs registered in India or exercisable in 
India. 
9. Other rights, including causes of action ex delicto, enforceable in India. 
14/5.2 
Aliens and Nonresident Individuals 
Aliens are taxed only on net wealth located in India. 
They are taxed 
- 
in full if they are resident or ordinarily resident, but receive a reduction 
of 50% of the tax if they are not resident (14/2.1). 
Citizens who are 
resident but not ordinarily resident or not resident, and Hindu undivided 
families which are resident but not ordinarily resident or not resident, 
are taxed in full on net wealth located in India but are exempt from tax 
on foreign net wealth (14/2.1, 14/2.3a). 
Aliens and taxpayers who are nonresident or resident but not ordinarily 
resident are not taxed on the value of assets in India represented by loans

14/5.3 
Foreign Corporations 
Under the law applicable through the tax years 1959-1960, a corpora- 
tion organized under foreign law is subject to the wealth tax if it main- 
tains a place of business in India. 
If its control and management are 
located wholly within India, it is classed as resident, and is taxed on its 
world-wide net wealth in the same manner as an Indian corporation 
(14/2.2). 
The reduction of 50% of the tax on foreign net wealth avail- 
able to individuals and Hindu undivided families is not available to 
corporations. 
If its control and management are not located wholly 
within India, the corporation is classed as nonresident, and is taxed only 
on the value of its net wealth located in India (14/2.2). 
The limited form of relief against double taxation which is granted to 
shareholders in domestic corporations is not available to shareholders in 
foreign corporations 
(14/7.3d). 
Shares in a foreign corporation are 
treated as being located outside India, whereas shares in a domestic 
corporation are treated as being located in India (14/5.1). 
A foreign 
corporation cannot qualify as an exempt banking corporation or as an 
exempt nonprofit corporation (14/2.4). 
It is expected that all corporations will be exempt from tax starting 
with the tax year 1960-1961 (14/2.2). 
14/5.4 
Tax Treaties 
There are no tax treaties or agreements for the relief of international 
double taxation 
of wealth, nor are there any special arrangements 
regarding diplomatic or consular personnel or employees of international 
organizations which apply to the wealth tax. 
14/5.5 
Foreign Tax Credit 
There is no provision for a credit for foreign net wealth taxes paid. 
The reductions of 50% of the tax on the foreign net wealth of ordinarily 
resident citizens and Hindu undivided families (14/7.8a) and of 50% 
of the tax on the domestic net wealth of nonresident aliens (14/7.3b) 
appear to have been designed in part to operate in lieu of such a credit.28

Tax Incentives 
The exemptions for assets or taxpayers listed below are designed to 
promote the industrial development of India. 
1. The exemption, accorded aliens and persons who are nonresident or who 
are resident but not ordinarily resident, of loans, deposits, and credits 
upon heat the interest is exempt from income tax (14/3.4f, 9/1.3, 
9/1:8). 
2. The exemption for five years of corporations newly organized to carry on

3. The exemption for five years of assets invested in new and separate units 
of industrial corporations (14/3.4e). 
4. The exemption of corporations organized to finance private industrial 
enterprises in India and accorded financial assistance by the central goy- 
ernment (14/2.4, item 4). 
5. The exemption of shares in an exempt newly organized industrial cor- 
poration (14/3.4f). 
14/7. 
Computation and Rates of Tax 
14/7.1 
In General 
In computing taxable wealth, all assets owned by the taxpayer on the 
valuation date (14/3.2), including attributed assets (14/3.3), must be 
taken into account, except assets which are exempt at the marginal rate 
(14/3.4a). 
Assets located outside India must be taken into account in 
computing the taxable wealth of a citizen who is ordinarily resident, a 
Hindu undivided family which is ordinarily resident, or a resident cor- 
poration. 
From the assets are subtracted deductible debts (14/3.5) to 
arrive at net wealth, which determines the applicable rate of tax (14/7.2). 
The tax computed on net wealth at this rate is then reduced by the 
amount of tax attributable to assets which are exempt at the average rate 
(14/3.4a, 14/3.4£) and by any special adjustments which may be applica- 
ble (14/7.3). 
Guardians or trustees holding assets for minors, incapacitated persons, 
or other ascertained beneficiaries must compute the tax on the assets 
held by them at the average rate applicable to the total net wealth of 
each beneficiary (14/2.1b).

14/7.3. 
Allowances and Adjustments 
a. FOREIGN NET WEALTH. A reduction of 50% of the tax attributable to 
foreign net wealth is granted to citizens and Hindu undivided families 
who are ordinarily resident (14/5.1). 
The tax on the total net wealth, 
domestic and foreign, must be computed at the average rate, and then 
reduced by an amount which bears the same proportion to it as 50% of 
the foreign net wealth bears to the total net wealth (WTA, Schedule, 
Rule 4). 
b. NONRESIDENT ALIENS. 
A reduction of 50% of the tax is granted to non- 
resident individuals who are not citizens of India (WTA, Schedule, 
Rule 3). Since such individuals are taxed only on the value of net wealth 
located within India (14/2.la), this is a reduction in respect of Indian net 
wealth. 
It is not available to Hindu undivided families or corporations. 
C, GOVERNMENT DEPOSITS AND SECURITIES. 
An adjustment is provided with 
respect to deposits with the central government or a state government, 
and securities of the central government, a state government, or a local 
authority, for which the central government has issued an appropriate 
notice in the Gazette of India (WTA, Schedule, Rule 1)(14/3.4b). 
The 
adjustment is at the average rate of tax, the tax being reduced by a frac- 
tion equal to the proportion which the above assets bear to total net 
wealth,

d. sHarEHoLpeERS. A limited form of relief is provided against the double 
taxation of shareholders in-corporations. 
The relief is available to a tax- 
payer, other than a corporation, whose net wealth includes the value of 
shares in a corporation organized under Indian law. 
The relief is com- 
puted as follows in respect of each corporation (WTA, Schedule, Rule 2). 
1. Determine the taxpayer’s wealth tax allocable to his shares in the corpora- 
tion. 
The tax so allocable is that proportion of the total wealth tax which 
the value of his shares in the corporation bears to his total net wealth. 
2. Determine the corporation’s wealth tax allocable to the taxpayer’s shares. 
The tax so allocable is that proportion of the corporation’s total wealth 
tax which the paid up value of the taxpayer’s shares bears to the aggre- 
gate paid up value of the share capital of the corporation. 
3. Compute 2% of the value of the shares included in the taxpayer’s net 
wealth.°° 
4. If the sum of the amounts determined in 1 and 2 exceeds the amounts 
computed in 3, reduce the taxpayer’s liability by the excess. 
€. LOSS CORPORATIONS. 
A corporation whose operations during the year 
ending on the valuation date have been unprofitable is granted a reduc- 
tion of wealth tax (WTA, Schedule, Part II; Schedule, Rule 5). 
If the 
corporation shows a net loss before deduction of additional depreciation 
allowances, unabsorbed depreciation allowances’ carried forward from 
past years (7/3.7), development rebate (10/6.4), or loss carry-over 
(7/4.2), the rate of tax on net wealth for that year is zero; if the cor- 
poration’s income before such deductions is less than the amount of 
wealth tax payable for the year, the wealth tax is reduced to the amount 
of the income before the deductions. 
Neither of the above adjustments 
are made if the corporation pays a dividend on “equity capital” for the 
year in question. 
The term “equity capital,” which is not defined, would 
presumably include common or participating preferred stock, but not 
limited preferred. 
14/8. 
Administration and Procedure 
14/8.1 
In General 
In general, administration and procedure under the Wealth-tax Act 
closely parallel administration and procedure under the Income-tax Act. 
The income tax authorities serve also as wealth tax authorities: Income- 
tax Officers serve as Wealth-tax Officers (WTA § 8); Commissioners of 
Income-tax and Appellate Assistant Commissioners of Income-tax are 
respectively Commissioners of Wealth-tax and Appellate Assistant Com- 
missioners of Wealth-tax (WTA §§ 9, 10).31_ 
Commissioners of Wealth- 
tax are authorized to appoint Inspecting Assistant Commissioners (WTA

§ 11). 
The body which serves as Appellate Tribunal in cases arising 
under the income tax performs a similar function under the wealth tax 
(WTA § 2(b) ) (1/86). 
14/8.2 
Returns, Assessment, and Collection 
Persons subject to tax are under an obligation to file a voluntary return 
before 30 June of each tax year without notice from the authorities 
(WTA § 14(1)). 
In addition, the authorities may notify a taxpayer that 
within a period of not less than 30 days he must file a return of net 
wealth as of a valuation date specified in the notice (WTA § 14(2)). 
Wealth-tax Officers are empowered to grant extensions of time for the 
filing of returns (WTA § 14(3)). 
Assessment is made by the Wealth-tax 
Officer, who is empowered in appropriate cases to make estimated assess- 
ments (WTA §16). 
After making an assessment the Officer serves a 
notice of demand on the taxpayer specifying the sum payable and the 
time within which it should be paid (WTA § 30). 
No information 
returns are regularly required to be filed, but the Wealth-tax Officer is 
empowered to demand from any person statements or information on 
specified points relating to the possible liability of other persons (WTA 
§ 88). 
The provisions regarding the collection of delinquent income 
taxes, interest, and penalties are extended to the collection of delinquent 
wealth taxes, interest, and penalties (WTA § 32)(18/1.6). 
If a Wealth-tax Officer has reason to believe that any part of the tax- 
payers net wealth has escaped assessment for any year, whether by 
under-assessment or by assessment at too low a rate, he may reassess the 
tax at any time within eight years after the tax year if the taxpayer omit- 
ted to file a return or failed to disclose fully the facts necessary for an 
assessment, or at any time within four years after the tax year if there 
was no such omission or failure (WTA § 17). 
Other provisions, including those concerning the review of returns 
(WTA § 16)(13/2) and penalties (WTA §§ 18, 36)(18/7) are similar 
to comparable provisions of the income tax. 
There is no provision com- 
parable to the refund provisions of the income tax (13/5). 
14/8.3 
Appeals 
Appeals may be taken from decisions of a Wealth-tax Officer to an 
Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Wealth-tax (WTA § 23). Decisions 
of an Appellate Assistant Commissioner may be appealed to the Appel- 
late Tribunal by either the taxpayer or the Wealth-tax Officer (WTA 
§ 24). 
Revision of an order of a Wealth-tax Officer or of an Appellate 
Assistant Commissioner may be made in favor of a taxpayer by a Com- 
missioner of Wealth-tax in cases in which, because of the lapse of time or 
for other reasons, an appeal cannot be taken to an Appellate Assistant

Valuation Disputes 
Special provision is made regarding disputes as to valuation where an 
appeal has been taken to the Appellate Tribunal. 
An appellant before 
that Tribunal may claim a reference to arbitration by two valuers, one 
to be named by the appellant and the other by the respondent. 
A deci- 
sion agreed upon by these two valuers is final and must be accepted by 
the Tribunal. 
If the valuers differ in opinion the parties, or the Appellate 
Tribunal in case of their failure to agree, name a third valuer whose 
decision is final (WTA §§ 24(6), 24(8)). 
Valuers must be named from 
among the persons appointed as valuers for purposes of estate tax (WTA

Registration of Gifts or Transfers of Real Property 
Under Indian law, instruments of gift of real property and nontesta- 
mentary instruments relating to transfer of real property or rights therein 
exceeding Rs 100 in value are not effective unless registered.** 
Transfers 
of nonagricultural property valued at more than Rs 100,000 may not be 
registered without a certificate of a Wealth-tax Officer permitting such 
registration (WTA § 
34). 
14/8.6 
International Aspects 
Assessment for wealth tax, like assessment for income tax (11/3.4), 
may be made against a person who is considered an agent of a taxpayer 
who “resides outside India” (WTA § 22). Any person employed by or 
on behalf of such a taxpayer or through whom such taxpayer is in receipt 
of any income, profits, or gains or who is in possession of or has custody 
of any assets of such a taxpayer is considered an agent for this purpose. 
The Wealth-tax Officer must serve such a person with a notice of inten- 
tion to treat him as an agent. 
The person considered an agent is liable 
for tax to the extent of assets of the taxpayer which are in his hands at the 
time a notice of demand is served on him. A notice of demand is served 
when a tax has been assessed (WTA § 80).

Administration and Procedure 
15/1. 
Introduction 
A tax on personal expenditure has been in effect in India since 1 April 
1958.1 
The enactment of an expenditure tax was among the proposals 
for an integrated direct tax system which were made in a study conducted 
at the request of the Indian government by Nicholas Kaldor of Cam- 
bridge University. The tax as enacted differs substantially from Kaldor’s 
proposal. 
1 The Expenditure-tax Act of 1957 (cited herein as ETA) was introduced in 
the lower house of the Indian Parliament on 15 May 1957 (Gaz. of India, Extra., 
Pt. II, Sec. 2, No. 8, 15 May 1957, p. 187). 
It was reported favorably, with amend- 
ments, by a Select Committee (Gaz. of India, Extra., Pt. II, Sec. 2, No. 27A, 26 
August 1957) and was enacted on 17 September 1957. 
The first returns, relating to 
base years commencing on 1 April 1957, were due on 30 June 1958 (ETA § 8(1)). 
2 Kaldor, Indian Tax Reform, Report of a Survey 40-47. 
See also Kaldor, An 
Expenditure Tax. 
In his report to the Indian government, Kaldor suggested that 
under the proper conditions an expenditure tax would provide a better measure of 
taxable capacity and more incentive for savings than an income tax, and that as part 
of an integrated system an expenditure tax could contribute 
to a more effective 
administration of all direct taxes (1/8.1). 
The idea of an expenditure tax has long 
been discussed by economists, including John Stuart Mill, Alfred Marshall, and Irving 
Fisher. 
An expenditure tax was proposed by the United States Treasury Department 
to the Senate Finance Committee in 1942 as a principal means of wartime taxation 
and inflation control, but was summarily rejected by that committee as unworkable. 
See Paul, Taxation in the United States 291-294, 312. 
India was the first country 
to enact such a measure; but in 1959 Ceylon adopted an integrated tax system, 
including an expenditure tax, based on proposals made by Kaldor in a report to the 
government of Ceylon.

EXPENDITURE 
TAX 
The tax is levied annually on expenditure incurred (15/3.1) by individ- 
uals and Hindu undivided families during a base year (15/3.2). 
It is 
based upon world-wide expenditure, expenditure within India, or expend- 
iture within India and expenditure outside India from Indian sources, 
according to the residence and citizenship status of the taxpayer (15/2). 
Expenditure above a standard allowance, generally Rs 30,000 (15/ 5.2a), 
is taxed at sharply progressive rates (15/5.4). 
The basic intent of the 
Act is to tax expenditure, exceeding the standard allowance, which is in 
the nature of personal consumption. Expenditure for expenses of busi- 
ness or employment, investments, capital outlays for personal use, and 
gifts are therefore exempt. 
In addition, certain expenditures which do 
represent personal consumption 
are exempted 
as basic living costs 
(15/3.6). 
15/2. 
Classes of Taxpayers 
15/2.1 
Persons Subject to Tax 
a. INDIvipuats. 
Liability of an individual to the expenditure tax depends 
on his status as ordinarily resident, resident but not ordinarily resident, or 
not resident, and also on his citizenship status.*? 
Residence during the 
assessment year is determined in accordance with the standards applied 
under the Income-tax Act 
(ETA § 5(0), Explanation) (5/1.2).4 
There are three classifications of liability to tax on domestic and foreign 
expenditure. 
1. Citizens who are ordinarily resident are taxable on world-wide expenditure 
regardless of the source of the funds from which the expenditure is made 
(ETA §3(1)). 
2. Citizens who are either resident but not ordinarily resident or not resident, 
and aliens who are either resident or ordinarily resident,® are taxed on 
expenditure in India regardless of source, and on expenditure outside 
India which is not made from income or capital accrued or realized out- 
side India (ETA §§ 8(1), 5(0)). 
3. Aliens who are not resident are taxed only on expenditure in India, but 
regardless of source (ETA §§ 3(1), 5(0)). 
3 The basic principles governing citizenship are to be found in articles 5 through 
11 of the Constitution of India and in the Citizenship Act of 1955. 
4Since 12 April 1954, the “taxable territories” to which these standards apply 
have included the state of Jammu and Kashmir (11/1.1), whereas the Expenditure- 
tax Act states that it “extends to the whole of India except the state of Jammu and 
Kashmir” (ETA §1(1)). 
It seems likely that the state of Jammu and Kashmir would 
not be considered 
a part of India in determining residence for expenditure tax 
purposes or in determining whether income or capital has been accrued or realized 
outside India. 
On the other hand, the exclusion of the state of Jammu and Kashmir 
from the territorial application of the Act probably would not affect the determination 
of citizenship status. 
5 Aliens are granted a special additional allowance of Rs 10,000 for expenditure 
outside India which would otherwise be subject to tax (15/5.2c).

b. MARRIED PERSONS, MINORS, AND INCAPACITATED PERSONS. 
Each spouse 
is taxed separately on expenditure incurred by him for his own benefit 
and out of his separate funds. 
However, an individual is subject to tax 
on expenditure incurred by him on behalf of his dependents, and also on 
expenditure incurred by his dependents (15/3.3, item 2). A spouse is 
also subject to tax on expenditure made on his behalf, or on behalf of his 
dependents, by the other spouse (15/3.3, item 3). 
No provision comparable to that under the income and wealth taxes 
(5/1.4, 14/2.1b) is made concerning the taxation of guardians or trustees 
for minors or incapacitated persons. 
Expenditure by a guardian or 
trustee on behalf of his ward would not be taxable to the guardian or 
trustee (15/3.6a), but might be attributed to the ward (ETA § 4(#)) 
(15/3.8). 
15/2.2 
Corporations 
Corporations are not subject to the expenditure tax (ETA § 3(1)). 
15/2.3 
Other Taxpayers 
a. HINDU UNDIVIDED FAMILIES. 
The liability of a Hindu undivided family 
to the expenditure tax depends on its residence status during the assess- 
ment year as determined by the standards applicable under the Income- 
tax Act (ETA §$5(0), Explanation) (5/8.2). 
Hindu undivided families 
which are ordinarily resident 
are taxed on world-wide 
expenditure 
regardless of the source of the funds from which the expenditure is made 
(ETA § 3(1)). 
Hindu undivided families which are either resident but 
not ordinarily resident or not resident are taxed on expenditure in India 
regardless of source, and on expenditure outside India which is made 
from income or capital accrued or realized in India (ETA 8§ 3(1), 5(o)). 
b. TRUSTS AND DECEDENTS ESTATES. 
No provision is made regarding the 
taxation of trusts or trustees. 
Expenditure by a trustee on behalf of a 
beneficiary would not be taxable to the trustee (15/3.6a), but might be 
attributed to the beneficiary (15/3.3). 
As under the income (5/3.8) and 
wealth taxes (14/2.3b), the executor, administrator, or other legal repre- 
sentative of a deceased person is liable to pay out of the estate of the 
deceased any expenditure tax which is payable by the deceased or which 
would have been payable by him if he had not died (ETA § 18(1)). 
As in the case of a trustee, expenditure by a legal representative would 
not be taxed to him (15/3.6a), but might be attributed to a beneficiary 
of the estate (15/3.3). 
C. PARTNERSHIPS, ASSOCIATIONS, AND LOCAL AUTHORITIES. 
Partnerships, 
associations, and local authorities are not subject to the expenditure tax 
(ETA §3(1)).

15/2.4 
Exempt Taxpayers 
Any taxpayer is exempt from the expenditure tax for any base year in 
which “income from all sources derived by him and his dependents,” 
after deduction of certain taxes, does not exceed Rs 36,000 (ETA § 3(1), 
Proviso).° 
“Income from all sources” may be assumed to include agri- 
cultural income or other income exempt from income tax, foreign income, 
and capital gains and other nonrecurring receipts. 
It also includes 
income which a trustee or any other person receives or is entitled to 
receive on behalf of the taxpayer or any of his dependents, as well as 
any sum in money or money's worth expended on behalf of the taxpayer 
or his dependents out of the income or property of a Hindu undivided 
family or association of persons of which the taxpayer is a member 
(ETA § 3(1), Explanation). 
In determining whether income exceeds Rs 36,000, total income is to 
be reduced by “the amount of taxes to which such income may be liable 
under any other law for the time being in force.” 
Only Indian taxes are 
included in this reduction. 
15/2.5 
Rulers of Indian States 
Former rulers of Indian States are not exempted but are treated spe- 
cially. 
Expenditure out of the privy purse of such a ruler for the com- 
pensation of his staff and the maintenance of his official residence is 
generally exempt (ETA §$5(q)). 
In addition, the Central Government 
is authorized to make special settlements concerning the expenditure tax 
payable by such rulers (ETA § 20). 
15/3. 
Taxable Expenditure 
15/3.1 
“Expenditure Incurred" 
“Expenditure” is defined as “any sum in money or money's worth, 
spent or disbursed or for the spending or disbursing of which a liability 
has been incurred” (ETA §2(h)). 
Amounts which are included in 
expenditure for any year in which liability is incurred but not satisfied 
are excluded from expenditure for any later year in which the liability 
is satisfied (ETA § 3(2)). 
In effect, expenditure is taxed when paid or 
accrued, whichever occurs first. Expenditure paid or accrued is referred 
to in the Act and hereinafter as “expenditure incurred.” 
15/3.2 
Tax Year and Base Year 
The expenditure tax is levied for each tax year (“financial year”) on 
expenditure incurred by the taxpayer during the base year (“previous

The tax year and base year are the same as for 
income tax purposes (6/3.1, 6/3.2), except that where, for purposes of 
the income tax, the taxpayer employs or is required to employ different 
base years for different sources of income, the base year for expenditure 
tax purposes is the year which expires last (ETA § 2(n)). 
If the tax- 
payer has a source of income for which there is no base year under the 
Income-tax Act, the base year for expenditure tax purposes is the year 
ending 31 March immediately preceding the tax year (ETA § 2(n)). 
Once an assessment has been made on the basis of expenditure in a par- 
ticular base year, the corresponding period must be taken as the base 
year in subsequent assessments unless the Expenditure-tax Officer grants 
permission for a change (ETA § 2(n)). 
15/3.3 
Attribution Rules 
The following expenditures incurred by persons other than the tax- 
payer are treated as incurred by him (ETA § 4): 
1. Expenditure incurred by other persons in satisfaction of any obligation or 
personal requirement of the taxpayer or any of his dependents, to the 
extent to which the aggregate of expenditure by other persons exceeds 
Rs 5,000 in the base year (ETA § 4(i) ).7 
2. Expenditures “wholly and necessarily in connection with the discharge 
(ETA § 4(ii)).8 
8. If the taxpayer is a Hindu undivided family, any expenditure incurred 
by a dependent of the family out of any income or property transferred 
directly or indirectly to the dependent by the taxpayer (ETA § 4(ii)). 
There is no attribution of expenditure which is by way of customary 
hospitality or of a trivial or inconsequential nature (ETA § 4, Explana- 
tion). 
In the case of an individual taxpayer, a dependent is defined as a 
spouse, a minor child, or any person wholly or mainly dependent on him 
for support and maintenance (ETA §2(g)). 
In the case of a Hindu 
undivided family, a dependent is defined as any coparcener, other than 
the manager, or any other member who is by law entitled to maintenance 
from the joint family property (ETA § 2(g)). 
There is no express indi- 
cation that amounts treated as expenditure of the taxpayer under these 
provisions may not also be treated as expenditure of the persons who 
actually incur them.

Because of constitutional prohibitions

2. Expenditures “wholly and necessarily in connection with the discharge 
of any duties assigned” by the central government or a state government 
(ETA § 5(c)).

b. INVESTMENT EXPENDITURE. 
Capital expenditure wholly and exclusively 
for the purpose of the taxpayer’s business is exempt from expenditure

15/6. 
Administration and Procedure 
Administration and procedure under the Expenditure-tax Act, as under 
the Wealth-tax Act (14/8), closely parallel administration and procedure 
under the Income-tax Act (1/8, 13/1-13/7). 
Income-tax Officers are 
ex officio Expenditure-tax Officers (ETA §7). 
The Central Board of 
Revenue is empowered to appoint Commissioners of Expenditure-tax 
and Appellate Assistant Commissioners of Expenditure-tax (ETA §§ 8, 9). 
Commissioners of Expenditure-tax are in turn authorized 
to appoint 
Inspecting Assistant Commissioners (ETA § 10). 
Persons subject to tax are required to file returns before 30 June of 
each tax year (ETA $13(1)). 
In addition, the Expenditure-tax Officer 
may notify a taxpayer that he must file a return (ETA § 13(2)). 
Assess- 
ment is made by the Expenditure-tax Officer, who is empowered to make 
estimated assessments in appropriate cases (ETA $15). 
After making 
an assessment, the officer serves on the taxpayer a notice of demand for 
payment (ETA § 28). 
Delinquent taxes may be collected by the same 
means as are available for purposes of the income and wealth taxes 
(ETA § 30)(18/1.6). 
No information returns are regularly required to 
be filed, but the Expenditure-tax Officer may require any person to give 
information relating to the liability of other persons (ETA § 34). Other

16/1. 
Tax Jurisdiction 
16/1.1 
Introduction 
This chapter contains a general description of the sales and purchase 
taxes of the various states of India and a more detailed analysis of the 
Central Sales Tax Act, which applies to interstate sales. 
A sales tax on motor fuel and lubricants was levied in Madhya Pradesh 
in 1938, but the first general sales tax was introduced in Madras in 1939. 
Prior to 1956 each Part A state and each Part B state except Jammu and 
Kashmir (1/1.2) had a sales tax. 
Since the states were reorganized in 
1956 most of the states have recodified their sales tax laws and extended 
them to newly acquired territory. The sales tax acts of neighboring states 
are applied in some of the Union territories. 
In addition to its sales tax 
act, each state has issued regulations, notifications, and press notes 
governing both substantive and procedural matters. 
Numerous decisions 
on sales tax matters have been made by the High Courts of the various 
states. 
The various taxes differ widely in their incidence and operation. 
In 
each system the most important characteristic is the point or points 
between production and retail sale to a consumer at which the tax is 
imposed 
(16/8.1), 
since this affects the qualifications 
of taxpayers 
(16/2), the classes of goods subjected to tax (16/4.1), rates of tax 
(16/4.2), and the method of administration (16/7). 
The evolution and 
character of the sales tax system in each state has been conditioned by 
its local economy and financial needs. 
In broad terms, states which have 
enjoyed a substantial urban trade and significant industrial and manu- 
facturing activities have tended to adopt a single-point tax imposed at 
only one point between production of goods and their sale to a consumer 
and on a limited group of dealers. 
In these states, a relatively high rate 
of tax is imposed on taxable sales and a large number of essential goods 
and basic raw materials are usually exempt. 
The incidence of a single- 
point tax is closely controlled, in keeping with the urban and largely 
commercial economy in which it operates. 
States with predominantly 
rural economies, on the other hand, have generally adopted multi-point 
sales taxes, imposed on every sale between production of the goods and 
their sale to the ultimate consumer. 
Since the incidence of such taxes 
is not controlled, the rates are relatively low, the exemptions from tax 
are few, and many dealers are subject to the tax. 
Changes in the econo- 
mies of some states, in their revenue needs, or in their revenue structures, 
or the prevalence of tax evasion, have prompted many states to adopt 
mixed features of both the single-point and multi-point sales taxes and 
to add novel features such as the purchase tax. 
1 For discussion of the operation of the various types of sales taxes, see 3 Report 
of the Taxation Enquiry Commission, 1953-54 1-33, 141-162.

16/1.1 
437 
SALES 
AND 
PURCHASE 
TAXES 
The Constitution, as adopted in 1950, gave the states exclusive power 
to impose taxes on the sales of all commodities except newspapers? but 
precluded any state from taxing any sale or purchase taking place either 
outside the state or in the course of the import or export of goods into or 
out of India; it also precluded the states, except as authorized by Parlia- 
ment, from imposing a tax on any sale or purchase taking place in the 
course of interstate trade or commerce.* 
The Constitution also required 
the assent of the President for the taxation by a state of sales or purchases 
of any goods which might be declared by Parliament to be “essential 
for the life of the community.” + 
As a result of their constitutional disability to tax sales in the course 
of interstate trade, the states lost considerable revenue which they had 
formerly received in taxes collected from dealers in their own territories 
on sales made to buyers in other states. 
However, the Constitution 
contained a provision that a sale or purchase should be deemed to have 
taken place in the state in which, as a direct result of the sale or purchase, 
the goods had actually been delivered for the purpose of consumption.® 
Under this provision the Supreme Court upheld the application to sales 
of goods in interstate commerce of a state law imposing tax on any sale 
under which the goods were delivered in the state for purposes of con- 
sumption, even though Parliament had not authorized the taxation of 
interstate sales by the states. 
The Supreme Court later reversed this 
decision and held that the provision referred to above did not empower 
the states to tax sales in the course of interstate commerce in the absence 
of authorization by Parliament.’ 
Parliament thereafter validated existing 
state laws as they applied to interstate sales. 
The difficulties regarding taxation of interstate sales resulted in the 
passage of the Constitution (Sixth Amendment) Act of 1956, which gave 
the Parliament exclusive power to tax sales in interstate trade, but re- 
quired the assignment of the proceeds to the states in which the taxes 
were levied. 
The amendments made by that Act also authorized the 
Parliament to formulate principles for determining when a sale takes 
place outside a state or in the course of export or import, and to restrict 
the taxation by the states of sales of goods which should be declared by 
Parliament to be of special importance to interstate commerce. 
The 
original provision restricting the power of the states to tax sales or

The Central Sales Tax Act determines which state has jurisdiction over 
an interstate transaction (16/1.3). 
If the transaction is taxable as an 
interstate sale of goods under the Central Sales Tax Act (16/3.2), the 
state having jurisdiction assesses and collects the tax, unless it exempts

The state applies the rates prescribed by the Central Sales Tax Act; 
special rates are applicable to sales to governments, sales to registered 
dealers (16/4.2), and sales of goods declared to be of special importance 
to interstate commerce (16/4.3). 
It collects the tax on behalf of the 
central government, using its own administrative machinery and pro-

ment under the Central Sales Tax Act (CSTA § 9(3) ) (16/7). Taxes and 
penalties collected are retained by the state; collections attributable to 
Union Territories become part of the Consolidated Fund of India 
(CSTA §9(4)).

Intrastate Sales 
The Constitution gives each state exclusive power to tax sales or 
purchases of goods, except newspapers, within the state.1° 
It also pro- 
hibits any state from taxing the sale or purchase of goods outside that 
state, and under the 1956 amendments authorizes the central government 
to formulate principles for determining when a sale or purchase of goods 
takes place outside a state.11 
The Central Sales Tax Act sets forth 
principles for determining whether a sale or purchase of goods takes 
place inside a state and further provides that a sale or purchase which 
has been found under these principles to take place inside one state must

SALES AND PURCHASE TAXES 
be deemed to have taken place outside all other states (CSTA § 4). The 
net effect of these provisions is outlined below. 
1. A sale or purchase of specific or ascertained goods may be taxed only by 
the state in which the goods are located when the contract of sale is made. 
2. A sale of unascertained or future goods may be taxed only by the state 
in which the goods are located when they are appropriated to the con- 
tract by either party with the consent, whether before or after the 
appropriation, of the other. 
Under these principles, when goods located in different states are 
sold under a single contract, each state involved may tax only the 
transfer of those goods which are within its borders at the critical time 
(CSTA § 4(2), Explanation). 
The principles provided under the Cen- 
tral Sales Tax Act for determining when a sale takes place in a state 
merely define the scope of the state’s disability to tax sales or purchases 
outside its borders; they do not confer on the states any jurisdiction to 
tax interstate transactions (CSTA § 4(1)). 
16/1.3 
Interstate Sales 
As a result of the 1956 amendments, the Constitution gives the central 
government exclusive power to impose taxes on the sale or purchase of 
goods in the course of interstate trade or commerce,'? but requires that 
the proceeds of the taxes be assigned and distributed to the states in 
which they are levied.* 
Parliament is also authorized to formulate 
principles for determining when a sale or purchase of goods takes place 
in the course of interstate trade or commerce.'+ 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act, the following transactions are deemed 
to take place in the course of interstate trade or commerce (CSTA § 3). 
1. A sale or purchase of goods which occasions the movement of the goods 
from one state to another is deemed to take place in the course of inter- 
state trade, unless the movement of the goods commences and terminates 
in the same state and the goods merely pass through another state in the 
course of transport. 
Delivery of goods located in the seller’s state to a 
buyer or his agent in the same state is not an interstate sale even if the 
buyer immediately thereafter ships the goods to another state, since the 
subsequent shipment is on behalf of the buyer and is not occasioned by 
the sale. 
However, an interstate sale takes place if the seller under a 
contract of sale ships the goods to a buyer in another state by common 
carrier. 
2. A sale or purchase of goods which is effected by a transfer of documents 
of title to the goods during their movement from one state to another is 
deemed to take place in the course of interstate trade. 
The movement 
of the goods for this purpose begins when they are delivered to a carrier

16/1.4 
Goods Declared to be of Special Importance to Interstate Trade 
The Constitution authorizes Parliament 
to impose restrictions 
and 
conditions on the taxation by the states of sales or purchases, whether 
or not in interstate commerce, of goods declared by Parliament to be 
of special importance in interstate trade or commerce.!® 
The Central 
Sales Tax Act lists certain raw materials which are declared to be of 
special importance for interstate trade (16/4.3), restricts taxes on sales of 
these commodities to a single-point levy at a special rate, and requires that 
any tax paid on a sale of any of these commodities in a state be refunded 
if the goods are subsequently sold in the course of interstate commerce 
(CSTA § 15). 
16/2. 
Persons Subject to Tax 
Although the central and state sales taxes are intended to be borne 
by the ultimate consumer of taxable goods, the taxes are imposed on and 
collected from registered dealers (16/7.2), and only a registered dealer 
is entitled to collect the tax payable by him from a purchaser (CSTA 
§9-A). 
A person who carries on the business of buying or selling goods 
qualifies as a “dealer” under the Central Sales Tax Act (CSTA § 2(b)); 
the definitions of “dealer” under the state acts are similar. 
The term 
comprehends individuals, corporations, partnerships, Hindu undivided 
families, and other organizations which carry on the business of buying 
or selling goods, whether as manufacturers, as wholesalers, or as retailers. 
The central government and state or local governments which carry on” 
the business of buying or selling goods are treated as dealers and are 
liable to tax under the Central Sales Tax Act (CSTA §2(b)), but some 
of the state sales tax acts do not treat governmental entities as dealers

Whether casual purchases and 
sales, or sales in the course of liquidating a business, may be considered 
as amounting to the carrying on of a business depends on the facts of 
each particular case. 
Some of the states impose sales tax liability for intrastate sales only 
on dealers whose annual gross receipts (“turnover”) exceed prescribed 
limits. 
Limits for wholesalers and retailers under single-point systems 
(Rs 50,000 in West Bengal) are generally higher than under multi-point 
systems (Rs 7,500 in Madras), in which the taxes are smaller but are 
applied to each transfer of goods from production to consumption. 
A 
few states prescribe limits for importers and manufacturers which are 
lower than the general limits for wholesalers and retailers. 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act every dealer is required to pay tax 
on his interstate sales regardless of his annual turnover (CSTA § 6(1)). 
A dealer is liable to tax on his interstate sales even if, under the law of 
the state having jurisdiction over the sale (16/1.3), he is not required 
to pay tax on his sales within the state (16/3.3). 
16/3. 
Taxable Event 
16/3.1 
In General 
Sales tax laws which exempt sales to registered dealers, as in West 
Bengal and Bihar, result in the imposition of single-point sales taxes at 
the retail level. 
In Andhra Pradesh, the point at which tax is imposed 
is specified in the rate schedule. 
Kerala, Madras, Mysore, and Uttar 
Pradesh restrict the imposition of their sales taxes on sales of certain 
goods to a single point, although for most goods the taxes are multi-point 
taxes. 
In some states, single-point purchase taxes are imposed when 
goods are first purchased by registered dealers from unregistered persons, 
and such a tax may be combined with a single-point retail sales tax in 
a double-point system, as in Bombay. 
In some states, appropriation of 
goods by a registered dealer for his own use is treated as a sale for tax 
purposes. 
Under the state acts, no tax is imposed on sales by dealers whose 
annual turnover is below prescribed limits (16/2). 
A tax imposed on 
the sale within a state of goods declared by Parliament to be of special 
importance for interstate commerce is refunded if the goods are later 
the subject of an interstate sale (16/4.3). 
Import sales and export sales 
are taxed neither by the central government nor by the states (16/6). 
16/3.2 
Sale of Goods 
Under the state acts and under the Central Sales Tax Act (CSTA 
§ 
2(g)), a sale is defined as a transfer of property in goods for a valuable 
consideration (except under a mortgage or pledge) including installment

Although the 
transfer of property in goods in the course of execution of a contract for 
services is expressly included under some of the state acts, the definition 
of a sale appears broad enough to cover such a transfer even in the 
absence of an express provision. 
In some states, a requirement that 
the consideration paid for the goods be in money excludes barter and 
exchange transfers from liability to tax. 
In general, tax is not imposed 
on casual sales not in the course of the dealer’s business as described in 
his certificate of registration. 
If goods delivered on approval or subject to other conditions are 
returned, no sale takes place, and no tax is payable either on the refunded 
sales price or on any part of the price retained by the seller as damages 
under the terms of the contract. 
If goods are returned otherwise than 
under a contract provision, however, the sale is exempt from tax only 
if the goods were returned within three months from the date of delivery 
to the buyer.'®6 
The burden of proving the return of the goods and the 
refund of the sales price is on the taxpayer. 
16/3.3 
Interstate Sales 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act, any sale (16/3.2) by a registered 
dealer in the course of interstate trade or commerce (16/1.3) is a taxable 
event whether or not the buyer is a registered dealer (CSTA § 6(1)). 
A sale to a registered dealer, however, is taxed at a lower rate than a sale 
to a consumer or other unregistered person (16/4.2). 
Liability to tax 
is not affected by the fact that the state which will impose it (16/1.3) 
would not have taxed an intrastate sale of similar goods by a registered 
dealer, unless any sale of goods of that class would have been exempt 
from the state tax (CSTA § 8(2A)). 
The tax is therefore essentially 
a multi-point levy, and can be imposed on each interstate sale in which 
particular goods are involved regardless of the stage or stages at which 
the state having jurisdiction taxes intrastate sales of similar goods. 
How- 
ever, where a taxable sale has taken place (16/3.2), a further sale of 
the same goods by transfer of documents of title during the same move- 
ment in interstate commerce is exempt from tax if (1) the sale is made 
to a registered dealer, (2) the goods are specified in his certificate of 
registration as intended for resale by him or for use by him in the manu- 
facture or processing of goods for sale, in mining, or in the generation 
or distribution of any form of power, and (8) the seller furnishes a

If the second sale is not exempt under this provision, 
tax may be imposed only by the state having jurisdiction over the dealer 
who makes the second sale (16/13).

16/4. 
Taxable Goods and Rates of Tax 
16/4.1 
Taxable Goods 
In general, the state taxes apply to sales of all kinds of tangible mov- 
able property; they do not apply to sales of real property or to sales of 
intangibles such as actionable claims or securities. 
The states have no 
authority to tax sales of newspapers 
(16/1.2), and newspapers 
are 
excluded from the definition of taxable goods under the Central Sales 
Tax Act (CSTA §2(d)). 
Intrastate sales of goods which have been 
declared by Parliament to be of special importance to interstate trade 
are subject to special treatment (16/4.3). A contract for the application 
of human labor and skill, as in the painting of a portrait, the repair or 
reconditioning of a customer’s property, the taking of X-rays by a doctor, 
or the preparation of etchings for a customer, is not a contract for the 
sale of goods. 
If the contract involves both remuneration for labor and 
a sale of movable property, tax may be imposed on that part of the price 
which is allocable to the sale of the property (16/3.2). 
In some states, 
the sales taxes are applied to sales of growing crops, grass, and trees 
which are to be severed from the property under the sales agreement. 
Various classes of goods are exempted, either by law or state govern- 
ment notification, from the state sales taxes. 
In general, states which 
impose single-point taxes exempt the necessaries of life and raw ma- 
terials. 
Since most of the essential goods do not change hands fre- 
quently between production and consumption, the total burden on them 
resulting from the low rates of tax at each stage under multi-point sales 
taxes is low, and the need for exemptions, which are always difficult to 
administer, is therefore less. 
Exemptions of sales of certain goods at 
specified stages under a multi-point system, however, may be used to 
effect concessional 
rates of tax 
(16/4.2). 
The exemptions 
granted 
under the various state laws may be classified as listed below. 
1. Necessaries or “essential” goods: goods purchased frequently and neces- 
sary to sustain life or goods for carrying on industrial processes, such as 
food, medicine, matches, inexpensive textiles, and agricultural or indus- 
trial raw materials. 
2. Goods subject to high taxes under other laws of the state or central 
governments, such as fuel oil, electricity, and tobacco, which are subject 
to excise taxes (17/4.1). 
3. Goods produced by small scale (cottage or village) industries, such as 
handmade textile fabrics and paper. 
The Central Sales Tax Act applies to all sales of tangible movable 
property except newspapers. 
Sales of actionable claims, stocks, shares, 
and securities are expressly excluded (CSTA § 2(d)). 
Goods exempted 
by a state are also exempt under the Central Sales Tax Act, provided the 
state exemption applies to all sales of such goods, to whomever made

and at any stage (CSTA § 8(2A)). 
Where the public interest requires, 
a state may also by notification exempt interstate sales of any classes of 
goods which are sold by dealers from places of business within the 
state (CSTA § 8(5)). 
16/4.2 
Rates of Tax 
The rates at which the state sales taxes are imposed range from less 
than 1% to more than 14%, depending on whether the tax is a single- 
point or a multi-point tax and depending on the goods sold. 
The rates 
applicable to each sale under single-point systems are generally higher 
than under multi-point systems, although the total of the taxes imposed 
from producer to consumer under a multi-point system may be as high 
as the tax under a single-point system. 
Some states grant concessional 
rates to sales of certain types of goods, which other states exempt from 
tax entirely (16/4.1). 
On the other hand, luxury goods, such as auto- 
mobiles, radios and other electric appliances, watches, furniture, arms, 
and cosmetics, are often taxed at higher rates than other goods. 
Under 
some multi-point systems, concessions may be granted to certain types 
of goods by taxing them only at one stage of sale. 
The Central Sales 
Tax Act prescribes special rates for sales within a state of goods declared 
by Parliament to be of particular impertance for interstate trade or 
commerce (16/4.3). 
The rates of tax on interstate sales are provided by the Central Sales 
Tax Act. 
For sales of goods other than those which have been declared 
by Parliament to be of special importance to interstate trade or commerce 
(16/4.3), the standard rate of tax is either 7% of the sales price, or the 
rate applicable to sales of similar goods in the state which has jurisdiction 
over the sale, whichever is higher (CSTA § 8(2)). 
In computing the 
applicable state rate, the fact that the seller would not have been liable 
to tax on the sale had it taken place within the state is disregarded. 
A special rate of 1% of the sales price, conditioiu.ed on the taxpayer’s 
filing a prescribed declaration (16/7.3), is provided for the categories 
of sales listed below (CSTA §§8(1), 8(3)). 
1. Sales to the government. 
2. Sales to a registered dealer of goods specified in the buyer’s certificate of 
registration as intended for resale by him. 
3. Sales to a registered dealer of goods specified in the buyer’s certificate of 
registration as intended for use by him in the manufacture or processing 
of goods for sale, in mining, or in the generation or distribution of any 
form of power, subject to rules made by the Central Government. 
The 
commodities which have been listed as qualifying for the special rates 
under this provision are goods intended for use as raw materials, process- 
ing materials, machinery, plant, equipment, tools, stores, spare parts, 
accessories, fuel, and lubricants.17

This provision, analogous to

is designed to extend concessional rates granted by state law for sales 
of certain classes of goods to interstate sales of those goods. 
When the public interest requires, a state government may by notifica-

sold by dealers from a place of business within the state (CSTA § 8(5)). 
16/4.3 
“Declared Goods" 
Pursuant to the constitutional authority of Parliament to impose re- 
strictions and conditions on the taxation by the states of sales or purchases 
of goods declared to be of special importance in interstate trade or com- 
merce (16/1.4), the Central Sales Tax Act lists certain raw materials 
which may be subjected to tax by the states only at a single point and 
at a special rate, and requires that sales taxes paid on sales of these 
commodities be refunded if the goods are subsequently sold in the 
course of interstate commerce. 
The “declared goods” to which the 
special treatment applies are cotton fabrics, cotton yarn, hides and skins, 
iron and steel, jute, oilseeds, rayon and other artificial fabrics, sugar, 
tobacco, woolen fabrics, and coal and coke (CSTA § 14).1§ 
The rate at which a state may tax an intrastate sale of “declared goods” 
may not exceed 2%, and a tax on sales of “declared goods” may not be 
levied at more than one stage (CSTA § 15(a)). 
Moreover, if the goods 
are thereafter sold in the course of interstate trade or commerce, any 
tax paid on the prior intrastate sale of the goods must be refunded to 
the seller who paid it (CSTA § 15(b)). 
Sales of “declared goods” in interstate trade or commerce are taxed 
at the special rate of 1% if they satisfy the conditions listed for other 
goods at 16/4.2. 
Sales which do not satisfy those conditions are taxed 
at the rate applicable to sales of similar goods in the state which has

16/5. 
Taxable Value 
The amount of sales tax liability is determined by applying the ap- 
plicable rate of tax (16/4.2, 16/4.3) to the “sales price” of the goods at 
the time of sale. 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act, the sales price of 
taxable goods is the amount paid or payable as consideration for the 
goods, reduced by any cash discounts allowed under normal practices 
of the trade (CSTA §2(h)). 
The sales price includes any sum charged 
for anything done by the dealer to the goods at or before delivery; 
freight, delivery, and installation 
costs are included unless they are 
charged separately. 
Damages received by the seller from the purchaser 
for breach of contract, or from a carrier for loss of goods during transit, 
are not included. 
Sales price under the state acts is determined in a similar manner. 
Some states have taken the position that since collection of the tax from 
the purchaser by the seller is not provided for in their sales tax acts, a 
dealer collecting the tax from a purchaser does so in his own behalf 
and must therefore include it in the sales price when computing the 
tax payable by him. 
16/6. 
International Aspects 
The Constitution prohibits any state from taxing the sale or purchase 
of goods in the course of import into India or export out of India.!® 
Under the 1956 amendments 
to the Constitution, 
the Parliament 
is 
authorized to formulate the principles for determining when a sale or 
purchase of goods takes place in the course of import or export.2° 
The 
Central Sales Tax Act provides that the following sales or purchases of 
goods shall be deemed to take place in the course of import or export 
and therefore may not be taxed by the state governments (CSTA §5). 
1. A sale or purchase of goods which occasions the import of goods into 
India or the export of goods out of India. 
Delivery of goods located in 
India to a buyer or his agent in India is not an export even if the buyer 
immediately thereafter ships the goods to another country, since the 
subsequent shipment is on behalf of the buyer and is not occasioned by 
the sale. 
However, an import or export takes place if the seller in India 
or a foreign country ships the goods to a buyer in the other country by 
common carrier. 
If a foreign buyer sells the goods in India without 
taking delivery, no export is deemed to have taken place,

16/7. 
Administration 
16/7.1 
In General 
The state sales taxes are administered by state departments established 
solely or principally for that purpose. 
In general, each department con- 
sists of a commissioner, his deputies, and tax officers, collectors, or 
inspectors. 
In most states, taxes are assessed by the tax officers or collec- 
tors, and the commissioners and their deputies serve appellate functions. 
In some states, the assessments are made and reviewed by the tax officers 
and collectors, subject to further review by administrative superiors and 
thereafter by appellate tribunals, boards of sales tax, or judges appointed 
specially for hearing appeals in sales tax cases. 
Under authority of their sales tax acts, the various states have issued 
rules governing the administration, and in some cases the substantive 
application, of their sales taxes. 
From time to time, the state govern- 
ments also issue notifications, usually published in their official state 
gazettes or journals, dealing with exemptions or rates of tax for various 
classes of goods. 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act, the tax on an interstate sale is 
assessed and collected by the state which has jurisdiction over the sale 
(16/1.3) in the same manner as its own sales taxes on intrastate sales 
(CSTA §$9(3)). 
The Central Government is empowered to make rules 
for the assessment and collection of tax in any state or part of a state 
in which there is no general sales tax law in force (CSTA §9(3), 
Proviso). 
The Central Government is also empowered to make rules 
governing registration, computation of turnover, forms of declarations 
and certificates, and fees payable for applications under the Central Sales 
Tax Act (CSTA § 13(1)). 
Under this authority the Central Government 
has issued the Central Sales Tax (Registration and Turnover) Rules, 
1957 2! and the Central Sales Tax (Union Territories) 
Rules, 1957.72 
Any rules made by the Central Government are subject to approval 
and modification by Parliament (CSTA §13(2)). 
The Central Sales 
Tax Act also authorizes the state governments to make rules, subject to 
the provisions of the Act and to rules made by the Central Government, 
for carrying out the purposes of the Act (CSTA §§ 18(3), 138(4)), and 
the various state governments have accordingly issued rules prescrib- 
ing the procedures to be followed by taxpayers and by the state tax 
authorities in the administration of their sales taxes as applied to inter- 
state sales.

16/7.2 
Registration 
Under the state sales tax laws, registration is required of all dealers 
whose annual gross receipts exceed the minimum limits established for 
tax liability (16/2). 
A manufacturer or dealer whose sales do not 
exceed the prescribed minimum may apply for registration. 
A manu- 
facturer who uses large quantities of taxable goods in his manufacturing 
process may find registration advantageous even when not required, 
since only registered dealers may pass the tax on to their purchasers, 
and since single-point taxes are imposed only when goods pass from a 
registered dealer to an unregistered person. 
In most states, no dealer 
liable for tax under the state sales tax law may carry on business unless 
he is registered. 
In order to minimize tax avoidance on the sale of certain 
goods, some states require special certification, in addition to registration, 
for dealers in those goods. 
Every dealer who is liable to tax on interstate sales under the Central 
Sales Tax Act is required to register in every state in which he has a 
place of business (CSTA §§2(a), 7(1)). 
“Place of business” includes 
a place where the dealer keeps his books of account, a warehouse or 
other place where he stores goods, and the place of business of any 
agent through whom he carries on business (CSTA § 2(dd)). 
A dealer 
who is not subject to tax under the Central Sales Tax Act may nonethe- 
less apply for registration under the Act to the authorities in any state 
in which he is subject to sales tax, or in any state in which he has a place 
of business if there.is no sales tax law in force in that state (CSTA 
§7(2)). 
Under the Central Sales Tax Act, a dealer liable for tax on interstate 
sales must apply for registration within 30 days after his first taxable 
sale; *8 a dealer who is not liable for tax may apply for registration at 
any time.** 
Application for registration must be made in each state in 
which the dealer maintains a place of business, but a single application 
will cover all of a dealer’s places of business in a single state.25 
The 
certificate of registration sets forth the nature of the dealer’s business and 
his accounting period, and lists his places of business. 
It also specifies 
the classes of goods intended for resale by the dealer or intended for 
use by him in the manufacture or processing of goods for sale, in mining, 
or in the generation or distribution of power (16/4.2). 
The forms of the 
application for registration under the Central Sales Tax Act are pre- 
scribed by the Central Sales Tax (Registration and Turnover) Rules. 
A dealer may apply for amendment or cancellation of his certificate 
(CSTA §§ 7(4), 7(5)); the granting authority may amend or cancel the

A certificate of registration may be

for central sales tax purposes. 
16/7.3 
Returns, Assessments, and Records 
Most of the states, under their sales tax acts and regulations, require 
the filing of returns. 
Ordinarily a return must be filed when payment 
is due, although in some states a receipt for payment must accompany 
the return. 
Assessment is usually based on the return; but if the tax- 
payer fails to file a return or files a return which the taxing authorities 
have reason to believe incorrect, assessment may be based on the tax- 
payers sales records, invoices, and vouchers. 
If these documents are 
lacking, assessment may be based on any evidence available to the 
authorities; and if necessary the taxpayer’s turnover may be estimated 
by adding a margin of profit to the purchase price of taxable goods shown 
in the taxpayer’s records. 
All the states require registered dealers to maintain true accounts of 
all purchases and sales and to retain them, together with invoices, 
vouchers, and other relevant papers, for periods ranging from three to 
six years in the different states. 
These records must be made available 
on demand for inspection by the tax authorities. 
Returns for interstate sales taxable under the Central Sales Tax Act 
are subject to the rules of the states having jurisdiction over the sales 
(CSTA §$9(3)). 
Some of the states have provided special rules for 
the preparation of returns on interstate sales under the Central Sales 
Tax Act. 
The state governments are expressly empowered under the 
Act to make rules as to the form of accounts relating to interstate sales, 
the furnishing of information relating to the business of a registered 
dealer, and the inspection of books and records (CSTA § 13(4)). 
16/7.4 
Interstate Sales to Registered Dealers 
In order to obtain the benefit of the special rate of tax applicable to 
interstate sales of taxable goods to a registered dealer (16/4.2, 16/4.3), 
the seller must file with his sales tax return a declaration signed by the 
buyer as to the buyer's registered status and the uses to which the goods

a prerequisite to obtaining the benefit of the exemption of a second sale, 
by transfer of documents of title, during a single movement of goods 
in interstate commerce (16/3.2). 
If the goods are sold to the govern- 
ment, the seller must file a declaration signed by an officer of the 
government to the effect that the goods were purchased by or on behalf 
of the government. 
Under the authorization of the Central Sales Tax 
Act (CSTA §13(4)(e)), the states have published rules regulating the 
issuance and use of the forms of declaration.

16/7.5 
Payment of Tax 
Sales taxes are payable on the aggregate of taxable sales (“turnover”) 
during a prescribed period (CSTA § 2(j)). 
Usually, the year of assess- 
ment for the state sales taxes is the tax year, 1 April to 31 March, but 
some states permit a taxpayer to use the customary accounting year of 
his trade. 
Some states require payment of tax semiannually, quarterly, 
or monthly, either on all sales or on sales of certain classes of goods. 
In some states, chiefly those imposing multi-point taxes, payment is due 
only when a formal notice of assessment is served on the taxpayer. 
For purposes of the Central Sales Tax Act, the period of turnover is 
the same as that prescribed for the submission of returns under the law 
of the state having jurisdiction to impose tax; a dealer who is not required 
to submit a return under the law of the state computes his turnover 
quarterly.?® 
Upon default by a taxpayer, tax may be recovered in one or more 
of the following ways: 
. Service of a demand on the taxpayer. 
. Arrest or detention of the taxpayer. 
. Attachment and sale of movable property belonging to a taxpayer. 
. Recovery as an arrear of land revenue by recourse to a taxpayer’s real 
property (3/2). 
Recovery of tax from a corporation may be made from corporate assets 
only and not against a shareholder or his assets. 
Tax arrearages cannot 
be recovered from the transferee of taxable goods which were the subject 
of a taxable sale, but generally may be recovered from the transferee 
of an entire business to the extent of the value of the business.

Under most of the state sales tax laws, appeals must be made within 
60 days of the date of assessment or final notice of demand. 
Appeals are
