heard in most states by administrative officials of the sales tax depart- 
ments, but some states have established special tribunals to hear appeals 
in sales tax cases. 
In most states, both the taxpayer and the department 
may appeal questions of law, but not questions of fact, to the High Court 
of the state. Appeal or reference to the High Court must be made within 
a prescribed period and is generally conditioned on prior payment of the 
tax. 
Refund of taxes paid erroneously is made only upon timely applica- 
tion based on a decision in the taxpayer’s favor on appeal from an 
assessment. 
Appeals under the Central Sales Tax Act are governed by the acts and 
rules of the states having jurisdiction over the sales on which tax is 
imposed (CSTA §9(3)). 
16/7.7 
Penalties 
The state sales tax acts provide fines, imprisonment, or penalty taxes 
for various offenses, which may be classified as follows: 
1. Failure to file returns, late filing, filing of fraudulent returns. 
2. Failure to pay tax when due. 
3. Intentional misrepresentation of books and records. 
4. Obstruction of an officer in inspection, search, or seizure. 
5. Assisting any person in the commission of any of the above offenses. 
The Central Sales Tax Act provides a fine or imprisonment up to six 
months, or both, for violations of certain of its provisions; and a con- 
tinuing offense subjects the taxpayer to a daily fine of Rs 50 so long as 
the offense continues (CSTA §10). 
The offenses which are subject to 
these penalties are listed below (CSTA § 10). 
1. Failure to register as required. 
2. False representation by a purchaser that he is registered. 
8. False representation by a registered purchaser that the goods purchased 
are specified by his certificate of registration as intended for resale or 
other favored use (16/4.2). 
4, Failure of a registered purchaser, without reasonable excuse, to use goods 
for the purposes specified in his certificate of registration (16/4.2). 
5. Illegal possession of forms of declaration (16/7.3). 
6. Collection of tax from a purchaser by an unregistered person, or by a 
registered dealer otherwise than in accordance with the Act and any rules 
made thereunder. 
As an alternative to fine or imprisonment, a purchaser of goods who 
has committed one of the offenses specified in items 2 through 4 above 
may be subject to a penalty of one and one half times the tax for which 
he is liable, imposed after a hearing by the authority competent to 
grant him a certificate of registration (CSTA § 10-A). 
Penalties for which a taxpayer may be liable under the Act are 
imposed and collected by the state having jurisdiction over the sale

17/1. 
India 
ANALYSIS 
OF 
OTHER 
TAXES 
454 
17/1. 
Introduction 
The principal tax treated in this chapter is the central government 
excise tax, or Union excise duty, which is the basic tax of this type. 
Certain miscellaneous excise taxes also are imposed upon designated 
industries by the central government, principally to defray expenses 
incurred in connection with those industries. 
These miscellaneous taxes, 
summarized at 17/4.4, are limited in both scope and impact. 
State 
excise taxes, which are levied solely on alcoholic liquors and narcotics, 
are briefly discussed at 17/4.5. 
The central excise tax is imposed under the provision of the Constitu- 
tion which reserves to the central government the exclusive power to 
impose excise taxes on tobacco and all other goods manufactured or pro- 
duced in India, except alcoholic liquors and narcotics, the taxation of 
which is reserved to the states.1. 
The tax schedule contains 27 designated 
commodities, one of which—salt—is presently exempt from tax. 
Of the 
remaining commodities, all but two—tobacco and coffee—are manu- 
factured goods. The tax is imposed principally at specific rates, although 
four commodities—tires, woolen fabrics, footwear, and electric batteries 
and parts—are taxed at ad valorem rates. 
The tax does not apply to 
imported articles nor to most exported articles. 
While the tax is intended 
to be borne by the consumer, it is imposed for administrative reasons on 
the manufacturer, producer, or curer. 
Procedures for payment and 
collection are extremely rigid and complex, and elaborate and detailed 
accounting is required prior to tax payment. 
Control by the authorities 
is extremely strict, involving close physical supervision of manufacture, 
and, in the case of tobacco, of warehousing and transport. 
The imposition and collection of the central government excise taxes, 
or Union excise duty, are governed by the Central Excises and Salt Act 
of 1944, as amended from time to time; ? Rules issued under the basic 
enactment 
(1/5.2), entitled the Central Excise Rules of 1944;? and 
various notifications amending the rules, exempting certain goods from 
tax, or reducing the rates applicable to certain goods. 
17/2. 
Persons Subject to Tax 
17/2.1_ 
In General 
Although excise taxes are intended to be borne by the ultimate con- 
sumers of the taxable goods, for administrative convenience the taxes 
are imposed on and collected from manufacturers, in the case of manu- 
factured goods, and on curers and wholesale dealers, in the case of 
unmanufactured goods. 
1 Const., Seventh Schedule, List I, Entry 84. 
2 Cited herein as CESA. 
3 Cited herein as Rules.

17/3.1 
455 
EXCISE 
TAXES 
17/2.2 
Manufacturers 
Excise taxes are imposed on all persons engaged in the manufacture 
of taxable goods (CESA § 3; Rules 7, 9). 
The term “manufacturer” includes the persons listed below. 
1. Persons who employ hired labor in the production or manufacture of 
taxable goods. 
2. Persons who engage in the production or manufacture on their own 
account of taxable goods intended for sale. 
8. Persons engaged in any process incidental or ancillary to the completion 
of a manufactured product. 
The manufacturer is personally liable to pay the tax and is responsible 
for any deficiencies which may be ascertained after the goods have left 
the factory, even though he may no longer be in a position to recover 
the amount of the tax from his purchaser or transferee. 
17/2.3 
Curers and Wholesale Dealers 
In the case of taxable unmanufactured goods (tobacco and coffee), 
the tax is normally imposed on the curers of the goods (CESA § 3; Rules 
19, 24). 
However, a curer may absolve himself from tax liability by 
transferring the goods to a wholesale dealer, provided that the dealer has 
a private warehouse licensed for the storage of the goods (Rules 24, 29). 
If a tax-free transfer of unmanufactured taxable goods to a wholesale 
dealer takes place, the dealer then becomes liable for the tax (Rules 144, 
157). A wholesale dealer is one who buys or sells taxable goods either 
for resale or for manufacture, including a broker or commission agent 
who retains taxable goods pending their sale (CESA § 2(k)). 
Curers and wholesale dealers are personally liable for payment of tax 
in the same manner as manufacturers (CESA § 11)(17/2.2). 
Where a 
curer transfers to a wholesale dealer taxable goods on which tax has not 
been paid, the curer remains liable until the transfer has been reported 
to and acknowledged by the proper tax official (Rule 29). 
17/3. 
Taxable Event 
17/3.1 
Manufactured Goods 
In the case of manufactured goods, the taxable event occurs, 
in 
theory, at the moment when the process of manufacture is completed.* 
The definition of “manufacture,” which includes any incidental or ancil- 
lary process requisite to the completion of the finished product, precludes 
the imposition of tax until all steps preparatory to completion of the

2(f)). 
While the tax becomes payable on the completion of manufacture, 
payment of tax is deferred for administrative reasons until removal of 
the goods from the factory premises (Rules 9, 47, 49). 
Goods may be 
retained in approved storerooms on the factory premises: pending re- 
moval (Rule 47). 
In order to remove the goods, clearance must be 
obtained from, and the tax paid to, the tax official, who is stationed either 
at the factory or nearby. 
Hence, any transfer of the goods from within 
the factory premises to a point outside imposes liability for the tax 
regardless of what happens to the title to the goods. 
Goods not properly 
accounted for (17/7.4) are subject to the tax on demand of the tax 
official unless the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the excise 
officer that they have been stolen or accidentally lost or destroyed 
(17/3.3). 
17/3.2 
Unmanufactured Goods 
In the case of unmanufactured goods (tobacco and coffee), the taxable 
event occurs when the goods have been cured and are suitable for sale. 
If manufacture is necessary to put the goods in salable form, as in the 
case of the manufacture of cigarettes from cured tobacco, the taxable 
event occurs when the goods have been cured and are suitable for 
manufacture (Rule 19).> “Curing” is defined to include wilting, drying, 
fermenting, and any other process necessary to make unmanufactured 
goods suitable for sale or manufacture (CESA § 2(c)). 
Any unmanu- 
factured goods retained by the curer for sale at retail are taxable on 
completion of curing (Rule 28). 
A curer may defer imposition of the tax, however, by any of the 
following three methods, singly or in combination. 
1. The curer may deposit the goods in a bonded storeroom on his premises 
and retain them there until not later than 30 June of the year following 
that in which the goods were harvested. 
On 30 June, or when the goods 
are withdrawn from the storeroom, if earlier, the curer must either pay the 
tax or utilize either of the other alternatives listed below (Rules 24, 27). 
2. The curer may deposit the goods in a licensed public warehouse for a 
three-year period from the date of initial deposit and, in certain instances 
where specific authorization from the tax officials is obtained (Rule 145), 
for two additional one-year periods. 
The tax must be paid on expiration 
of the appropriate period or periods, or on sale (Rules 24, 157). 
Transfer 
of the goods to another licensed warehouse during the three-year period 
is permitted without payment of tax (Rule 152). 
3. The curer may transfer the goods to a wholesale dealer possessing

During the balance of the three-year period from the date of 
first warehousing, and for such further periods not exceeding two years 
as may be specifically permitted, the dealer may store the goods in his 
own warehouse, or transfer them to another licensed warehouse, without

The tax must be paid when the

Transfer of the goods to a licensed public warehouse or to

Under 
this method, a tax-free zone is created within which, during the per-

17/3.3 
Nontaxable Dispositions of Goods 
The imposition of the excise tax on unmanufactured goods is deferred 
if the goods are transferred to a warehouse or to a dealer as described at 
17/3.2. 
Since the tax is imposed on goods sold or intended for sale for 
private or industrial consumption, goods which would be taxable if sold 
may none the less be exempt from the tax if they are disposed of in one 
of the ways listed below. 
Ve Unmanufactured goods, whether cured or not, are not taxed if they are 
consumed 
personally by the grower 
or members 
of his household 
(Rule 20). 
. Goods manufactured or produced by a state government are not taxed 
if they are not used for or in connection with a trade or business carried 
on by or on behalf of the government (CESA § 3). 
. Subject to certain conditions, a refund of the tax is allowed for manu- 
factured goods previously sold and taxed, when returned to the factory 
for remaking, refining, reconditioning, or any similar process within one 
year after the tax was paid. 
However, the reconditioned goods are 
taxed again on their departure from the factory premises; the tax paid 
on the original sale is refunded to the manufacturer on the completion 
of reconditioning, subject to specified conditions (Rule 97). 
. Subject to the discretion of the proper tax officers, taxable goods which 
are lost, destroyed, or stolen while in the possession of the manufacturer, 
if they are manufactured, or in the possession of the curer or wholesale 
dealer, if they are unmanufactured, 
are not taxed (Rules 49, 147).® 
Unmanufactured goods stored in warehouses, which are found to be unfit 
for sale or use in manufacture, are not taxed if destroyed (Rule 149); 
manufactured goods damaged at the factory prior to shipment are not 
taxed if destroyed (Rules 49, 61). 
In addition, taxable goods specified by central government notifica- 
tion are not taxed when sold or utilized for special industrial purposes. 
Many such notifications have been issued; they are discussed at 17/4.2.

17/4. 
Taxable Goods and Rates of Tax 
17/4.1 
Taxable Goods 
Taxable goods (“excisable goods”) are those manufactured commodi- 
ties subject to excise tax upon completion and those unmanufactured 
commodities subject to excise tax on curing. 
The Central Excises and 
Salt Act of 1944 sets forth in its First Schedule a list of 27 classes of 
taxable commodities, some of which are divided into subclassifications 
for the purpose of applying varying rates. 
Most of the commodities are 
described in some detail in the schedule, principally in order to clarify the 
application of the tax to the classes of goods enumerated. 
The designa- 
tions of the commodities and the range of rates applicable to each com- 
modity are reproduced in Table 23 at 17/4.3. 
17/4.2 
Exempt Goods 
In some cases, the commodity definitions exempt certain classes of 
goods from the tax, either specifically or by implication. 
Thus, while 
fabrics and motor vehicles generally are taxable, certain types in each of 
these classes are exempt. 
In addition, the Central Government is em- 
powered to exempt any goods within a commodity classification from 
part or all of the tax by a notification in the Gazette of India (CESA 
8§ 87(xvii), 38; Rule 8). 
For example, while motor fuels are subject 
to the tax, the Central Government has decreed that certain types of fuel 
are exempt if used as ingredients or solvents in chemical processes. 
In 
exceptional instances, the Central Board of Revenue also may exempt 
taxable goods from duty on a case-by-case basis. 
Numerous notifications 
have been issued to give total exemption from the tax or reduction of 
rates for certain types of goods within each commodity classification. 
The schedule of excise duties, incorporating the effects of these noti- 
fications, appears in the Central Excise Manual, which is published 
periodically under authority of the Central Board of Revenue, and also 
in Indian Customs Tariff (4/5.1). 
The exemptions and rate reductions 
do not follow a uniform pattern. 
Some are intended to encourage the 
growth of small-scale and cottage industries, and others to encourage 
the production of necessities of life and raw materials needed for indus- 
trial development. 
Administrative problems concerned with tax super- 
vision and collection are responsible for other exemptions and reductions.

are exempt from the tax either because they are manufactured without 
powered machinery, are produced in factories employing less than a 
designated number of workers, or are not produced in greater than 
specified minimum quantities.

17/4.4 
Miscellaneous Central Government Excise Taxes 
In addition to the Union excise duty, a number of other excise taxes 
are levied by the central government upon designated industries, most 
frequently for the purpose of defraying the costs of government activities 
undertaken on behalf of the industry taxed. 
A small number of these 
taxes are supplementary to the Union excise duty on the same commodi- 
ties. 
Thus, a tax is levied at varying specific rates per bale of cotton 
produced or per yard or square yard of certain natural and synthetic 
fabrics manufactured, 
in order to finance research, dissemination 
of 
information, and other activities beneficial to the industries.7 
For the 
same purpose, tax is charged at specific rates on vegetable oils and salt, 
although the latter commodity presently is exempt from the Union ex- 
cise duty.§ 
A special additional excise duty is imposed at graduated rates on 
exports of cotton fabrics exceeding a prescribed quota.® 
Additional 
excise duties are levied by the central government on sugar, tobacco, 
cotton fabrics, rayon 
or other 
artificial fabrics, and woolen fabrics 
produced or manufactured in India.° 
The proceeds of these taxes are 
assigned to the states to replace their revenues from former taxes on 
sales of goods now “declared to be of special importance to interstate 
trade” (16/4.3). 
Other commodities, not subject to the Union excise, are subject to 
special excise levies at specific rates. 
Three different coal and coke 
excises, at specific rates per ton, have been imposed to improve worker 
safety and welfare and for similar purposes.1!_ A rubber “cess” is imposed 
on the owners of estates on which rubber is produced.!* 
The central 
government has imposed excise taxes on medicinal and toilet prepara- 
tions containing either alcohol or narcotics, but the states both collect 
these taxes and retain the revenues therefrom.!* 
A coconut cess 
is 
imposed on copra consumed in any manufacturing establishment, whether 
obtained domestically or imported.14 
Some of these duties are imposed 
on exported goods as well as on goods intended for domestic consump- 
tion (4/5.3).

ANALYSIS 
OF OTHER TAXES 
462 
17/4.5 
State Excise Taxes 
State governments 
are empowered to levy excise taxes 
solely on 
alcoholic liquors suitable for human consumption and on opium, Indian 
hemp, and other narcotics; these commodities must be produced or 
manufactured in the taxing state or, if manufactured in another state, 
enter the taxing state’s jurisdiction. 
Opium, Indian hemp, and other narcotics generally are subject to 
excise tax at varying rates in all states which have not prohibited their 
sale. 
Opium consumption has been closely controlled by the central 
government, which has a monopoly on its production. 
Since 1959, pur- 
suant to a resolution of the All-India Opium Conference of 1949, all sales 
of opium, except for medicinal or scientific purposes, have been pro- 
hibited, although sales of other narcotics continue to be a matter of state 
option. 
Alcoholic liquors are subject to excise tax, at varying but uniformly 
high rates, in all those states which have not adopted a policy of prohibi- 
tion. 
Bombay and Madras, for example, both have adopted policies of 
state-wide prohibition, while such states as Uttar Pradesh and Mysore 
have adopted policies of partial prohibition either by enforced absti- 
nence in certain districts or by restriction of consumption. 
The govern- 
ment of India, as early as 1905, adopted a policy of sharply restricted 
liquor consumption which later became a constitutional directive to the 
states to “endeavor to bring about prohibition of consumption” of all 
intoxicating liquors or drugs, except for medicinal purposes.1®¢ 
For a 
majority of the states, however, the tax on alcoholic liquors has been of 
considerable importance (1/7.3b). 
Therefore, a national program of 
uniform prohibition is unlikely at present. 
17/5. 
Taxable Value 
The value of taxable commodities enters into the computation of the 
tax only in the case of tires, woolen fabrics, footwear and electric bat- 
teries and parts, manufactured tobacco products, and mechanical lighters. 
The amount of excise tax liability on commodities subject to ad valorem 
rates is computed by applying the applicable rate of tax (17/4.3) to the 
value of the commodities. 
“Value,” for this purpose and for the purpose of ascertaining the 
specific rate applicable to manufactured tobacco products, is the cash 
wholesale price, exclusive of excise tax, which the taxable commodities 
or those of like kind and quality would bring by sale on the open market 
15 Const., Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 51. 
Excise taxes on medicinal and 
toilet preparations containing alcohol or narcotics are imposed by the central govy- 
ernment but are collected by and accrue to the states (17/4.4). 
16 Const. art. 47.

in wholesale lots under certain standard conditions (CESA §4). 
The 
wholesale price of the goods must be determined objectively but with 
reference to the class of goods involved, the place of sale, and the 
customs of the trade which prevail at that place. 
Since the price must 
be one at which an independent buyer of a normal wholesale lot can 
purchase, any special relationship between buyer and seller which would 
vitiate the objective character of the sale is disregarded. 
The sale is deemed to occur at the time when the taxable commodities 
are removed from the place of manufacture or production for delivery. 
Where the tax is imposed on lost goods, the time of sale is governed by 
the standards which determine the rate to be applied to the goods 
(17/4.3). 
Both sale and delivery are deemed to occur at the place of 
manufacture or production. 
However, where no representative whole- 
sale market for the same or similar goods exists at the locus of manu- 
facture or production, sale and delivery are deemed to occur at the 
nearest place where similar transactions occur, normally the location of 
a selling organization, agent, or distributor. 
No adjustments or deductions 
are permitted in ascertaining value 
except for the tax itself and normal trade discounts for cash payments or 
quantity purchases generally available to independent wholesale pur- 
chasers which are not dependent on the fulfillment of special conditions 
before or after delivery. 
The price includes the cost of packaging. 
17/6. 
International Aspects 
17/6.1 
Imported Goods 
Imported commodities are not subject to the excise tax since the tax 
applies only to domestically manufactured or produced items (CESA 
§3). 
Customs duties (4/5), however, perform the revenue-producing 
function of excise taxes with respect to imported commodities, and 
historically excise duties have been enacted to offset the revenue loss 
caused by high protective customs duties imposed on imported com- 
modities in order to foster domestic production. 
17/6.2 
Exported Goods 
The Central Government is specifically authorized to grant total or 
partial rebates of the tax paid or to be paid under the Central Excises 
and Salt Act with respect to exported goods, subject to such limitations 
as it may wish to make (CESA §87(xvi); Rule 12). 
Pursuant to this 
authorization, the government has exempted most taxable commodities 
from tax when exported; but certain iron and steel products are subject 
to tax when exported, although at lower rates than those prevailing for 
the same items consumed domestically.17 
However, all goods exported 
17 Notification No. 10 C.E. (5 April 1949).

17/7.

464 
to any country which has a common land frontier with India, except 
Pakistan,!8 are subject to tax. 
The taxation of goods exported to Nepal 
is governed by special arrangements, and the export of certain com- 
modities to Tibet is exempt from tax. 
A special additional excise duty 
is imposed on exports of cotton fabrics exceeding a specified export 
quota (17/4.4), and some of the special excise duties imposed on certain 
commodities apply only to exported goods or to exported goods as well 
as to goods intended for domestic consumption (4/5.3, 17/4.4). 
In order to obtain a rebate of tax already paid or a tax exemption for 
exports, compliance with certain stringent procedures is required (Rule 
185). 
The goods must be exported directly from the factory or ware- 
house, unless special authorization is obtained. 
Export must take place 
within two years after the tax has been paid or within such shorter period 
as may be prescribed for certain classes of goods, often no more than 
four months.!9 
Where goods are to be exported free of duty, a bond 
is required to guarantee proper exportation 
in conformity with all 
applicable controls. 
The bond, with surety or adequate security, may 
be limited to a specific shipment, or may encompass all exports by a 
particular manufacturer or producer (Rules 13, 14).?° 
17/7. 
Administration 
17/7.1 
In General 
The excise tax is administered by the Central Board of Revenue 
through Collectors of Central Excise who are the heads of excise depart- 
ments (Rule 2(ii)).. 
Each department normally supervises the adminis- 
tration and collection of the tax for at least one state and, in some 
instances, more than one. 
Each department or collectorate is divided 
into divisions; these are divided into circles comprised, in turn, of ranges, 
which are the basic units of excise tax administration. 
Principally, the 
ranges are either tobacco ranges, administering the growing, curing, 
warehousing, and transport of unmanufactured tobacco, or factory ranges, 
which are divided into subclasses for various manufactured products 
subject to tax. A large manufacturing plant may comprise a single range, 
whereas smaller plants may be grouped together to form one range. 
Manufacturers and storers of taxable goods must provide satisfactory 
accommodations for excise officers within factory or warehouse prem- 
ises and, where required, manufacturers must provide suitable homes 
18 Notification No. 19 C.E. (28 May 1959). 
2 
19 Notification No. 10 (5 April 1949), which also provides certain other require- 
ments, 
20 Rule 14A provides penalties for failure to export or to furnish proof of export 
as required, 
Rules 185-191 provide for the mechanical procedures, such as number 
of copies of applications and the marking of shipments, which must be complied 
with if exemption or rebate is to be obtained.


<!-- page 501 of 600 -->

India 
17/7.3 
465 
EXCISE 
TAXES 
for the officers at rentals not exceeding 10% of their salaries (Rule 
229). 
The Central Government is given broad authority to make rules for the 
administration of the excise tax and, by notification, to amend the list of 
taxable goods and rates applicable thereto (17/4.2). 
The rules and 
notifications become effective upon publication in the Gazette of India. 
All rules, however, must be presented as soon as possible to Parliament 
while it is in session and must remain before Parliament for a 30-day 
period, during which they may be modified or annulled (CESA § 38). 
17/7.2. 
Payment of Tax 
The excise tax on manufactured goods is payable when the goods leave 
the factory or warehouse on the manufacturer’s premises (17/3.1). 
The 
tax may be paid in one of three ways: by cash; by an “account current” 
under which a debit is made to an advance fund deposited by the manu- 
facturer with the Treasury (Rule 9); or, in the case of matches and 
manufactured tobacco products, through “banderols” or tax labels which 
the manufacturer may purchase in advance from the Treasury and affix 
to the goods. 
The excise tax on unmanufactured goods is payable when the goods 
are cured or are otherwise put in salable form. 
However, in most 
instances, these goods are stored in licensed warehouses or storerooms, 
and the tax need not be paid until transfer from such locations for the 
purpose of domestic sale or the expiration of a prescribed tax-free period 
(17/3.2), whichever occurs first. 
The tax may be paid either in cash, 
by money order, or through an account current. 
If the excise tax is not paid when due, the taxing officer may deduct 
it from any money in his possession or control which is owed to any 
person from whom the tax could be recovered—for example, by suit 
against the taxpayer’s surety on his bond, or against the security pledged 
by the taxpayer (17/7.3). 
Alternatively, it may be recovered by attach- 
ment and sale of the goods themselves. 
Where neither of these methods 
is successful, the local land revenue collector may be authorized to 
recover the tax as if it were a land revenue arrearage (CESA § 11) 
(3/2). 
Provision is also made for recovery of excise tax arrearage by 
detention of the taxable goods, even if sold to a bona fide purchaser, and 
all property used in their production or manufacture (Rule 230). 
17/7.3 
Licensing and Permits 
In order to ensure tax collection and prevent avoidance, all persons 
performing any function with respect to taxable goods, whether or not 
liable at any time for the tax, are required to be licensed or to obtain 
permits or make declarations (CESA §§ 6, 7). Manufacturers of taxable


<!-- page 502 of 600 -->

17/7.4 
India 
ANALYSIS:-OF: 
OTHER 
TAXES 
466 
goods, persons receiving taxable goods for special industrial purposes 
and, in some instances, manufacturers of component parts or ingredients 
of manufactured goods, are required to give notice of intended manu- 
facture and to obtain licenses (Rules 43, 174). 
Manufacturers also are 
required to furnish bonds, with adequate security, in amounts not exceed- 
ing Rs 50,000 (Rule 48). In practice, the amount is equivalent to either 
the tax imposed on two weeks of normal production, or the value of the 
maximum amount of taxable goods ordinarily held in storage at the 
manufacturer's premises at any one time, whichever is less. 
In the case 
of unmanufactured goods, licenses are required of curers, brokers, com- 
mission agents, wholesale dealers, and holders of private bonded store- 
rooms or warehouses (Rule 174), while producers of such goods, if not 
in the above group, must make declarations as to production (Rule 15). 
Any of the aforementioned persons who ship the goods must obtain pre- 
scribed transport documents (Rules 31-35). 
At the discretion of the 
tax officials, security may be required of producers, curers, or whole- 
sale dealers to assure proper accounting for taxable goods and payment 
of the tax (Rule 18). 
All persons licensed to keep private warehouses 
and curers who store their goods in public warehouses are required to 
post bonds with security or a surety, guaranteeing proper tax payment 
(Rules 140, 153, 164). 
The rules prescribe the procedures for obtaining licenses and the 
fees therefor (Rules 174-181A, 221), for giving notice of intended manu- 
facture and for making declarations of equipment and the premises used 
(Rules 15-17, 43-46), and for securing appointment and license of a 
warehouse for the purpose of storing unmanufactured goods (Rule 139). 
17/7.4 
Returns and Records 
Each manufacturer is required to file a monthly return detailing the 
quantity of taxable goods manufactured during the month and their 
disposition (Rule 54). 
At the end of each calendar quarter or, if the 
manufacturing operations are not continuous, at the end of each manu- 
facturing period, a further return is required showing the materials used 
and goods manufactured during that period (Rule 55). Each producer 
or curer of unmanufactured goods is required to file an annual return 
of goods grown or cured (Rules 36, 37). 
For the purpose of tax computation by the excise officer, each manu- 
facturer is required to maintain a daily stock account in a prescribed 
manner, detailing production and delivery (Rule 53). Specified account- 
ing records and registers also are required, varying somewhat in content 
depending on the commodities involved (Rules 67, 83, 84, 94, 96K, and 
96N ). Each grower, curer, or wholesale dealer in an unmanufactured 
product is required to keep an entry book as prescribed (Rules 21, 22,

India 
17/7.7 
467 
EXCISE 
TAXES 
42), while each warehouse keeper is required to maintain a register of 
all activities concerning taxable products (Rules 168, 173). 
17/7.5 
Audits and Investigations 
The Central Excise Officers have broad powers, where authorized by 
the Collector of Central Excise, to enter any licensed premises or other 
places where taxable goods are grown, stored, manufactured, or sold 
(Rule 197); to detain persons in possession of taxable goods and examine 
the goods (Rule 199); to detain and search any means of conveyance 
(Rule 200); and to enter and search any other location or object on 
reasonable cause (Rule 201). 
Certain excise officers are empowered to 
summon anyone to give evidence and produce documents in connection 
with any inquiry related to excise tax (CESA § 14). 
17/7.6 
Refunds and Appeals 
Refund of a tax paid erroneously will be permitted only if a written 
claim is filed with the appropriate officer within three months following 
the date of payment or of adjustment to an account current (Rule 11). 
Rebate or refund of a tax paid on exports (17/6.2) must be claimed 
within five months after the date on which the goods were sealed by 
an excise officer immediately prior to dispatch.2? 
A refund of excise 
tax paid on goods returned to the factory for reconditioning may be 
claimed under certain conditions if the goods are returned to the factory 
within one year of the date of payment of the tax (Rule 97). 
Appeal from an order or decision of a Central Excise Officer to the 
Central Board of Revenue or to any officer designated by it to hear 
appeals must be made within three months from the date of the order 
or decision 
(CESA § 35; Rules 213, 214). The three-month period com- 
mences on the date the order is dispatched to the appellant. 
The appeal 
must bear a court fee stamp (4/3.1) to be valid. 
The Central Govern- 
ment may reverse or modify any decision or order on application of an 
aggrieved party, provided that the party has exhausted all other rights 
of appeal (CESA § 
36). 
17/7.7 
Penalties 
Numerous and varied penalties are provided for any violations of the 
laws or rules relating to the excise tax. 
In general, operating without a 
license when a license is required, possessing tobacco in excess of the 
quantity allowed, evading tax or aiding in evasion, failing to supply 
information when required, or supplying false information may result in 
imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to Rs 2,000, or both, as well

as confiscation of the taxable goods involved (CESA §§ 9, 10). Obstruct- 
ing any excise officer in the performance of his duty may subject the 
obstructor to fine and imprisonment (CESA § 27). 
Other violations 
generally may be penalized only by confiscation or a fine not exceeding 
Rs 2,000, or both, but not by imprisonment (Rules 14A, 57, 181, 210). 
Where a ship of under 300 tons is involved in the sea transport of 
taxable goods, the vessel may be confiscated (CESA §§ 24, 28). Where 
an owner or occupier of land or his agent charged with management 
of the land willfully aids in any violation of the Acts or rules thereunder, 
including willful failure to report the manufacture of contraband taxable 
goods on the land, he may be punishable by imprisonment for up to 
six months, a fine of Rs 500, or both (CESA §§ 16, 17).
